#3140. Uber Eats starts drone deliveries with Zipline in Houston

Customers can choose "by drone" in the app, with Dallas and more US cities next.

Zipline’s delivery pod sets down an Uber Eats order. Houston customers can now choose “by drone” in the app.

Zipline has started delivering Uber Eats orders by drone in Houston, the first launch under the companies’ August partnership. Dallas comes next, and the pair are aiming for 1 million drone deliveries a day by 2029.

Uber Eats customers in Houston can now get food delivered by drone, Zipline announced on Tuesday. Customers pick “by drone” on the Uber Eats home screen, and a Zipline aircraft brings the order to their door. Dallas is next, followed by more US cities.

It is the first launch under the companies’ August partnership, which aims for 1 million drone deliveries a day by 2029. Uber also agreed to invest in Zipline, but did not say how much.

Zipline’s aircraft fly at up to 70mph and carry up to 8 pounds over 10 miles. They stay about 330 feet up and lower orders to the ground on a tether, which Zipline says keeps the noise down.

“Being able to reach people’s homes autonomously in under 10 minutes opens up a whole new opportunity for Uber Eats and its customers,” said Uber’s autonomous delivery head, Aaron Emrich.

Zipline says more than 80% of its orders are new business for restaurants, not orders they would have got anyway. It has made 1 million deliveries in the Dallas area alone.

Houston is not new ground for Zipline. In April, it opened early access there for the first 5,000 residents through its own app.

The drone delivery race is speeding up. Zipline raised $1.5B at a $21.5B valuation this month, as Walmart agreed to add 300 drone sites. Amazon plans to offer drone delivery in nearly 500 US cities and towns by the end of the year.

Food delivery rivals are moving too. DoorDash has unveiled its own drones, and Irish startup Manna is building a US drone factory in Oklahoma.

#3139. Former Apple chairman Arthur Levinson files to sell $31.8 million in company stock

Arthur Levinson, who currently serves as Apple’s lead independent director, informed the SEC today of his plans to sell 90,000 shares of Apple stock worth approximately $31.8 million. Here are the details.

If you’ve been following Apple for a while, you likely know the name Arthur Levinson, as he served as the company’s chairman from 2011 until September of this year, when Tim Cook took over as executive chairman as part of the leadership transition that saw John Ternus become CEO.

Back in May, Levinson made headlines when he sold 250,000 Apple shares for approximately $71.2 million. Three weeks later, he sold another 50,000 shares for $15.55 million. On the same day, he also transferred another 65,000 shares as a gift. Still, he retained approximately 3.7 million directly held shares in the company.

Today, Levinson informed the SEC in a Form 144 filing of his plans to sell 90,000 common shares with an aggregate market value of $31,765,885.00, though the disclosure did not specify how many Apple shares he currently holds. The shares are held in The Homeplace Trust, with Levinson acting as trustee and handling the proposed sale on the trust’s behalf.

The filing lists all shares as acquired in cash on February 27, 2001, though it does not disclose how much Levinson originally paid for them. For reference, Apple stock was trading at approximately $0.29 per share on a split-adjusted basis on that date, compared to roughly $353 today.

Importantly, Apple has undergone three stock splits since then, meaning the 90,000 shares listed in the filing don’t necessarily correspond to the number of shares Levinson originally purchased in 2001.

According to the filing, the transaction was expected to take place today through Charles Schwab. However, it is worth noting that Form 144 is only a notice of a proposed sale, meaning the filing does not confirm that the transaction has already been completed.

#3136. Jensen Huang offers to return as Nvidia CEO if the board asks, CNBC reports

In a statement obtained by CNBC, Jensen Huang apologised to Nvidia’s board for the problems he caused. The board is not considering his return and is searching for a new CEO.

NVIDIA founder and CEO Jensen Huang during his GTC 2026 keynote at the SAP Center in San Jose, 16 March 2026

Jensen Huang says he would return as Nvidia’s chief executive if the board decides it wants him back. He made the offer in a written statement obtained by David Faber of CNBC on Tuesday. It is his first public comment since he resigned as chief executive on 12 November. CNBC’s Kif Leswing published the statement in full.

“If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO,” Huang said.

The statement landed hours before Nvidia reports third-quarter results, its first without him.

Huang apologised to Nvidia’s directors and said he would cooperate with the board’s independent investigation.

“I did not live up to the standards expected of everyone at NVIDIA, and I have made serious mistakes in my personal life. I created problems for the Board that I deeply regret,” he said.

He said he had seen an outpouring of calls for his return from Nvidia staff, investors, business partners and customers. Many still contact him directly, he said. An open letter asking the board to reinstate him now has more than 180,000 signatures, CNBC reported. President Donald Trump said on Monday that he would not mind Huang coming back.

Huang also wrote about his own story. He came to the US 53 years ago. He called becoming an American citizen one of the proudest moments of his life. He described Nvidia as his life’s work.

Huang resigned days after admitting to an affair, CNBC reported. News reports alleged affairs with Nvidia employees and with Alice Huang, who worked for a customer and is alleged to have contact with Chinese intelligence.

Nvidia’s board is not considering bringing Huang back, CNBC reported on Monday. When he resigned, the board started a formal search for a permanent chief executive, according to Nvidia’s announcement. It will look at internal and external candidates. Colette Kress, the chief financial officer, is interim CEO. The board said on Friday it was choosing a search firm, CNBC reported.

Nvidia has hired the law firm Wachtell Lipton to lead its investigation, according to CNBC. The probe covers Huang’s conduct and whether it compromised national security or company secrets.

Huang has separately agreed to answer questions from three House committees on 1 December.

#3135. iPhone Duo gets one of Face ID’s best features with upcoming iOS 27.3 update

Soon, your alarms, timers, and phone calls will be less disruptive on iPhone Duo.

With today’s iOS 27.3 developer beta 2, iPhone Duo gained a new feature: Unlock with Front Camera. This lets you unlock your iPhone Duo in a similar fashion to Face ID, but using the front selfie camera, rather than Face ID’s TrueDepth 3D camera system. But, Face ID is more than just unlocking: it also provides Attention Aware features.

Attention Aware features, which were first introduced with iPhone X, check for when you’re looking at the phone before performing certain actions:

iPhone will check for attention before dimming the display, expanding a notification when locked, or lowering the volume of some alerts.

Previously, Attention Aware features required Face ID, but iOS 27.3 extends it to iPhone Duo. Like the new face unlock feature, Attention Aware features only work when using the outer display. However, the face unlock feature does not have to be set up to use the Attention Aware features.

After updating to iOS 27.3, the features should be automatically enabled. You can enable or disable the feature in Settings → Accessibility → Face Recognition & Attention. You can also enable Haptic on Successful Unlock there, just like an iPhone with Face ID.

In my experience, Attention Aware features will lower the volume of alarms, timers, and incoming calls when your iPhone is already unlocked. It also will prevent the display from dimming and locking while you are actively looking at it. Finally, it will expand and show notification content on the Lock Screen after unlocking with the new face unlock feature.

#3133. Apple hears Liquid Glass feedback, tests small but welcome change

Liquid Glass was one of the most controversial and polarizing UI changes Apple has made for a long time. The company listened to the feedback and made a number of changes, the most significant of which was to introduce a sliding transparency scale.

Apple is currently testing a change some will consider insignificant but I personally find very welcome: softer edges when scrolling …

The term 'polarizing' implies a difference of opinion over UI aesthetics. However it seems to me that the proponents often speak in aesthetics - 'new', 'fresh'; while opponents often speak of newly introduced UI problems (ex. window resizing). The point being that articles should be more definitive and not conflate aesthetics with usability. So, how would the author describe this change, looks like aesthetics to me.

Apple’s introduction of the Liquid Glass UI split the Apple community, some hailing it as one of the best improvements seen for many years, and others rejecting it as a usability disaster.

As is often the case with any change, the controversy dampened significantly once people had a chance to get used to it. That is not the same as everyone being happy with it, however. Apple later tried to please most of the people most of the time with a slider that allows people to customize the level of transparency, from a very frosted glass look to an almost completely clear one.

Code sleuth pdfu has spotted that the company is currently testing a small but welcome additional choice.

They heard the feedback: Apple is testing the return of iOS 26’s softer scroll-edge effect in navigation bars when glass tint is set to 25% or lower.Currently disabled behind UIKit/clear_glass_soft_pocket. Applies to the default/auto style. pic.twitter.com/D2NvKfESYa

The difference is somewhat subtle, and some may consider it irrelevant, but as someone who has transparency maxed-out I’m a fan of the softer fade and would welcome the option to be able to reinstate this.

#3132. Suno adds AI video to its music app, with filters for artists’ faces

Visuals makes lyric videos and album art for users' songs, but blocks prompts that copy real people.

AI music company Suno has launched Visuals, which makes images and video clips of up to 15 seconds to match users’ songs, including lyric videos that lip-sync. It is on the web now, uses separate credits, and comes with filters meant to block likenesses of artists, public figures and copyrighted work.

AI music company Suno has launched Visuals, a tool that makes images and short videos to go with users’ songs, it announced on Tuesday. Users can create lyric videos, album art and clips of up to 15 seconds. It is on the web now, with iOS and Android apps due in the next few weeks.

Suno says its video model is built around music. Clips follow a song’s structure, pick up on its lyrics and lip-sync to them. Users can start from Suno’s own characters or upload an image, then extend and edit clips with text prompts.

Visuals runs on its own credits, bought separately from song credits. It follows Suno’s Speech tool, launched in October for spoken audio such as poems and meditations.

New filters will block prompts and uploads that try to show specific artists, public figures or copyrighted characters, Suno says. Videos will also carry hidden watermarks before they can be shared outside Suno. ByteDance added similar guardrails to its Seedance video tool in March.

“This means that prompts that work on other video platforms may not work on Suno and that’s by design,” the company wrote.

Those guardrails come as Suno fights fresh legal battles. Last week, Elvis Presley’s music owners and Eminem’s publisher sued Suno, and the Presley suit claims it misused his voice.

Suno has been trying to look more legitimate. It launched music models trained on licensed songs from Warner and BMG in September, and plans audio watermarks for its tracks. Investors valued the company at $5.4B in June.

#3131. How Microcredentials Can Help Engineers Build Trustworthy AI

IEEE Credentialing Program pairs AI governance standards with microcredentials

Kaitlyn Ridel is the IEEE microcredentials marketing specialist.

Engineering teams are moving at breakneck speed to integrate artificial intelligence, but they are running into a formidable new barrier: compliance issues. Translating high-level AI ethics, governance, and auditing into daily operational workflows has become one of the industry’s toughest challenges.

“AI ethics” refers to the principles developers use to govern and operate workflows. “Governance” refers to the rules and procedures an organization establishes for AI workflows and how they interact with organizational data. Auditing is the process of assessing and validating systems to ensure safety, fairness, transparency, and legal compliance.

Technology leads and systems engineers are responsible for adhering to a structured set of guidelines for standards and processes usually issued by a governing body such as the European Union, the U.S. National Institute of Standards and Technology, and the International Organization for Standardization.

The regulations aim to mitigate issues such as systemic bias, security vulnerabilities, and transparency risks, but they also highlight a critical skills gap.

Most traditional computer science, software, and electrical engineering degree programs were built around technical design and system architecture. They do not yet include training in AI auditing, data tracking, or safety protocols for how AI systems interact with people and other technologies.

Expecting mid-career engineers to leave their job to attend a full-time two- or four-year program to learn about the topics is not feasible. Yet treating safety and governance as an afterthought can lead to costly product delays, legal exposure, and broken public trust.

Targeted microcredential programs can bridge the knowledge gap by helping engineers build skills in compliance, AI ethics, and governance.

Skills-based microcredentials represent the mastery of expertise gained through a learning program. To earn them, learners must demonstrate the skill through a validation assessment. The microcredentials can be stacked, showing a growing skill set in a defined area and allowing learners to earn several microcredentials in one program.

Microcredentials also allow engineers to upskill and master critical competencies, such as bias mitigation, algorithmic transparency, and risk auditing, without interrupting their career. Through rigorous skills-validation assessments, microcredentials give tech leaders verifiable proof that their teams can audit systems effectively before deployment.

For engineering organizations, microcredentialing creates an agile upskilling pathway. It connects software engineering and hardware design directly to regulatory frameworks, empowering teams to certify systems for safety and compliance within their development life cycles.

Bridging technical capability and ethical responsibility requires a trusted foundation. IEEE has long been a pioneer in socio-technical standards, most notably through the IEEE 7000 series for ethics in AI system design, a framework created to address ethical considerations during the development life cycle.

The IEEE Credentialing Program translates the organization’s world-class standards into actionable, industry-aligned microcredentials. For more than three decades, IEEE has set the gold standard for technical validation and professional certification. By pairing cutting-edge AI governance standards with targeted microcredential programs, IEEE provides engineers and IT leaders with clear, standardized road maps to build systems that are not just technically advanced but also safe, compliant, and worthy of public trust.

To learn more about the credentialing program, explore the offerings or connect with an IEEE expert.

Kaitlyn Ridel is a marketing specialist for the IEEE Microcredentialing Program

#3129. Face unlock is a good compromise for the iPhone Duo – now let’s have it for the Mac

When Apple first announced Face ID, the company talked a great deal about how secure the system is, contrasting it to the far less secure image-based facial unlock systems used by the likes of Google and Samsung.

Fast-forward to 2026, and Apple is itself now offering that less secure approach as an option on the iPhone Duo – but in a way I consider a sensible balance between convenience and security …

The first smartphone to offer a face unlock feature was the Galaxy Nexus back in 2011. This didn’t include any extra hardware, simply using the front-facing camera to take a photo and compare this to a stored image of the user.

It took just days to discover just how insecure this approach is, with unlock achieved simply by holding up a photo of the owner’s face on another device. Yet even as late as 2019, Samsung was continuing to use this approach.

Meantime, in 2017 Apple launched Face ID in the iPhone X. This has an entire hardware module devoted to it, with infrared emitters and receivers used to create a 3D map of the shape of our face. This cannot be fooled by photos or even models, and Apple said at the time there was a less than a one in a million chance of it being fooled (with riders for twins, etc).

Face ID projects more than 30,000 invisible IR dots. The IR image and dot pattern are pushed through neural networks to create a mathematical model of your face and send the data to the secure enclave to confirm a match, while adapting to physical changes in appearance over time. All saved facial information is protected by the secure enclave to keep data extremely secure, while all of the processing is done on-device […] The probability that a random person in the population could look at your iPhone or iPad Pro and unlock it using Face ID is less than 1 in 1,000,000.

Given the massive contrast in security of the two approaches, it might seem odd that Apple is now adapting a purely visual face unlock feature. The only reason the company is doing this is because the lack of Face ID has been far and away one of the biggest complaints about the iPhone Duo.

I suspect Apple made the decision reluctantly and over the protests of security engineers. But while face unlock remains a very insecure approach compared to Face ID, Apple’s approach tries to strike a good balance between convenience and security. The following safeguards apply:

That latter restriction means it can’t be used for Apple Pay, to unlock password-protected apps, to open the Passwords app, or to do anything else that requires authentication – such as changing your passcode or adding a fingerprint to Touch ID.

I do not see any downside provided the feature is off by default and only those who want it will turn it on. Presumably with an explanation of the reasons it gives reduced security.

For myself, I have got so used to using touch ID on my keyboard that I'd likely not make use of it in my business. If anything goes wrong with client information, I want to know, and be able to demonstrate, that I have taken security seriously.

There’s only one other safeguard I’d like to see Apple introduce: geolocking. Personally, I’d want to be able to allow face unlock at home, but disable it when I’m out and about. Currently, the only two ways to temporarily disable it are to toggle it off or to restart the phone. I’d like to see an option to set safe locations, like home and work, with the feature disabled in public.

Given that Face unlock requires only a front-facing camera, there’s absolutely no reason why Apple couldn’t also make it available on the Mac.

Face ID has been something MacBook users have been wanting for a great many years, and despite a decade’s worth of Apple patents for just this, it still hasn’t happened. Face unlock would be a compromise option that would at least get us some of the way there. I see I’m not the first to suggest this, with Macworld’s Roman Loyola beating me to it.

What’s your view? If you own an iPhone Duo, will you choose to enable this? If you own a MacBook, would you like the same option on that? Please take our poll and share your thoughts in the comments.

#3128. Google buys Howie, an AI assistant that books your meetings

The scheduling agent was already built on Gmail and Google Calendar, and its team is joining Google Labs.

Google Labs has bought Howie, an AI scheduling tool that users copy into emails to arrange meetings, Bloomberg reported. Terms were not disclosed; PitchBook valued Howie at $14M in 2024. Google said it wants to build AI tools for small businesses with the team.

Google has bought Howie, an AI tool that schedules meetings and manages calendars, Bloomberg reported. Google Labs, the company’s experimental arm, announced the deal on Monday in a post on X. It did not share the price.

Howie works like a human assistant. Users copy it into an email thread, and it finds a time and books the meeting. PitchBook valued the startup at $14M in 2024, according to Bloomberg.

Google Labs said it wants to build “the next generation of intuitive AI tools” for small businesses with the Howie team.

Howie’s co-founder and CEO, Austin Petersmith, said the team will keep building the tool at Google. He noted on LinkedIn that Howie has always run on Gmail and Google Calendar. Google has not said whether Howie will be built into its own apps.

The deal adds to Google’s push into AI agents that act for users, not just answer questions. In May, it launched Gemini Spark, an always-on agent that takes tasks by email. In October, it gave workplace agents their own email addresses.

OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta and xAI all offer rival agents, and OpenAI bought travel agent Odessia last week.

Google Labs has been busy. Last week it released Tabletop, a tool for building group planning apps with AI. In February, it bought music app ProducerAI, which runs on Google DeepMind’s Lyria model.

Google and Xreal's spatial computing AR glasses have finally arrived and I've been wearing them for just a few days. They're an interesting hint at the future of both computing and wearables.

In the smart glasses space, there isn't anything like the Aura's. They're not quite a VR headset, but they're far more advanced than display glasses like Xreal's own One Pro Plus.

Xreal's only potential rivals exist in tech that has yet to actually hit shelves: the Snap Specs (which are supposed to ship "this fall") and the Meta VR Glasses that don't drop until sometime in Spring 2027.

There's a lot going on here, and we'll have a full review soon, but here are some early first impressions. As we dig into the glasses, if there's something you want to know reach out to scott.younker@futurenet.com or leave a comment below!

Beyond the puck, the Xreal Aura glasses won't look out of place next to any other display spectacles made by the company. There is an aesthetic to this kind of glasses and you can see it mirrored in Xreal's rival Viture with the recent Pro 2 glasses.

Where you'll notice the difference is in the cameras. Like the best smart glasses, the Aura features cameras at the temples plus one on the nose bridge. These are built to enable the gesture controls and 6DoF spatial computing, something no other Xreal glasses have natively.

The Aura sits somewhat between Meta's VR Glasses and Snap Specs; mostly, it comes down to software and cameras. Meta glasses have more cameras that can "see" your hands even if they're in your lap.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

With the Aura's, moving your hands down to your lap means you're most likely using the puck as a trackpad, which works pretty well.

The puck is a computer for the glasses thanks to the powerful Snapdragon Reality Elite chipset. If you work in the Google suite, you have access to all of the Google apps and services you could want. Plus, it comes with Gemini AI, which you can access via voice controls.

Nicely, you don't need the puck for mirroring. You can connect the glasses to any device, save the Switch 2 (more on that below), and they will work like your normal Xreal glasses.

If you've worn a pair of Xreal glasses, the Aura feels about the same. I think they're fairly comfortable, and they do come with different nose pad sizes. Plus, the arms can be adjusted by three levels, which helps settle the glasses.

I want to highlight the speakers in the Aura. I hate speakers in display glasses and often find them tinny, preferring to use headphones. Also, especially since I travel or use the glasses to not disturb my partner at night even if the speakers are siloed, sound still leaks out.

Now, the Bose speakers in the Aura won't beat the best headphones, but they sound way better than any other glasses I've tested.

The included puck has both the computing chipsets and the battery. The puck is about the size of a thick iPhone 16, and does have some heft. You could use the included belt clip so that you don't have to hold the puck when you're out and about (which gives cellphone belt guy vibes).

The Xreal Aura are rated for about 3 hours of continuous use. I haven't done a full rundown test yet, but in my usage I've found that to be fairly accurate.

Perhaps that's for the best. I've found that the portion of the glasses that rests on your eyebrows gets warm. Not uncomfortably so, but noticeably enough that I wonder how that settles out over the long term. The puck, however, does seem to dissipate heat fairly well, and I never felt it get warm.

Xreal partnered with Google on the Aura and you can feel Mountain View's presence in the Android XR platform that lives in the puck. If you've ever tested the Samsung Galaxy XR headset, then you've seen the Android XR interface before.

It's the exact same here, with fewer capabilities thanks to fewer cameras and a little less power. The Aura also has a smaller FOV of 70 degrees. VR enthusiasts won't like that, but I think most people will find it more than usable.

You can use pinch gestures or the trackpad puck to control the interface. So far I've found the gesture controls smooth and intuitive. The Aura comes with a delightful setup process that teaches you how to use the gesture controls and puck so you can open the glasses up ready to go. It's honestly one of the better startup tutorials I've come across.

In previous hands-on sessions, the gesture controls felt a bit laggy at times, but whatever work Xreal and Google have done in the meantime has really made the controls much better.

Honestly, it's not as exciting as the eye-tracking in the Meta VR Glasses, but it works well, so I'm not knocking it too much.

Since the system runs on Android XR there are a lot of AR (and some VR-lite) games that you can play on the Aura. Xreal recommended the excellent Demeo, which is available in the Play Store.

I've already enjoyed Demeo in VR and the AR translation is a delight, using pinch controls to move the map, zoom in, and make choices. You'll need to pay attention to your hand position so the cameras can catch it.

I do think you'll need a controller to enjoy the most out of what the Aura can do or a mouse and keyboard. Fortunately, you can connect a surprising number of accessories to the Aura via Bluetooth (more on that below).

But what makes the Aura standout is the connectivity. As mentioned, you can just use the glasses to run a Steam Deck or mirror using a cable on your laptop. Have I been running WoW: Forever through the Aura glasses? Yes. Should I? That remains to be seen.

We got a sneak peek during AWE 2026 back in June, but the Xreal Aura is one of the few glasses that can connect to the Switch 2. Compared to the mini dock and larger pro dock that Viture makes, the Aura puck is lighter, smaller and does more than just act as a passthrough and battery pack. And it does so through the USB-C connection into the puck.

It's a delight to pop in Mario Kart World or the Ocarina of Time remake on the glasses. I still don't know how Xreal and Qualcomm got this to work, but I'm happy it does.

Xreal has said that you can accessorize the Aura with peripherals to enhance your use. With that in mind, the company did send us a wireless gaming controller built by GameSir, a wireless folding keyboard and a USB-C DP-in for mirroring external devices.

All three add an extra cost on top of the initial $1,299 glasses price. The GameSir controller costs $99 and can be used wirelessly or wired and has an AI button.

GameSir makes good controllers and the Xreal one is pretty decent. However, if you already have an Xbox, PlayStation or other Bluetooth controller, the Aura will support them. You won't have the Gemini button, but if you're like me and don't use that anyway, it shouldn't be a problem.

The Xreal keyboard is $79 but comes with Aura-specific keys in the FN row that enable you to control the glasses like you would your monitor on a laptop. It's actually a pretty comfortable keyboard, and the foldability for travel makes it an excellent companion. Honestly, so far you should add the $79 as part of the cost of getting a pair of Auras. You can also pair it with other devices, including laptops and tablets.

The cable is a Silkland USB-C one that costs $12.99. If you already have a USB-C DP in cable, it should work, but you're not out too much if you're looking to do wired mirroring.

At over $1,000, the Xreal Aura is pretty expensive, but these glasses are a lot of compute shrunk down into a pair of glasses and a cell phone-sized puck.

I don't know that everyone needs these glasses, and it's not quite the super portable laptop replacement yet, but it is an exciting glimpse at the future of AR glasses. Between the Aura, Snap Specs, and Meta VR Glasses the next generation of glasses has some true potential.

There's also room for the Aura to grow from both a software and hardware perspective.

We're not there yet, but the Aura feels like a true step toward the sci-fi eyewear that we saw in movies and shows as kids.

#3126. Apple memory suppliers expect price increases through at least 2030 [U]

Key Apple memory supplier SK Hynix has warned that RAM and flash memory shortages are likely to last through at least 2030, keeping product prices high. Apple is believed to be one of 14 customers who have locked in priority orders, but the contract does not protect against price increases related to the balance of supply and demand.

Update: Apple is reportedly about to sign a similar contract with Samsung, also permitting market-driven price increases.

SK Hynix says that while AI continues to drive demand and growth, there is little that can be done in the short to medium term to increase supply.

Supply, on the other hand, is not keeping pace with the growth of the market. Given technical difficulty of leading-edge processes and the long lead time required to build new production facilities, it expects the structure in which demand exceeds supply to persist through 2030.

The Register reports that SK Hynix has long-term deals with 14 tech giants for priority orders, but these allow for market-based price increases.

14 big buyers […] will collectively buy more than half of its output during 2027 and 2028, and some of them want to extend those agreements. The Korean giant doesn’t mind that because the deals include “a mechanism that reflects market conditions within a price range agreed upon with customers”

Apple is used to being in the driving seat when it comes to negotiating with suppliers, but this is not the case where memory and flash storage is concerned. Here, the shortages mean that it will have been forced to agree to contracts that allow significant price hikes in order to obtain guaranteed supplies.

Nikkei Asia also reports that printed circuit boards may be the next component to experience constrained supply. Once a humble commodity item, advances in the technology has turned them into specialist tech, with more layers and higher bandwidth requirements. The report says “that complexity shrinks the supplier pool and extends lead times.”

Apple said back in June that the company was doing its best to mitigate the price increases, but it has so far been unable to do so.

#3125. 28 Zero-Day Findings in Under Two Days. Is Robotics Security Keeping Pace?

VicOne’s AI-assisted research reveals what faster zero-day discovery means for robot safety

VicOne is a Physical AI cybersecurity company protecting vehicles and robots from cyber threats that can alter behavior and compromise safety.

VicOne used AI to find 28 zero-day vulnerabilities in Physical AI tools —these weaknesses can impact robot training, testing, and real-world control.

This article is brought to you by VicOne.

VicOne identified an initial set of 28 zero-day findings in less than two days using AI-assisted research across software and tools supporting the Physical AI ecosystem. These include projects developed or maintained by Google, NVIDIA, and Meta, among others.

Based on initial validation, all 28 findings are classified as zero-day vulnerabilities. The count may change following vendor and vulnerability-authority review, and some findings do not yet have CVE tracking numbers.

Many of these tools help teams train, simulate, test, and operate robots. Weaknesses in them could influence the models teams build, the test results they trust, and the instructions sent to robots.

These findings create two demands for robotics teams: responding as AI helps uncover weaknesses faster, and assessing how each one could affect robot safety and operations.

Vulnerability discovery involves examining code, tracing how systems communicate, and testing whether a suspected weakness can actually be exploited. AI can accelerate parts of this work, helping researchers analyze more software in less time. Attackers could use similar capabilities.

When the weakness is a zero-day — previously unknown and without an available fix — faster discovery can leave teams with little time to respond. While that exposure does not necessarily mean an attack has occurred, teams still need to determine whether they use the affected software and what an attacker could access or change.

VicOne’s findings span three stages of the robotics lifecycle: development and training, simulation and validation, and deployment and runtime. Weaknesses at each stage could affect what a robot learns, how it is tested, and how it is controlled.

Figure 1. In this research set, 75% of findings involved development, training, simulation, or validation tools, highlighting risks that can arise before a robot is deployed.VicOne

The following scenarios show how a compromised component could influence the robot at each stage.

These are potential consequences and not demonstrated outcomes for every finding. Actual effects depend on the attacker’s access, the system’s design, and whether other safeguards prevent the changes from reaching physical behavior.

In a separate demonstration, VicOne researchers provide a concrete example of a weakness affecting a protective function. The researchers exploited a vulnerability to prevent a robot’s remote-stop command from working. The case shows why teams need to test whether safeguards remain effective when the software supporting them is compromised.

Video 1. VicOne researchers demonstrate a vulnerability that prevents a robot’s remote-stop command from working. VicOne

AI can shorten the search for weaknesses, but a robotics team still needs to determine whether a fix is safe to deploy. Even after a software maintainer releases a patch, teams must identify affected systems, check compatibility, and verify that the update preserves intended behavior.

An earlier successful test remains useful evidence. However, a newly discovered weakness may reveal conditions that test never examined.

When immediate updating is impractical, teams may need temporary safeguards, such as restricting access to an affected service, while a validated fix is prepared.

As details from the 28 findings become available through coordinated disclosure, the next step is for robotics manufacturers is to connect each finding to its potential effect on development, deployment, and robot behavior.

That work also requires understanding how threats could affect robot behavior and how to protect systems already in operation. VicOne Radeis helps teams identify potential zero-day vulnerabilities, assess AI model and system security, and use simulation to evaluate how these risks could affect robot behavior before deployment. VicOne Rthena supports threat detection and responses within approved policies during operation.

Figure 2. Cybersecurity strengthens robot safety evidence throughout the lifecycle. VicOne helps teams test safety limits against manipulation before deployment and monitor the conditions behind safe behavior in operation.VicOne

Faster vulnerability discovery matters when teams can turn findings into action: identify what needs attention, verify that safeguards still hold, and confirm that a fix does not introduce new risks. That is how cybersecurity strengthens robot safety as systems continue to change.

For a deeper look how cybersecurity can affect robot safety, download our white paper, “Why Robot Safety Depends on Cybersecurity: Protecting the Information That Safety Decisions Rely On.”

#3124. Ambience’s AI now helps hospitals plan rounds and discharges

The new tools sit beside software that already writes notes and suggests billing codes.

Ambience’s new tools suggest tasks for each shift and flag barriers to discharge.

Ambience Healthcare has added Rounding Assistant and Discharge Readiness to its hospital AI software, to help care teams prioritise tasks and spot barriers to discharge earlier. The company also points to customer results on billing, including a 6.5% rise in case mix index at Onvida Health.

Ambience Healthcare has added two AI tools that help hospital teams decide what to do next for each patient, the company announced on Tuesday. They join its existing software, which writes clinical notes and suggests billing codes for hospital stays.

Rounding Assistant pulls together overnight events, changes in a patient’s condition and a list of suggested tasks for each shift. Discharge Readiness flags medical, practical and social problems that could delay a patient going home, earlier in the stay.

Ambience is backed by Andreessen Horowitz, Kleiner Perkins and the OpenAI Startup Fund. It counts Cleveland Clinic and Mayo Clinic among its customers, and ties its fees to results. Cleveland Clinic has also backed Dyania, another hospital AI startup.

Much of the pitch is about money. Ambience aims to raise hospitals’ case mix index, a measure of how sick patients are that helps set what insurers pay. At Onvida Health, discharges handled with Ambience scored 6.5% higher than a year earlier, the company says.

“To justify the investment, we needed roughly a 1.5% improvement in case mix index,” said Mike Lewis, chief financial officer of Onvida Medical Group.

Lewis said Onvida’s own finance team checked the results. Ambience also says admission notes written with its tool captured 59% more of the diagnoses used in quality rankings, in one health system’s review of 1,100 stays. None of the figures come from independent research.

AI note tools are still under scrutiny. In August, England’s patient watchdog warned that AI scribes were getting drug names and diagnoses wrong. Rivals are growing fast too: Heidi raised $340M in September, and Google launched Gemini for healthcare last week.

#3122. Major websites compromised to steal crypto from iPhone users

A security researcher has discovered that some of the world’s most popular websites were compromised in an attempt to steal cryptocurrency from iPhone users.

A total of 178 websites were affected, including BBC, CNN, HSBC, IKEA, and Zoom. Reasonably recent versions of iOS are safe, and so far it appears that only a few thousand dollars have been stolen …

Reuters reports that hackers attacked Optimizely, a website optimization platform used by many major websites.

Several of the affected companies said that they have disabled the Optimizely scripts and are investigating potential impacts. Helme says almost all of the rogue code has now been removed, and that Apple patched iOS after an identical attack method was detected last month.

The Coruna loader is byte-identical to a sample we analysed in October from a different campaign. The kit’s own comments say iOS 18.7.3 and later, and 26.3 and later, are patched.

Helme monitored the attacker’s wallets and discovered that only $7,040 has been stolen, though it’s not possible to see how many payment card numbers were obtained.

As always, the best protection against this type of attack is to promptly update all your Apple devices to the latest OS versions they support.

#3121. Is IONIX the best-kept secret in cybersecurity?

AI is shrinking the time between a vulnerability’s disclosure and its exploitation. IONIX is building exposure management that finds, validates and mitigates external risks at machine speed.

As organizations expand their digital infrastructure, their external attack surfaces are becoming increasingly difficult to secure. Cloud environments, third-party vendors, subsidiaries, web applications and AI services introduce new potential entry points. At the same time, AI is accelerating how quickly attackers can discover vulnerabilities, identify exposed assets and turn weaknesses into opportunities for exploitation.

The result is a shrinking window for defenders. IONIX argues that the likelihood of an individual exposure being exploited has shifted dramatically. It has moved from a historically low probability (statistically safe by default) to approaching a default-breach scenario. While the exact risk varies by vulnerability and environment, the broader point is clear. Maintaining a complete inventory and validating exposures continuously are becoming essential security requirements.

IONIX has built its approach around this challenge. Through its External Exposure Management Platform, the company combines autonomous asset discovery, continuous security assessment, exploitability validation and agentic remediation. Its central premise is that if attackers operate at machine speed, defenders need to do the same.

Enterprise attack surfaces rarely stop at the boundaries of internally managed infrastructure. Vendors, cloud providers, subsidiaries and acquired businesses can introduce internet-facing assets that remain outside traditional security monitoring.

IONIX addresses this visibility gap through autonomous discovery that maps external assets, vendor-managed infrastructure and digital dependencies. The company says its platform discovers 30% to 50% more assets than competing approaches. This helps organizations identify shadow IT, overlooked applications and third-party exposures.

Through its Continuous Threat Exposure Management (CTEM) capabilities, IONIX aims to continuously discover, monitor and prioritize exposures across an organization’s external environment. This broader visibility becomes increasingly important as enterprises adopt new technologies and expand their digital supply chains.

Identifying vulnerabilities is only part of the problem. Traditional security assessments can generate extensive findings, but not every issue represents an immediate or exploitable threat.

IONIX combines continuous security testing with non-disruptive active exploitability validation to distinguish actual exposures from theoretical risks. Its Exposure Validation capabilities examine vulnerabilities, misconfigurations and exposed technologies, testing whether identified weaknesses represent genuine security risks.

The platform then prioritizes findings according to severity, exploitability, potential blast radius and asset importance. The objective is to help security teams concentrate on exposures that present meaningful business risks rather than working through undifferentiated vulnerability lists.

IONIX is also extending exposure management beyond continuous discovery and assessment through its Live Exposure Defense solution.

The technology addresses a particularly urgent challenge: what happens when a new vulnerability is publicly disclosed? Instead of requiring security teams to manually determine which systems might be affected, IONIX automatically ingests newly published CVEs. It then correlates them against its mapped external attack surface.

The platform then uses agentic analysis to identify potentially affected assets, validate actual exploitability through safe, non-intrusive testing. It also recommends concrete mitigation measures. IONIX targets a 12-hour window from public CVE disclosure to validated exposure and actionable mitigation.

For confirmed exploitable web assets, this can include generating specific remediation workflows and mitigating actions. Specifically, it can generate Web Application Firewall (WAF) rules through supported providers such as Akamai and Cloudflare. The approach gives security teams a practical mitigation path rather than another vulnerability alert to investigate.

IONIX’s approach has attracted interest from organizations managing complex digital environments. These include Warner Music Group, BlackRock, Infosys, the Telegraph, E.ON and Grand Canyon Education.

John Remo, former SVP of Global Cloud, Infrastructure and Cybersecurity at Warner Music Group, described the platform as delivering almost immediate value without adding pressure to technical staffing. Mike Manrod, CISO at Grand Canyon Education, highlighted its ability to provide a dynamic view of an organization’s external attack surface from an attacker’s perspective.

These examples reflect a broader consideration for enterprise security buyers. The value of exposure management is not simply how many vulnerabilities a platform discovers, but whether it helps organizations understand and reduce their actual risk.

The cybersecurity market is crowded with platforms promising better visibility and vulnerability management. IONIX is pursuing a more integrated approach, bringing asset discovery, exploitability validation, risk prioritization and agentic mitigation into one continuous process.

Its focus on digital dependencies and machine-speed response addresses a growing challenge for enterprises. That challenge is keeping security controls aligned with an attack surface that never stops changing.

As AI accelerates both the discovery and exploitation of vulnerabilities, organizations will have less room to rely on incomplete inventories and periodic assessments. IONIX is betting that continuous visibility, validated exposure and faster mitigation will become fundamental requirements for the next generation of enterprise security.

#3119. Advanced Metrology for Defect Detection, Tool Health, and Semiconductor Yield Enhancement



In advanced semiconductor manufacturing, small defects can have a large effect on yield. Thin film deposition tools must stay stable and qualified. Process drift must be caught early. When a defect does appear, engineers need to know where it came from and how it affects device performance. This webinar shows how in-line inspection and offline characterization combine into one workflow, from tool monitoring to root-cause analysis.

In the first half, Dr. Bitan Chakraborty from Intel, explains how surface scan metrology fits into station monitors for thin film tools. The session shows how baseline signatures and real-time monitoring reveal hardware wear, particle generation, and process drift before they reach production wafers. It then moves to in-line scans on patterned wafers. These scans expose layer-level defects and show how they form and spread through multi-layer device stacks. Linking this defect data to electrical test results helps teams find root causes and focus their yield improvement work.

In the second half, Dr. Jacob Petersen from Evident Scientific, addresses a common question: what happens after an in-line tool flags a problem? In-line tools are fast, but they cannot always provide the details needed for a firm conclusion. Offline 3D optical profilometry fills that gap by combining three complementary inspection techniques in a single system. It delivers dimensional measurements and helps determine whether a defect lies within the sample or comes from foreign material. The session covers how several optical techniques support inspection from bare silicon to fully packaged chips. It also shows how automation enables fast measurement of features down to the sub-nanometer scale with minimal operator handling.

What You Will Learn:

  • How surface scan metrology in station monitors tracks tool health and supports the qualification of thin film deposition processes
  • How baseline signatures and real-time monitoring detect particle generation, hardware degradation, and process drift before production is affected
  • How in-line scans on patterned wafers reveal layer-level defects and show how they propagate through multi-layer device structures
  • When offline 3D optical profilometry should follow in-line inspection, and how it measures dimensions and separates sample defects from foreign material
  • How correlating tool health data, inspection results, and electrical performance links physical defects to yield loss and guides targeted improvement projects

#3116. How to hide the new macOS 27.3 menu bar indicator

macOS 27.3 beta 2 adds a blue menu bar indicator for apps using System & App Protection Override. Apple describes itas a transparency indicator that appears when one app is controlling another.

If you regularly use trusted automation tools and utilities, that can mean a persistent pill taking up space in your menu bar. Prefer to hide it? There’s a Terminal workaround.

I’ve tested this on macOS 27.3 beta 2 and confirmed that the indicator disappears after a restart.

Open Terminal and run these two commands:

sudo mkdir -p /Library/Preferences/FeatureFlags/Domainsudo defaults write /Library/Preferences/FeatureFlags/Domain/TCC AX_TRANSPARENCY_INDICATOR -dict Enabled -bool false

Enter your Mac administrator password when prompted, then restart your Mac.

The command disables the internal AX_TRANSPARENCY_INDICATOR feature flag. It doesn’t remove apps from your permissions list, although you’ll no longer see this activity indicator.

To restore Apple’s default behavior, run:

sudo defaults delete /Library/Preferences/FeatureFlags/Domain/TCC AX_TRANSPARENCY_INDICATOR

Restart your Mac again to apply the reversal. This removes only the indicator override, preserving any other flags you may have configured.

This is an undocumented workaround tested on the current beta, so Apple could change or remove it in a future update.

#3114. OpenAI for Chile aims to train civil servants and back startups

The non-binding pact covers civil servant training and startups, with a US export scheme behind it.

OpenAI has signed a memorandum of understanding with Chile’s science ministry to explore AI in public administration, train civil servants and support local startups. The deal sets no investment or purchasing commitment, and is backed by a US Commerce Department programme that promotes American AI abroad.

OpenAI has signed an agreement with Chile’s government to bring AI into public offices and help local startups, the company announced on Tuesday. Science minister Ximena Lincolao signed for Chile at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World conference in California, where Sam Altman also spoke.

The two sides will explore using AI in the science ministry’s paperwork and training civil servants to use it safely. Startups could get help from OpenAI, including tech advice and mentoring. A joint team will set goals and a first work plan.

The deal is a non-binding pact, not a contract. The details, including what each side provides, will be agreed later. Abu Dhabi, by contrast, signed four deals with OpenAI this month, covering permits and investments.

“The MoU sets no investment or purchasing commitment,” OpenAI wrote.

The pact is backed by the US Commerce Department’s American SI Exports Program, which helps US AI firms win deals abroad. OpenAI is one of its anchor partners. Washington has also pushed federal financing for American AI exports.

Chile is the latest country to join OpenAI for Countries. Malta agreed in May to give citizens free ChatGPT Plus, and OpenAI’s head of countries, George Osborne, has courted Canada for data centres. Chile already has its own AI plan, with 177 actions across 14 ministries.

#3113. Can Robots Bring Stroke Surgery to Remote Hospitals?

Remedy Robotics is testing whether surgeons can operate from afar

At Remedy Robotics, the N1 System’s prototype console [lower left] awaits its operator, with cofounders Jake Sganga [left] and David Bell and the surgical robot in an adjoining room.

I am practicing brain surgery on a patient lying 6 meters away, out of my sight and reach. I press a foot pedal, activating the controller in my hand, and carefully steer a thin flexible tube called a catheter up through the patient’s blood vessels. I head for what I believe to be the brain, tracking my progress on the live X-ray feed. As I imagine finding a blood clot, David Bell, the surgeon seated to my right, helpfully reminds me that every minute a stroke goes untreated, millions of brain cells suffocate, swell, and die.

The patient under the X-ray in Bell’s office is not flesh and blood, but a plastic container holding long branches of silicone tubing. The controller I hold comes from an Xbox. But the surgical robot is real. The Remedy N1 is designed for emergency operations, including thrombectomies, the standard brain operation for acute ischemic strokes caused by blood clots. Ischemia, a restriction of blood flow, is the most common cause of stroke.

“We want it to feel a bit like a video game—a bit easy,” Bell says. “But we don’t want to dehumanize it as if there’s just another ‘game over.’ ” Bell, a clinician and former cardiac-surgery trainee from Australia, cofounded Remedy Robotics, based in San Francisco. With a team of engineers, he developed this robotic catheter and its related software to help ischemic stroke patients in remote and rural places, who lose crucial hours while being transferred away from hospitals incapable of providing care. According to 2025 data, at least 5 million people around the world suffer ischemic strokes every year. In the United States, stroke is the fourth leading cause of death.

When Remedy Robotics cofounders Jake Sganga [left] and David Bell initially met, they matched each other’s energy right away.Christie Hemm Klok

The screen shows my catheter at a fork in the narrowing road, and I decide to take a sharp right; I think I can make it. This device feels easier to drive than a typical robotic instrument that I controlled on a hospital tour the summer prior. I say to Bell that here my movements are smoother, more precise—exactly the talking point you’d expect to hear from a surgical robotics company. Never mind that, Bell corrects me: “Smoothness and precision are not clinical outcomes. Neither is a surgeon’s ergonomics.”

For Bell, the outcome that matters is whether the robot can get stroke treatment to patients who otherwise wouldn’t receive it in time. Today, only about 1 in 10 patients eligible for thrombectomy receive one. That’s where the long-unrealized promise of telesurgery is meeting an urgent problem: providing access to thrombectomies before life-threatening damage takes hold.

But can putting a robot in one hospital and a surgeon somewhere else actually close that gap? Remedy has already taken a first step, remotely testing its system on a small group of patients. “The remote stroke need is well known,” says Jake Sganga, who cofounded Remedy with Bell and leads the technology side. “It’s just a hard problem to take on.” Making telesurgery a practical part of stroke care will require more than a capable robot: It will depend on communications infrastructure, hospital resources and workflows, and ultimately, evidence that patients actually benefit.

As recently as the early ’90s, physicians who treated stroke struggled with “therapeutic nihilism.” A 1991 editorial by two lamenting neurologists expressed hope that a successful drug therapy for stroke would emerge that would “reverse the trend of nihilism.” Five years later, clot-busting drugs revolutionized stroke treatment, followed about a decade later by mechanical thrombectomy, in which a blood clot is physically removed from an artery.

In a standard thrombectomy a surgeon snakes a flexible wire through a small opening in the patient’s groin. This guide wire sets the route for a fine hollow tube around it, the catheter, to travel through the blood vessels to the brain, where instruments remove the clot. Suddenly a stroke was no longer a sentence of profound disability or death but a treatable event.

Yet decades later, thrombectomies remain inherently blind expeditions. The surgeon stands beside the patient, physically pushing these lines up, inch by inch. The only view comes from a live X-ray, which can’t see soft tissues like blood vessels. The surgeon shoots brief puffs of contrast dye through the catheter to illuminate the path ahead. A nimble operator can avoid scraping or piercing artery walls while bending the guide wire’s rounded tip around corners. But even these left or right turns are not intuitive. The guide wire can twist inside the body, and because the surgeon sees only a flat silhouette, steering it left may actually rotate the guidewire to the right.

The N1 robot feeds the catheter along a rail lined with seven modules, using a thin wire that allows precise control through a patient’s vascular system, even from kilometers away. Christie Hemm Klok

If all goes as planned, the doctor reaches the brain and pushes instruments through the catheter to dislodge the clot, then carefully pulls everything back out. Bell remembers how thrombectomies felt when he performed them. “I’m one and a half meters away from my catheter tip. I’m not in control of it. I can’t see where the blood vessels are. I thought, what is the ideal way to do these procedures? It’s certainly not what I’m doing now.”

Sganga and Bell want their robots to do two things: see what surgeons can’t see and be where surgeons can’t be. When I visited Remedy’s office in January, the team showed me their robotic arm and instruments that snap onto it. Motorized cartridges live on the robotic arm, one containing several actuators that use small gears to grip the threadlike instruments to move them in and out of a body. The instruments include a stent, an expandable wire-mesh tube used to pierce, grab, and yank a clot back out. It’s all typical stroke operation equipment—except for the catheter.

Remedy’s catheter is steerable, so it doesn’t need a guide wire to pave its path. Outside the body, a robotic arm advances the catheter while tiny wires tug its leading tip in any direction, as if an inquisitive worm is navigating the narrow branches of a bloodstream. As I maneuver the catheter with the Xbox controller, Bell and Sganga tell me they made wayfinding a priority. Sganga toggles on a CT scan to overlay on the X-ray feed. Suddenly I see the bright three-dimensional routes of blood vessels along a path that had been invisible on X-ray.

I noticed a pattern of small markings on the catheter. Sganga tells me they’re not for the surgeon, but for a computer-vision algorithm that tracks the catheter’s rotation inside the body. If an operator wants to steer right, Remedy’s software automatically translates that intention into the correct action. Instead of squinting at a 2D silhouette on an X-ray and mentally compensating for every twist in the catheter, the surgeon simply toggles to the right on the X-ray image, the Remedy system adjusts, and the catheter moves in the correct direction.

This system grew out of ideas that Bell and Sganga were pursuing when they met at Stanford in 2019. Already a physician, Bell was completing an MBA and enrolled in a robotics class in hopes of meeting an engineer who might share his interest in creating a medical robot. The professor connected him to Sganga, a bioengineering doctoral student who was developing pathfinding algorithms for an FDA-approved robotic bronchoscope to navigate the lungs.

Outside the body, a robotic arm advances the catheter while tiny wires tug its leading tip in any direction, as if an inquisitive worm is navigating the narrow branches of a bloodstream.

Sganga’s engineering work had exposed him to surgical robotics companies that failed because they hadn’t chosen a valuable enough problem to solve. He sought a medical problem where a robot could prove its worth well before human trials, and stroke stood out. “It’s an already verified clinical need,” Sganga says, “Time.” When he and Bell met for coffee, they matched each other’s energy right away: “It was like ‘Hey how you doing?’ and then we were looking at medical images of blood vessels together off of his phone,” Sganga says.

About a year after they both left Stanford, Bell and Sganga rented a two-car garage in Southern California and X-ray-proofed it with lead lining. “We called it the bunker because it had exposed lead on all sides, including the ceiling,” Sganga says. “It was just big enough to fit a bed and this rickety old C-arm [X-ray].” There they test-drove a prototype of their steerable catheter through silicone arteries—first controlling the robot on-site from another room, and then from a laptop hundreds of kilometers away. “We were trying to get an initial sign of life,” Sganga says. “And it was that moment that we realized that this could work.”

Dreams of remote surgery predate modern stroke care. In the 1980s and 1990s, the companies Computer Motion and Intuitive developed bedside robots to assist surgeons. Then, in 2001, French surgeon Jacques Marescaux and Canadian surgeon Michel Gagner removed a patient’s gallbladder from more than 6,000 km away. In New York City, Marescaux used a computer connected via high-speed fiber optics to control a Computer Motion robot in Strasbourg, France. The milestone, known as the Lindbergh Operation, was completed safely with no complications.

But telesurgery did not take off after Lindbergh. Instead, companies invested in robots operated by surgeons in the same room. Computer Motion and Intuitive merged in 2003, more companies sprang up, and robotic surgery steadily entered the mainstream. Today thousands of surgical robots operate in hospitals around the country, assisting in roughly 22 percent of surgeries. In 2023 alone, more than 2 million surgeries were performed with da Vinci, Intuitive’s flagship platform.

Remedy mechanical engineer Chris Hapstack [left] and software engineer Campbell Crowley adjust the N1 robot. Christie Hemm Klok

In the summer of 2025, telesurgery appeared to regain momentum when surgeons near Orlando, Fla., removed the prostate from a man 11,000 km away in Luanda, Angola. Around the same time, Intuitive demonstrated what it called “telecollaboration,” in which two surgeons on different continents operated together on a tissue model. Meanwhile, India-based SS Innovations has been testing cardiac telesurgery; in Panama, the Texas-based medical robotics company XCath has tested a steerable guide wire for thrombectomies. These companies are building on advances in computer vision and machine learning, yet remote robotics is hardly a sure bet.

“The first procedures are going to be those procedures where time is critical,” says Brad Nelson, who develops surgical robots at ETH Zurich and is not affiliated with Remedy. Last year, Nelson coauthored a report in Science Robotics arguing that telesurgery’s future success hinges on finding emergency operations where patients can’t always reach specialists in time, including stroke, heart attack, and fetal operations.

Surgeries that occur within blood vessels seem an attractive proving ground for teleoperation in emergencies. “If you have a hiccup, the nice thing about vascular procedures is nothing bad can happen other than the thing stops moving,” Nelson says. There’s neither a large open cavity to tend to, nor the urgent choreography one might need in organ transplants. If the surgeon loses connection to the robot while the catheter is inside a blood vessel, the operation can pause in place without damage.

Nelson’s lab is also working on a stroke solution. He has partnered with the Mayo Clinic in Arizona to build microscopic robots—the size of a coffee grain—steered with magnets to dissolve a clot.

After preliminary success in the garage, Sganga and Bell turned their focus to the environment where the Remedy N1 would live. Doctors and nurses advised them to improve the live audio-video feed, as any surgery is a coordinated team effort requiring constant communication. They were told to improve setup time, maintenance, cleaning, and began a series of conversations about secure communication and cybersecurity.

In 2021, CEO David Bell naps next to Remedy’s first X-ray machine in a lead-lined garage in Venice, Calif. Remedy Robotics

Absent a cyberattack, the elephant in the room for any telesurgery hopeful is latency. Experts speak about latency, or lag, in terms of how many thousandths of a second it takes for a small packet of data to reach a destination then ping back to its original source. In a major city with strong 5G or fiber-optic internet, latency might measure in the tens of milliseconds. In rural areas, even in the United States, lag can drag above 100.

Noticeable lag may not be a dealbreaker. When researchers in Japan analyzed five years of surgical simulations and demonstrations, they reported surgeons adapting to the connection speed. They paused. They moved more slowly. Remedy has noticed similar behavior in test runs. “We’ve actually found that operators are quite resilient to latency,” Sganga says.

Still, Remedy targets a round-trip latency of no more than 150 milliseconds, below the average human reaction time of 200 milliseconds. Whenever latency sneaks above that threshold, the system pauses all surgical action. Bell and Sganga say they’ve tailored their system to work with the slower internet speeds common in rural areas that would benefit from better access to stroke care, claiming they recently operated their system from across the Pacific using a mobile hotspot.

But sorting out the engineering details raises more questions about how telesurgery might change surgical practice. Bell told me he worries about what a telesurgical future could bring. What if surgeons’ skills erode? What if trainees become dependent on specific platforms? What if two patients need care from the same remote surgeon at the same time? “Is the person suffering a stroke in America necessarily more important than the person suffering a stroke in India? No,” Bell says. “So how do you figure that out? That’s something I think about a lot.”

During a stroke, a blockage in the brain triggers symptoms within seconds or minutes. The following hour is the so-called golden period for saving the brain before the risk of permanent damage grows. “Every minute wasted or delayed, 2 million brain cells are going to die,” says neurologist Archit Bhatt of Providence Medical Group in Portland, Oregon. “You really need to act fast.” Yet decades after the advent of thrombectomies, one in five Americans lives more than an hour from a hospital that offers the procedure.

Medium and small hospitals often lack the 24-hour surgical team, experience, or equipment for thrombectomies, so they must transfer stroke patients to large hospitals. As a result, standard stroke care is concentrated in urban areas. For example, Alaska’s only two thrombectomy centers serving the 739,000 people who live or work in the state are both in Anchorage, leaving more than half of residents out of range.

But the places most in need of telesurgery may also be the hardest places to deploy it. For starters, they may not have the high-quality network connections that remote surgery requires. Last June, experts from five major robotic corporations coauthored a list of technical standards for what they called “surgical-grade networks.” Mike Teodorescu, an information systems researcher with the University of Washington, says experts usually consider 100 milliseconds a safe threshold, but his team recently reported that many rural communities—and even most countries—struggle to meet it.

Neuroradiologist Hal Rice of the Australian Stroke Alliance remotely operates Remedy’s N1 System.Remedy Robotics

And connectivity is only part of the problem. The smallest and most remote hospitals may lack other support needed for thrombectomy, including neurologists, catheterization teams, CT scanners, and specialized intensive care units. “It’s an infrastructure problem,” Teodorescu says.

Medium-size regional hospitals may be a better target. Although they rarely offer thrombectomies, many already have the right support, experience, and patient volume. “There is a window for a thrombectomy center in a reasonably sized town where there is a stable economy,” says neurologist Bhatt.

“Every minute wasted or delayed, 2 million brain cells are going to die.”–neurologist Archit Bhatt

Telesurgery could do more than bring a distant specialist into the operating room. Jasdeep Bahra, an emergency medicine physician and lecturer in Kilifi, Kenya, worries that telerobotics could concentrate expertise in cities—widening the skill gap between rich cities and poor towns. The thrombectomy access problem is real, Bahra says, but lower income communities might benefit more if a system like Remedy’s could both treat patients and help train clinicians on-site. Sganga says Bahra’s idea fits Remedy’s mission.

“Digital operating rooms where you have surgeons that are over your shoulder as a mentor,” Bahra says. “If that’s what we’re talking about in telesurgery, that is the future for me.”

If smoothness and precision aren’t clinical outcomes, as Bell told me, what would count as success? One target is safety. In more than 1 percent of thrombectomy operations, surgeons unintentionally slice open a blood vessel, a feared and sometimes fatal occurrence that Bell believes robots can prevent.

In September 2025, Bell flew to Toronto for Remedy’s first test in human patients. Ten patients had consented to nonemergency procedures with Remedy’s robot. A neurosurgeon with a laptop would operate on six patients in an adjoining room; two elsewhere in the hospital; and two at an entirely different hospital across town. The Remedy team had experimented for years on silicone models, like the one I test-drove. Tests on lab animals suggested that, compared with a human, their robot collided less often with blood vessels and finished procedures faster.

Neurosurgeon Vitor Mendes Pereira pilots the N1 system in 2024 for its first in-person robotic procedure, in Toronto. Remedy Robotics

In the run-up to the Toronto procedures, the team measured internet latencies meticulously. Now they could only hope that their results would translate to human patients. “You’re never sure of how that leap is going to look, and it’s actually really hard to test,” Bell says. The night before the first operation, Bell barely slept.

The procedures—recording images called angiograms from within patients’ blood vessels—were a success, and were completed nearly twice as quickly as the current standard. “I cannot explain the relief,” Bell says. Remedy considers speed one measure of success because it can allow doctors to treat more people.

In 2025, neurosurgeon Vitor Mendes Pereira and his team at Unity Health Toronto perform the first fully remote robotic neurointerventional procedures. Remedy Robotics

A few months after my visit, Remedy announced US $62 million in new funding to support upcoming clinical trials. A portion of that investment came from the University of California system, which will host the clinical studies within a year, according to Bell. Remedy’s first trials will be on-site elective procedures, such as treating unruptured aneurysms, before expanding to remote surgeries in Australia or within the University of California system, near the end of 2027.

Sganga emphasizes that the on-site trials are not just a stepping stone. He’s come to believe that Remedy’s success depends on improving operations even when the surgeon is in the room. “The remote solution—it’s very flashy, it’s very obvious what that patient need is—but in order to get there, we believe you have to solve a meaningful problem on-premise,” he says. “Otherwise, doctors simply won’t use the system, and if they don’t use the system, they’re not going to gain the expertise required to operate remotely.”

The steerable catheter and computer-vision algorithm are two features he claims will improve thrombectomies, remote or not. And as trials ramp up, Sganga says they will look at factors beyond safety and surgical speed. “How quickly are doctors picking up on this new technique? How smoothly are the bedside interactions going? How quickly are folks able to set up the draping and interact with the tools?” he says. Bell has wondered whether to add a photo or video of the patient’s face to the surgeon’s display to preserve the emotional stakes of surgery.

These ambitions draw Bell and Sganga’s 25-person company into uncharted waters. Beyond one-time demonstrations, no robotics company has earned full regulatory approval for telesurgery, and no patient has been operated on remotely in the United States. Remedy hopes to change that. Decades after stroke research conquered the “therapeutic nihilism” that once defined the field, Remedy hopes telesurgery can bring thrombectomy to everyone who needs it, no matter where they might be.

Max G. Levy is an independent science journalist based in Los Angeles. His work has appeared in Wired, Quanta Magazine, and MIT Technology Review.

This is a tantalizing, multidisciplinary technology, but the latency issue seems really important. It seems like once they're through the medical hoops national telecoms regulators will have to figure out whether the necessary connections as emergency or critical infrastructure that deserve special spectrum allocation or similar, especially since this seems to have the most promise in more rural or remote settings.

#3111. Jensen Huang says he’s ready to rejoin Nvidia as CEO (if asked)

Jensen Huang’s resignation as Nvidia CEO shook up the AI market and US economy last week, but now via The Wall Street Journal Huang has spoken out publicly for the first time since stepping down, and he signals he’s ready to return as CEO if asked.

Today Robbie Whelan at The Wall Street Journal published Jensen Huang’s first public statement since departing Nvidia last week.

“Since my departure, I’ve seen an outpouring of calls from Nvidia’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO,” Huang said in a short statement. “If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.”

Home Depot isn’t hiring for the festive season?

The timing is likely no coincidence, as Nvidia is set to report its quarterly earnings later today.

Even though Huang technically resigned as CEO rather than being fired, it was clear that his ouster wasn’t exactly his choice. Thus, today’s statement is the former CEO formally putting it out into the world that he’s ready to return if asked.

Since Huang stepped down, President Trump publicly called on Apple’s Tim Cook to step in as Nvidia CEO. But it’s expected that a new CEO—assuming it’s not Huang—will take much longer for the company to find and Cook is unlikely to want the job.

What do you make of Huang’s remarks today? Let us know in the comments.

Cellular IoT has extended low-power connectivity to many remote places. Even so, about four-fifths of the earth’s surface remains outside the range of a base station. Non-terrestrial networks (NTN) address this gap by adding satellite access to the 5G standard. One modem can then connect through a satellite when no terrestrial cell is available.

This shift changes how devices are designed. Satellites are in motion. Signals therefore face long propagation delays and changing Doppler shift. Link budgets are tight and device antennas are small. A device can pass static conformance tests and still fail on a real satellite link.

This White Paper explains these challenges. It also outlines the test conditions and measurements needed to evaluate synchronization, signaling, receiver performance, and link reliability.

#3109. Anthropic lets apps bill Claude costs to their customers

Linked billing lets developers choose who pays for each request, but not every customer can use it.

Anthropic has launched Linked billing in beta, letting apps built on Claude bill API usage to a customer’s own Claude organisation. Customers can set a spend cap or unlink the app, but only organisations that pay Anthropic directly qualify, and their own data protections do not carry over.

Apps built on Claude can now charge their AI usage to their customers’ own Claude accounts. The feature, called Linked billing, launched in beta on Tuesday, according to Anthropic’s release notes.

A customer first links its Claude organisation to the app and approves it. The developer then chooses, on each request, whether the customer or the developer pays. The request still runs on the developer’s account, with its usage limits and model access.

Customers can set a monthly spending cap for each app in the Claude Console, or unlink it at any time. If Anthropic cannot bill the customer, the request is refused rather than charged to the developer. Anthropic is strict on limits elsewhere too: it ends enterprise discounts once customers use up their tokens.

Not every customer qualifies. It only works for organisations that pay Anthropic directly, not those billed through AWS, Google Cloud or Azure, or with only a Claude subscription. Credits from Claude plans and Anthropic’s startup programmes cannot be used either.
