#3081. Epic accuses Apple of withholding 122,000 documents, seeks daily fines

In a new filing, Epic Games accuses Apple of withholding more than 122,000 documents related to its proposed App Store commissions and asks the court to impose daily fines until the company complies. Here are the details.

As a result of the lawsuit Epic Games brought against Apple in 2020, Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers ruled in 2021 that Apple would have to, among other things, allow developers to direct users to alternative payment methods outside the App Store.

Apple responded by allowing external payment links, but imposed a commission of up to 27% on purchases made through them. This, in turn, led the court to find Apple in civil contempt for violating its injunction. Since then, Apple has been trying to overturn that ruling, a dispute that has now reached the Supreme Court.

At the same time, district court proceedings will determine what, if any, commission Apple may charge on purchases made through external payment links. Apple submitted its proposal on August 13, calling for commissions ranging from 5% to 15%, and Epic is expected to respond after Apple completes its document production.

In a new filing, however, Epic is accusing Apple of withholding more than 122,000 documents related to how it arrived at its proposed commission rates.

One of the many aspects of the ever-sprawling battle between Epic Games and Apple centers on document production.

In its new filing, Epic says Apple has repeatedly failed to produce documents detailing how it arrived at its proposed commission rates, accusing the company of withholding materials it deems irrelevant to the proceedings.

Epic argues that Apple previously used questionable claims of attorney-client privilege to withhold documents during the contempt proceedings, but has now changed tactics.

Apple does introduce one tactical change from its prior campaign of delay. Whereas during the contempt proceeding Apple used bogus claims of privilege to evade its discovery obligations, this time Apple withholds thousands of documents on bogus claims of irrelevance. For example, Apple is withholding well over 99% of the documents returned by running the agreed-to search terms on the files of the four custodians Apple says decided on the proposed fee (Tim Cook, Eddy Cue, Carson Oliver, and Kevan Parekh (Apple’s new CFO)) and three other key individuals (Nate Barton, Alex Roman, and Phil Schiller). Apple claims these withheld documents are not relevant to this proceeding-even though they hit on case-specific terms such as “proffer,” “contempt,” “injunction,” and “link-out.” To put this into context, while Apple produced 632 custodial documents returned by these search terms (including families), Apple is withholding over 122,000 based on a claim of non-responsiveness. Moreover, Apple claims that it completed its production from the files of these custodians, yet its production does not include a single substantive email discussing the rates Apple ultimately proposed; any notes or communications reflecting what occurred at any meeting where these rates were discussed or decided; any internal analysis of the financial or business impact of the proposed commissions; any App Store profit and loss statements; or any support for Apple’s assertion that its incremental link-out costs are “essentially zero.”

Epic goes on to state that “Apple cannot be trusted to fix this problem on its own,” proposing instead that the court order Apple to produce all non-privileged documents matching the search terms agreed upon by both parties, regardless of whether Apple considers them relevant.

Under this proposal, Apple would still be allowed to review documents for attorney-client privilege, but it would be up to Epic to determine which of the remaining documents are relevant to the case. Epic argues that existing confidentiality protections would prevent it from using any of the information for purposes unrelated to the litigation.

Given Apple’s position, Epic respectfully submits that the Court should order Apple to produce to Epic all non-privileged documents that hit on the Parties’ agreed-upon search terms, so that Epic itself can sift the wheat from the chaff. Doing so will avoid further delays and place no burden on Apple. Moreover, doing so would not raise any of the concerns that required Special Master involvement in the prior proceeding, namely concerns around the production of privileged Apple information to Epic. Under Epic’s proposed remedy, Apple would be allowed to continue its review for privilege. For these reasons, Epic asks this Court to order Apple to produce all non-privileged documents that hit on any of the Parties’ agreed-upon search terms by December 2, 2026 (one week after Apple’s deadline to substantially complete production), irrespective of any relevance or responsiveness assessment.

Finally, though Epic does not propose a specific dollar amount, it “asks that the Court impose on Apple a daily monetary sanction for each day Apple fails to comply after December 2, 2026.”

According to the court docket, a hearing on Epic’s motion was initially scheduled for November 24 before Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers. However, a new order filed today, which has yet to be made public, refers the discovery dispute to a magistrate judge and includes a notice terminating deadlines and hearings.

#3079. Report: iPhone set to gain market share in 2027 amid industry-wide slump

Apple could see iPhone shipments rise 7% next year, giving it a 26% share of global smartphone shipments, according to a new report. Here are the details.

As detailed by AppleInsider, a new Morgan Stanley research report says Apple is poised to ship approximately 270 million iPhones in 2027, a 7% bump from 2026.

The forecast comes amid a change of pace for Apple, which launched only the iPhone 18 Pro models and iPhone Duo this fall, with the rest of its iPhone lineup reportedly set to arrive early next year.

Morgan Stanley notes that this could push some purchases from late 2026 into 2027, contributing to the projected shipment growth without necessarily reflecting an increase in underlying demand.

The report also comes as Apple and the rest of the smartphone industry continue to grapple with rising memory and storage prices, though previous reports have suggested that Apple is better positioned than many of its competitors to absorb those costs.

Apple raised iPhone prices in September, after keeping them stable for much of the year while competitors had already introduced price hikes. In some cases, they raised prices more than once within a matter of months.

Back to the report, it notes that global smartphone shipments are expected to drop 5% next year, compared with a previous forecast of 3.6% growth. That said, it’s still an improvement over the estimated 13.8% decline in 2026.

When it comes to Apple and the iPhone specifically, Morgan Stanley notes that consumer interest in upgrading has remained largely unchanged year over year, with 37% of iPhone owners saying they are extremely likely to upgrade within the next 12 months. That’s compared with 41% of smartphone owners overall, a figure that dropped by 2 percentage points year over year.

As for the market’s reaction to the iPhone Duo, Morgan Stanley found that 22% of non-iPhone users surveyed expressed interest in switching to Apple’s foldable device, with that figure reaching 34% in China.

Importantly, Morgan Stanley’s survey was conducted after the iPhone Duo was announced, but before it launched, so these figures reflect consumer interest rather than actual purchasing behavior.

Apple Intelligence was another factor examined in the survey, with Morgan Stanley concluding that AI features are becoming less important in driving iPhone upgrades, while factors such as battery life and upgrade eligibility are gaining importance.

Finally, Morgan Stanley found that Apple’s customer retention rate increased three percentage points to a record 93%, while its net switching rate improved to 12%.

Huawei was the only other major smartphone brand to show a positive and improving net switching rate, while Samsung and Google remained relatively neutral, and Xiaomi, Motorola, Honor, Oppo, and Vivo recorded negative rates.

#3077. WhatsApp’s first-party chat history backup service moves ahead

Select WhatsApp beta testers on iOS are now seeing an option to use the app’s own backup service as an alternative to iCloud. Here are the details.

A few months ago, WABetaInfo reported that WhatsApp was working on its own backup service as an alternative to the current method of backing up chats, which relies on Apple’s iCloud.

At the time, the feature wasn’t available even to beta testers, but WABetaInfo’s report provided details on how it would work, including 2GB of free storage, optional paid plans for larger backups, and mandatory end-to-end encryption for backups stored on WhatsApp’s servers.

Now, the site reports that some WhatsApp users running the latest TestFlight build are seeing the option to switch from iCloud to WhatsApp’s own backup service, suggesting that a wider rollout may not be too far off.

Users can switch to WhatsApp cloud storage from the Chat backup screen. Here, users will have to choose the backup provider they want to use. If they choose WhatsApp, they will have to secure their backups using end-to-end encryption. Since encryption is mandatory, users cannot skip this step. However, they can choose a different method to encrypt their backups. For example, users can secure their backups using a 64-digit encryption key. Users who do not know what to choose can opt for the passkey, which is the default method WhatsApp recommends. After users complete the setup, they can back up their chat history on WhatsApp’s servers. WhatsApp keeps the backup on its servers for four months after a subscription expires. If users do not renew their subscription, WhatsApp deletes the backup permanently.

Importantly, the site notes that backups stored on WhatsApp’s servers cannot currently be used to restore chats across platforms, meaning users switching from iPhone to Android, or vice versa, will still need to rely on WhatsApp’s built-in chat transfer feature.

Although the feature appears to be rolling out to beta testers first, the report notes that “the latest version available on the App Store is also compatible with this functionality,” meaning WhatsApp could theoretically enable it for users running the public version without requiring another app update.

#3076. Airbnb vs. Booking: Quarterly Revenue Scale and Historical Growth

Booking has out-earned Airbnb in every quarter of the past two years, yet the gap may be narrowing as Airbnb's third-quarter peaks grow.

Airbnb (ABNB -2.82%) primarily generates its revenue by managing a global digital marketplace that connects individual property hosts offering private rooms, primary residences, and vacation homes with travelers seeking unique lodging experiences, custom local activities, and tailored vacation rentals worldwide.

It recently entered an exclusive property booking partnership integrating over one million listings into the American Express platform, and it formally introduced updated operational policies restricting hosts from assigning specific professional checkout chores to visiting guests.

Booking (BKNG -1.95%) functions as a global provider of digital travel and dining reservations, earning revenue through a diverse portfolio of consumer platforms that offer extensive accommodation bookings, airline tickets, rental cars, vacation packages, cruise itineraries, and online restaurant reservations across international markets.

It recently introduced a new artificial intelligence-powered personal travel agent tool to enhance consumer booking experiences, while simultaneously navigating a Federal Trade Commission investigation regarding specific marketing and billing practices at its Priceline brand.

Revenue here refers to the data provider's standardized income-statement revenue line item, which serves as a fundamental financial tracking metric that shows individual investors exactly how much total money a business brings in from its core operations before any administrative, marketing, payroll, or operational expenses are deducted by the company's management.

Airbnb vs. Booking Revenue over the last 8 quarters.

Normally, the first thing to note when examining a company's revenue trend is seasonality: some times of the year have stronger buying patterns than others. In normal times, seasonality holds true for consumer-driven stocks like these. Airbnb and Booking Holdings get exceptional volume for summer months in the Northern Hemisphere, which translates into third-quarter revenue being booked.

To properly evaluate the revenue trend of companies with strong seasonal trends, compare each quarter to its comparable prior-year quarter. Note that Airbnb's 2026 third quarter rose sharply over Q3 2025, adding $800 million in revenue. Interestingly, Booking's revenue actually dipped year-over-year, suggesting some weakness could be appearing. Despite Booking's large international business, third-quarter results felt no effect, for better or worse, due to foreign exchange considerations.

Revenue is the simplest metric investors use to judge a business. Ideally, on a chart like this, a company would show sequentially rising bars, left ot right. But even when seasonality exists, a trend is visible.

#3075. iFixit tears down Apple HomeView, finds lots of glue and endless frustration

iFixit’s teardown of the new Apple HomeView is now up, revealing a device that seems nearly impossible to take apart and repair. Watch it below.

Following last week’s launch of the Apple HomeView, iFixit today published its teardown of the device.

Contrary to recent teardowns, which found significant repairability improvements with greater component modularity and easier access to internal components, the HomeView put up a fight nearly all the way through.

With heavily glued or adhesive-bonded components, including the display, speakers, antennas, and logic board, the teardown proved particularly challenging, even after the adhesive securing the display’s speakers was soaked in isopropyl alcohol.

At one point, one of them broke apart during removal, while the logic board required considerable force to separate from the chassis due to the thermal adhesive holding it in place.

iFixit’s teardown covered the two HomeView variants: the tabletop model and the wall-mounted version. Interestingly, there are some internal differences between them, as the wall-mounted model has a slightly wider logic board to accommodate capacitors that are housed in the base of the tabletop version.

As a result, the wall-mounted HomeView also has smaller internal speakers, which helps explain the differences in their audio systems that Apple had already acknowledged at launch.

Back to the tabletop model, iFixit’s teardown also showed that separating the display from the base requires either specialized tools or extensive, potentially destructive disassembly of the display assembly, thanks to the way Apple routed the connecting cables through the pivot mechanism.

Once iFixit was in the base, however, there was some good news: the USB-C port is modular and relatively easy to access, as are the passive radiators and the board powering the lower assembly.

Still, an extremely short cable connecting the woofer to the board underneath made disassembly difficult, with iFixit questioning how anyone would be able to reconnect it during reassembly.

Given all these repairability challenges, Shahram Mokhtari joked that while iFixit doesn’t have an official repairability scorecard for this category of device, he would give the Apple HomeView a “BEEP this thing” out of 10.

To check out iFixit’s blog post, which features an interactive 3D CT scan of the HomeView, follow this link.

Be sure to also catch 9to5Mac’s review of the Apple HomeView.

#3071. Should You Buy Anthropic Stock at Its IPO? Here's What History Says.

Anthropic is expected to go public at a $1.4 trillion valuation.

Anthropic is preparing for one of the largest initial public offerings (IPOs) in stock market history. The company behind the Claude chatbot is expected to begin trading on the Nasdaq under the ticker symbol ANT on Nov. 19. The offering price is reported to land between $70 and $78. At the upper end of that range, Anthropic could raise $64 billion.

IPOs can attract meaningful attention from institutional investors, momentum traders, and retail investors hoping to capitalize on the next multibagger. Historical evidence suggests that buying stock immediately after a highly anticipated public debut can be a risky strategy.

IPO stocks often experience outsize volatility because the offering price and the price retail investors actually pay when trading begins can differ by a wide margin. When demand exceeds the available supply of shares, prices can surge during the opening session as investors scramble to build a position. However, initial enthusiasm tends to fade as day traders take profits.

Research published by LPL Financial illustrates how the prices of new public companies can fluctuate. The firm studied IPOs that raised at least $50 million between April 1995 and April 2025. The data showed that average first-year returns were positive even though median returns were negative. This disparity suggests that a relatively small cohort of winners helped offset otherwise disappointing performances across a larger portion of newly public companies.

The research documented severe drawdowns during the first year following several high-profile technology IPOs. Meta Platforms experienced a maximum decline of approximately 54%, while Uber and electric vehicle manufacturer Rivian witnessed drawdowns of 68% and 88%, respectively.

This volatility underscores why investors should not confuse an exciting opportunity with an attractive entry point.

On the surface, Anthropic's IPO looks tempting. The company is at the forefront of an enormous addressable market, is experiencing unprecedented revenue growth, and is directly benefiting from euphoria around AI.

At the upper end of its proposed offering price, Anthropic's valuation could reach $1.4 trillion. This would immediately propel Anthropic among the world's most valuable companies.

With that said, this valuation inherently reflects extraordinary expectations around future growth, even as the company invests heavily in model development, computing infrastructure, and customer acquisition. As a result, investors need to determine whether Anthropic can eventually generate enough earnings and free cash flow to justify its market capitalization.

The distinction between growth and profitability is important because AI development is extremely capital-intensive. Anthropic faces intense competition from OpenAI, Alphabet's (GOOGL -1.24%) (GOOG -1.30%) Gemini, and other well-funded developers.

Meanwhile, the cost of training generative models continues to rise. Even if the company delivers impressive revenue growth, disappointing profit margins or slower-than-expected progress toward profitability could easily pressure Anthropic's valuation.

Historical IPO performance offers an important lesson, but it doesn't necessarily mean investors should always avoid new public companies. Alphabet’s and Amazon's (AMZN +0.05%) IPOs provide a compelling counterexample, with shares gaining 281% and 179% during their first year of trading, according to LPL's research. Investors who bought stock early and maintained a long-term perspective ultimately made generational wealth from these companies' expansion.

Nevertheless, waiting for Anthropic to settle as a public company rather than chasing the initial momentum appears to be the more prudent strategy. Investors will have ample opportunities to evaluate quarterly earnings, monitor profitability trends, and determine whether the company's growth justifies its valuation. Meanwhile, allowing the initial excitement to subside should create more attractive entry points.

The takeaway here is that Anthropic's long-term potential will not be determined by what happens during its first few trading sessions. Ultimately, the company's success will depend on competitive advantages, customer adoption, financial performance, and the economics of developing AI models. For investors focused on building wealth over a long-term time horizon, buying Anthropic stock at a reasonable valuation matters more than owning the stock on its first day.

#3070. Fitbit users can’t see Google Health metrics after update – how to fix it

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Google says it's working on a fix - meantime, users have found workarounds.

Fitbit users are having trouble seeing several key metrics on the Google Health app. The glitch, Reddit users are speculating, occurs after users update to the latest Fitbit update 5.12.

One user reported that Fitbit Air stopped tracking metrics n the Vitals section of the app, including breathing rate, blood oxygen, resting heart rate, HRV, and skin temperature. Many users on the Reddit thread said they’ve experienced the same issue over the past few days.

Also: Google’s new Fitbit Edge solves my biggest gripe with the Pixel Watch

Users are complaining that it’s taken Google so long to fix this bug, which appeared in the app for some users about six days ago.

“This is getting extremely frustrating and disappointing that Google, a multi-trillion-dollar company with AI models built to fix these issues and high-tier engineers, can’t even fix a little issue like that,” one user wrote in a thread.

Google acknowledged in a customer support reply that it was aware of the issue and looking to fix it.

On the Reddit thread, users have suggested logging out and back in, or uninstalling and reinstalling the app, as a solution to the disappearing data issue.

Also: After one week wearing the Pixel Watch 5, here’s what I want most

Another user suggested clicking through each stat that doesn’t populate and then selecting the monthly view. Doing this, the user reported, should repopulate the main screen with the latest information, without requiring one to log out and log back in. Users in the thread said that this fix helped solve the issue.

Google said it is rolling out a fix for the issue. “A small number of iOS users were missing metrics like vitals and daily totals for steps, distance and energy burned. Updating to app version 5.12.2 will fix the issue. No user data was lost,” Google said in an email to ZDNET.

And some really key milestones in the very near future as we approach that integration of Hulu + Live TV on Disney+ and the integration of Fubo into ESPN's commerce flows. So yes, we feel confident about our ability to grow. The second component of that growth trajectory is on prioritizing our higher value, better retaining tiers here in North America.

We'll talk more, I'm sure, as other questions come in around how we leverage the full breadth of the flexibility in our portfolio but orienting our organization around prioritizing those higher-value tiers is a key part of our growth strategy. We are confident in it. And I want to really underscore though that our definition of growth going forward is going to be measured in that revenue and profit outcomes that we're committing to. On your second question, the international part of our strategic review is still ongoing. We really focused our priority on the domestic market.

That's the area where we believe we have very strong competitive differentiations in the criteria we need to really succeed in continuing to grow the business. That's where we have a truly differentiated product proposition. It's where we have our relationship with Disney that we can leverage the best outcomes there and we have scale in this market. So we're very committed to prioritizing our resources to support the U.S. business. Our international review is ongoing, as you say and we'll update you when we have more to conclude on that front. The one add I'd make to your comments is, you are right that the international businesses were in part delivering some technology capabilities to the core U.S. business.

And I think it's a really good call out because we have succeeded in bringing together the platforms that we had from those acquisitions into one now. So here in the U.S., we're enjoying the benefits of a unified platform that brings together many of the innovations that were first delivered in France on the Molotov platform. And our AI capabilities that were part of our acquisitions in India are now embedded throughout the platform experiences and our engineering teams across each of those 3 locations are now truly operating as one. So we have yielded the benefits of those initial hypotheses around the value of the acquisitions from a technology capability perspective.

And we're really pleased with how the efficiencies and the distribution of those capabilities has been incorporated into the U.S. product and tech platform.

Operator: Your next question comes from the line of Kutgun Maral with Evercore ISI.

Kutgun Maral: Two, if I could, one on the product road map and one on advertising. So first, on product, you laid out a lot this morning with 2 brands and Hulu Live TV moving over into the Disney app by year-end. How do you think about the technology platform across both services over time? And how should we think about technology spend as the plan rolls out given the efficiencies you're already seeing and getting from AI? And then on advertising, you had strong ad revenue growth in the quarter, helped by the move to the Disney Ad Server.

Earlier this year, you said that with the gains in CPMs and fill rates, you expected Fubo's ad ARPU to converge with Hulu Live's once that move was done. How close are you in that journey? And from there, where do you see the next leg of ad growth to come from, including mobile and maybe fan engagement opportunities that you flagged?

Alisa Bowen: Thanks, Kutgun. Both great questions. On innovation, technology and AI, I think as we said in our prepared remarks, continuing to innovate our fan experience is a key focus for the growth agenda. Innovation has been part of the Fubo DNA and it's certainly an area that we want to double down on now. I think we see significant opportunities to evolve the level of focus that we've had. I mentioned, for example, the core viewing experience inside the Fubo app but also the companion experience that we can deliver through the mobile app. They're both areas of focus. And you're also right that AI is helping us move faster.

I said in my prepared remarks that we more than doubled our development velocity this year, thanks to AI and its coding efficiency. So that really gives us confidence that we can accelerate our ambition for what we're going to deliver and the output without increasing our costs significantly. And by the way, some of those same cost advantages apply to the way that we're using AI in our marketing applications as well.

Marketing tech has been an area of focus and AI capabilities in that area are allowing us to do more to launch more campaigns, to harness better targeting, to generate greater volumes of creative, a whole range of ways that we're helping to accelerate the volume that we're doing without increasing our costs in that space, too. In terms of how we think about the road map, I mentioned a couple of platform issues or areas of focus, mobile being one. But the road map overall, really, we think about where we're focused there in the categories that are driving our business.

So that's acquisition and monetization initiatives, things like improving our marketplace and how we merchandise all the soft bundles and add-on options that we have to consumers or the data signals that we're using in our marketing campaigns to improve the conversion rates. The second area is in engagement and retention initiatives, things like, say, for example, improving our content merchandising and discovery capabilities or even the video playback experience. And then the third is supporting the platform for scalability and efficiencies. The way we go to market with partners, for example and the way that we extend our distribution in -- on different platforms and different devices without significantly increasing our technology resource overhead each and every time.

So they're the sort of 4 areas that we've segmented the road map into. And as we get into delivering that, in future quarters, we're looking forward to sharing greater velocity of deliverables in each of those areas. With regards to your second question on advertising outcomes, I'm going to ask John to comment firstly on those and then I'll jump in at the end.

John Janedis: Kutgun, thanks again for the question. So we continue to see strength in the ad business since that migration to the Disney Ad Server in terms of both the fill rates and CPMs. During the quarter, we did see double-digit growth in CPMs and a meaningful improvement in the fill. So in terms of convergence from a CPM perspective, we've actually largely converged already. And I'd say given Fubo's relative exposure to sports, there was a tailwind during the fourth quarter. And then I would say, looking at it on an annual basis, we'd expect relative CPMs to actually be very similar and converge in '27.

Alisa Bowen: And I'll just point out one other highlight. In the last quarter, we saw real improvements in the sale of our entertainment inventory on the Fubo platform. I think that's a great example of the benefits that come with Disney's scale as it relates to audience sales and audience tracking across different platforms, as well as Disney's ad platform targeting capabilities. So as we go through the usual seasonality that we expect to see in the future, as John mentioned, that ability to better monetize our non-sports inventory is a real bright spot and something that we look to continue.

Operator: Your next question comes from the line of Patrick Sholl with Barrington Research.

Patrick Sholl: I just had one kind of around the capital allocation. As you mentioned you have priorities around technology investments to expand mobile, looking into niche sports rights. I was just kind of curious, as you make your push into mobile and the expanded sports rights, do you kind of view that as also adding add-on services to add to the content offering? Or would you be investing in owning sports rights as part of that?

John Janedis: Why don't I start with that, Patrick and maybe Alisa will follow up. But let me start on the capital question. I'd referenced my earlier comments that we ended the quarter in the strongest financial position in Fubo's history with more than $270 million in cash in the balance sheet and we generated $36 million in free cash flow in that seasonally strong fourth quarter. And then again, looking ahead, we expect to generate free cash flow in both fiscal '27 and '28.

And then if you take a step back and look at our business combination, while we'll have quarter-to-quarter variations, again, given the seasonality, on an annual basis, the conversion from adjusted EBITDA to free cash flow is significant. And remember, all of the adjusted EBITDA from Hulu Live converts to free cash flow. And then more broadly, we have minimal tax obligations and fixed interest payments. And so that dovetails with our investment priorities where we'll continue to invest in content, marketing, tech and product and those align with the areas of focus that Alisa spoke to in her remarks.

So rather than focus on rights acquisitions, we're really focused on making sure that the marketplace represents the broadest possible set of options for consumers to package and put together a service that reflects what their needs are. So add-ons, bundles, hard and soft bundles and then obviously, the addition of licensed content through expanding our channel propositions and other opportunities to integrate content into the platform would be our focus as opposed to rights acquisition.

Operator: Your next question comes from the line of David Joyce with Seaport Research Partners.

Our approach as we go into each of our renewals and each of our content negotiations is to think about it as a partnership. We're very committed to the philosophy that a healthy ecosystem with maximum reach is in everyone's interest, ours and the programmers. And we're really pleased with the way the programmers are partnering with us to try and achieve those outcomes so far.

Operator: Your next question comes from the line of Drew Crum with B. Riley.

Andrew Crum: Alisa, you've discussed the uniqueness of Fubo extensively here. Having undertaken the business review, any further learnings in terms of the company's positioning versus your peer set? And how would you characterize the competitive dynamics, your ability to compete entering fiscal '27? And then, John, you did not offer EBITDA guidance for fiscal '27. Why not? And can you address any variables that we should be thinking about that would influence the range of outcomes for profitability and EBITDA specifically in the upcoming year?

Alisa Bowen: Okay. Thanks, Drew, for your question. I'll jump in first and then hand over to John. You're right, the pay TV ecosystem is extremely competitive across both legacy and virtual players. But in terms of innovation and differentiation, I think you're seeing a lot from us actually. As we've gone through the strategic review, we've really honed in on what we think those differentiations are. Our brand strength from both Fubo and Hulu, having both brands in the market, we see as a core advantage. We think that those brands speak really strongly to very different segments of the market and having both in our portfolio is a specific advantage.

So together with those kind of innovations as well as the integration of Hulu Live onto the Disney+ app, I think we have some really key competitive differentiators and we're really confident that consumers are starting to see it too. On your question around 2027 and -- or fiscal '27, let me pass that one to John.

And so for '27, to your point, we're not specifically guiding to adjusted EBITDA. But I'd say, given the upcoming launch of our key initiatives, maybe some more context for you, over the next several quarters, the year-over-year improvement won't be linear or maybe said differently, we would expect the growth in adjusted EBITDA over the next 2 years to be weighted towards fiscal 2028.

Operator: Your next question comes from the line of Tyler DiMatteo with BTIG.

Tyler DiMatteo: Two for me, please. I wanted to come back to just the broader Disney relationship, Alisa. How should investors think about Disney's involvement in the company today, their role, the level of commitment and just their role in the overall strategic direction of the business? I know you gave a lot of highlights on the product, the advertising, the bundling opportunity, et cetera. Just curious for some incremental color at a higher level in terms of their overall role in the strategic direction of the business. And then my second question, wanted to come back to the bundling opportunities. I know you highlighted on Disney a variety of opportunities. But what other incremental opportunities are there out there?

How would you kind of describe the state of play for bundling and just how investors should think about the bundling opportunities for the business?

Alisa Bowen: Okay. Great. Thanks, Tyler. Your first question may be a better question for Disney. I can't speak to their strategy specifically. But what I can talk about is what the Disney partnership means for Fubo and for our business here. And I think I've highlighted in our prepared remarks and in some of the other responses that I have given this morning that our strategic arrangements with Disney are really central to each of the 4 focus areas that we're driving for near-term implementation.

I think I would reiterate a earlier response I gave as well that, first and foremost, continuing to have those 2 brands that really target 2 different audiences in the marketplace, we see as a very big advantage and something that we're really leaned into. I've mentioned many of the other examples already today. The Disney bundle inclusion, we're confident that, that's an example of something that's going to yield both acquisition and retention benefits on the Fubo side. And then the addition of Hulu Live to Disney, that's a great opportunity to significantly increase the visibility of Hulu Live to a whole new SVOD audience in the marketplace.

And then Fubo being part of the ESPN commerce flows in 2027, again, an opportunity to introduce the brand and to generate cost-effective customer referrals to the Fubo plans, including our sports bundle. These are all ways that we see the commercial agreements benefiting the Fubo business and we're really pleased with how that's evolving. The success of our combination with the Disney ad platform, I think we've mentioned that several times as well. That's a very clear and bright spot in the partnership and we're looking forward to more from that coming. So on several of these initiatives, I would characterize it as us just getting to the starting point here.

But we're now at that starting point and we're really pleased with the way the collaboration is evolving. And I think that fiscal 2027 is going to be a pivotal moment as we continue to double down on these initiatives and learn what works together with Disney in partnership with them, what works for the audiences and how we evolve the details of the implementations once we're up and running. On your first question around bundling, I think that's a great one, too. Bundling is a fairly natural response, I think, to the fragmentation. And for sports fans, in particular, which is really relevant for the Fubo market positioning, fragmentation is a real frustration.

I hear all the time that what fans really love about Fubo is that it addresses that fragmentation, that the pay TV bundle and Fubo specifically is still an opportunity to bring together all the rights that fans care about, all in one place. And we still offer that -- the best value in terms of the rights that people care about, all in one place at a price point that's affordable. So not only do those live rights come together in a meaningful way through pay TV and Fubo specifically but it also comes with a library.

And I think this is an example of something that's perhaps not as well understood by consumers and by the marketplace as it should be, that library of more than 65,000 on-demand titles, which is a core part of the Fubo proposition, along with all the live rights and the local sports rights. So that concept, that bundling is important to address fragmentation is very real. And the Fubo proposition, which does that means that we have a real value proposition that consumers are after, a certain segment of the market is after. So along with that, I think we're also leaning into the soft bundles that give consumers an opportunity to customize what that bundle looks like for them.

We also mentioned, I think, that the packaging of the SVOD services with Fubo Elite and Pro is another opportunity. In fact, adding Disney+ and Hulu follows an earlier addition of ESPN Unlimited. And the data shows us that customers who have activated those SVOD services in addition to their core Fubo subscription do have greater engagement and better retention than those who haven't. So getting Disney+ and Hulu in front of our base and making sure that those who are now entitled fully activate and make use of that incremental value is going to be a key priority. And then, of course, we continue to look for additional ways to bundle value where it makes sense.

Operator: Your next question comes from the line of Alicia Reese with Wedbush.

Alicia Reese: Congrats, Alisa and John, great results, particularly on the ad tier. It's really nice to see growth in that line item, finally. And to what extent -- I'd like to dig in on to what extent the -- there was a clear early benefit from layering Fubo ads onto the Disney ad platform. But I do wonder if you could talk about what kind of leeway you have to improve ad monetization, kind of optimizing that ad load against the different tiers and the high-value tiers where you're adding on some more Disney content, for example and then you have the mobile opportunity there. The ad load is already quite high.

And so you wouldn't want to disturb those most high-value subscription tiers. But maybe you could refine targeting a little bit more and adding on all of the mobile. What are your opportunities there to just increase the ad optimization?

Alisa Bowen: Thank you for the question. And we agree, it is a real bright spot. We're really pleased with those results as well. And I think that as we go forward, the opportunity is the clearest and most obvious opportunity is for us to increase engagement with the platform overall. And clearly, our product road map is designed to underpin that. I also think that we'll continue to see and John alluded to this earlier, we're going to continue to see the benefits of overall innovation on the Disney ad serving platform as it relates to new targeting capabilities, the ability to automate ad plans, the ability for advertisers to generate creative in the platform.

So we're really focused on that and I think additional benefits from a technology perspective are going to flow to us as they materialize in the entire ecosystem that Disney is managing. Ad loads is an area that we will continue to take a look at. It's something where I think we have some opportunities to iterate. Frankly, we're just beginning to get into that. So nothing to say specifically about that yet. But specifically as it relates to the consumption of VOD content and other non-broadcast content, there may be an opportunity for us to iterate and extract some incremental value there.

Operator: Your next question comes from the line of Brent Penter with Raymond James.

Brent Penter: First one for me. You called out the more general entertainment focus of Hulu Live TV relative to Fubo. But clearly, still a large contingent of sports fans there. So I'm wondering your thinking in terms of offering more sports-focused tiers in Hulu Live and possibly even adding regional sports networks to Hulu Live.

Alisa Bowen: Well, thanks for the question, Brent. The focus right now is really on doubling down on the core differentiations that we see between those 2 services. I've said a couple of times on this call, we see the distinct market positioning of the 2 services, Fubo and Hulu + Live TV as being a key advantage. And the most immediate priority is in leaning into those respective strengths. And that's what we're really focused on doing.

And I think as we get further into testing and learning what's working in that regard, as I mentioned earlier, we'll continue to iterate on our strategy. But for now, we see those 2 market positionings as being particular advantages and we want to focus on that.

Brent Penter: Very clear. And on that point, as you think about Fubo kind of being a sports fans service, it's been a while since Fubo has had the Warner Bros. Discovery networks and you all in the past have talked about that not having a significant impact. I'm just wondering now that the Skydance merger has closed, if you've had any discussions with them or see any opportunity to get those networks back on Fubo.

And it's one of the advantages of us having this combined portfolio now that we can really lean into how we market those differences to different consumer segments.

Operator: This concludes the question-and-answer session and this concludes today's call. Thank you for attending. You may now disconnect.

#3068. Google’s Pixel Tag tracker won’t work as well on older Android phones – check our list

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Tech > Services & Software > Operating Systems > Mobile OS > Android

Several of the tracker’s best features require Bluetooth 6.0-compatible device.

Google’s Pixel Tag, the company’s take on an Android-exclusive Bluetooth tracker, is finally here, following its August announcement during the Google I/O developer conference.

Also: Google’s new Android XR glasses have lower ‘creep factor’ than competitors

Pixel Tag is a complete Bluetooth tracker for Android users that appears less confined to device-specific ecosystems than Samsung’s Smart Tag 3 and Apple’s AirTag.

However, if you look at Google’s footnotes, the Pixel Tag’s functionality is diminished when an older Android phone is involved. Several of the tracker’s best features require a compatible device running Android 9.0+ and Bluetooth 6.0+, according to Google.

Android 9 and newer encompasses a lot of devices, but Bluetooth 6.0 and newer doesn’t. Here’s what to check before you buy.

Smartphones began shipping with Bluetooth 6.0 in 2025, starting with the Samsung Galaxy S26 Plus and Galaxy S26 Ultra. The following phones also have Bluetooth 6.0:

If your Android phone is older than any of the listed above, even by a generation, it likely supports Bluetooth 5.3 or 5.4 — not enough for the Pixel Tag’s best features.

The Pixel Tag’s precision-finding capabilities are powered by Bluetooth Channel Sounding, a key feature introduced in Bluetooth 6.0. Nearly every review I’ve seen of the Pixel Tag, including our own, tests the tracker when paired with a Pixel 10, Pixel 10 Pro, Pixel 11, or Pixel 11 Pro.

I assume that Android users whose phones run Android 9.0+ but lack Bluetooth 6.0+ can use the Pixel Tag for very basic, general location tracking. These users may see the tracker’s general location, but Google’s device compatibility footnote appears several times throughout its press release.

The following features require Android 9.0+ and Bluetooth 6.0+, according to Google’s release:

So, on older Android devices without Android 9.0+ and Bluetooth 6.0+, the following aren’t supported: locating the exact direction and distance of your tracked devices, pinging a tracker when you don’t see it, or giving your tracked devices a custom name.

Also: 3 ways Bluetooth 7 upgrades your devices beyond lossless audio

Additionally, shorter-distance tracking requires an ultra-wideband chip inside your Android phone. Channel Sounding handles distance and direction at longer ranges, while UWB takes over for shorter ranges. Most premium Android phones with Bluetooth 6.0 also have UWB chips, but several of Google’s base-model phones lack a UWB chip.

Samsung’s base-model, A-series, and Z Flip-series phones also lack UWB, resulting in more phones that can’t access the Pixel Tag’s short-range precision finding capabilities.

With all the specs in mind, the Pixel Tag is the best option for users of recent premium flagship Android phones. Those without the latest Bluetooth connectivity will find that the Pixel Tag works like any other Bluetooth tracker, with basic functionality.

Also: These are the closest things to AirTags for Android users

The good thing is that a single Pixel Tag is $30, so it’s not much more expensive than a Tile Tag, and cheaper than a Chipolo Loop. Still, if your phone doesn’t support Bluetooth 6.0, you might be better off looking for a cheaper option until you’re ready to upgrade.

#3066. Google Wallet just turned your Android phone into a digital house key – how it works

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Home & Office > Smart Home > Home Security

Google is moving digital keys out of individual smart lock apps and into the Google Wallet.

Google is adding digital home keys to Google Wallet, letting users tap their phones to unlock compatible smart locks. The home key functionality, which will integrate with Google Home, will roll out this month.

Also: This tiny box gives your older tech smart home superpowers

Apple introduced Home Keys in 2021 with iOS 15, allowing users to store digital keys in the Apple Wallet. This lets you tap your iPhone or Apple Watch on the lock to unlock it. More recently, the addition of Express Mode to Apple Home lets users unlock smart locks without first unlocking their iPhones with Face ID.

Google’s digital keys use tap-to-unlock via NFC on smart locks. Like the Apple Home Key, you don’t need to unlock your phone to use your digital key, though you can change your verification settings as you wish.

Google’s announcement confirms that the company is embracing Aliro and UWB unlocking technologies as well. UWB unlocking for smart locks is supported on Google Pixel 10 Pro and newer models, as well as select UWB-enabled Samsung Galaxy phones. Aliro is a common standard for compatible smart locks and devices.

Before Google’s announcement, compatible smart locks could be controlled on Android through their accompanying app and Google Home. Smart lock companies also offered their own digital access methods, like NFC cards, Bluetooth, and geolocation.

One digital key will be created for each Google Home, so it can unlock all compatible smart locks in that home. You won’t need to search through digital keys in Google Wallet to find the one for your front door, back door, or bedroom door — just tap your phone and Google Home will recognize the lock as one in your smart home ecosystem.

At launch, Google Wallet will support digital keys for the Aqara U400 with UWB and NFC, and NFC on the Schlage Sense Pro and Nuki Keypad 2.

Google Wallet already supports digital car keys for compatible vehicles.

#3065. Midera (MFP) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Midera's new guidance reflects strong backlog and a fresh poultry acquisition.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Midera Food Processing (MFP -2.44%) completed its first full quarter as a standalone public company following its separation from Middleby. Management reported growth across all geographic regions and product categories, specifically highlighting the snack category as the fastest-growing segment due to the resolution of previously delayed shipments. The company emphasized its strategic shift toward Total Line Solutions, where it manages entire production lines rather than individual machines, to drive deeper customer relationships and recurring service revenue. Financial results were supported by a 26% increase in backlog and the completion of the Phoenix Innovations acquisition, which expanded the company's poultry processing capabilities.

This conference call is being webcast live within the Investors section of our website at Midera.com, and a downloadable version of today's presentation is available there as well. A webcast replay will be posted to our site following the call. You can also reach our Investor Relations team at [email protected]. These statements are subject to risks and uncertainties that may cause actual results to differ materially from those projected. We will also refer to certain non-GAAP financial measures.
