Historical reconciliations to the most directly comparable GAAP measures are available in today's earnings release and accompanying materials posted on our Investor Relations website. A reconciliation of forward-looking adjusted EBITDA to the most directly comparable GAAP financial measure, net earnings, is not available because the timing and magnitude of certain items cannot be reasonably estimated at this time without unreasonable effort. With that, I would like to turn the call over to Mark.

Mark Salman: Thank you, Rob, and good morning, everyone. Before I turn to the quarter, I want to recognize our people. This was our first full quarter as an independent public company, an important milestone for Midera and one our team should be proud of. We marked it with the move into our new home office in Rosemont, Illinois. It is a place that is ours, and it has helped us define who we are as Midera. But ultimately, the building does not make a company. People do. I want to thank our entire team for their commitment, energy and individual contributions. Our results-driven entrepreneurial culture is what makes Midera special, and it is what will drive our success going forward.

Last quarter, I told you I had never seen this team more energized or more aligned around where we are headed. This quarter, that energy and focus showed up in our results. I'm once again pleased the team exceeded our expectations and delivered a great quarter. Net sales of $228.9 million grew 13% with organic growth of 12%. Adjusted EBITDA of $42.9 million grew 45% and a margin of 18.7% expanded approximately 410 basis points relative to an estimated stand-alone adjusted EBITDA in the prior year. Orders grew approximately 13% versus a year ago to $229 million, and our backlog of $446 million is up 26% over that same period.

On today's call, I'll take you through some key highlights of the quarter against the 4 pillars we laid out at our Investor Day in May: total line solutions, market penetration, aftermarket and acquisitions. Then I'll hand it over to Amy for the financial review, and we will take your questions. Before I get into the pillars, I want to take a moment for those who are newer to our story to describe who Midera is and what we do. We believe we are the largest pure-play further food processing company. Midera operates at the highest value, most mission-critical parts of our customers' production lines where automation, differentiated technology, reliability and system integration matter most.

We design, integrate, commission and support total line solutions, complete production lines for protein, bakery and snack producers from preparation, portioning and thermal processing through slicing, packaging and facility automation. Our portfolio of more than 30 industry-leading brands, our installed base of more than 100,000 units and our approximately 2,900 team members serve customers on 6 continents. Our customers depend on our equipment every day to produce some of the most widely consumed foods in the world, and they choose Midera because we help them improve yield, efficiency, food safety and labor productivity. Every decision we make begins with the customer, and that discipline anchors how we operate as an independent public company.

With that, let me start with Total Line Solutions, which is the central pillar of our operating strategy. When we sell a line instead of a machine, we own the outcome. And increasingly, customers are moving towards having Midera integrate the complete line rather than integrating it themselves. Last quarter, I talked about our first major total line solution with newly acquired Frigomeccanica in the charcuterie category. This quarter, we won 1 of the largest charcuterie projects in Italy for a leading Italian producer. Winning a project of this scale in a category so central to Italian food culture says a lot about our position.

That customer is Salumificio Coati, which is building a new dry cured meat facility in Northern Italy. Coati selected Midera as its single technology partner for the further processing part, bringing together 4 of our brands and the line was conceived at our new innovation center. They chose Midera for the design of the line, which we anticipate will deliver a lower total cost of ownership and greater product uniformity and for our ability to manage the entire project from bringing together the right expertise to commissioning the line. In bakery, we won a large bun line in the U.S. for a leading U.S. grocery retailer. And in snack, we won a complete tortilla chip line in India.

These are just 3 examples, and they fit a pattern. Each 1 is a line where we own the outcome, and we create a customer relationship that lasts for the life of that line through the service that follows. We are winning projects across multiple categories and geographies, and our pipeline suggests this will continue. Our second pillar is market penetration, and the headline this quarter was that demand continued to be broad-based. On a year-to-date basis, we grew across all of our categories and across geographies in North America and even more significantly in the rest of the world. That is by design. Every company in our industry has its own angle.

Ours is agnostic to the end product and squarely focused on further processing, which is where we believe value is created to the customer. Our advantage is not tied to any 1 food category. It comes from innovative precision-engineered technology, deep process expertise and strong material know-how that we can apply whether a customer is producing bacon, chicken, bread or tortillas. Categories ebb and flow, so diversification across them gives us a greater resilience, allows us to capitalize on growth whenever it occurs and wherever and ultimately drives more consistent, durable growth over time. That includes the Middle East.

It has been a difficult period for the region, yet our customers there continue to invest in their operations, and we continue to win business with them. I had the pleasure of attending Gulfood Manufacturing, 1 of the world's leading food and beverage sourcing events that took place earlier this month in Dubai, where we showed customers from across the region, including those from growing markets like Turkey and Pakistan, what our innovation can do for their lines. These are markets with growing populations to feed, and we had an exceptional show that speaks to the shifting needs of today's food manufacturer. Taking a look at a few wins in the quarter. I will start with portable protein snacks.

ALKAR, a leader in continuous thermal processing systems for protein located in Wisconsin, had a particularly strong quarter as the consumption of portable protein continues to grow, driving demand for cooked ready-to-eat protein snacks. In poultry, our customers continue to invest to meet demand, reduce costs and make more value-added product. That is where our newest acquisition, Phoenix Innovations, fits, and I'll come back to that. In bakery, growth accelerated in the quarter. The world loves bread, and sourdough and long fermentation formats continue to be a bright spot. In snack, we told you last quarter that the equipment shipments delayed by a third-party vendor were a matter of timing.

As expected, these units shipped in the third quarter, contributing to snack becoming our fastest-growing category in the quarter. Beyond the timing impact, we continue to see strong demand from our customers in this space. Every time a customer reformulates or launches a new format, they need different equipment, and that's the moment they call us. And that is the real point. Customers are working hard to protect their margins. We don't just win because we sell a better machine. We win because we help them make more product with less waste and less labor and with the payback they can see.

Whether they serve the premium end of the market or the value end, that is a conversation every customer wants to have. Our third pillar is aftermarket, and it continues to be a consistent revenue stream, as we discussed at our Investor Day, represents a compelling opportunity for growth. Aftermarket sales grew approximately 16%, including double-digit organic growth and represented 42% of net sales in the quarter. Growth came across all 3 subcategories: parts, service and modernization projects, driven by higher demand, share capture and pricing actions that have been taken over the last year. Last quarter, I talked about the importance of delivering for our customers to ensure maximum uptime.

I'm proud of our team for continuing to support our customers every day. How we answer the call is what earns us the next order, and you can see it in these results. And the more we install, the stronger this gets. Every line and every machine we put in the field adds to the installed base our service team supports for the life of that equipment. During the quarter, we made further investments in our service organization, adding technicians to expand our customer support capabilities. We are also advancing our connected equipment solutions with a focus on predictive maintenance and increasing equipment uptime.

We see uptime and proactive service as key competitive advantages that deepen customer relationships, differentiate our offering and create opportunities for continued aftermarket growth. Our fourth pillar is acquisitions. And in October, we completed our first as a stand-alone company, Phoenix Innovations. Phoenix is based in Russellville, Arkansas, which is strategically located in the heart of many poultry processing plants. It designs and manufactures needle injection, marination, tumbling and thermal processing solutions with a focus on poultry and has an annual revenue run rate of approximately $25 million. That is exactly the kind of deal we described at our Investor Day, adding the capability where buying it is faster and more capital efficient than building it from scratch.

Phoenix expands our offerings of complete further processing poultry lines, supporting our total line solutions strategy and adds an installed base for our aftermarket team to serve. Phoenix is a founder-led business and its team lives and breathes poultry processing. The team will continue to lead the business and the Phoenix name stays on the door. When a founder chooses Midera as the home for what they spent years building, we take that seriously, and we are excited to extend our global reach to them. Acquisition timing is difficult to predict, but it's a perpetual process for us. Our pipeline remains active, and we are continuously looking for the next business that fits our strategy and our culture.

We underwrite every deal to target double-digit ROIC by year 3. And with net leverage of 1.2x, we have significant capacity to keep executing. Let me finish with profitability because it was a highlight of the quarter with adjusted EBITDA margin expanding to 18.7%, up 410 basis points relative to estimated stand-alone adjusted EBITDA in the prior year. This was also 170 basis points higher than the margin we reported in Q2 on an estimated stand-alone adjusted basis. This reflects a healthier backlog, the operating efficiencies our team are driving and lapping prior year tariff pressure. Longer term, we believe the opportunity to drive margin expansion using the Midera Operating System framework is compelling.

The biggest levers we are focused on are material costs and supply chain management, logistics, purchasing power, low-cost sourcing and make or buy decisions. And we continue to believe that we are in the early innings. Fundamental to our operating system is our culture. We empower our world-class team because we believe the best team wins. We continue to advance visual management across the organization using a consistent SQDC&G framework, that is safety, quality, delivery, cost and growth to drive faster, more informed decision-making and greater accountability. Combined with a lean toolkit and the aggressive deployment of technology across our manufacturing operations, these initiatives are improving productivity and execution.

Importantly, we see a clear path for these efforts to contribute to sustainable margin expansion over time. With that, I'll turn it over to Amy for a detailed financial review.

Amy Campbell: Thank you, Mark, and good morning, everyone. Today, I'll cover our third quarter results, followed by a review of our balance sheet as well as our outlook for the fiscal quarter. Before I begin, I want to reiterate Rob's comments about the presentation of results. Midera's separation from Middleby was completed on July 6 at the start of the third quarter. Therefore, our third quarter results are on a stand-alone public company basis. Our results for the first 6 months of 2026 and prior year results are presented on a carve-out basis.

Where we refer to the non-GAAP measure, estimated stand-alone adjusted EBITDA, that measure reflects management's view of profitability, fully burdened by our estimated stand-alone public company costs, which are not reflected in Middleby's historical segment reporting and are not fully captured in the carve-out financial statements on a like-for-like basis. I also want to point out to avoid any confusion that in the quarter, we revised the definition of acquisition-related adjustments in the calculation of adjusted EBITDA to include third-party transaction costs related to M&A transactions, which we believe to be outside core operating results. All materials filed today reflect this definition change for all periods.

This change in definition does not change estimated stand-alone adjusted EBITDA for historical periods as previously disclosed. With those administrative details out of the way, let's cover the quarter. Third quarter net sales grew 13% to $229 million. Organic net sales growth was 12%, which excludes the impact of acquisitions and foreign exchange rates. The impact of foreign exchange was negligible. Inorganic sales contributed 2% to top line growth, reflecting the contribution from our Frigomeccanica and Oka acquisitions prior to the anniversary of those deals closing in the third quarter of last year.

From an organic perspective, growth was driven by strong aftermarket parts and service, which grew across the installed base and higher equipment sales that were broad-based across categories, including the impact of the snack category shipments that were delayed from the second quarter. Geographically, we saw 30% growth outside the United States and Canada versus the prior year period, with particular strength in Europe. Investment priorities continue to vary by region. In Europe, customer spending is weighted toward automation that addresses labor constraints and improves energy efficiency. In the U.S., the emphasis is more on increasing yield and throughput.

Across both regions, customers remain disciplined in their capital allocation with spending focused on projects that offer a clear and relatively near-term payback. Aftermarket parts and service represented 42% of net sales in the quarter and 41% on a trailing 12-month basis as of the end of the third quarter. Aftermarket parts and service provide steady recurring revenue from a large installed base. And as Mark mentioned, we continue to invest to further accelerate growth. Adjusted EBITDA was $42.9 million.

A 45% increase in adjusted EBITDA relative to estimated stand-alone adjusted EBITDA in the prior year was driven primarily by higher sales of aftermarket parts and service, higher equipment sales, improved pricing and improved operating efficiencies, partially offset by the impact of cost inflation. Adjusted EBITDA margin was 18.7% compared to 14.6% in the prior year period on an estimated stand-alone adjusted basis. The 410 basis point year-over-year increase in margin percentage primarily reflects improved operating leverage on higher equipment and aftermarket sales, operating efficiencies and price actions, partially offset by cost inflation. Operating efficiencies benefited significantly in the quarter from a much healthier backlog than where we started the comparable quarter last year.

A strong backlog impacts how you run the business from commercial decisions to improved planning and manufacturing operations and is a significant part of the margin growth story this quarter. The third quarter has now largely lapped the prior year tariff pressure that weighed on margins. We did recognize a small amount of tariff refunds in the quarter, impacting margins by approximately 30 basis points. To address inflation, we continue to price contracts against expected cost, lock supplier contracts where we can on large projects. And at midyear, we took additional pricing actions on aftermarket parts. Now shifting to results on a year-to-date basis.

As a reminder, we believe it's important to evaluate Midera's performance over a number of quarters and not in a specific quarter, given the value of our equipment and the reality that shipments can pull forward or slip for any number of reasons, including customer needs. Therefore, we discourage drawing conclusions and trends from the results of any single quarter, but instead look at the business over time. And the last 9 months' results reflect a business that continues to be very healthy. Net sales were $699 million through the first 9 months of the year, an increase of 19% compared to the prior year period with organic net sales growth of 12%.

Higher year-to-date sales have been a result of strong demand across all categories as customers invest to drive returns in their businesses and meet changing consumer preferences. Year-to-date, estimated stand-alone adjusted EBITDA grew 32% to $118 million and margin expanded by approximately 170 basis points year-over-year to 16.9%. This performance was primarily driven by higher equipment and aftermarket sales, partially offset by inflationary costs. With 170 basis points of margin improvement year-to-date, we are tracking as expected toward the 2028 margin targets we laid out at our Investor Day in May. Orders in the quarter were $229 million, up approximately 13% from the prior year, including approximately 11% organic growth.

Backlog ended the quarter at $446 million, up approximately 26% year-over-year, all of which was organic. And backlog as of the end of the quarter gives us visibility to over 90% of our fourth quarter equipment sales assumed in the guidance we provided today. Book-to-bill was 1.0x in the quarter, consistent with the third quarter of last year. Book-to-bill was 1.1x for the trailing 12-month period through the third quarter. This is a reflection of continued strong broad-based demand and the willingness of our customers to invest where there is a quantifiable return. Free cash flow for the quarter was approximately $9 million, below our expectations, primarily reflecting the timing of certain receivable collections around quarter end.

Those receivables have since been collected, reinforcing our view that this was largely a timing issue rather than a change in the underlying cash generation of the business. We remain focused on disciplined working capital management and continue to expect annual free cash flow conversion above 50% of adjusted EBITDA when we transition to a full year of financial results on a reported stand-alone basis. We ended the quarter with cash of $49 million and total debt of $249 million for net debt of approximately $200 million.

Net leverage was 1.2x based on LTM estimated stand-alone adjusted EBITDA, and we ended the quarter with $829 million of liquidity, which includes cash and cash equivalents, along with $780 million of availability under the revolving credit facility. Our capital structure is deliberately simple. It was designed to support growth and our capital allocation priorities, which are unchanged from our Investor Day: first, organic reinvestment to protect and grow what we have; second, disciplined return-driven acquisitions; and third, we manage all of it within a net leverage framework of below 3.0x. Capital expenditures were $10.7 million for the first 9 months of 2026 compared to $35.2 million during the first 9 months of 2025.

Capital expenditures in the first 9 months of 2026 were primarily for upgrades of production equipment and manufacturing facilities to drive operating efficiencies. Capital expenditures for the prior year period included significant investments for our innovation center in Italy and the purchase of a previously leased building in Texas. During the third quarter, we repurchased 14,700 shares for approximately $600,000 under our $50 million share repurchase program. To date, we have repurchased approximately 59,000 shares for approximately $2.5 million and have $47.5 million of remaining authorization. Our share repurchase program is primarily intended to mitigate stockholder dilution from equity grants. Turning to our outlook.

Given our strong performance and including the expected contribution from Phoenix, we are updating our full year 2026 guidance to reflect an increase in the midpoint of expected ranges for net sales and estimated stand-alone adjusted EBITDA. At the midpoint, the revised guidance represents an increase of $13 million in net sales and $5 million in estimated stand-alone adjusted EBITDA versus our prior guidance. While there are puts and takes, the raise to the guide essentially passes on the organic beat in the quarter and adds our expectations for Phoenix, which will be a part of our portfolio for about 2 months of 2026. We continue to take a disciplined approach as to how we deliver guidance to investors.

For the full year 2026, we expect net sales in the range of $953 million to $973 million and estimated stand-alone adjusted EBITDA in the range of $168 million to $178 million. At the midpoint, that implies expected organic sales growth of 7% and estimated stand-alone adjusted EBITDA margin expansion of approximately 160 basis points versus 2025. Our guidance reflects the health of the equipment backlog, strong aftermarket parts and service growth and improved operating efficiencies. In lieu of an adjusted earnings per share estimate, we are providing additional modeling assumptions, including depreciation and amortization, stock-based compensation, interest expense and weighted average diluted shares outstanding. These are all detailed in our press release that was issued this morning.

The fourth quarter is typically our strongest for both net sales and adjusted EBITDA as customers focus on getting capital projects delivered before their fiscal year ends, and we anticipate the seasonality again this year. We also expect margin to improve sequentially on improving mix in the backlog, improved pricing, absorption of fixed costs on higher sales and realization of benefits from the Midera Operating System. Before I turn it back to Mark, I do want to call your attention to a fourth quarter fiscal calendar-related headwind that impacts organic sales growth versus the prior year. Fiscal 2025 included a 14th week in the fourth quarter under our 4-4-5 fiscal calendar, a situation that happens every 5 to 6 years.

This additional week in the prior year period creates a slightly more difficult year-over-year comparison as the duration of the prior year period was approximately 7% longer. With that, I'll turn it back to Mark.

Mark Salman: Thank you, Amy. Before we take questions, let me pull the key takeaways together. Our first full quarter as a stand-alone company delivered what we said it would. We delivered strong profitability with margin up 410 basis points on an estimated stand-alone adjusted basis. Demand is broad-based across our categories and geographies, reflected in strong order books and backlog as we look to 2027. We are not dependent on any 1 category or any 1 region, and that balance is a strength. That growth is structural, not cyclical. Rising protein consumption, dietary shifts, labor scarcity and food safety and security all make our equipment the preferred solutions for customers. This spending is need-based, not discretionary.

The margin story from here is largely in our control. It comes from innovation, growth, absorption, acquisitions maturing to our platform margins and the Midera Operating System powered by our people and the culture they have built. And we are playing offense. Phoenix is our first acquisition as a stand-alone company, and our pipeline remains active. In a fragmented $70 billion market, the acquirer of choice becomes the compounder of choice. We intend to be both, and we intend to keep earning that distinction. We are committed to generating a return on your time and on your investment. With that, operator, please open the line for questions.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] Our first question comes from Justin Ages with CJS Securities.

Justin Ages: Pretty good results. I wanted to ask about total line solutions. Can you give us any more color? I know you called out 3 wins, but can you give us a sense of what percentage they are of orders or what percentage they are of equipment sales?

Mark Salman: Yes, Justin. So we do not share the specifics on Total Line Solutions. However, what I can share with you is it continues to be a strong growth driver of our revenue. I can give you some data points. I mentioned I was in Dubai earlier this month. We closed several total line solutions in the bread category. We've closed -- we talked about Coati in the earnings release on the charcuterie. We -- across all 3 end products in snacks, we continue to see a lot of demand on corn chips full line solutions. But it is definitely 1 growth driver that is proving to be a winner for us.

Justin Ages: Okay. And then switching to guidance and the CapEx guidance. Based on my math, it seems like it's implying a pretty big step-up in 4Q CapEx to get in that 2% to 2.5% range. Can you talk about what you guys are investing in? Is it further the innovation centers? Or is it something else?

Amy Campbell: Yes. No, Justin, just to clarify, we didn't provide CapEx guidance for the full year. The 2% to 2.5% of sales, I'd really say is over time, what we expect CapEx to be. That said, we do expect CapEx to increase in the fourth quarter. And I'll turn it over to Mark Bowie, our COO, to talk about where we're making those investments in the fourth quarter.

Mark Bowie: Justin, from a CapEx perspective, I mean, obviously, we want to make the right investments and be super smart with how we deploy that incredibly impactful resource for us. And where we've really tried to do that in a meaningful way is looking at our operations and making investments around technology that support our ability to serve our customers and compete on the cost front in a meaningful way. So we've got a lot of investments that are in flight today that will improve our manufacturing operations from a cost perspective. And really, we'll see that on the productivity front.

And that's 1 of the multiple pillars that we have that gives us confidence around our margin expansion story going forward. So we do believe Q4 will be strong in where those investments lie, and we will continue to reap rewards for those investments for years to come.

Operator: Our next question comes from Mig Dobre with Baird.

Peter Kalemkerian: This is Peter Kalemkerian on for Mig this morning. I want to start with 1 on margin. Implied fourth quarter margin is in, call it, just shy of 21%. How much of that step-up reflects structural operating improvements or a catch-up on price cost versus seasonal volume or shipment mix? And is the margin -- let's -- there is some normal seasonality from 4Q to first quarter. But is the margin in that 20-ish percent range a reasonable run rate to think about into the start of next year? Any color on that would be appreciated.

Amy Campbell: No. Thanks, Pete. I'll take that. So if you look at that step-up of margin implied at the midpoint, it's about 200 bps from the third quarter, certainly not unprecedented. In fact, it's half of the step-up in margin accretion we had from the third quarter to the fourth quarter last year, where we saw a 400 bps margin improvement. So we do tend to see that fourth quarter historically have the highest EBITDA margin percent of the quarters. It does come from -- and I'm going to talk about from a sequential basis, it certainly comes from better fixed cost leverage on higher sales. Sales are up 15% implied at the midpoint versus the third quarter.

The backlog does continue to get healthier from a price/cost perspective, which allows us to run our plants much more efficiently. And then we do -- we have started and further expect to see the benefits from the Midera Operating System and in fact, some of these CapEx projects that we were spending in the third quarter. So it is both, I would say, fixed cost leverage on higher cost, the highest cost with the fourth quarter being our highest sales quarter and then operating leverage, healthier backlog coming through, which is certainly sustainable as we move into 2027. I'm not going to provide 2027 guidance, certainly not going to provide quarterly guidance at this time into 2027.

That said, I would expect margins to step back in the first quarter from what we deliver in the fourth quarter. That's seasonally what we see happen. I wouldn't expect that not to be the case for 2027. And I would expect us for the full year 2027 to continue on the trajectory towards the 2028 margin targets we laid out back in May.

Peter Kalemkerian: Got it. I guess on pricing, the announced price increase, how has customer acceptance been to these price increases? And we're halfway through the fourth quarter now. Are you seeing any impact on order conversion or competitive win rates? Anything to call out there? And then second piece of the question, is there a way to quantify that cost inflation headwind that we saw this quarter? And when do you expect to achieve full price/cost neutrality given the timing of shipments out of backlog? Is that something that's in the 4Q guide? Or is that a first half of '27 story?

Mark Salman: All right. I'll take a pass at the first part of your question. We are in the business to deliver solutions that makes money to our customers. And therefore, when the ROI is there, the pricing becomes a secondary discussion. So it is true. We did take a pricing adjustment on aftermarket to mitigate some of the inflation pressure that we see. But our equipments are bespoke. We cost each line at that time with the data that we have, and we're able to mitigate some of the inflation by really buying forward some of our key material on these lines.

But at the end of the day, you should look at our edge, the innovation edge is that we allow our customers to produce great food in an affordable fashion. And therefore, pricing becomes a secondary discussion.

Amy Campbell: And on the second half of that question, Pete, which I think was when do we reach full cost price neutrality. What I would say there is if you think back a year ago in the second half of 2025, where we had tariff pressures on margins that came from actually really several different operational commercial issues. We believe as we entered the second half of 2026 that, that -- those headwinds that drove margin pressure in the backlog are behind us at this point. So we're now addressing inflation, pricing projects with known inflation, things have settled down certainly from where we were a year ago this time. That said, inflation certainly continues.

And so we will continue to track inflation to take price increases as necessary. I don't see in the midterm that we're going to stop having to stay on top of inflationary pressures, be they from fuel costs, be they from materials cost, whatnot. That's going to be a continuing focus of the teams.

Operator: Our next question comes from Ian Zaffino with Oppenheimer.

Ian Zaffino: Would you be able to give us the -- either for the past quarter or maybe in the guide or maybe how that's changing price versus volume? So what will be that split for last quarter and then in the guide or any acceleration in pricing? Or how do we think about that going forward?

Amy Campbell: Yes. Ian, we don't break out price versus volume. It's, in fact, very difficult for us to do given the bespoke nature, the one-off nature of our equipment sales specifically. So we don't break that out. We have disclosed that midyear, we took -- it differed by brand, but on the average, about a mid-single-digit price increase on parts. Now certainly, a lot of that was to offset the inflationary headwinds that we see out there. So I think that math is pretty easy to do. But outside of that, every one of these projects is priced individually. They tend to be very unique projects.

And so breaking out price volume is just a very difficult thing to do, and we don't have that data to disclose certainly at this time.

Ian Zaffino: Okay. And then maybe as far as the margin improvement, would you be able to maybe bucket it as far as how much is it mix aftermarket? How much would it be volumes? And how much is it kind of recovering price versus cost?

#3064. Roku drops smart home products to focus on streaming – what that means for your devices

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Roku is winding down its smart home business following its sale to Fox. Here's what to know.

Roku is stepping back from smart home gear.

In an exclusive first reported by freelance journalist Janko Roettgers via his newsletter, Lowpass, the streaming device maker confirmed it won’t be making any additional smart home products going forward, as its existing home devices run out of stock.

“We’re sharpening our focus on Roku’s core mission: being the top streaming platform,” a Roku spokesperson told Roettgers via email. “As part of that, we plan to wind down sales of smart home hardware and will provide continued support and services for Roku Smart Home products.”

Also: Worried about Fox buying Roku? Here are three popular concerns – and why I’m optimistic

Roku was recently acquired by Fox, with the formal sale closing on Nov. 6.

Roku, primarily known for its streaming stick and TV devices that rival competitors like Amazon’s Fire lineup, expanded into the smart home space in 2022 with a series of affordable home security cameras, smart plugs, and lights, developed with white-labeled hardware from Waze. Roku launched its own product lineup with proprietary hardware in 2025.

Also: Roku is taking away a fan-favorite screensaver – but you have alternatives

In 2024, the company launched TV features connected to its smart home products, including a view that let users cycle through their live camera feeds on their TV and a picture-in-picture feature that pins a feed to your screen while users have another app open. It’s unclear how this change will impact support for these cameras and associated features for those who already own them, but ZDNET has reached out to Roku for comment.

Roettgers said in his newsletter that, based on Roku’s own website, the number of products available for purchase appears to have dwindled. Currently, all but two of Roku’s smart home gear are listed as out of stock.

At other retailers like Home Depot, Amazon, and Walmart, many Roku listings have been removed or marked for clearance, while some retailers are only selling refurbished items.

It’s likely, as Roettgers identified in a previous newsletter, that Fox did not see long-term value in smart home gear for Roku, a fact certainly exacerbated by AI-induced hardware cost increases that have hit nearly every tech manufacturer, including Apple.

Also: Why your RAM options cost 4X more now than last year – even legacy tech prices aren’t immune

The closure of the sale of Roku to Fox also emphasizes the return to streaming as the company’s main priority. Roettgers said the reason for that has been publicly noted in Roku’s financial disclosures, including last week’s 10-Q, where the brand clearly emphasized that smart home gear does not contribute to Roku’s streaming hours or revenue.

#3063. John Mulaney’s SNL Sister Eldercare Ad Is an Instant, Painful Classic

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

How long did it take you to text it to your sibling group chat?

Did SNL just add another legendary fake commercial to the show’s hall of fame? On Saturday night, host John Mulaney and the cast delivered a winning pretaped parody commercial that hit a nerve in more than a few households.

In the ad, Mulaney and others fret about their aging parents. Nursing homes don’t appeal, yet in-home care would cost too much. Fortunately, Mulaney has heard about Sister, “a live-in, 24/7 eldercare provider that is completely free, and also your sister.”

“I love my mom more than anything,” says another adult son, played by Andrew Dismukes. “That doesn’t mean I want to help her in the bathroom. Sister doesn’t either. But she will, whereas I won’t. That’s the Sister difference!”

Jane Wickline plays a frantic sister who drops everything, quits her job, breaks her lease, and moves halfway across the country to take care of her elderly dad (Tommy Brennan, ironically one of the youngest cast members).

Mulaney says he just had to text his sister, “Dad fell,” and voilà, she instantly appeared.

Mikey Day plays a doctor who, as the author of the astutely named book Not It! A Son’s Guide to Elder Care, explains how it works.

“Years of internalized sexism warps Sister’s brain into thinking caretaking is her responsibility, and somehow, not yours,” Day says. “Next, your text arrives, instantly activating her. And that’s it! You’re done for life! See you at the funeral!”

Anyone who’s ever had to care for elderly parents can relate to Sister’s duties: Making those torturous, endless calls to doctors, insurance companies and pharmacists, all while screaming, “Speak to human!” at unhelpful phone trees.

Meanwhile, Kenan Thompson rejoices that he’s still in the will despite doing nothing, and Mulaney and Brennan bond over griping about Sister’s diet restrictions. Mulaney urges viewers to sign up now for the free addition of Sister’s Husband, who just doesn’t know why this burden has to fall on his (defensive) wife.

A quickly flashed line at the end of the ad notes, “Offer void if Sister has a good therapist,” who’d presumably tell her to insist her brothers do their share.

It wasn’t just a fictional sketch to some SNL viewers on Reddit.

“This isn’t funny, this is life for a lot of women,” wrote one person.

“I watched this skit earlier today with my husband, and I started crying,” said another. “It’s exactly the situation I’m in while my brother travels the world.”

The point of the ad is that the duties fell on one very human family member. But tech companies are increasingly eyeing that responsibility as an opportunity for AI or robotic help — if that’s something you and your family are willing to try.

One device we’ve seen is a companion robot, ElliQ, that’s meant to live with elderly family members and serve as a digital assistant, social companion and health advocate. (We tried it out with some of our parents and grandparents.) And a 2025 University of Michigan survey found that older adults often find AI smart home devices and voice assistants useful in helping them age in place. CNET also has a roundup of the most reliable smart tech to help people age in place.

No robot or AI can replace the personal touch and self-sacrificial dedication of Sister. I haven’t replayed an SNL parody commercial this many times since the now-classic 2017 ad for Alexa Echo Silver: For the Greatest Generation.

And yes, I texted the Sister ad to my two sisters (but not my brothers).

#3060. ‘We need more reviewers’: Finding Linux bugs is easy now – fixing them is another story

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Some Linux maintainers are quitting under the crushing strain of AI bug reports, while others see signs for hope.

Recently, Microsoft’s FORGE Lab reported that its AI scanning system, MDASH, turned up 59 upstream Linux kernel bug reports, including one flaw at least 21 years old. That’s less impressive than it sounds. For 2026, through Nov. 2, the Linux Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) team reported an average of 27 CVEs a day.

Why so many? Easy: in Linux, any bug can be a security bug. As Linux Torvalds told me in 2024, “Bugs will happen, and anything can be a security bug if somebody is clever enough to just figure out how to abuse it.” Besides, since Linux runs everything from smartphones to refrigerators to supercomputers, what may be a serious bug in one device may not even appear at all on another.

It’s not just Linux, though. In the latest Windows Patch Tuesday security release, Microsoft reported 726 CVEs. The vast majority of these bug reports are coming from AI programmers. Finding bugs on anything is no longer the hard part. But reviewing and fixing them is, and both Microsoft developers and kernel maintainers are struggling to keep up.

Also: Microsoft fixes over 1,000 Windows flaws – and one is being exploited

As the FORGE Lab said, “Finding bugs and fixing them are drastically out of balance.” Turning its findings into reports took more than four person-months because “human effort [is] the bottleneck.”

That’s hurting the overworked maintainers. On Nov. 10, an ARM engineer and Linux kernel maintainer Lorenzo Stoakes gave up reviewing code. He’d been a reviewer for the memory-management core, misc, reclaim, and Rust-related sections. Stoakes, a kernel contributor since 2014,  wrote, “Given the current throughput in the kernel resulting from AI-generated series, I unfortunately lack the bandwidth to generally be able to offer review except in those areas I maintain.”

Stoakes added, “Of course the AI wave has been horrible, and is getting significantly worse. At first it was once in a while that I’d see slop. Then it was at least once a week. Then every few days. Nowadays it’s pretty much half of what I see, if not more.”

Also: Filing bugs for open-source apps is a huge help for devs – and easier than you think

He’s not alone. As Greg Kroah-Hartman, the Linux kernel stable maintainer, said in a Q&A session at Open Source Summit Europe, “We don’t have enough people to review them, the onslaught of the LLM-generated patches. We need more reviewers. We don’t have enough. All of the maintainers are burnt out, and we have been for ten years.”

It’s not all doom and gloom, though. Linux Torvalds, Linux’s creator, said in a recent Linux Kernel Mailing List (LKML) message that much of the new code in the Linux 7.4 rc 2 “was driven by various AI fixes.”

He continued, “that on the bpf [Berkeley Packet Filter]- side at least the fixes are now coming in faster than the new reports, and that sounds lovely if true. I think most other areas haven’t reached that point yet, but it’s at least a sign that we _may_ be starting to see the tide starting to turn. Don’t hold your breath, but maybe cross your fingers we’ll be getting there in the not entirely distant future.”

We can but hope. In an interview, Kroah-Hartman isn’t so optimistic. “We are getting closer, yes, but not quite there yet.”  He’s not even willing to give a guesstimate of when human-approved AI fixes will catch up with and overcome AI bug reports.

Also: I locked down my OpenClaw agent with Claude Code – then dared it to escape

Daniel Steinberg, the creator of the open-source cURL project, is also cautiously optimistic. Steinberg, who’s been especially critical of AI slop bug reports, told me in an interview that he now believes “we manage the flood pretty well so far, even if it goes a little up and down in periods depending exactly on who sends us a new set of findings this particular week.”

Still, while AI bugs remain a major headache for now, AI bug fixes, along with the work of thousands of maintainers, may finally be starting to stem the AI bug flood. I still foresee long days and nights of work ahead.

I also expect we’ll see more serious security breaches. In November alone, we saw a serious Linux TCP networking security hole revealed; the nasty Alpine Linux OpenSSH flaw; Alpine’s GitLab near-miss; and the wide-open PHP2Shell security problem, which many groups still haven’t patched.

#3059. Google Pixel Tag Hands-On: Android Fans Get Their Own AirTag-Style Tracker

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Google's tracker has a few features we'd like to see Apple adopt.

If a company releases a product in an already established market, is it worth the effort? If you think I’m talking about Apple and Google, you’d be right – but this isn’t the iPhone Duo muscling into the folding phone fray. This time, the roles are reversed: Google has released the Pixel Tag, a small Bluetooth tracker that it hopes will be the Android ecosystem’s answer to Apple’s near-ubiquitous AirTag.

The Pixel Tag is available now for $30 each or $100 in a pack of four. It works with Android phones and uses Google’s Find Hub technology for tracking over distances beyond Bluetooth range. If you use an Android phone and have wanted the capability to track things such as keys, bags, bikes, vehicles and other indispensable items, and you want the tech to come from the company that designed the system, the Pixel Tag is an excellent choice.

It isn’t the first Android-compatible tracker. Motorola introduced its Moto Tag 2 earlier this year, and Tile has been the de facto AirTag alternative for several years. There’s also now a growing ecosystem of other items that tap into Apple’s Find My and Android’s Find Hub networks, ranging from slim credit-card-sized devices like the Rolling Square AirCard Pro and Peak Design’s Beacon Finder Card, to novel approaches like Falcam’s TagBatt, a battery for some Sony and Canon mirrorless cameras that integrates Apple Find My tracking.

Google jumping into this more crowded field tells me the company thinks there’s profit to be made by manufacturing its own hardware and software. It’s also investing in the infrastructure it’s already built out, and not leaving the hardware side to a constellation of other vendors.

Trackers like the Pixel Tag and AirTag can be a surprisingly deflating purchase: You pair them with your phone, put them into something you don’t want to lose track of – then forget about them. They’re usually not tactile the way a phone, watch or laptop is each day. And their value doesn’t kick into action until you think an item has gone missing.

After slinging AirTags into bags and dangling them off keychains, one thing I really appreciate about the Pixel Tag is its thinness. Apple chose a small, round footprint, even keeping the exact design for the second-generation AirTags. Google instead opted for a longer lozenge shape, at 1.8 inches (46.1mm), that is about two-thirds the height of the AirTag at 0.2 inch (5.4mm).

Google sent a Bellroy leather keychain as a sample accessory for review, and paired with the Pixel Tag, the two are a fine size for a pocket or clipped to an inside bag pocket. I thought the longer design would get in the way, but it’s not bad at all.

The Pixel Tag uses a CR2032 coin-sized battery that should last about a year (the same as the AirTag). It also has an IP67 rating, which is durable in 1 meter of water for up to 30 minutes.

Another departure from the AirTag is a physical button, making the Pixel Tag even more tactile. When you’re using Find Hub on your phone to locate it by sound, press once to stop the chirps it makes. Or, if you have the tag in hand (on a keychain, for example) and need to find your phone, press twice to ring the phone – it makes a pleasant sing-songy chime that gets louder and more intense as it continues, so I’m confident it’ll be easy to locate, even among couch cushions.

Speaking of the chimes, credit to the Google sound designers who came up with the Pixel Tag’s tune. It has three levels of loudness you can set, and seems plenty audible enough when you’re spelunking the living room for it. I measured it at 80 decibels, which when compared to the second-generation AirTag volume, is 7 less than the 87 decibels of Apple’s tracker.

One more nice touch compared to the AirTag: the Find Hub app shows the tag’s battery status. If that gets to Low or Very Low, the app sends you notifications every two weeks until the battery is replaced. After Apple showed battery statuses on AirTags in early versions of the Find My app, the company changed the Find My app so it only indicates battery when it’s low and needs to be replaced.

The best feature of either tracker is the ability to locate its exact location – not which building or room it’s in, but to tell if the item fell behind the couch or was accidentally dropped in the driveway. (Yes, I’m making up these examples from personal experience.)

Precision Finding uses a combination of Bluetooth 6.0 (via a feature called Channel Sounding) and the ultra-wideband chips inside the tag and the phone to directionally find the tracker when it’s within Bluetooth range. You hold the phone upright, perpendicular to the ground for the best connection. Then you wander your space, watching the indicator change as you get closer to the tag.

On the Pixel Tag, that indication is a wobbly circle shape that fills in as you get closer; when you’re on top of the tracker, the shape is fully filled. The Find Hub app also uses the camera and UWB chip to include an estimated distance in feet and inches (or meters and centimeters). When you’re close enough, the tracking shape becomes a directional arrow to point you the right way. UWB is compatible with the Pixel 8 Pro, Pixel 8 Fold and newer Pixel phones.

In my testing, the Find Nearby feature performed fairly well. Find Hub using a Pixel 11 Pro XL connected from within about 25 feet, including on multiple levels of a house when I was above or below it.

Perhaps because I was raised on science-fiction devices like the trackers in Aliens, though, I expected more consistent readings. There were times when both I and the tag remained stationary. The distance estimates would fluctuate by several feet.

Since I’ve had this review unit for only a few days, I haven’t yet had a chance to send it off with someone else and see if I can track it remotely using the Find Hub network. When nearby Android devices detect the Pixel Tag’s presence, they should securely and privately relay the tracker’s location to Google’s servers. (Apple’s Find My network operates the same way.) I’ll update this article once I’ve taken the tag on such an adventure.

Tracking all your stuff is invaluable – I learned this first-hand earlier this year when I left a small bag containing my passport in a hotel room, and was able to convince the hotel that the bag was still on the premises. But unfortunately, smart tags are being used to track people without their knowledge.

Google is taking the same approach as Apple to help thwart this type of tracking. If a tag is separated from the phone it’s paired with (or the phone of someone else you’ve chosen to share the tag location with), and the tag is moved, its chime activates.

The idea is that you’ll hear an unfamiliar chirp and investigate. It has an NFC chip that displays its information when you tap it using the NFC built into a phone.

#3058. Every Gigawatt of GE Vernova's HA Turbines Is Expected to Generate $500 Million in Services. Here's Why That Outlasts the Boom.

Record gas turbine orders are rapidly expanding GE Vernova's installed base, locking in decades of high-margin, recurring service revenue.

Data centers and utilities are scrambling for power, and GE Vernova (GEV +2.14%) has seen incredibly strong demand for its high-efficiency, air-cooled, heavy-duty (HA) gas turbines. The company is experiencing unprecedented growth as technology companies, data center developers, and utilities seek to secure power amid rising electricity demand.

GE Vernova's large-scale HA gas turbines provide multiple gigawatts of behind-the-meter power, a capability that has become increasingly important as utilities and hyperscalers seek to increase capacity without driving up electricity prices.

The company is seeing strong product sales and slot reservation agreements extending to 2032, highlighting the robust demand for gas turbines. But that's not all: For every gigawatt of HA turbines, GE Vernova expects to generate roughly $500 million in high-margin service revenue. Here's why that's the real story for GE Vernova that outlasts this historic equipment boom.

During its third-quarter earnings call, GE Vernova CEO Scott Strazik said we are in the early stages of an "electricity investment supercycle," driven by robust demand from data centers and the electrification of the power grid, with utilities scrambling to add power capacity. All these forces have been a powerful tailwind for GE Vernova's stock, which is up 515% since its 2024 spinoff from General Electric (now GE Aerospace).

In the third quarter, GE Vernova's remaining performance obligations (RPO) reached nearly $197 billion, a 45% increase from one year ago. This backlog is driven by strong growth in equipment sales, which grew 92% from last year to $104 billion, while its services backlog increased 14% to almost $93 billion.

Equipment sales include everything from heavy-duty HA gas turbines to aeroderivative turbines, transformers, switchgear, and wind turbines. Over the next five years, GE Vernova expects to recognize 97% of its equipment RPO.

That said, GE Vernova has a massive installed base that powers up to 25% of the world's electricity, providing a major source of services revenue for routine maintenance, upgrades, and plant life extensions. For every gigawatt of HA gas turbines installed, Strazik expects GE Vernova to earn $500 million in service revenue.

While equipment provides a boost to earnings over the next few years, the services revenue attached to that equipment will continue for decades. Over the next five years, GE Vernova expects to collect 54% of its services revenue, and 91% within 15 years.

GE Vernova has seen significant volatility as AI stocks face a big test, with investors questioning the sustainability of the AI build-out amid recent election results and pushback from residents around data center developments. That said, Strazik noted that roughly 20% of GE Vernova's power sales are from data centers, with the remainder coming from conventional customers like utilities.

GE Vernova continues to see a historic boom in demand for its power equipment and has slot reservation agreements in place over the next five years, which should boost services revenue over the next couple of decades. This makes GE Vernova a solid long-term stock to invest in the ongoing power boom.

#3057. I checked Gemini’s new Memory summary to see what it knew about me – how to see and edit yours

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

A new option called Memory summary lets you see and control the things that Gemini AI knows about you.

Like any AI, Google Gemini wants to remember things about you. The purported reason is to help tailor and personalize your conversations. But remember that your personal details may also wind up training the AI or even being reviewed by actual humans. With that in mind, you might want to find out just what Gemini knows about you. And now you can.

Also: I tried Claude Sheets on 3 tasks – and it saved me hours of work

With a new option called Memory summary, you’re able to view the details that Gemini has gathered about you over time. These may be tidbits from your conversations or things that you directly told the AI. Even better, you can add or remove any details just by editing the memory or issuing your request directly to Gemini.

This new capability is available in Gemini across the board, so you can access it at the Gemini website, in the mobile iOS and Android apps, and in the Windows and Mac desktop apps.

Launch Gemini via the web or in one of the mobile or desktop apps. In the left pane displaying your previous chats, select the Settings icon at the bottom. At the Settings screen, select Personal Intelligence and then click or tap Memory summary. If the option is grayed out, it means the Memory feature is turned off. To proceed, turn it back on. You can always turn if off again afterward if you wish.

You’ll then see the individual details by category. My summary arranged the information across such categories as Essentials, Business & Career, Reading & Interests, and Culinary Preferences. Go down the list to see the individual items in each category. To view a recent history, tap the three dot-icon at the top and select Memory history. This shows you the latest changes and updates to Gemini’s memory.

Also: Stop sharing your passwords with AI agents

What if Gemini’s memory includes details that are too personal or just incorrect? No problem. You can alter the AI’s memories of you. At the website or in one of the desktop apps, click the pencil icon at the top. Now you’re able to directly edit the text to add, remove, or revise specific details. After you’ve made your changes, just click Save.

For example, my summary said that I lived in Madison County. I have no idea where Gemini got that notion, as I live in New York. Here, I revised the text and saved the changes, which then synced across the Gemini website and apps.

The mobile apps have no direct editing capability. But there’s another method that works both on mobile and on the desktop. Just tell Gemini what change you want to make. At the prompt, type and speak your request, and the AI will carry it out for you.

As an example, my summary said that I run a business called Batter Up selling collectible baseball cards. That’s not at all true. I had once referred to such a store only to test Gemini’s image creation skills to design a logo for a baseball card seller. Here, I simply told Gemini that I don’t run a business called Batter Up and asked it to remove that item from its memory. Poof, that detail quickly disappeared.

#3056. Five iOS 27 Toggles That Make Your iPhone Easier to Read and More Private

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Tech > Services & Software > Operating Systems

Whether it’s a new iPhone or an updated one, these five iOS 27 settings are worth checking before you settle in.

The iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo ship with iOS 27’s default settings, and so does any older iPhone that updated this fall. Those defaults include a strong Liquid Glass effect, automatic subtitles on videos and a Siri that saves and syncs your conversations.

They’re easy to change once you know where to look. Here are five settings worth adjusting, whether you’re setting up a new phone or finally getting around to it on your current one.

Read more: Win a New Apple Watch in CNET Big Guessing Game Contest

Apple introduced Liquid Glass with iOS 26, giving menus, buttons, notifications and other interface elements a translucent appearance. Not everyone was a fan of the new design, and with iOS 27, you now get more control over exactly how transparent the interface looks.

Go to Settings > Appearance > Liquid Glass. Drag the slider to the right to add more tint and opacity, making buttons and text easier to distinguish from whatever is behind them. Moving it left makes the interface more transparent.

If the most opaque setting still isn’t enough, go to Settings > Accessibility > Display & Text Size and turn on Reduce Transparency. This makes translucent backgrounds more solid across iOS, although it overrides the regular Liquid Glass appearance controls.

More tint makes Liquid Glass easier to read.

The new Siri AI works similarly t ChatGPT or Claude in iOS 27. It now comes complete with a dedicated app where you can revisit previous conversations. Those chats sync through iCloud so you can start a conversation on your iPhone and continue it on another Apple device, such as your Mac.

By default, iOS 27 keeps those conversations forever, but there is a way to automatically get rid of older conversations if you don’t want them piling up.

If you don’t need a permanent archive of everything you ask Siri, go to Settings > Siri > Keep Conversations and choose 30 Days or 1 Year. Selecting either option permanently deletes conversations beyond that timeframe.

Siri keeps your conversations forever unless you choose a shorter limit.

While you’re there, tap Opens To and select A New Conversation if you want the Siri app to open with a blank chat instead of showing your recent conversations every time.

Siri AI requires an iPhone 15 Pro or 15 Pro Max, iPhone Air or an iPhone 16 or later.

iOS 27 puts a new Write with Siri button above the keyboard in apps including Messages, Mail and Notes. You can ask Siri AI to draft something from scratch, proofread what you’ve written or rewrite it in a different tone.

The thing is, I’m not a big fan of the AI writing tools, so I don’t use them at all.

Screen Time lets you completely disable Siri’s writing tools.

This disables access to the writing tools across your iPhone, rather than simply hiding the keyboard button, so only do this if you don’t use Apple’s AI writing tools at all. You can return to the same menu and choose Allow if you want them back. Apple documents the restriction under its Apple Intelligence Screen Time controls.

Introduced back in iOS 17, Siri can now wake up when you simply say “Siri” instead of “Hey Siri.” The one-word command is convenient, but it also makes accidental activations more likely whenever someone says Siri’s name in a conversation or a video they’re watching online.

Siri goes absolutely bonkers whenever I’m in work meetings about Apple features.

To disable the feature, go to Settings > Siri > Talk to Siri. Choose “Hey Siri” instead of “Siri.”

Requiring “Hey Siri” can help prevent accidental activations.

You’ll still be able to bring up Siri with your voice, but the extra word makes it less likely to wake up when you aren’t talking to it directly.

This isn’t exclusive to iOS 27, but it’s been annoying me more recently, so thought I would throw it in here, especially with Siri AI being the prominent feature on this update.

iOS 27 now automatically shows subtitles on videos in Photos, Safari and other apps that use Apple’s video player. I don’t mind captions when I need them, but they can take up too much of the video and distract me from whatever I’m watching.

They don’t appear randomly though. By default, iOS can turn them on when the video is in another language, when your iPhone is muted or when you skip back.

Whenever subtitles appear in Apple’s video player, you can tap the video to show the playback controls, tap the More Controls button, select Subtitles and choose Off.

If iOS keeps turning them on because it thinks the video is in another language, go to Settings > Accessibility > Subtitles & Captioning. Under Automatic Subtitles, turn off When Languages Don’t Match.

The same menu also has switches for Show When Muted and Show on Skip Back, so you can disable those behaviors individually without turning off every automatic subtitle feature.

You can also disable each automatic subtitle trigger individually.

Some apps and websites use their own video players, so you may need to find a separate CC or subtitles button instead.

For more on iOS 27, check out this article on the features it brings to your iPhone and how Siri AI helped one of my colleagues avoid eating diarrhea lettuce.
