#3055. AECOM (ACM) Q4 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Record backlog and record margins close fiscal 2026 amid legacy project drag.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

AECOM (ACM +11.08%) reported record backlog and margin expansion to conclude its 2026 fiscal year, supported by high win rates and accelerating growth in its design and advisory businesses. Management reported that the company is successfully navigating legacy liabilities while shifting its portfolio toward higher-margin, lower-risk professional services. The company stated that technology and AI investments are already yielding operational efficiencies and expanding the addressable market through new client wins. Guidance for fiscal 2027 anticipates continued top-line growth and record margins as the company capitalizes on global infrastructure investment cycles and favorable funding environments.

Operator: Hello, everyone. Thank you for joining us, and welcome to AECOM's Fourth Quarter 2026 Earnings Conference Call. [Operator Instructions] I will now hand the conference over to Will Gabrielski, Senior Vice President of Finance and Investor Relations. You may begin.

Will Gabrielski: Thank you, operator. I would like to direct your attention to the safe harbor statement on Page 1 of today's presentation. Today's discussion contains forward-looking statements about future business and financial expectations. Actual results may differ significantly from those projected in today's forward-looking statements due to various risks and uncertainties, including the risks described in our periodic reports filed with the SEC. Except as required by law, we undertake no obligation to update our forward-looking statements. We use certain non-GAAP financial measures in our presentation. The appropriate GAAP reconciliations are incorporated into our materials, which are posted to our website. Growth rates are presented on a year-over-year basis unless otherwise noted.

Any references to segment margins or segment adjusted operating margins will reflect the performance for the Americas and International segments. When discussing revenue and revenue growth, we will refer to net service revenue, or NSR, which is defined as revenue excluding pass-through revenue. NSR growth rates are presented on a constant currency basis, unless otherwise noted. Today's remarks will focus on continuing operations. Also, as a reminder, for the fiscal fourth quarter and the full year, our business was impacted by fewer workdays compared to the prior year's period. Accordingly, our discussion of NSR growth rates will adjust for this impact unless otherwise noted.

On today's call, Troy Rudd, our Chief Executive Officer, will review key developments and accomplishments this quarter as well as our outlook for the business. Lara Poloni, our President, will discuss key trends across our markets; and Gaurav Kapoor, our Chief Financial and Operations Officer, will review our financial performance and outlook in greater detail. We will conclude with a question-and-answer session. With that, I will turn the call over to Troy. Troy?

W. Rudd: Thanks, Will, and thank you all for joining us today to review our financial results and key strategic priorities. We had several accomplishments in fiscal 2026 that give us confidence in the business, highlighted by record wins, backlog and fourth quarter margins. Before discussing our performance in greater detail, I want to provide an update on the two construction management projects we discussed last quarter. I'm pleased to report these projects are on track with the delivery time lines and budgets communicated previously, including having achieved substantial completion on the first phase of one project in the first quarter of fiscal 2027. We expect delivery of the second project near the end of the second fiscal quarter.

I want to reiterate that the risk profile of these projects, which were bid and won many years ago, differs significantly from the rest of the business. Over the past 6 years, we have transformed the backlog of our CM business, and there are no other projects in our backlog with similar risk exposures. Beyond these projects, the Construction Management business is performing exceptionally well. Backlog increased 25% during the year, and we expect revenue growth to accelerate in the second half of fiscal 2027 and beyond, with several key projects ramping up as the year progresses. Now turning to our performance. A few highlights stand out. First, the benefits of our competitive advantages continue to be apparent.

Our win rates set a new all-time high this year, and many of our wins feature duration spanning several years, which further extends our growth visibility. As a result, our backlog increased by 13% during the year, and our full year book-to-burn was very strong at 1.3x. Second, reflecting strong trends across our markets and backlog, design growth accelerated to 6% in the fourth quarter. Third, we continue to expand our industry-leading margins, delivering a new all-time high adjusted EBITDA margin of 19.2% in the fourth quarter, up 170 basis points over the prior year. This expansion reflects the benefits of our strategic investments and strong execution across the business.

Finally, free cash flow exceeded our expectations for the year, reflecting the strength of our balance sheet and our expectations for strong cash flow, our Board of Directors approved a 10% increase in the quarterly dividend. We have now grown our dividend at an 18% CAGR since initiation, demonstrating our continued commitment to shareholder returns. During the year, we also made great progress on our strategic initiatives, including our investments in Advisory and Technology or AI. Starting with technology. Our investments are helping transform how we deliver work and extend our competitive advantage while demonstrating greater value to clients on their projects. Importantly, our business has already realized benefits from these investments.

This includes some of our largest wins this past year, as shown by our 9-figure Scottish Water engineering win and a recompete win with an energy client earlier this year, where our book of business with this client went up fivefold. A large component of our success on these wins was built on the Technology we deliver to these clients today and the road map of what we're working on for tomorrow. In addition, our pipeline of opportunities is increasing as new clients not only benefit from our technology on their existing projects, but are also bringing us into a greater breadth of work. Next, our strategy to grow the Advisory business continues to bear fruit.

We are expanding our addressable market along with increasing our win probability by filling a void in the market with our domain and technical-led expertise, which elevates our role with clients. In fact, Advisory was one of the fastest-growing businesses within AECOM in fiscal 2026, and we expect to hire aggressively to continue to drive this growth. Concluding with our financial guidance. Today, we provide our initial outlook for fiscal 2027, where we forecast NSR growth of 4% to 6%, along with continued adjusted EBITDA and adjusted EPS growth to $1.37 billion and $6.25 at their respective midpoints. Our growth is driven by our backlog, strong end markets where we have #1 ranked practices.

Additionally, we expect another year of expansion in our industry-leading margins. Gaur will share more on this in a moment. Taken together, we believe AECOM is well positioned to create lasting value for our clients, our communities and our shareholders. With that, I'll turn the call over to Lara.

Lara Maria Poloni: Thanks, Troy. Our robust backlog demonstrates that our investments in our strategy are generating strong returns. Our wins were broad-based across our markets and geographies, and there are a number of positive trends that are supportive of our growth. This is apparent in our Americas design business, where our backlog is at a record level and our pipeline has grown at a double-digit rate for a fifth consecutive quarter. One key driver of our growth was Transportation. As an example of our momentum, we were selected for two of the largest transportation capital programs ever undertaken by their respective state departments of transportation.

These awards in Q4 and the current quarter reflects our technical leadership and the continued priority our clients are placing on modernizing critical infrastructure. Looking ahead, the U.S. market environment remains healthy, and we are optimistic the new Congress will create additional growth opportunities, which we are poised to capitalize on. This includes work to advance the Surface Transportation reauthorization, where we continue to expect bipartisan support for the next 5-year bill. In the meantime, more than half of the IIJA funding available to our markets has yet to be spent. While political transitions can cause some short-term uncertainty, we have managed through these cycles many times and have delivered consistent growth through these periods.

Infrastructure more broadly also maintained strong support from politicians and voters alike. Just this month, U.S. voters approved billions in state and local transportation ballot measures by 2:1 margins on average. The government of Canada also recently released its 2026 federal budget, which continues to reflect a commitment to long-term investment in infrastructure. And just as important, governments in the U.S. and around the world are pursuing permitting reforms and other measures intended to accelerate investment. We are seeing similarly positive trends in Water and Energy. In the U.K., Energy was a very strong contributor as our work on the Great Grid Upgrade, the largest grid infrastructure investment in the country's history, continues to progress as expected.

Growth in our Water business is also accelerating with increasing engagements from clients tied to the AMP8 cycle. In Australia, strong Water and Defense investment provides for large durable programs where our scale, technical capabilities and client relationships position us well to deliver continued growth. In addition to a strong long-term growth outlook in our core markets, we are also prioritizing investment in key end markets with outsized growth potential. A great example is the substantial opportunity we see to help private capital move into infrastructure. Through our Advisory business, we can help investors identify, accelerate and derisk projects while creating opportunities for our broader design capabilities.

We are also investing to expand in markets where clients are advancing large capital investment programs in which strategic partners like us are competitively advantaged, such as in Aviation and Energy. Across these markets, the common thread is our ability to bring together deep domain expertise, trusted client relationships and technology to help clients plan, fund and deliver increasingly complex infrastructure programs. This is extending our competitive advantages and creating a larger high-value addressable market for AECOM. With that, I'll turn the call over to Gaur.

Gaurav Kapoor: Thanks, Lara. We delivered strong results during the year despite some unexpected impacts in our markets, including the ongoing conflict in the Middle East and a slower ramp on some of our larger Construction Management wins, which are on track to accelerate in the second half of fiscal 2027. Importantly, we exited the year with a great deal of momentum. In the fourth quarter, we delivered 9% adjusted EBITDA growth and 20% adjusted EPS growth. Turning to our segment performance. In the Americas, design NSR increased 6% this quarter.

The adjusted operating margin was 20.6%, up 20 basis points from the prior year. n the fourth quarter, backlog in the design business was up high single digits as well as up sequentially while the pipeline growing even faster. This positions us well for continued growth in fiscal 2027 and beyond. Turning to the International segment. NSR growth accelerated again this quarter, up 5%, led by ongoing strength in the U.K. and Australia. The adjusted operating margin was 14.8%, which set a new quarterly record and was up 270 basis points. This performance reflects growth in our higher-margin markets, improved utilization and initial returns on our strategic investments.

Our International backlog growth also continues to be strong with several large wins this year, including a significant metro rail project in Ireland during the fourth quarter. Turning to cash flow and capital allocation. We exceeded our prior free cash flow guidance for the year, reflecting underlying business performance. When combined with our strong balance sheet position with net leverage of 1.3x, we are able to continue to operate with certainty. As Troy noted, we increased our quarterly dividend by 10%, and we remain committed to double-digit annual growth in per share value of our dividend for the long term.

We will have additional capital allocation flexibility once the CM project headwinds subside near the end of the first half of fiscal 2027. Importantly, our capital allocation priorities are unchanged and returns-based. Over the past several years, we have bought back approximately $3 billion of stock and returned approximately $600 million in dividends. Now turning to our guidance. We expect net services revenue growth of 4% to 6% in fiscal 2027, excluding the CM charge in fiscal 2026 and supported by our book-to-burn of 1.3x and strong backlog and pipeline. For your modeling, there is no workday impact for the full year. We expect segment adjusted operating margin and adjusted EBITDA margin expansion to 17.6%.

Our margins are benefiting from our overall growth mix shift from growing our higher-margin advisory business and benefits from our restructuring and technology investments. Adjusted EBITDA is expected to increase to $1.37 billion at the midpoint and adjusted EPS is expected to increase to $6.25 at the midpoint. As always, this does not include any potential benefits from capital allocation actions not yet taken. Our tax rate is expected to be approximately 22%, and, consistent with prior years, we expect a lower rate in the first quarter. We expect to deliver free cash flow of approximately $300 million, driven by healthy underlying performance consistent with our expectations for at least 100% free cash flow conversion.

This is offset by approximately $500 million used during the year on the 2 CM projects, which is consistent with the forecast we shared last quarter. In summary, our expectations for fiscal 2027 reflect strong NSR growth, record margins and continued earnings growth. With that, let's turn to Q&A, operator.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] Your first question comes from the line of Sabahat Khan with RBC.

Sabahat Khan: I just wanted to start with the commentary you shared in the materials about the ongoing projects. It sounds like they're on track with regards to the timing you shared before for kind of one this quarter and one the next. Maybe if you can detail what's been completed, what's remaining? And maybe just sort of the update there on what's happened in the last few months since we last heard from you on them?

W. Rudd: With respect to the first project, that project, I would describe it as this first phase is complete. We have delivered the asset to the customer, and the customer is spending a few weeks going through their testing with their tenants, and there is a planned opening for that asset in the very near future. So that asset has been delivered. So there's no real update beyond that. There is a second phase to that project, which represents about 25% of the total work to be done on that asset. That work will start in the beginning of the new calendar year and will extend into fiscal '29.

And at this point, we have confidence based on our experience delivering the 75% of the scope of the project that, that will be delivered successfully sort of on schedule and on budget. On the second project, that project is still ongoing, and there is a lot of work to do. But if you remember, the work that we were doing was not the physical asset. The physical asset is actually complete. The work that is ongoing really relates to all of the systems commissioning and testing and sign-off. I do want to make one other point about both of these projects, which is these are projects that the CM business and our teams have had a lot of experience in delivery. So this is not a new asset type or something that we're not familiar with. This is just -- we've had a couple of challenging situations that we've had to work our way through. But we certainly have confidence in delivering that and principally because these are assets that we have delivered, that our teams have delivered in the past.

Sabahat Khan: Great. And then maybe this one is for Gaur. On the guidance that you laid out, I think in the prepared comments, there was something about kind of the cadence between sort of earlier in the year and later in the year. Would you be able to share some thoughts on how should we expect top line and earnings to flow either through the quarters or the halves? And then similarly, any commentary on the flow-through of cash flow over the course of the year to get to the guidance range?

Gaurav Kapoor: Yes. I'll take that question. So in terms of the cadence or the phasing throughout the year, overall, from a earnings standpoint, the expectation should be consistent with our historical delivery as we phased earnings in first, second half, including the quarter. There will be no change -- significant change from that standpoint. And when we look at NSR, it's a good question. Because as you recall, we had mentioned this last quarter as well, and we forecasted consistently. In the first half, our NSR is going to be burdened because our CM business as it is pivoting off delivering some really large projects.

Right now, it is in the phase of what we call more agency work before the meat of our scope is delivered, that those large projects are going to kickstart in the second half of the year. And we also have -- even though for the year, there's no workday impact, just in the first quarter, we do have about half a day of impact as well. So when you look at the overall business, the design business, given the backlog growth, the CM business as well, that significant backlog growth in the first half, design business and second half is going to consistently going to deliver, but it will be tempered overall growth because of the CM business.

So there will be a ramp. I would say we're probably going to be at the low end of the range, maybe a little bit below low end of the range in the first quarter, and it will ramp up from there. In regards to cash flow, cash flow, if we take a normalized, which would have been approximately $800 million. What that represents is 100% conversion of our adjusted net income, consistent with our long-term algorithm. But we are impacted in delivery of these 2 projects where we have said we're going to spend a little -- approximately $0.5 billion in cash.

So when you look at the phasing of it, in a normalized year, we would deliver 15% to 20% of free cash flow in the first half of the year. Most of that $0.5 billion is going to be spent in the first and second quarter. So you should expect negative free cash flow for the first half of the year and then our normal cadence of cash delivery will kick in, in Q3, Q4 to deliver a net free cash flow result of approximately $300 million. And from a margin standpoint, I would say the delivery and the phasing is going to be very consistent to what you guys have seen last few years, including FY '26.

Between the first quarter and the second quarter, there generally is about 170 to 200 bps of differential, just given the number of workdays hours that are available. Therefore, our overhead cost and period costs are absorbed at a better clip in Q4 compared to Q1, and that consistently ramps up as well.

Operator: Your next question comes from the line of Adam Bubes with Goldman Sachs.

Adam Bubes: I think the margin guidance implies roughly 60 basis points of margin expansion year-over-year. Can you just help us bridge that outlook? How much is coming from the increasing mix of Advisory work versus restructuring and AI-driven productivity? And what are you embedding for AI investment costs in 2027?

Gaurav Kapoor: Yes. What I would say is the second part of your question in terms of AI investments, our investments continue to be consistent with what we spent in FY '26. So they're flat. However, as you recall, consistent with what we had originally planned out, in FY '27, we're already starting to see, and we saw this in end of FY '26, why we were able to deliver better margins than what we had planned. We started to see a ramp in those margins. So when you look at it on a net basis, the AI investments are net neutral in FY '27, consistent with what we had said.

In terms of the margins, I would almost put that growth for FY '27 into 3 different buckets. One is our strategic investments, including our advisory business, will continue to uplift the enterprise margins. Growth, anytime we have growth in our business because we always have this focus of continuous improvement on our cost base, which we'll continue to deliver, that will provide you with a natural lift in organic margins. And the third part outside of the AI, which we've already spoken about, is continued focus on our EC delivery centers. We continue to ramp up our direct labor hours going through EC, which also provide a good uplift to our margins.

So those are the different pieces leading to that 60 bps year-over-year increase.

Adam Bubes: And then on AI, can you just update us on the rollout of AI tools across the portfolio, which workflows are being impacted today? Any way to sort of quantify the early efficiency gains? And as those productivity benefits start to materialize, are you seeing any changes in how clients are asking you to contract?

W. Rudd: Yes. So let me sort of break this down into a couple of components of what we see in terms of our -- the impact of our technology investment. First is we are seeing efficiencies that are resulting ultimately in improved margins. And we started that process back in effectively the second quarter of this past year. And we started to see that improve over the course of the year. But as we followed our development road map, as the development has become more robust and started to impact what we can actually deliver for our customers, it's not that we're focused on margin efficiencies or efficiencies. We are gaining those and those will continue to improve.

But what we are seeing is actually a change, I'll even call it a profound impact on how customers are seeing the value that we can provide to them from design. And so think about that as actually dramatically improving the outcomes or the returns on their infrastructure assets because of the way we're able to take technology and effectively partner with our teams of engineers working on those projects.

And so that -- I mean, you can think about that as having an impact on margins, but we think of that actually at this point is starting to have an impact on our ability to win, to win relationships, win projects and actually through those new relationships, actually win work that we hadn't done before even outside of engineering and design. So again, we're a year into this process. We're kind of working through our thoughtful road map of development and deployment. We've moved from efficiencies into demonstrating new value for our customers and winning work.

Operator: Your next question comes from the line of Andrew Wittmann with Baird.

Andrew J. Wittmann: I guess maybe I just wanted to build on that last question a little bit and talk about your long-term outlook on margins -- and certainly, the progress has been good since you've announced this plan. It feels like there's a little bit sharper ramp or...

W. Rudd: I'm sorry, Andy, we're not hearing your question. Your line is breaking up.

Andrew J. Wittmann: I'm sorry about that. Maybe I'll try again.

W. Rudd: That's okay. You're cutting out. Maybe you can repeat the question, please.

Andrew J. Wittmann: Sure. I'll try one more time. Just I was wondering about the 2028 margin bridge. It feels like you're making good progress towards it, but it feels like there's still a decent ways to go. I recognize that the exit of '28 is the run rate for 20%. But I was just wondering what factors drive the out year, the '28-year benefit to margins. There's a little bit more you're expecting then, than you're realizing here at least in the '27 guide.

Gaurav Kapoor: Andy, thanks for the question. This is Gaurav. I'll take it. So you're right. In FY '28, we've said we're going to exit at 20-plus percent -- 20% plus. And to achieve that, on an annualized basis, what that equates to in FY '28 is approximately 18.6% margins. When we gave our guidance in FY '26, our plan was at 16.6%. So if you just take a linear growth curve and say, are we on track or not, you would have expected 100 bps of increase in margin for FY '27 and then another 100 bps of increase in margins for FY '28 to achieve that exit ramp we had laid out.

The good news is we've achieved that for FY '27. So if -- again, planned FY '26 was 16.6% margins. Our planned margins for FY '27 are 17.6%. So it's exactly that linear 100 bps of increase we were -- we had committed to and we've now delivered. And as you know, in our history of operating as this management team for the last 6 years, we are appropriately focused on not only delivering on the commitments we put forth on the margins, but we make every effort during the year as we execute to do a little bit better, just like we did compared to plan versus actual delivery in FY '26.

So as we look -- sit back here, look at the strategic investments across the board, as I laid out to the previous analyst questions on the different towers that are contributing to this margin expansion, we have a lot of confidence in exiting FY '28 at 20-plus percent, and we don't see a sharp curve for the reasons I explained.

Andrew J. Wittmann: Great. I just wanted to ask my follow-up question on the top line then. Obviously, the Backlog is up 13%. All year, it's been pretty steady good growth, and that's great. Your outlook, obviously, 4% to 6% on the organic, there's -- that's a difference. Like the backlog is certainly much higher than the outlook. And I guess you talked about longer duration awards. So maybe that explains it. But I was just wondering if there's any change in customer behavior in terms of the time between award and the notice to proceed is changing. Certainly, we've talked to others in the industry where they have seen a little bit of that.

So I was just wondering if you could comment on that. And maybe, Gaurav, if you could talk about how the portion of next year's guidance or expected revenue is already under contract. Is it more booked this year than a typical year? Or is this more like a typical year?

W. Rudd: Yes. Andy, I'll sort of confirm a few points that you already made for us. First of all is we are winning work that is longer in duration, so larger projects. And as we said, that does create more durability and visibility into long-term growth. So that is certainly part of the equation. The other thing is that we have, over the course of this past year, we have seen a longer period of time for some of the larger projects in terms of award to actually beginning work. And if you think about this past year, we've seen that most significantly has been in the Middle East. But we have seen that across most of our business.

So I don't know if, you know, if that's temporary or long term. But what we have planned in the guidance this year is we have planned that based on the backlog that we've won and our pipeline, something similar in terms of conversion to our awards to turn it into deliverable work. And then the other important thing to point out is that, again, I think Gaurav already made this point, our Construction Management business, we spent many years repositioning that business. As a result of that repositioning, we have a very different looking backlog, but we have also seen a very significant increase in that backlog.

And so in the guidance this year, certainly, the first half of the year is muted because the construction management business is not ramping up to revenue growth, but it is in the second half of the year. And so there are two very different periods. I think as you sort of look longer term, you'd say, well, the construction management and the design business, if you didn't have this ramp up in our fiscal '27, that it would look a little bit better as you would move forward.

Operator: Your next question comes from the line of Sangita Jain with KeyBanc Capital Markets.

Sangita Jain: If I can follow up on the previous questions regarding margins and all the commentary, Gaurav, you've given so far. Is it fair to assess that to get to the margin targets that you've laid out for 2029 would also imply that your NSR growth will trend towards the higher end of that 5% to 8% rate that you've given for this period?

Gaurav Kapoor: Yes. Thanks for that question, Sangita. No, that's the simple answer because there's so many different levers to margin. We're absolutely anticipating margin -- I'm sorry, NSR growth, especially with CM stabilizing in end of FY '27 going into FY '28. So our expectation, given the overall backlog growth, the visibility we have and the duration, as Troy just answered in the previous question, it provides us good confidence in NSR FY '28.

But as I also mentioned, all the strategic investments we're making, our Advisory business, our focus on making sure we're leveraging EC to our maximum capacity and capability, our focus on cost, continuous improvement culture and the technology investments that we've made in terms of driving internal efficiency, all of those things will contribute. And they're not directly linked to make sure that there is significant NSR growth to drive that margin expansion. So we have -- there's a lot of different blocks we have put in place, and that's why I say we have a lot of confidence and why we've delivered for the last 6 years, industry-leading margins.

Sangita Jain: Understood. And then is there any update that you can provide on the dispute resolution for the challenged Construction Management projects that you're pursuing? And any kind of updated time line on when we may hear more on those?

W. Rudd: The simple answer is it's going to take a long time for those disputes to be resolved. But I will point out that on one of the projects, there is a mechanism that allows us to sort of resolve individual differences along the way. And so we still are working through that process. It is slow, cumbersome and the amounts that you can dispute in that process are smaller. And -- but I will say that in that process, we have been very successful to date. So I think that, again, just sort of gives us confidence about the longer term.

But the simple answer to your question is it's going to be a long time before we can resolve these matters.

Operator: Your next question comes from the line of Lauren Sullivan with UBS.

Lauren Sullivan: Just first, in terms of the $500 million cash usage, could you just break down what's driving the cash intensity on those 2 projects in their final stages? Could this potentially be less or like any risk that it could be more than that?

Gaurav Kapoor: Lauren, thanks for that question. This is Gaur. I'll take it. Yes, the $500 million is on both of those projects, including completing the one large project we've talked about. And in terms of the detail, it's just the completion on those projects. There's not any more further detail we can provide on it.

Lauren Sullivan: Got it. And then just from your CM customers, I was wondering if you were hearing anything about higher interest rates and inflation causing any project delays? And then what types of projects do you have the most confidence to ramp in the second half of 2027?

W. Rudd: Yes. So the answer to your first question is no. At this point, we're not hearing anything from customers on their sensitivity to interest rates for construction management projects. And I would say that, that goes even more broadly across the entire business. There are always exceptions to that, but it's not something that we're hearing from our customers nor is it a trend in the work that we have ongoing. And then sort of think about the confidence in the projects is our confidence is, I would say, equal amongst all of the projects we have in backlog for a number of reasons.

One is because they are very important pieces of infrastructure that drive pretty significant economic outcomes, either for the individual private clients or for government organizations or communities. And the other thing is that what we put in the backlog is supported by funding. If those projects are not funded, then we don't put unfunded elements into our backlog. So again, in terms of funding and in terms of the importance of those projects, we have confidence in kind of everything that sits in our backlog today.

Operator: Your next question comes from the line of Michael Dudas with Vertical Research Partners.

Michael Dudas: Two questions. First, maybe just to highlight first your International business, I mean, your execution and the growth and the margin has been quite positive over the past few years. Maybe how can that momentum continue? And is there any areas that are going to provide some more better opportunities or maybe ability to enhance those margins at a better rate?

And then secondly, maybe in your Federal business, remind us how much of your business is with the U.S. federal government and given the recent FAA issues that we saw last week and the IIJA you mentioned, your confidence on this new Congress and stuff coming -- getting through on a bipartisan basis to maybe help the visibility in the infrastructure side going into '28 and beyond?

Lara Maria Poloni: Yes. Thanks, Mike, for the question. It's Lara. I'll take that. With respect to the International performance, this was a really strong quarter from the various segments of International. We had 7% growth in both the U.K. business, really led by strong performance in our Energy and Water segments, and we continue to have a really positive outlook for both of those. And also our Australia and New Zealand business grew by 7%. So that momentum and this next wave of infrastructure spending and the long-term positions we've secured with many of the water clients, which gives us that durability and long-term visibility is really starting to ramp up now. And even in the Middle East, we grew 5%.

And I think we remain really positive about our long-term sort of market leadership there, and we had some great wins despite the ongoing conflict and the sort of tempered growth in tourism. We're finding that we're getting real acceleration in growth in terms of the infrastructure segment. We had a great large rail project win in KSA. So the various segments of International really contributed to a strong quarter and a growing momentum there. And I think with respect to the federal sort of outlook, I think Troy is going to take that.

W. Rudd: Yes, I'll take that. I guess -- so first of all, Mike, our federal government -- U.S. federal government business represents about 9% of our overall revenues. So it is an important client. I will say this, I mean, look, everybody loves infrastructure. And I think that when you sort of look at the new Congress, we believe, based on history, that they do have a very strong commitment to infrastructure. And we believe that there should be bipartisan support for continued investment in infrastructure. So we are positive on that. But it's simply too early for us to have an opinion.

I think we'll find out more when the new Congress is in session, and we'll see the working relationship that develops with the current administration. But we are -- again, we are positive. People are asking us a lot about the surface transportation bill, and there is a short-term reauthorization. And again, we have confidence that it will continue. The exact form and duration of that, we don't know. But the one thing I will point out beyond the federal government is just the U.S. elections were also positive for state and local investment in transportation infrastructure.

There are a whole number of voter-approved ballot measures that are very significant and will provide funding for transportation projects at the state level. And we see that coming into, again, roads, bridges, a little bit of transit. And so we think that also provides support for what is an important part of our business, our state and local government clients.

Operator: Your next question comes from the line of Kevin Wilson with Truist Securities.

Kevin Wilson: Calling on behalf of Jamie Cook. Just one for me. It sounds like growth in Advisory continues to be really strong. You mentioned one of the fastest-growing areas of the company last year. How do you see that business continuing to evolve this year? Maybe any more color on the aggressive hiring you mentioned and the impact to margins from that? And are you still on track to double the Advisory business by next year?

Lara Maria Poloni: Thanks for the question, Kevin. It's Lara. We are absolutely on track to double that business by next year as we committed to. And you mentioned just the recruitment piece. We've been really excited and pleased with our progress in terms of just attracting talent. I think our proposition is really resonating with the talent that is coming across. We have secured some very senior hires, not just in the U.S. but across all segments of our Advisory business internationally as well. And those recruits are coming from other management consultants and Big 4. So the hiring is going really well.

And most importantly, the proposition and the support from many of our long-term clients is really going well as well. So I think we remain really excited about the prospects with advisory, and it's very complementary to our sort of market leadership in all of the other verticals. So we're absolutely on track and excited for the future of this business.

Operator: There are no further questions at this time. I will now turn the call back to Troy Rudd for closing remarks.

W. Rudd: Thank you, operator, and thank you, everyone, for joining the call today. We appreciate your support and interest. And I want to say thank you to all of the employees and folks across AECOM. This has been a long and this has been a tough year, and I thank them all for their commitment, and we do look forward to '27. And we think this is going to be a good year for infrastructure. Thank you.

Operator: This concludes today's call. Thank you for attending. You may now disconnect.

#3053. AI finds zero-day flaws for just $4 now – even mediocre hackers can cash in

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Rapidly advancing AI models are making it cheaper and easier to uncover critical vulnerabilities, but it's a double-edged sword - and a gift to hackers.

The best AI models on the market couldn’t find zero-days earlier this year, but now they can in less than 15 minutes and at a cost of a few bucks, according to a new report from penetration testing firm Xint.io. The findings raise questions about how vulnerabilities will be discovered and exploited in the future.

Every major AI developer is working at breakneck speed to improve model effectiveness. At the same time, token prices continue to fall, with studies showing that the average cost of tokens, which varies by domain, has dropped by about 47% per quarter since 2023 and 15% last month alone, due to intense competition among companies including OpenAI and Anthropic.

This is good news for businesses trying to harness AI for productivity and new services, but as token prices fall, it has also become cheaper for attackers to launch AI-assisted attacks, including software breaches caused by exploiting unknown vulnerabilities.

Also: How AI security failures are endangering your supply chain

A report published by Xint.io examines how popular AI models have evolved over the past year to the point where cybersecurity tasks that would have failed only months ago now succeed. The team analyzed seven models launched since February 2026: two from OpenAI, three from Anthropic, and two open-source models from DeepSeek and Z.ai. The team tracked, over time, how they performed in finding a target vulnerability.

The target of this research was a security flaw in Google’s V8 engine. Tracked as CVE-2026-102321, the type confusion bug leading to remote code execution (RCE) was disclosed to the Google Vulnerability Reward Program (VRP) by Xint researcher Taisic Yun and so was not present in the AI models’ training datasets.

The research scope was limited to a set of source files, including the file containing the vulnerability, and each model was instructed to search for security issues within these files.

Xint’s first test was conducted in February. After 25 hours and $350 of scanning, the best models then available still couldn’t find the critical vulnerability.

In July, GPT 5.6 Sol found the zero-day flaw for $22 in 44 minutes.

Also: Finding Linux bugs is easy – fixing them is another story

By September, GPT 6 Sol discovered the bug in 13 minutes for only $4.24 with its first guided prompt.

Only three of the seven models found the bug: GPT 6 Sol, GPT 5.6 Sol, and Claude Opus 5, all launched from July onward. GPT 5.6 Sol needed two prompts, while Claude Opus 5 found it on its first try but at a higher cost of $43.40.

DeepSeek’s and Z.ai’s models failed the task.

The researchers say that the combination of AI model development and low token prices means that “mediocre hackers” can now use frontier models effectively to discover and potentially exploit vulnerabilities, and “while we are still far from complete amateurs using unharnessed models to hack systems and applications, what used to be considered too hard and costly to be worth the effort of the average hacker is now reachable.”

As a result, organizations need to adjust their security posture accordingly — but falling token costs and evolving AI skills and speed can also work in your favor.

Also: How I safely run my OpenClaw AI agent 24/7 on a Mac

There’s nothing stopping an organization’s security team or pentesters from running the same checks themselves to find vulnerabilities before threat actors do. AI-assisted tests, arguably, are no longer something that can be pushed back to next year’s budgetary review. By performing a risk assessment that focuses on likely weak spots, such as public-facing services or a digital supply chain that hasn’t been audited for years, organizations can mitigate the risk AI-enabled cyberattacks pose.

Zero-day vulnerabilities are unknown to vendors, and a patch might not be available when they go public or are actively exploited in the wild. So, AI can only go so far, but it can free up your defenders for tasks that need the human touch. Furthermore, maintaining zero-trust access controls, segmenting and shoring up your network’s defenses, and monitoring endpoints for signs of suspicious behavior can do as much as, or more than, AI.

As Xint notes, “expertise still matters” when it comes to instructing AI models to discover vulnerabilities. In some cases, the models couldn’t find the target vulnerability without guidance, so additional runs were needed, increasing time and cost.

“Software breaches still require some level of technical proficiency,” the researchers say, “but no longer top-of-the-distribution expertise.”

#3052. Samsung Galaxy S27 Lineup Could Have a Personal AI Assistant Built-In

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Galaxy Claw could make calls and send text messages for you.

Samsung is expected to unveil its Galaxy S27 lineup early next year, and a personal AI assistant might be arriving as well. The so-called Galaxy Claw could perform a variety of functions, including making phone calls, sending text messages and creating appointments, according to Android Authority.

The tech news website discovered Galaxy Claw while digging into Samsung’s Personal Agent Core app, which is a new AI system that connects AI across Samsung apps and Google services. This new system can also pull data from your calendar, Gmail, text messages, delivery info and other sources and also autonomously perform tasks upon your instructions.

Android Authority said that coding details for the Personal Agent Core app were shared by The Cipher Project, a Telegram channel that often leaks Samsung software updates, One UI features and unreleased device functions.

A representative for Samsung did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Samsung has had AI functionality on its phones and other devices since January 2024, when the company introduced Galaxy AI. The main capabilities at that launch included Circle to Search — allowing users to search for anything on the screen — as well as live language translation and photo editing.

Over the past two-plus years, Samsung has integrated more AI functionality into its devices, including Google Gemini and Gemini Live. Although Samsung devices have plenty of AI to do things for you, it primarily operates on your command rather than acting as an autonomous agent.

The new Galaxy Claw system might launch at Samsung Unpacked in January or February, when Samsung could release the Galaxy S27 series, which could include the Ultra flagship. Samsung has not officially announced what products it will launch at Unpacked.

According to Android Authority, the Galaxy Claw could connect to various apps on your phone and perform functions for you. Those apps could include Calendar, Contacts, Gallery, Gmail, Messages, Notifications, Perplexity, Phone and Voice Recorder.

So, in essence, the Claw could create appointments, write and send emails and make phone calls. For example, you could have Claw set up a meeting and send calendar notifications to the attendees with an attached agenda. Or perhaps Claw could call someone for you to tell them where you’re going.

Android Authority said other components could be included — Daily Brief, Device Cleaner, Travel Planner and a dedicated widget.

Those tasks would be a major step up from what Galaxy AI can currently do on Samsung phones — live translation, text drafting, photo editing, scam call detection and more.

Adding agentic AI won’t justify the $1,400 or even $1,500 price tag for the S27 Ultra but could help generate customer loyalty, says tech reviewer Jon Rettinger.

“People buy the Ultra for the camera, the screen and the S Pen, and that won’t change next year,” Rettinger told CNET. “Where an agent could matter is keeping people. If Galaxy Claw is reading my Gmail, my calendar and my texts and quietly handling the busywork, switching phones gets a lot harder, because I’d be walking away from an assistant that knows how my week runs.”

Rettinger said Samsung would be wise to include the Galaxy Claw with the new devices and not as a separate subscription service.

“So, now the pitch is $1,500 for the phone, then a monthly fee for the feature that’s supposed to justify the phone,” Rettinger said. “That’s a tough sell. If Samsung wants this to move hardware, it should come included on the Ultra.”

People apparently will maintain authority and control over Galaxy Claw, according to Android Authority. The new system would request access to sensitive data such as contacts, photos and calendar events, as well as permission to execute functions such as sending text messages and making calls. The Claw wouldn’t go rogue on you, in other words.

Samsung users might also be able to schedule the Claw to do tasks and functions regularly. Perhaps you need to email or text weekly reminders to someone about something. You could instruct the AI on the task and when to do it each week. It might only require a simple prompt from you, such as, “Please remind my son to take out the garbage by 8 a.m. Monday mornings.”

Android Authority said tasks could be scheduled by hour, day, weekly and custom intervals. Users would also be able to cancel or modify scheduled tasks and check task history.

#3050. NIO vs. Tesla: Which EV Stock Is a Better Buy for 2027?

NIO's battery-swapping model and fast revenue growth face off against Tesla's scale and cash flow, but only one balance sheet carries the lower-risk profile.

As the transition to electric transportation accelerates, investors often weigh the rapid growth of NIO Inc. (NIO +3.31%) against the established dominance of Tesla Inc. (TSLA +0.10%) to determine which is the better buy today.

NIO focuses on the luxury segment in China and Europe, utilizing unique battery-swapping stations to address charging concerns. Conversely, Tesla leverages massive manufacturing scale and software integration to lead the global market. Comparing these two involves balancing NIO's high-speed expansion against Tesla's proven profitability and massive capital reserves.

NIO designs and sells smart electric vehicles under several brands, including its namesake line and the newer ONVO and Firefly labels. It targets premium buyers across 24 countries, emphasizing a user enterprise model that integrates lifestyle services with vehicle ownership. No single customer accounts for more than 10% of its revenue, providing a diversified sales base.

In FY 2025, revenue reached approximately $13.1 billion, an increase of approximately 33.1% from the prior year. Despite this growth, the company reported a net loss of about $2.2 billion for the period. While the net margin improved from the previous two years, it remained negative at roughly 17.1%. (Note that figures have been converted from Chinese Yuan as of the publication date).

As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio is approximately 6.3x, which measures total debt against the value of shareholder equity. The current ratio, which gauges the ability to cover short-term obligations with current assets, is roughly 1.0x. Free cash flow, or cash from operations minus capital expenditures, was negative $461.2 million. Note that stock-based compensation represented roughly 59.8% of operating cash flow, which inflates reported cash generation since SBC is a non-cash expense added back in the cash flow statement.

Tesla operates as a vertically integrated manufacturer of electric vehicles and energy storage systems, selling directly to consumers without a traditional dealership network. It serves a diverse group of residential and utility-scale customers, while partnering with firms like Contemporary Amperex Technology Co. Limited (CYATY +0.35%) for battery cells. This strategy allows the company to capture value across the entire energy ecosystem.

For FY 2025, revenue reached approximately $94.8 billion, a decrease of nearly 2.9% year over year. The company recorded net income of roughly $3.8 billion, resulting in a net margin of close to 4%. This represents a decline from the double-digit net margins seen in previous fiscal years.

As of the December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio is approximately 0.1x, indicating a very low level of debt relative to equity. The current ratio is roughly 2.2x, suggesting a strong ability to meet immediate financial commitments. Tesla generated significant free cash flow of nearly $6.2 billion, providing ample capital for reinvestment.

NIO faces challenges related to its capital-intensive battery-swapping network and its expansion into highly competitive international markets. The company must manage heavy research and development costs while striving for profitability among consumer discretionary stocks facing fluctuating demand. Geopolitical tensions and trade barriers in Europe and North America also pose significant hurdles for its global growth ambitions.

Tesla encounters risks involving the complex production ramp-up of new products like the Cybercab and Optimus robot. It is also heavily dependent on the continued advancement of autonomous driving software and the time and attention of its chief executive. Intense competition from global manufacturers and sensitivity to macroeconomic factors, such as interest rates, can further affect vehicle demand and pricing.

NIO currently trades at a significantly lower sales multiple than Tesla, although Tesla remains the only profitable company between the two based on recent earnings.

Valuation metrics include those sourced from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from those of other data providers.

The P/S ratio measures a company's market price against its sales over the past twelve months. Meanwhile, the Forward P/E compares the share price to future earnings estimates.

For investors seeking EV automaker stocks, NIO and Tesla offer two strong brands in two significant global car markets.

Looking at NIO, the EV market in mainland China is booming: fully two-thirds of all vehicles sold in the country these days are classified as EVs or plug-in hybrids (PHEVs). Still, new car sales in China plunged about 20% in the first half of 2026 compared to the first half of 2025, even as EVs and PHEVs continued to gain market share. The central government halved its credit for buying EVs this year too, which should be impacting demand, although in the current five-year plan, the Communist government has EVs as a core part of its central economic plan.

NIO management is saying it will be able to post 8% sales growth for the third quarter of the current fiscal year, but August deliveries of almost 36,000 units were about 10% of the run rate needed to hit that mark, according to a report from CFRA. Wall Street sees NIO tallying sales of $19.2 billion in 2026, growth of more than 46%. It should come with a much narrower net loss of $300 million, according to consensus estimates.

Tesla, meanwhile, faces a muddled outlook in the U.S. The Big Beautiful Bill removed incentives for buying EVs in the U.S., an obvious negative for Tesla. Third-quarter EV sales were down sharply from 2025, although that quarter is believed to have pulled forward consumer demand for EVs ahead of the expiration of the GOP's signature bill in recent years. Yet in October, EV sales posted their first rise over 2025, as elevated gas prices from the Iran war sent shoppers seeking alternatives to fossil fuel vehicles. On the other hand, Tesla is killing off the Cybertruck, a massive failure on the scale of the famous Edsel from Ford Motor Co. (F -1.99%) in the late 1950s.

Wall Street has also long been expecting that Elon Musk will seek to combine Tesla with Space Exploration Technologies (SPCX +3.16%), which has brought a type of arbitrage to the shares.

So which is the better buy? Leave the inside baseball of a potential SpaceX merger to the pros. NIO is the simpler story here and the far better-valued automaker, even as it operates in a fiercely competitive Chinese market and does not come cheap in its own right, valuation-wise.

#3049. Your enterprise AI access can be sold for pennies – beware ‘LLM Mixers’

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Underground brokers are selling access to hijacked enterprise AI accounts, with companies footing the usage bill, Google reports.

In just a few years, businesses have adopted AI and large language models (LLMs) to manage everything from calendar invites to data analysis and programming. Bad actors steal credentials for those models through LLMjacking — and the marketplace is evolving.

Google’s latest report on AI threats, the Q4 AI Threat Tracker from the Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG), found that gateways called LLM Mixers are selling access for cents on the dollar.

Also: 6 essential strategies to defend against AI-powered threat actors

Organizations have poured billions of dollars into AI development and deployment, although the amount they spend on AI tokens every month varies. According to Ramp AI index data, among firms paying for AI, the top 1% spent over $10,000 per employee per month, compared with around $16 for the median firm. When employees have access to AI models, companies may introduce spending caps, but smaller outfits may overlook them.

LLMjacking is the theft of AI-related credentials, including usernames and passwords, or API keys, used to access AI models. This gives cybercriminals the opportunity to use tokens and AI resources belonging to a victim organization (or individual), typically with usage-based billing or subscriptions with no fixed cap.

With these credentials, an unauthorized user could run high-resource computing tasks, manage their own malicious AI deployments, extract and steal corporate data from the AI’s memory, or even poison training data. To add insult to injury, if demand outstrips the limits of the victim’s subscription, cybercriminals can rack up high usage costs that the victim is then on the hook for.

Also: Rogue AI incidents hit ‘tens of thousands’: Can businesses trust these tools?

John Hultquist, chief analyst for GTIG, previously said the cybersecurity unit has seen a “major increase” in LLMjacking over 2026, so we can assume this trend will likely continue into 2027 and beyond.

AI access is now a lucrative illegal business in its own right, leading to what Google calls LLM Mixers: “illicit storefronts” that provide unauthorized access to AI services and underlying proxy infrastructure.

After analyzing LLMJacking vendor advertisements on Russian- and Chinese-language marketplaces, GTIG researchers found that most offer access not only to frontier models from AI labs, but also to jailbroken models marketed as suitable for malicious purposes.

However, it doesn’t seem that many of these cybercriminal groups can agree on “reasonable” pricing, with prices swinging wildly depending on the models offered and the credentials available.

Also: How I safely run my OpenClaw AI agent 24/7 on a Mac – with Claude Code standing guard

Free trial credentials fetch far less than enterprise credentials, as you would expect. Token prices for business use ranged from $0.10 to $25, and one vendor, APIMart, increased its token price fivefold once a prompt exceeds 100,000 tokens. Other vendors offer subscription-based pricing.

This might not seem like much at the lower tiers, but Sysdig estimates LLMJacking could cost around $46,000 based on earlier models, and even over $100,000 per day on cutting-edge models. Mandiant research published earlier this month recorded incidents with illicit AI usage exceeding $100,000 in only 24 hours, with cumulative charges at some organizations reaching $1 million before access was revoked.

While direct credentials can be sold, the infrastructure element is also an interesting service offering. Google’s threat team said in the report that the sale of LLM infrastructure “routes buyer traffic through a pool of stolen credentials and compute instances to ensure reliable access, while also offering the ability to spread query volume across multiple victim environments to reduce the likelihood of detection.”

LLM Mixers look similar to the rest of the cybercriminal underground economy, in which traders tend to specialize in one or two parts of an attack chain. For example, an LLM Mixer offers the access and infrastructure needed to exploit an enterprise AI model, while its partners might break into victim networks to secure initial access or buy stolen credentials from operators of infostealer malware.

Avoid LLMjacking and having your organization’s AI added to a Mixer’s menu similarly to how you would prevent intrusions into SaaS applications and cloud setups: managing access, monitoring, and imposing restrictions.

Usage and spending are the first areas to tackle. By setting limits on how many tokens can be issued and used across every AI service and account, and by alerting when usage suddenly spikes, organizations can limit damage if an account is compromised and stop massive bills before they rack up.

Organizations should also try to prevent their keys from ending up in the hands of cyberattackers in the first place. Google recommends using a secrets manager that securely stores and frequently rotates API keys, and running audits to detect quiet probing, misconfigurations, or shadow accounts.

It’s also advisable, across the board, to implement phishing protections and multi-factor authentication (MFA) to make the business of stealing credentials or compromising your accounts and networks more difficult in the first place.

#3048. A New Study Finds Hyperscale Data Centers Emit as Much Carbon as Denmark

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Harvard researchers collected metrics on more than 400 data centers to determine their energy use and carbon emissions.

During the midterm elections, Americans made one thing very clear: Data centers must be reined in.

A vast majority of communities across the country voted to ban or restrict the construction of data centers, as concerns about their impact on the environment and public health grow.

A new study by Harvard researchers shows that these fears are not unfounded. The findings published today in Nature Sustainability show that the carbon emissions and energy use of hyperscale data centers amount to as much as those of entire states and more than those of the country of Denmark.

I spoke with Gianluca Guidi, a postdoctoral fellow in the Department of Biostatistics and lead author of the paper, to discuss how the team collected data on energy use despite a lack of industry transparency, the rapid evolution of AI infrastructure and future research goals.

Hyperscale data centers are the largest and most powerful data center facilities, featuring thousands of servers to power cloud computing, model training and the global use of AI. Guidi said he was inspired to look into data center emissions and the broader impacts of generative AI after reading a paper on bitcoin mining’s electricity use, which found that just 34 mining facilities, combined, consumed as much electricity as the entire city of Los Angeles.

The study narrowed in on 403 of these facilities to provide the most up-to-date and transparent measures of their electricity use and carbon emissions between May 2024 and April 2025.

Tech companies are not quick to disclose their energy use, so Guidi and his team had to circumvent these obstacles to get accurate metrics. The team used satellite imagery to narrow down 675 candidate sites to 403 verified facilities, estimated annual electricity consumption, and linked them to Environmental Protection Agency data to measure each facility’s carbon emissions.

“I would say the data preparation, data collection and validation were 100% the toughest part of the whole project,” Guidi said during a phone interview, explaining that there is a need for transparency and people should have access to this data.

During the study, the team found that these hyperscale data centers emitted 25.7 million metric tons of carbon dioxide, more than the entire country of Denmark and far exceeding the last peer-reviewed estimate from 2018. The 403 facilities also used between 68 and 99 terawatt-hours of electricity during the testing period — about 1.8% of all US electricity consumption.

A majority of the electricity (54%) that powers these hyperscale data centers comes from natural gas and coal, despite many tech companies signing corporate pledges to make substantial investments in renewable energy. Fossil fuels have long been known to generate massive amounts of carbon dioxide, exacerbating global warming and climate change, despite many of these tech companies. “We need to distinguish between what companies commit to on paper, and then the actual physical emissions associated with the whole powering of these infrastructures,” Guidi said.

The Harvard team also pointed out that the paper’s data is from last spring, meaning the industry’s 2026 footprint is certainly substantially larger today.

“I feel like the pace at which the industry is growing is really outpacing the pace at which people like us — scientists — are working in order to understand (HDC) impacts,” Guidi said. “And we’re lagging behind because of the way the system is made.”

As data centers scale and expand, the research will need to as well, the researchers said. The team is already working to expand its dataset to investigate the broader public health consequences of hyperscale data centers, including water consumption and noise pollution.

The level of collaboration we have seen across our divisions is outstanding and to our employees across all the geographies where we work and live, a job well done. This year has been outstanding, and our team members are the reason that we are able to say yes to the opportunities that our customers have and continue to bring an award to Powell.

Turning to our results for the quarter. Revenue grew 33% to $397 million compared to the fourth quarter of the prior year. Our continued focus on productivity and project execution delivered a gross margin of 34.9%, resulting in earnings of $2.23 per diluted share. We booked $710 million of new orders in the quarter, which was up 162% compared to the prior year and was the second highest order total in Powell's history, surpassed only by the record $934 million that we booked in the prior quarter.

We booked $2.6 billion of new orders, more than double what we booked in fiscal 2025 for a full year book-to-bill of 2x. As a result, we ended the year with a backlog of $2.7 billion, up over $300 million sequentially and $1.3 billion higher than a year ago.

Our visibility now extends well into fiscal 2028 and in some cases, beyond, and the composition of our backlog remains healthy and well balanced. Equally as important is the mix of projects by size, complementing our mega projects that provide an anchor from a scheduling and execution perspective, we continue to see a steady flow of core projects below $10 million and larger projects in the $10 million to $50 million range. That blend of project scope and size lets us efficiently schedule around the natural stop and hold points that often arise in larger projects and enables us to optimize the variable costs of production.

Reflecting on fiscal 2026 results, I am particularly pleased with the continued progress we are making in our efforts to diversify Powell across the markets we serve. Traditionally, Powell has focused on delivering complex engineered-to-order electrical distribution solutions for customers spanning our important core industrial markets. Today, we are not only effectively serving these traditional Powell markets, but we are also successfully leveraging these same engineering and manufacturing competencies to continue to grow our presence across the electric utility and the commercial and other industrial end markets globally.

The current commercial demand spanning these end markets today demands process and structure that is embedded across our footprint, and it is a testament to our teams globally in their ability to scale and leverage the processes, engineering talent and manufacturing capabilities across the business. We are confident that this Powell attribute is a fundamental reason driving our success and an important competitive advantage for our business. Specific to our core industrial end markets, commercial activity remains strong. We continue to expand our position across the natural gas value chain, particularly in LNG as demonstrated by roughly $350 million of new LNG orders in the fiscal fourth quarter.

We were also encouraged by the fertilizer project awarded earlier in the year, which we believe is an early sign of a potential recovery in the petrochemical market following a period of softer market demand. Overall, the progress we have made against our decade-long strategy to diversify the business is increasingly evident in our results. The electric utility and commercial and other industrial markets represented 50% of revenue in fiscal 2026 compared to 41% in fiscal 2025. For perspective, these markets accounted for less than 30% of revenue on a significantly lower revenue base just 5 years ago.

We believe that this diversification is contributing to a more balanced business, reducing cyclicality and providing greater visibility to plan and invest beyond the current market cycles. Over the past year, we have taken a series of deliberate steps to add capacity. And together, they have expanded our manufacturing, office and warehouse footprint by more than 20% versus the end of fiscal 2025. In Ohio, we've added an incremental 60,000 square feet of manufacturing and warehousing capacity through a lease signed late last calendar year as we begin to execute on growing demand for our data center backlog. In Houston, we recently leased an additional 50,000 square feet of manufacturing and integration capacity.

Additionally, we recently decided to further expand this location by an additional 80,000 square feet. This will be a world-class fabrication yard spanning roughly 1 million square feet with 1,200 feet of bulkhead for water access, ideal for shipping large single-piece power control rooms and large offshore modules.

With this expansion, we plan to support the accelerating demand for custom power control rooms targeted at core industrial applications, but this capacity will remain fungible across all the markets that we serve. At full utilization, we expect it to support well over $100 million of incremental annualized revenue. We are also looking forward and initiating the next phase of our capacity expansion strategy. During our fiscal third quarter of 2026, the Board authorized the lease of a new facility that will add approximately 275,000 square feet of manufacturing and integration space, which we expect to bring online in our fiscal third quarter of 2027.

Finally, we continue to evaluate a purpose-built greenfield Powell-owned factory of somewhere between 250,000 to 300,000 square feet, which would further support increased future fabrication needs for the markets that we serve. Now turning to the current operations. Labor availability and supply chain constraints remain 2 areas that we are closely monitoring. We are beginning to see increased competition for skilled craft labor across a broad geographic footprint. While this has not had an impact on our ability to execute our backlog to date, we remain mindful of the potential risk due to the increased demand for skilled labor as we look ahead to fiscal 2027 and 2028.

On the supply chain front, our teams continue to work closely with our key suppliers and partners to ensure material availability and delivery schedules remain aligned with our project commitments. As we enter fiscal 2027, the environment across each of our key verticals remains very active. We see continued momentum across most of the markets that we serve as evidenced by the fiscal 2026 order strength across our oil and gas, electric utility and commercial and other industrial market sectors. In our oil and gas sector, the most active end market is clearly being driven by the demand for LNG.

And we believe we are in the early innings of a multiyear infrastructure build-out and anticipate that this market domestically will remain active into the foreseeable future. Turning to our Electric Utility segment. The outlook remains robust and balanced across the customers and geographies that we serve. Demand continues to be underwritten by structurally undersupplied power generation and grid capacity and the growing wave of investment in electrical infrastructure is broad and durable. And finally, with respect to the data center opportunities that we are seeing, these are much more standard electrical applications versus our traditional engineered-to-order configurations, and we continue to find strong partners commercially that enable Powell to further penetrate this market.

On the electrical automation front, we are 1 year on from closing the Remsdaq acquisition, and it has proven synergistic and accretive across the company. The domestic data center market has pulled Remsdaq technology into the U.S. faster than we had planned, and it complements our medium voltage offerings on many of the data center orders that we secured throughout fiscal 2026. Additionally, we see a unique and valuable opportunity in U.S. government and defense, leveraging our U.S.-centric supply chain, operations and workforce, which position us well to support national defense or other governmental institutions for critical electrical distribution applications.

And finally, on M&A, our pipeline is healthy, and we are focused on complementary electrical products and/or markets expanding our breadth in automation and on building our services franchise. Valuations across the space are rich, so we will stay disciplined and act where we see both strategic fit and value. Overall, we are very pleased with both the execution across the business, driving record revenue levels for the year as well as our orders performance throughout fiscal 2026. Compared to the fourth quarter of fiscal 2025, domestic revenues of $348 million increased by $118 million or 51%, while international revenues decreased by 29% to $48 million, driven primarily by the softer Canadian end market.

From a market sector perspective, revenues from our oil and gas and utility sectors were higher by 24% and 22%, respectively, on the solid commercial environment in the U.S., driving demand for the industrial build-out across both electrical infrastructure as well as LNG export terminals along the Gulf Coast. Additionally, our commercial and other industrial sector was higher by 179%, driven predominantly by the ongoing strength across the data center end market. Modestly offsetting this growth, our petrochemical and traction sectors were lower versus the same period 1 year ago by 49% and 24%, respectively.
