The forward-looking statements are as of today, and we assume no obligation to update or supplement these statements. We may also refer to certain non-IFRS financial metrics, which are reconciled and described in our press release posted on our Investor Relations website at ir.viking.com. Leah and Linh will begin today's call with a strategic overview of the business, including a recap of our third quarter results and an update on the current booking environment. Following their remarks, we will open the call for your questions. To supplement today's discussion, an earnings presentation is available on our Investor Relations website. With that, I'm pleased to turn the call over to Leah.

Leah Talactac: Thank you, Carola, and good morning, everyone. It has been an eventful quarter for Viking, and I am pleased to provide an update on our performance and outlook. Turning to Slide 3, I will share some highlights. During the quarter, we generated total revenue of $2.2 billion, an increase of 9.2% year-over-year. This growth was driven by continued fleet expansion and higher revenue per Passenger Cruise Day. Moreover, this performance also reflects the benefits of our diversified business and the enduring appeal of the Viking brand. Today, our portfolio is balanced across River and Ocean, providing multiple drivers of growth and enhancing the resilience of our operating model.

This strength is also evident in our year-to-date results with Adjusted Gross Margin increasing 11.3% and Net Yield up 4% year-over-year. Now the diversification proved particularly valuable this quarter as historically low water levels affected portions of our European river operations. As we have done in prior disruptions, we leveraged our experience, scale and operational flexibility to minimize the impact on our guests. Drawing on nearly 30 years of river cruising experience and the flexibility of our identical fleet of Longships, we operated all scheduled voyages through ship swaps, itinerary modifications, alternative transportation and additional accommodations where needed.

We are incredibly proud of and grateful to our onboard crew and shoreside teams whose extraordinary efforts enabled us to continue serving our guests throughout this period. Importantly, the vast majority of affected guests chose to continue their journeys with Viking, reflecting both the strength of our guest experience and the trust they place in our brand. Throughout this disruption, our priority remained clear: caring for our guests and preserving their confidence in Viking. To support that objective, we enhanced guest communications prior to departure to provide greater flexibility into potential itinerary changes and, where appropriate, offered vouchers as a gesture of goodwill. We believe these actions were the right long-term decisions for both our guests and the Viking brand.

Having said this, it is important to put this year's disruption into context. While some level of low and high water occurs each season, 2026 was unique due to the unprecedented combination of duration, severity and geographic breadth. Multiple sections of the Rhine, Main and Danube rivers were affected simultaneously and remained impacted for an extended period. Based on our experience operating in these regions, we view this season's conditions as atypical rather than a new normal. Encouragingly, I am glad to share that recent rainfall has already improved conditions across key regions and current forecasts call for additional precipitation in the coming days.

As a result, we are seeing signs of recovery and are anticipating water levels to continue to improve across the impacted river network during mid-November and into December. River cruising is a unique way to travel and explore the world. We remain confident and excited in its great appeal and the demand for destination-focused experiences. In addition, Ocean continues to perform exceptionally well with advance bookings, pricing and guest demand all remaining at strong levels. Now turning to Slide 5, I would like to highlight how our order book is strengthening our business model. One of Viking's advantages is the balanced and increasingly diversified nature of our business.

Through thoughtful fleet expansion over the last decade, we have evolved from a company primarily focused on river cruising into a global travel company with a portfolio spanning River, Ocean and Expedition voyages. Today, our capacity is evenly split between River and Ocean, creating a balanced earnings profile and reducing our reliance on any single product category or operating environment. This diversification also expands our addressable market, extends our global reach and strengthens the lifetime value of our guests. Looking ahead, we expect the Ocean segment to be the largest driver of our growth through 2036, accounting for approximately 70% of our newbuild capacity.

We believe that this deliberate diversification allows Viking to benefit from the attractive opportunities in the Ocean segment while continuing to leverage the scale, brand strength and market leadership we have established in River. In River, we have a leading position with more than 50% of the North American outbound river cruise market. Since our last earnings call, we secured options for 10 additional river vessels to operate in Europe, underscoring our belief that river cruising is an attractive way to travel and reinforcing our long-term commitment to the River segment and our leadership position within it. In Ocean, we currently hold approximately 27% of the luxury ocean cruise market, providing significant opportunity for future growth.

We believe this combination of market leadership in River and substantial runway for expansion in Ocean positions us well to continue growing both revenue and earnings over the long term. Turning to Slide 6. As we continue to expand our fleet and global reach, we remain committed to delivering the exceptional experiences that define Viking. We are proud that Viking was once again ranked the #1 Cruise Line for Rivers and #1 Cruise Line for Oceans in Condé Nast Traveler's 2026 Readers' Choice Awards, marking the sixth consecutive year we have received both distinctions. Viking was also recognized as the World's Best by Travel + Leisure.

I will highlight that no other travel company has received these distinctions from both publications simultaneously. These recognitions are especially meaningful because they come directly from travelers and reflect the experiences we strive to deliver every day. We believe this continued recognition underscores the quality, consistency and differentiation of the Viking experience as well as the dedication of our teams around the world. With that, I will turn the call over to Linh to discuss our financial results.

Linh Banh: Thank you, Leah, and good morning, everyone. I will now walk you through our results for the third quarter, which are summarized on Slide 8. On a consolidated basis, total revenue for the quarter increased 9.2% year-over-year to $2.2 billion. This growth was driven by increased capacity and higher revenue per PCD. As Leah mentioned, we delivered this level of revenue despite historically disruptive weather conditions. Overall, this performance reflects strong demand across our portfolio, the benefits of diversification and disciplined execution. During the third quarter of 2026, Capacity PCDs increased 10.2% compared to the same period in 2025, and Occupancy was 91.3%, lower than last year, mainly driven by guest cancellations and low water disrupted sailings.

Adjusted Gross Margin increased 4.1% year-over-year to $1.4 billion, resulting in a Net Yield of $612. The third quarter was impacted by lower Occupancy and incremental costs related to the low water disruption. Vessel expenses, excluding fuel per Capacity PCD increased 5% year-over-year. Regarding SG&A, expenses were slightly lower as a percentage of AGM when compared to the same time last year. Adjusted EBITDA for the third quarter was $674 million, down 4.3% compared to the prior year. The year-over-year decline reflects the impact of historically low water conditions. Even so, our performance reflects the strength of our broader portfolio and our ability to respond effectively in a complex operating environment.

Net income was $498 million and Adjusted Net Income attributable to Viking Holdings Ltd was $497 million. Adjusted EPS was $1.11 for the third quarter. Before I discuss year-to-date metrics for our 2 reportable segments, I would like to address the impact that historically low water levels had on our river operations during the third quarter. While we were able to maintain operations and did not cancel any scheduled cruises, low water conditions resulted in itinerary disruptions and increased guest cancellations. Approximately 70% of our river capacity cruise days were affected during the third quarter and approximately 12% of guests booked on affected itineraries elected to cancel.

We estimate that the low water disruptions reduced third quarter revenue by approximately $100 million. The impact on Adjusted Gross Margin was also approximately $100 million, reflecting the lost margin from guest cancellations as well as incremental direct costs incurred to mitigate the disruptions. With respect to vessel operating expenses, the weather disruptions had no material impact on the quarter. Low water levels continued into the fourth quarter. As of mid-November, approximately 70% of our river capacity cruise days have been affected and approximately 20% of guests booked on affected itineraries have elected to cancel. Now the quarter is still ongoing, and we are encouraged by the improved weather conditions.

To this end, it remains too early to reliably estimate the ultimate fourth quarter financial impact. Overall, we remain focused on navigating the situation while positioning the business for a strong finish to the year. I now want to provide some additional context on how we supported guests affected by these disruptions as there are 2 distinct types of vouchers with different financial implications. You can see this on Slide 9. For certain guests who elected to cancel a disrupted sailing, we issued vouchers equal to the amount they had paid for their cruise. As of November 8, 2026, we have issued approximately $165 million of these vouchers.

It is important to note that the financial impact of the guest cancellations is reflected in the period of the guest's scheduled sailing. Accordingly, the impact from cancellations of the third quarter sailings, which equated to approximately $100 million, has already been reflected in our 2026 results, including the related revenue and Adjusted Gross Margin impacts described earlier. To this end, the vouchers issued to those guests should not be viewed as having an additional financial impact other than described nor in future seasons. I would like to highlight that more than 60% of these guests who had canceled have already rebooked a cruise.

Notably, the vast majority chose a 2027 river itinerary, underscoring our belief that river cruising is a very appealing way to travel. Separately, guests who chose to travel despite a disrupted sailing received a Future Cruise Voucher, or FCV, as a goodwill gesture. These goodwill vouchers are issued for a specified dollar amount depending on the level of disruption experienced and can be applied toward a new booking made within 1 year of issuance for any itinerary available for sale at time of booking. For reporting purposes, when one of these FCVs is applied, the value is reflected as a reduction to river Advance Bookings for the applicable season, regardless of which Viking product the guest ultimately books.

As of November 8, 2026, we have issued approximately $265 million of these goodwill FCVs. Notably, 50% have already been redeemed and approximately 60% of them were applied toward travel in the 2027 season. As previously noted, the value of the FCVs applied for the 2027 season are a reduction to 2027 river Advance Bookings regardless of the Viking product the guest ultimately books. We view these vouchers as an investment in our guests and the Viking brand. Moreover, we are encouraged by the strong redemption rates, which demonstrate continued guest loyalty and confidence in Viking.

We believe that recognizing our guest experience, maintaining their trust and encouraging them to travel with Viking again is the right long-term decision and will support repeat business over time. Now I will briefly discuss year-to-date metrics for the 9 months ended September 30, which are on Slide 10. Overall, the resilience of our business model is reflected in the year-to-date performance with consolidated Adjusted Gross Margin increasing to $3.5 billion, up 11.3%, and Net Yield equal to $621, increasing 4%. In the River segment, Capacity PCDs increased 5.4% year-over-year and Occupancy for the period was 91.3%. Adjusted Gross Margin increased 1.9% year-over-year to $1.4 billion. As a result, Net Yield was $599, up 1.6% year-over-year.

For Ocean, Capacity PCDs increased 9.8% year-over-year and Occupancy for the period was 96%. Adjusted Gross Margin increased 16.6% year-over-year to $1.8 billion, while Net Yield increased 5.5% to $624. Now moving to the balance sheet. On Slide 11, you can see that as of September 30, 2026, we had total cash and cash equivalents of $4.1 billion. We had an undrawn revolver facility of $1.0 billion. Our Net Debt was $2.3 billion, and our Net Leverage was 1.2x. Also on Slide 11, we show our bond maturity outlook with maturities in 2028 and beyond. I would like to briefly touch on capital return.

During the third quarter, Viking returned $350 million to shareholders through share repurchases under the Board's previously announced $1.0 billion authorization. We believe this authorization reflects confidence in the long-term outlook for our business and provides flexibility to return capital to shareholders while continuing to invest in our fleet and pursue growth opportunities. With this, I'd like to confirm our debt amortization for 2026 and 2027. As of September 30, 2026, the scheduled principal payments for the remainder of 2026 were $94 million and $233 million for full year 2027. From a committed capital expenditure perspective and for full year 2026, the total expected committed ship CapEx is about $2.0 billion, or $750 million net of financing.

And for the full year 2027, the total expected committed ship CapEx is about $1.0 billion, or $300 million net of financing. Let's now talk about the booking curves, which are all as of November 8, 2026. On Slide 13, we show our consolidated metrics for our Core Products. Turning first to 2026, our Core Products are now 93% booked with Advance Bookings of $6.2 billion, which is 11% higher than the 2025 season at the same point in time. The 2026 season is mostly sold out. Nevertheless, when compared to our last earnings release, Advance Bookings declined, primarily reflecting guest cancellations related to low water levels in the River segment. Turning to 2027.

Overall, we are encouraged by the underlying demand environment. Capacity for the Core Products is expected to grow approximately 15% year-over-year, and we have already booked approximately 68% of the inventory, representing $5.8 billion of Advance Bookings. Now I will talk about the advance bookings curves for the segments. On the next slide, you will see our curves for Ocean Cruises, which look very good. This is Slide 14. I will begin with the yellow line, which represents bookings for 2026. Overall, we have sold 96% of our Capacity PCDs for the year.

Advance Bookings are 17% higher than they were at the same point in time last year, and rates have remained very strong, equal to $765 compared to $717 last year. Now if you look at the purple line, you will see the booking trend for the 2027 season. As you can see, we are in very good shape, too. Ocean capacity is projected to increase by 18% year-over-year and approximately 77% of that capacity has already been booked. This represents approximately $3.2 billion in Advance Bookings at average rates of $873 compared with $785 at the same point for the 2026 season.

Given the significant increase in capacity, being in this booked position is a clear testament to the continued strength of demand for our ocean itineraries and the appeal of the Viking brand. If we move to Slide 15, you will see the curves for the River segment. I will start with the yellow line, which graphs the Advance Bookings for 2026. Advance Bookings for 2026 totaled approximately $2.8 billion, reflecting a decline from the level reported at our last earnings update. As noted earlier, this was driven by guest cancellations related to low water levels. Overall rates for the 2026 season remained strong as they equal $871 compared to $820 at the same point in the 2025 season.

Now let's turn to the purple line, which reflects Advance Bookings for the 2027 river season. As of November 8, we had booked 56% of the river capacity, which is growing approximately 13% year-over-year. Advance Bookings totaled $2.2 billion with rates equal to $957 compared to $919 at the same point in the 2026 season. As previously mentioned, Advance Bookings for River includes the goodwill FCVs that have already been applied for the 2027 season regardless of the product ultimately booked by the guest. Now beyond the impact of the FCVs, the low water disruption also affected our normal booking cadence for Rhine, Main and Danube itineraries.

This is not surprising given the unprecedented duration, severity and geographic breadth of the conditions experienced across these rivers. Importantly, we have always viewed our advance bookings curves as a key Viking advantage. As of early November, we are already 56% booked for the 2027 season, even as capacity grows 13%. This level of forward visibility gives us time and flexibility to manage through periods of disruption. Overall, the business remains very healthy with the first half of the 2027 season already well sold. And as noted before, we are very encouraged by the recent improvement in weather patterns and water levels in Central Europe.

Strong demand across our offerings, combined with the resilience provided by our diversified operating platform and highly loyal guest base, continues to support our long-term growth outlook. Now Leah will add some color to our order book and capacity.

Leah Talactac: Thank you, Linh. Xian Siew Hew Sam: Okay. Understood. That makes sense. Leah Talactac: Yes, sure. Brandt Montour: Okay. That's helpful. And then maybe just a question on the way that your customers are behaving in this period with the disruption. And I guess for Ocean specifically, it does -- it seems like the booking -- advance bookings per PCD slowed a little bit there and the bookings that you've added since the last quarter, by our math was a little softer. Is that mix, softer pricing environment? Or is the river guests moving to Ocean having an impact there?

Linh Banh: Sean, so as we noted in the call, as our guests utilize the goodwill voucher, the voucher will impact the revenue for Rivers for that particular season. And so I think Steve asked earlier, directionally speaking, if we exclude the goodwill voucher impact for 2027 season for Rivers, it would be higher, obviously. I think Steve mentioned 6% to 7%, which is directionally accurate. As it relates to Ocean, I think we went from 11% to 9% ahead year-over-year from the last earnings call to this earnings call. That's just the natural progression of the curve. It really is dependent on what we've sold to date, what we have remaining to sell.

That being said, I think the price increase for '27 with the capacity increase for oceans is a very nice position to be in.

Sean Wagner: Okay. And I guess you've adjusted some Christmas market itineraries despite what appears to be the forecast improving for water levels. Is that just precautionary? Or do you expect there to still be some disruptions to sailings in the fourth quarter?

Leah Talactac: I think this was an effort to be more transparent with our guests. That adjustment was made. Of course, when this adjustment was made, we did not -- there was -- it's hard to predict weather patterns, right? And so when we made that adjustment, it was in an effort to be more transparent with our guests because we understand that people like to plan and people like to know what to expect and to give people choice. Having said that, we are glad it's raining.

We are glad that the other Christmas market itineraries will be operating as planned, and we are glad that the other river cruise itineraries that are currently operating are operating with either no or very minimal disruptions.

Operator: Your next question is coming from Lizzie Dove from Goldman Sachs.

Elizabeth Dove: I guess on that topic, we're kind of several months into this now. So I'm just wondering what your kind of learnings have been from all of this? Any changes you've been making to your approach, be that in terms of voucher percentage that's issued, cost management, some proactive deployment changes? And when you're thinking about all of that in the context of Q4 and next year, what you're kind of assuming might be within that low to mid-singles, the ultimate kind of voucher issuance by year-end, I guess?

Leah Talactac: Yes. Thanks for the question, Lizzie. So our fleet has been designed with the identical ships and the 2 ships operating starting from opposing endpoints, they are really designed to be able to operate within normal low or high water conditions. And so we still remain convicted that, that is an appropriate strategy for the varying water levels. Having said that, we do have a vast network of operators within the region so that if we do need to make adjustments outside of the ship swaps, we can do that fairly quickly. And I think that's one of the advantages of the fact that we own and operate our vessels. We control the entire guest experience from beginning to end.

And we're able to even modify itineraries if the pivot would be would be of a lesser experience, we're able to even pivot where we would take guests to destinations that they wouldn't have expected. For example, in the Rhine Getaway, we took them to Luxembourg and Brussels, which was a great surprise and people really enjoyed that. And having said that, I think with the fact that we are now taking options for 10 additional Longships also for Central Europe, we remain convicted in just the overall demand for river cruising, and we don't see any real disruption to the long-term the long-term strength of this particular way of traveling.

And there was another part of your question, Lizzie, that I think I forgot. Can you remind me what it is?

Elizabeth Dove: Yes, I can use this as my follow-up because I asked a lot there. But I'm just wondering if you could put a finer point on what you're assuming in terms of kind of future cruise credits that will be issued by year-end when you're thinking about that low single digit to mid-single digit for next year and what you're kind of factoring in there, I guess, in terms of number of FCVs and redemption patterns.

Leah Talactac: Okay. Now you triggered -- so our learnings. I think that was one of your questions is what are our learnings. So our learnings is that early communication, giving guest choice, really informing them what to expect, I think, goes a long way in maintaining trust in the brand and also supporting quality scores. So we've seen that once we started more transparent communication with our guests and kind of keeping that touch point with them, our NPS increased from the first maybe, let's call it, 2 to 3 weeks in July when the disruptions began. And at that point, it was really difficult for us to ascertain what is the severity of this disruption because it was so early.

But as it became more obvious that the disruption would be more impactful than prior seasons, then we adjusted. As far as FCVs are concerned, I think Linh alluded to the fact that those adjust up and down depending on how impacted guests were. So this year, we gave some, in some cases, 50%, 60% for those guests who were impacted more severely. What is more severe? It could be more than one or multiple ship swaps. It could be the length of any coaching that they may have to do. For those guests who were moderately or not really impacted, we gave less FCVs. And I think that strategy remains a good one for us.

And as we start to see river cruising kind of return back to normal, in some cases, our ships are operating end-to-end now. So there would not be FCVs given to those guests. For some guests who maybe may be impacted slightly, we would reduce the FCVs down.

Operator: Your next question is coming from Trey Bowers from Wells Fargo.

Raymond Bowers: One kind of micro question and then more of a macro question. But on the short term, I just want to make sure everybody has the numbers right. When you guys are talking to an LS low single-digit to mid-single-digit number, that's more specific to '27 and kind of a post-cruise credit impacted number. And related to that, is the longer-term expectation of the algorithm still more of a mid-single-digit number going forward?

Linh Banh: Trey, that's right. I think for 2027, we are being mindful of the vouchers that we have issued thus far that would be applied to 2027 if the guest chooses to rebook '27. As we look forward, we have a lot of conviction in the business. You can see from our order book, we placed more Longship orders. We have more options. We have obviously all of our order book for Oceans and Expeditions as well. So with that, I think our goal will always remain mid-single-digit yield growth for the long term.

Raymond Bowers: And then kind of longer term, just in terms of capital allocation, great to see you guys were pretty active in the quarter with the buyback. As you think about that going forward, though, you guys are still very free cash flow positive and that cash is going to continue to pile up. So is this just the first stage of maybe a more concerted effort to start using your cash to buy back? Or do you expect it to be more taking advantage of kind of dislocation in the stock price going forward?

Leah Talactac: Okay. Thanks, Trey, for the question. So the share -- you're right. So we did buy back some shares. We bought $350 million of them through share repurchases. Our share repurchase strategy or our approach to it is consistent with our broader capital allocation philosophy. So our first priority, it remains investing in the business and pursuing attractive growth opportunities that we believe will create long-term shareholder value. And at the same time, given our cash generation and balance sheet, we believe share repurchase can be an attractive use of excess capital. Having said that, we do intend to be disciplined and opportunistic about our share repurchases.

The authorization that the Board gave us for up to $1 billion gives us flexibility, but it's not really a commitment to repurchase a specific amount of time with a specific time frame. I think we will continually evaluate our share repurchase program against other opportunities to deploy capital. But again, it's really -- our objective is straightforward: allocate capital where we believe it will generate the best long-term returns for our shareholders.

Operator: Your next question is coming from Andrew Didora from Bank of America.

Andrew Didora: Just a couple more questions here on the vouchers and book position. I guess first, just given your experience with these vouchers, would you expect '27 or 2028 to be the most impacted from your consumers' rebooking decision? It certainly seems like it would be '27, but just want to get your thoughts on that. And then second, I know it's hard to parse out the impact here, but could you tell if there was any -- if any of the river booking decel came from some of the political instability in Europe? Like was there a blip in bookings when a lot of the protests were at peak? Or just curious what you saw around that.

Linh Banh: Andrew, so as -- I'll take your first question first. As it relates to the goodwill vouchers, so as of early November, already 50% redeemed. And of that 50%, 60% redeemed for the 2027 season. So just where we're seeing the numbers to date, I think that is where we would say that at least half or more than half has already applied it for '27 season. Our hope is that our guests do use the goodwill vouchers. I think from our perspective, we want our guests to return, and we want them to have a great experience. That's what builds guest loyalty and also repeat rates. So from our perspective, that would be a great thing.

And the strong redemption rates thus far is very encouraging. As it relates to demand, I think it is a little too hard for us to say whether or not the few days or that week of instability in Europe had an impact. This is where we go back to our booking curves and how advanced they are and how much of an advantage we feel that is. It gives us time and flexibility. And so now as we look into 2027 with the first half well sold, our goal, of course, is to sell out the second half and have a good year for '27 as well.

Leah Talactac: And I think it's important to also when you take a look at the booking curves, Ocean is 77% sold already for the 2027 season. So while there is -- there could have been impact. It's a little hard to untangle it given all of the things that occurred this year. When you look at Ocean being 77% sold relative to River at 56%, I think there is some extrapolation that could be done there. We're not being entirely specific because, again, it's hard to extrapolate given everything that's happening. But the 77% sold in Ocean shows that despite what is happening, guests are continuing to look forward to traveling in 2027.

And again, with the 56% in River, most of that is the first half of 2027, that gives us time to finish up the second half in the next few months.

Operator: Our next question is coming from Stephen Grambling from Morgan Stanley.

Stephen Grambling: When you look back at prior windows where you had vouchers given out, I'm curious how close-in pricing and onboard spending may have changed in the subsequent years when they were used. And really, the heart of the question is whether you see incremental demand from customers rebooking or even if customers actually plan around a set dollar amount to spend on their vacations. So perhaps these vouchers just end up being leveraged to upgrade cabins or reinvest into excursions.

Linh Banh: Stephen, I think it's kind of hard for us to say either way, but our belief is that when a guest does have a voucher, depending on the value, they do upgrade and/or add additional ancillary revenue. As you know, we have a lot of choice as it relates to shore excursions, pre and post extensions. And so our hope is that our guests return with these vouchers and they augment their cruise because as we've said in the past, when a guest does augment their cruise, we do see that quality scores are higher as well.

Stephen Grambling: Got it. Maybe just a very quick follow-up would just be if you can remind us maybe how many guests kind of sail with you typically every year versus every other year versus new to cruise.

Linh Banh: So I think your question relates to our past passenger repeat rate versus new-to-brand. Obviously, that is -- we try to balance the 2 because we need new-to-brand to come in to become a past guest, right? And so for the 2027 season, our past guest repeat rate was about 52%, 53%, which we feel is a really good rate, especially with the order book and the capacity growth that we have had in the past and what we have coming up in the coming future.

Operator: I will now turn the conference back over to Torstein Hagen, Viking's Chairman, for closing remarks.

Torstein Hagen: Well, thank you. I want to thank you very much for attending this earnings call after an interesting quarter. But I think when you see the position we are in, we feel very good about it. You see we are ordering ships, rivers and oceans. We have options. We have a strong balance sheet. And above all, we have satisfied customers. So I think we are in excellent shape for moving onwards. Thank you very much.

Operator: Thank you. This does conclude today's conference call. You may disconnect at this time, and have a wonderful day. Thank you once again for your participation.

#3033. iPhone Duo 2 prototypes suggest Face ID, Action Button, other potential 2027 features

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

With manufacturing deadlines looming, it's unclear which of several feature upgrades may have to wait until the foldable's third generation.

Although the iPhone Duo was released just this fall, Apple is finalizing the foldable’s second generation. According to a Bloomberg report, Apple has already created prototypes for the second iPhone Duo, codenamed V78, and some include a sought-after feature: Face ID.

Apple reportedly wants to bring Face ID to the foldable, potentially integrating it into the outer display. However, Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman notes that Apple appears to be running out of time to finalize its plans for the Duo ahead of a fall 2027 launch.

Also: iPhone Duo review: Hard to recommend, even harder to put down

iPhone launch events typically take place in early September, when Apple releases its new smartphone lineups. To have the iPhones ready for sale on the heels of their announcement, Apple must manufacture the new models well before the launch event.

Because of this timeline concern, Face ID isn’t guaranteed for the iPhone Duo 2, though it could come to a third generation instead.

Other planned uogrades — including an Action Button, a telephoto camera, and a thinner, lighter construction — are also noted in the report.

Apple reportedly wants to add an Action Button, the customizable button that performs an action when pressed. The iPhone Duo 2 may combine the Action Button and the Camera Control buttons into a single button, providing a useful physical shortcut instead of adding a new button.

The report indicates that many users don’t use the camera control button as often as Apple expected. Combining the camera and action buttons gives Apple the real estate necessary to add both options in an already constrained space.

Apple also wants to incorporate a telephoto camera into the iPhone Duo, though this is likely to happen in one of the next couple of generations. A telephoto camera would give users greater flexibility to zoom in and capture clear photos of distant objects, which would be an upgrade to the Duo’s photography features.

Technically, equipping the Duo with a telephoto camera is feasible, but the biggest obstacle is space constraints. A telephoto camera needs more room than a wide-angle one, since it requires additional optical elements to magnify distant objects.

Apple already uses a tetraprism design in its Pro iPhones, which allows a longer optical path without too much physical depth.

Apple also wants to reduce the weight and thickness of the iPhone Duo, which is legitimately clunky and cumbersome. To do this, Apple needs to balance the large internal and outer displays, battery capacity, camera array, and the hinge mechanism.

Also: The iPhone Action Button you’re hardly using has a superpower

For many users, reducing the weight and thickness of a passport-sized foldable could matter more in buying decisions than adding another button or camera.

Gurman’s latest report doesn’t mention any planned changes for the iPhone Duo’s hinge mechanism, even after concerns with the first generation’s durability. With manufacturing deadlines fast approaching, however, it’s unlikely that Apple will be able to make changes to the Duo 2 based on consumer feedback. More than likely, these changes would come with the third-generation model.

CNET tested the iPhone Duo’s hinge mechanism and found that, after around 440,000 cycles, the hinge stopped opening flat on its own. Loosening and other signs of wear were evident after 390,000 folds.

Also: The best iPhone Duo cases: Expert recommended

Given the thinner, lighter construction of a future Duo model, one could assume that changes to the hinge and the foldable’s internal structure are imminent, but this has not been confirmed.

Because Apple will not have enough time to gather feedback on the iPhone Duo before the manufacturing deadlines for the iPhone Duo 2, I don’t expect the second-generation iPhone Duo to be significantly different from its predecessor. We do expect a thinner iPhone Duo 2 and a way to incorporate the Action and Camera buttons.

#3032. Oura Ring Adds a Jet Lag Feature for Time Zone Travelers

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Traveling to new places is good for the soul, but then there’s jet lag, which can cause fatigue, headaches, insomnia and even nausea during your trip. Oura, maker of the Oura Ring, wants to help you combat these effects with its latest feature, Jet Lag Plan, which launched on Tuesday.

A press release explained that Jet Lag Plan was developed using a March 2025 study conducted by the National University of Singapore. The study analyzed de-identified data covering 1.5 million nights of sleep from over 57,000 Oura members to determine how sleep shifted before and after about 65,000 long-distance trips.

Jet Lag Plan is specifically designed for users who travel across at least three time zones and is based on typical sleep patterns, flight itinerary and chronotype. The latter describes whether you’re a morning person, a night person or somewhere in between.

Oura uses 40 to 90 days of sleep timing and activity and average body temperature trends to assign users one of six chronotypes: early morning type, morning type, late morning type, early evening type, evening type and late evening type. This can change over time.

Both your chronotype and sleep history also inform your circadian low point. Usually around 4 a.m., this is when your body temperature is at its lowest and you’re the most ready for sleep.

In the Oura app, you can start a Jet Lag Plan in one of four ways: by adding travel from the Today tab, selecting “Jet Lag” from the app menu, asking the AI-powered Oura Advisor to create a plan for your upcoming trip or responding to a prompt when Oura detects that your phone has changed time zones.

In addition to your flight details, you’ll also want to share the reason for your trip, as a work-related Jet Lag Plan will differ from a vacation one.

Your Jet Lag Plan will then populate with a recommended schedule for sleep, caffeine, activity and light exposure before, during and after your trip, with reminders and the ability to mark actions as complete. You can request adjustments to this plan using Oura Advisor.

During your trip, you’ll be able to compare your readiness score to the typical score for similar trips. This is based on data from 10 million trips already taken by Oura members.

Once your trip ends, you’ll receive a report comparing your sleep and readiness scores before and during your trip.

Jet Lag Plan is now available to Oura members whose language is set to English. It works with an Oura Ring 3 or newer on both Android and iOS.

The latest Oura Ring 5 starts at $399, while a membership is $6 per month or $70 per year.

#3031. Opera (OPRA) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Advertising growth and a new local AI push shaped the quarter.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Opera (OPRA -7.99%) reported third-quarter financial results that met or exceeded management's previous guidance, driven by growth in both advertising and search query segments. The company is transitioning its listing from American Depositary Shares to ordinary shares on the NASDAQ to lower holder fees and improve eligibility for various equity indices. Strategic focus remains on integrating artificial intelligence natively into the browser architecture, specifically through local inference capabilities and agentic tools. Management indicated that the advertising business is diversifying its vertical mix, with gaming and travel increasingly contributing to the top line alongside the primary e-commerce segment.

Operator: Welcome to the Opera Limited Third Quarter 2026 Earnings Call. [Operator Instructions] Please be advised that today's call is being recorded. [Operator Instructions] I would now like to turn the call over to your speaker today, Jake Graves, Head of Investor Relations. You may begin.

Jake Graves: Thank you, operator, and thank you all for joining us. Today, I am joined by our CEO, Song Lin; and our CFO, Frode Jacobsen. Before we begin, I would like to remind you that some of the statements made today regarding our business, operations and financial performance may be considered forward-looking. Such statements are based on current expectations and assumptions that are subject to a number of risks and uncertainties. Actual results could differ materially as a result of various factors, including those set forth in today's earnings press release and in our most recent annual report on Form 20-F filed with the SEC. We undertake no obligation to update any forward-looking statement.

During this call, we will present both IFRS and non-IFRS financial measures. A reconciliation of IFRS to non-IFRS measures is included in today's earnings press release. The earnings press release and our investor presentation are available on our Investor Relations website at investor.opera.com. Comparisons to prior periods will be on a year-over-year basis, unless stated otherwise. With that, let me turn the call over to our CEO, Song Lin, who will cover our operational highlights and strategy; and then our CFO, Frode Jacobsen, who will discuss the details of our financial results and expectations. Song?

Lin Song: Sure. Thank you, Jake, and thanks to everyone for joining us today. Last quarter, we talked about both the resilience and opportunity that comes with our position as an independent, well-established and innovative browser provider. Q3 further validated this. In a time when Internet search is evolving with monetization catching up, we are generating healthy query revenue growth from connecting users with partners that are relevant for their intentions. And in a time when e-commerce platforms are adapting to new regulations, we are generating healthy advertising revenue growth through an always broadening partnership base. In sum, Opera continues to deliver strong financial results.

For over 30 years, Opera has been guided by a simple principle, the browser should serve the user. This principle has shaped everything we have built from early innovations like tabs and space to the free built-in VPN to products designed for specific audiences such as Opera GX. As AI changes everyday tasks and workflows and the landscape of tools and services for them, we believe our position as a leading independent browser company becomes increasingly valuable. The range of AI use cases is vast, spanning personal and professional life from supporting human judgment and creativity to carrying out complex work.

Different users want different levels of assistance and may rely on several AI sources as their preferences and habits change. For many use cases, the browser is the natural place to utilize AI assistance. At Opera, we have been working hard to facilitate native integration of AI tools from our own Opera AI and its agentic browsing capabilities to support the connections with the largest AI tools and model providers. While most browsers restrict users to one model provider or their own cloud service, Opera browsers offer users optionality across their preferred models. Earlier this year, we shipped Browser Connector, which connects Claude, ChatGPT and other agentic models directly to our browsers.

With such great benefits, one might ask, why doesn't everyone use local AI today? The answer is the complexity of setting it up. Docker installation, specific model downloads, terminal commands, et cetera, get in the way. However, with the launch of Opera's WebAI, users are now able to access open-weight models on their machine with a simple toggle. WebAI is an evolving standard backed by industrial-leading open-weight model providers. It gives websites and extensions access to local models through the browser, allowing developers to add AI features without operating their own AI infrastructure. We are also releasing example extensions to demonstrate what developers can build with users controlling which websites may access their local models.

Cloud-based models will continue to be important for the most demanding tasks. However, we see local AI and cloud intelligence developing together with the browser enabling users to benefit from both. And over the months ahead, you will see us expand these capabilities. As we develop more products that leverage local AI and agentic tools, our unwavering focus is to help users take full advantage of this new technology by bringing together leading models with the context and utility of the browser. Shifting to our results. We continue to see solid progress in our advertising business, which grew 22% in Q3 as we expand our capabilities as well as number of clients we serve.

We have adapted well to evolving conditions and opportunities across our markets and partnerships, allowing us to continue growing e-commerce as our single largest vertical while also driving high relative growth in travel and rapidly scaling gaming to become a material contributor. Opera Ads is our advertising and monetization platform that combines our own inventory and hundreds of millions of users with audiences reached through third-party inventory. By combining our strong first-party data asset from our browsers and modeling of it, we deliver strong ROI performance to many of the largest advertisers in the world. As we look to increase the performance of Opera Ads, cross-channel capabilities are an important area of focus.

This year, we are seeing encouraging signs from newly adapted CTV inventory through an audience extension. While it's solid, we are observing strong campaign performance, especially as advertisers deploy a cross-channel approach. CTV represents a premium, highly engaged audience that provides a strong complement to our current omnichannel. Our strong growth speaks to Opera's differentiated advertising platform and our ability to drive incrementality for our partners. As we continue to recursively improve our targeting and measurement capabilities, I expect ROI on our platform to continue to increase. In Q3, our query revenue grew 17% year-over-year, reflecting the resilience of our business model and growth in key developed markets.

While traditional search remains a core part of revenue, browser recommendations and AI conversations are creating new avenues for query growth. This revenue category directly captures the traffic monetization potential of increased engagement in our browsers with native AI functionalities benefiting both time spent and the browser's ability to connect the right partners with our users at the right time. Our commerce platform integrates merchant product information into relevant browser experience, helping users discover and compare products closer to a purchase decision. Direct integrations give us access to information such as product descriptions, images and prices, so recommendations can be useful within the browsing experience.

Switching to MiniPay, our self-custodial stablecoin wallet simplifies holding and transferring of digital dollars with local payment connections and card functionality adding practical ways to use them. That can mean sending money to family abroad or use a balance to pay locally while traveling. As of Q3, MiniPay had over 20 million activated wallets and processed nearly 600 million cumulative transactions. Building on strong user momentum, MiniPay now features frictionless deposits via Stripe. Users can instantly top up their accounts using a card, Apple Pay or Google Pay through a familiar experience trusted by over 300 million people.

This integration with Stripe makes it easier for users in the U.S. and Europe to get started with MiniPay and marks the beginning of a broader collaboration. Today, MiniPay is generating revenue through integrating and promoting partners within the ecosystem. Over time, we believe broad usage and additional services can support transaction and service-based revenue. This is how we see MiniPay developing into a larger business, a platform that attracts users efficiently and offers a range of valuable services to them. For now, our focus is adoption and utility while continuing to develop unique opportunities for monetization. Finally, turning to our user base.

While the third quarter is always affected by summer holiday seasonality, especially in Europe, we continue to see strong user growth in high ARPU markets and products. In Western markets, we added 1 million MAUs year-over-year in Q3. For Opera GX, we added over 4 million MAUs year-over-year in Q3. And as we've embarked on Q4, our recent user updates point to a very strong post-summer season with new records across our key platforms. I want to congratulate our PC team on reaching the major milestone of 100 million monthly active users in October, which represents 16% year-over-year growth. On the mobile side, we are pleased to report that Opera One for iOS grew 20% in October.

This success of our browsers and the strong engagement we have with our community reinforces our conviction in building compelling alternatives to default browsers. Opera One, GX, Mini and Neon solve different needs on the shared browser foundation. By developing differentiated experiences, we are serving our users to the fullest extent. Across the business, we are investing in capabilities that can strengthen user relationships and expand monetization while sustaining healthy profitability. Frode will now discuss our financial results, capital allocation and outlook. Frode?

Frode Jacobsen: Thanks, Song. As previewed a couple of weeks ago, we are pleased to report yet another quarter at the top end of guidance, which allows us to nudge up our full year revenue guidance even further while still maintaining appropriate caution and room to invest in growth initiatives for the near term. Revenue in Q3 was $182.8 million, representing growth of 20% year-over-year. We continue to observe strong user dynamics across key products and geographies, and our Opera Ads platform scaled particularly well in both high-value U.S. and fast-growing Asia. This led to an even stronger ARPU growth of 22%. Advertising revenue was $116.8 million, up 22%.

We have adapted well to evolving conditions and opportunities across our markets and partnerships. As a browser company with a massive O&O reach, we continue to focus on verticals with the most natural integration opportunities. E-commerce continues to represent our largest vertical, while gaming is also becoming a material contributor. We continue to see strong potential for both of these verticals as well as travel, which is already impressive on a relative basis, though growing from a smaller base. Query revenue was $65 million, up 17%. We benefit from the continued mix shift toward a higher engagement user base and a continued broadening of the category as nonsearch query benefits from addressing user intent.

Over the medium and long term, we expect to increasingly benefit from AI-generated search responses as search partners monetize them at higher rates. Adjusted EBITDA was $43.2 million, representing a 24% margin, both just above the top end of guidance. Cost of revenue items totaled $74.1 million, representing 40.5% (sic) [ 41% ] of revenue as Opera Ads continued to scale with revenue reaching the high end of guidance. As a reminder, while Opera Ads carries a higher cost of revenue profile, it also requires a few additional operating expenses and drives healthy incremental profitability to our overall business. Marketing expense in Q3 was $36 million, flat versus both the prior year and the prior quarter.

Cash-based compensation was $20.7 million, in line with the prior year and 10% down versus the prior quarter, which included accelerated bonus accruals. Other operating expenses before adjusted EBITDA also came in according to indications at approximately $9 million. Net income was $27.6 million with diluted EPS of $0.30, up 49% year-over-year and benefiting from a full reversal of the Q2 impairment of nonfinancial assets, specifically a result of the market value fluctuations of the Celo community grants we received earlier this year. Adjusted net income was $30.1 million or 17% of revenue. Adjusted diluted earnings per share was $0.34, growing 16% year-over-year in the quarter and 23% year-to-date.

Operating cash flow was $37.4 million in Q3, representing 87% of adjusted EBITDA or 80% year-to-date. Free cash flow from operations was $32.6 million or 75% conversion of adjusted EBITDA in the quarter and 67% year-to-date. While we will always see fluctuations in cash conversion between quarters, both cash flow metrics in Q3 strengthened the year-to-date ratios as expected and the lean capital requirements of our operating model continue to benefit us. Then turning to capital allocation. During Q3, we paid the July installation of our semiannual dividend of $0.40 per share, totaling $35.6 million.

We also repurchased 2 million shares for $37.7 million, reducing the number of shares outstanding by 2.2% during the quarter to $86.95 million as of September 30. The resulting total shareholder returns in the quarter amounted to $73.3 million. Since the start of our share repurchase program in March, we have repurchased a total of 3.8 million shares for $66 million at an average price of $17.33 per share. Taken together with our January and July dividends, year-to-date shareholder returns then amounts to $137 million. We ended September with cash of $109 million and no debt. As a browser, we are in a great position to benefit from advances in AI without reliance on major CapEx investments.

That model gives us operational flexibility and is what allows us to combine healthy growth with returning capital to shareholders at such a high ratio. Now turning to our updated guidance. We are pleased to translate the continued momentum in our business into a reconfirmation of our most recent full year guidance with a further upward nudge of the low end of our revenue range. Taken together with the significant increases in guidance earlier this year, our final 2026 guidance ranges for both revenue and adjusted EBITDA now have low ends starting at their original high ends. For the full year 2026, we expect revenue of $735 million to $742 million, representing 20% year-over-year growth at the midpoint.

The range reflects our ability to deliver at or above the high end of quarters to date and our ongoing expansion of monetization partners and formats, though still preserving an appropriate caution given the broader monetization environment. For adjusted EBITDA, we continue to expect $172 million to $175 million, representing a 23.5% margin for the full year. For the fourth quarter, this translates to revenue of $198 million to $205 million or 14% growth at the midpoint. As a reminder, we are lapping 2 strong periods of growth in both Q4 2024 and Q4 2025, evidenced by the far above average sequential growth in those periods when we scaled e-commerce to become the most significant advertising vertical.

You might remember that Q4 2025 revenue came in $12 million or about 7% above the high end of our guidance. This year, we forecast a more normal seasonality profile with Q4 guidance implying 8% to 12% sequential growth from the third quarter, in line with the 3-year average prior to 2024 and representing the strongest sequential growth of 2026. Looking across a multiyear period, the Q4 guidance corresponds to a 3-year CAGR of 21%, same as it was for Q3. For adjusted EBITDA, we expect $44 million to $47 million, representing a 23% margin at the midpoint.

In Q4, we benefit from the strong advertising seasonality with cost of revenue representing a larger part of the quarterly cost mix as a result. We will also take the opportunity to invest in new gaming clients and new sources of third-party inventory like CTV to establish additional growth vectors in 2027. With that at the new midpoint, we expect cost of revenue items to increase by 5 to 6 percentage points to represent about 46% of revenue in Q4 or just over 40% for the year as a whole. We expect marketing spend to reduce somewhat, resulting in low single-digit annual growth and representing just below 20% of full year revenue.

Cash-based compensation expense is expected to continue reducing relative to Q3 with annual growth in the high single digits and representing below 12% of full year revenue. To sum of all other OpEx items, pre-adjusted EBITDA is expected to remain quite stable at about 5% of revenue for both the quarter and the year as a whole. In sum, cash-based compensation and marketing will then decline from representing 36% of revenue last year to representing about 31% of revenue this year, supported by economies of scale and the inflow of revenue from Opera Ads that carries cost of revenue but limited incremental OpEx.

This enables us to guide to an increase in adjusted EBITDA margin relative to 2025 of about 30 basis points. And finally, the fact that we were once again able to deliver results at the top of expectations and extend our elevated guidance in a period with monetization adaptations, both within Internet search and e-commerce also points to some potential future tailwinds as they renormalize. Before we move to Q&A, I'll briefly comment on our separate announcement today that Opera is moving from American Depositary Shares or ADSs to ordinary shares listed on NASDAQ.

Listing our ordinary shares makes Opera simpler to own and eliminate the recurring depository fees that ADS holders pay for each of our semiannual dividends and annually for the program itself. By listing ordinary shares, we also remove a barrier for inclusion in certain equity indices and investment funds whose mandates restrict investment in depository shares. Each ADS will be exchanged automatically for 1 ordinary share and no action is needed. The ADSs will trade on NASDAQ until Friday, December 4, and the ordinary shares will begin trading on Monday, December 7, under the same ticker. More details can be found in today's separate press release on the ADS exchange and in the FAQ on our investor website.

All in all, we find ourselves in a great position as we enter the fourth quarter and look ahead to 2027. We are excited about our commercial opportunities as well as the broader strategic picture. With that, I'll turn the call back to the operator for questions.

#3030. 5 ways AI will change how you defend your business in 2027

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Security leaders reveal the future consequences of AI outpacing human defenders.

At the beginning of the year, few organizations were utilizing large language models (LLMs) and AI agents in their cybersecurity workflows, including for discovering and patching vulnerabilities. According to Google, this is now happening at scale.

Also: Rogue AI incidents hit ‘tens of thousands’: Can businesses trust these tools?

The capabilities of agentic AI are fast outstripping the speed and scale at which traditional security operations centers (SOCs) can operate. Like it or not, AI has an integral role in the new reality — for the defenders and threat actors.

Speed and scale are the main reasons enterprises consider adopting AI in SOCs and for security more broadly, and these factors underpin Google’s new security forecast for 2027 — Cloud CISO Perspectives. However, without the right precautions, AI security adopters could inadvertently increase their attack surface rather than shrink it.

With this in mind, these are five ways AI will change the security industry over the next year and what CISOs need to consider going into 2027.

Alert fatigue is well-known across SOC teams. Alert after alert needs to be trawled through; many are irrelevant or false positives, tying up skilled staff with the mundane, tedious, time-consuming task of triaging them.

Now that autonomous, AI-driven threats can probe a network, gain entry, and move laterally across it in minutes, chasing threat data and security alerts from multiple systems logged days or weeks ago can’t help a business mitigate them — and certainly not at the speed of the threat.

According to Google’s forecast, AI will mean the alert queue quietly disappears. Ramya Chitrakar, VP of engineering at Google Cloud Security, believes that “2027 is the year analysts stop chasing alerts and start shaping outcomes.”

Also: AI is both a cyber weapon and a massive target

How? CISOs must change the alert model itself. Instead of human defenders triaging alerts at the start of a cybersecurity incident, the alert becomes final output, with autonomous agents handling “data enrichment, correlation, and triage automatically, surfacing a verified conclusion rather than a raw ticket,” according to Google.

This means cybersecurity experts can oversee alert handling and verify automated actions, potentially freeing them to focus on other tasks.

Custom agentic AI is often designed — or at least intended — to work autonomously, with human oversight. However, having thousands of individual agents working across multiple environments can create high-value entry points into corporate networks that cyberattackers target.

We need to think of agentic AI as more than a tool: each one needs its own identity, like a human employee, to operate within a zero-trust architecture, retain control, and reduce the risk of compromise.

Also: Your enterprise AI access can be sold for pennies – beware ‘LLM Mixers’

However, Heather Adkins, VP of security engineering at Google, thinks this needs to go further and suggests the zero-trust concept shouldn’t stop at the network layer. Instead, Adkins believes it needs to reach the transaction layer.

A paper trail for each agent needs to be established, which is impossible to handle manually, and even within a zero-trust framework, AI agents could be given too much scope. Instead, implement verification for each transaction and for every authorization, and assign each AI agent its own least-privilege set of credentials that can be revoked if there is a security incident or the agent is no longer required.

“When backed by real-time autonomous reasoning, we can dynamically allow a transaction on Tuesday and block the exact same request on Wednesday if conditions look anomalous,” the report notes.

AI is being used to speed up the development and deployment of new software, and in 2027, security will have to become a continuous system embedded in the software delivery pipeline, according to Google.

Threat actors have carried out software supply chain attacks over the years, one of the most notable being the SolarWinds incident of 2020. Sandra Joyce, VP of Google Threat Intelligence, says cybercriminals are now poisoning everything from open-source code to software libraries, which AI coding assistants often pull automatically into codebases.

Also: How AI security failures are endangering your supply chain

Bug-fix tickets that take days to respond to and security appearing at the end of a software development cycle no longer work. Instead, writing and securing code must happen simultaneously, with the help of agentic AI, so speed doesn’t compromise security.

“It’s also crucial that we link live production environments directly back to source code so that defenders can trace a real-world exposure to the exact line of code, validate whether it is genuinely exploitable, and deliver a pre-tested fix at machine speed without breaking production,” Google added.

As organizations rush to implement AI into their applications and services to appear “AI-first,” innovative, and modern, security may be ignored or treated as an afterthought.

As a result, we may face a new, broader attack surface than we realize, as AI introduces new security issues, including software vulnerabilities, misconfiguration, bypasses, and indirect prompt injection attacks. Now that AI is also in the hands of all cyberattackers — from script kiddies to state-sponsored groups — auditing corporate networks and infrastructure is crucial.

Also: Who’s responsible for catching rogue AI agents? You are

Penetration testing and red team exercises now need to cover agentic AI. This wasn’t in scope for many red teams only a few years ago, but now that businesses have run with the idea of implementing AI in their workflows, processes, and products, organizations need to identify and fix security issues introduced by AI before threat actors take advantage of them.

CISOs should task pen testers with auditing before an autonomous workflow hits production, then combine the results with threat intelligence to ensure defenders have the information they need to bolster network defenses and harden classifiers against new and novel attacks.

The final significant trend we are likely to see in 2027 is tackling agent sprawl to create coordinated teams of AI agents that can rapidly handle security tasks at scale.

Single AI agents given general instructions won’t cut it when AI-assisted attackers can compromise endpoint devices, enter networks, move laterally, or start stealing data in a far shorter timeframe than before. Instead, CISOs should replace these “generalist” AI agents with specialized, orchestrated teams of AI agents that can meet the demands of defending against AI-driven attacks by employing specialist tooling and skill sets.

Also: AI agent kill switch urged by Okta-led alliance

CISOs also need to ensure that each agent has its own domain training and understanding, memory, and dedicated tools, and can act on its own within set limits, with a central coordinator that knows when to hand a decision to a human. This requires oversight, but in return, organizations will avoid agent sprawl, which the tech giant believes is the next iteration of shadow IT and its associated threats.
