#3029. Google’s Xreal Aura, Reviewed: The Weird Evolution of VR Into Glasses Is Already Underway

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Tech > Computing > Gadgets > VR/AR Productivity

The most fascinating and frustrating device I've used in a long time pushes at the edges of where headsets are heading, and glasses are evolving.

Let me tell you about a strange, fascinating and rough tweener product called Xreal Aura.

There are VR headsets, and there are smart glasses. And there’s a new class of devices that’s falling right in between. What do we call these things? I have no idea. The category includes the Meta VR Glasses coming next year and now the Aura, a collaboration by Google and Xreal.

The Xreal Aura shoots for the moon, aiming to bridge glasses and VR, and to shrink everything down on the go. It’s often fascinating, and more often frustrating. At times, it almost feels like a VR headset. At other times it feels like a superpowered version of the tethered display glasses that Xreal and several others already make, that act like wearable monitors for your phone or laptop or almost anything else.

I think it’s actually an experimental bridge to a future where phones will play nicer with advanced smart glasses. Those future glasses could create floating displays and workspaces all around you, if you wish. Consider the Aura, in a way, Google’s early attempt to get there.

Emphasis on early. Right now, the Xreal Aura’s features, OS and especially inputs feel rough to use at times and sometimes hard to get into a natural flow with. But it shows what something of this size could be capable of with more software and input-flow tweaks. And when it does work, it feels wildly like a portable VR/AR headset in a way I’ve never really seen before.

The Aura aspires to be a shrunk-down version of last year’s Samsung Galaxy XR, an expensive mixed-reality headset similar to Apple’s Vision Pro. Like the Galaxy XR, the Aura runs Android XR, a variant of Android that floats apps all around. It even runs VR apps. At times it gets close. Other times, it’s not nearly close enough.

What’s wild about the Aura is that it folds down into a case that’s truly small enough to slide into my bag. But setting up and using the Aura often involves patience and experimentation. When it works, it’s a heck of a peek at a future that’s likely around the corner. But the hoops you have to jump through to make it happen sometimes make me want to hop out.

Android XR is Google’s OS for AR/VR/AI devices and wearables, and aims to connect glasses and headsets of all shapes and sizes to Google and Gemini services and apps. The Samsung Galaxy XR, released last year, was the first. Coming up next, in just a few weeks, are Google and Samsung’s Warby Parker- and Gentle Monster-designed AI smart glasses.

The Xreal Aura is more Galaxy XR than smart glasses, in concept: It’s an AR/VR headset that you can take on the go. The glasses connect with a USB-C cable to an included processor puck that runs Android XR. It can display Android apps in both 2D and immersive 3D.

The Aura supports hand tracking and can allow full spatial movement to place floating 3D objects or play immersive games. It can float apps all around you, and you can navigate apps at the same time. You can use hand tracking to open or tap those apps, or a trackpad that’s built into the top of the processor puck. You can also pair a Bluetooth keyboard, or game controller, or a mouse, like I’m doing.

The kit tucks into an included carry case that’s smaller than the one I carry my Nintendo Switch 2 in. It’s easy to pack away for travel. I love this part of the Aura so, so much.

It’s $1,279 for the version with 256GB of storage and 12GB RAM or $1,499 for 512GB/16GB, but it’s on sale until the end of the year for $1,099/$1,299. That onboard storage is all you get, though. There’s no expandable microSD card slot. I reviewed the 256GB version.

The display tech in the Aura is an enhanced version of what’s already on Xreal’s other tethered display glasses, and similar to what Viture and TCL RayNeo use. The twin micro OLED displays are impressively bright and crisp, projected via prisms to look like they’re floating in the room with you. The “birdbath” display tech means the lenses are chunky and odd-looking, but they’re also a lot bigger and better-looking than what’s possible on display-enabled wireless glasses like Meta’s Ray-Ban Displays.

They have a 70-degree field of view, something that beats out previous generations of AR glasses like Magic Leap or the upcoming Snap Specs. The fidelity, although capping at 1,920×1,200 pixels per eye, is also really crisp and great for movie watching or games (up to 120Hz refresh). It’s enough to feel like a big movie screen is projected across the room or to lay out a virtual computer monitor, but there are clear edges where the image is still cut off compared to VR headsets (which tend to have 90 degree or better fields of view).

When running VR apps, which this can shockingly do, the graphics look sharp but narrowly framed. It’s good enough to use VR in a pinch, though: I floated through 3D Immersive Google Maps, dragging and scrolling with my fingers in the air, or played the VR role-playing game Demeo, exploring a tabletop board game dungeon, or played back 360-degree videos on YouTube. But the limits of the viewing field become a lot more stark in these modes, making me wish I had a VR headset instead. Then again, I never travel with VR headsets, and I’d travel with this.

The display’s visuals seemed to tear a few times while playing YouTube videos. Tracking, using the built-in cameras, also sometimes drifted. Mostly, the displays stayed where I put them, but sometimes they’d shift slightly out of alignment.

The processor puck means the Xreal Aura can open up most Android and Chrome-based apps I can think of, but not all of them. The Qualcommm Snapdragon Reality Elite chip on the puck seems more than zippy enough to handle whatever multiple games and apps (even VR ones) I throw at it, but not all Android apps are available: Developers can choose not to opt in, as with Netflix and Disney Plus, but they can be loaded up in-browser.

Other apps aren’t necessarily optimized for the fluid way the Aura can open an app in any size. I watched a Jets game on Paramount Plus on the Aura, and it stayed in a fixed window size. I could move closer or further away, but it wouldn’t enlarge.

The whole Aura interface feels new-ish, even if you’ve used VR. The glasses enable hand tracking that’s surprisingly OK: Tapping and pinching works, and an extended pointer can reach at a distance and click and drag or adjust windows. When my hand passes in front of the Aura’s display, it even gets overlaid with a virtual hand mapped onto mine, like VR.

There’s no eye tracking, though, something Apple Vision Pro, Samsung Galaxy XR and Meta VR Glasses do. Eye tracking is helpful: It means you can lock into something and click it without lifting your hand. Here, I found I had to lift and aim my hand a lot, like an interactive remote. Hand tracking does work somewhat below the display’s field of view, but you often won’t know if you’re interacting until that hand’s lifted up higher. This is where the Aura’s smaller-than-VR viewing area becomes a problem.

It’s particularly an issue when playing some VR games. I tried Synth Riders, a popular fitness music movement game that’s also on Android XR. I could see what was further off in front of me, but the limited viewing area meant my hands were out of sight when in my peripheral vision, so I couldn’t reach for targets near me or off to the sides.

There’s a second way to control Aura: The processor puck itself has a touchpad across its whole top. Hold it and it’s a touch remote: I can drag my finger and touch-click. On a table next to a paired keyboard, it’s a trackpad.

That’s super clever, but the trackpad’s performance ranged from OK to poor depending on the apps I ran. There are some multitouch elements too, but it still felt less effective as a headset control than I wanted.

The puck has discrete volume controls and a power button with a fingerprint sensor for secure logins. But the side button wasn’t always in an easy place to press, depending on how I held the puck.

You could also just use voice to control things: Saying “Hey Google” or launching live Gemini can open apps, handle dictation and feel like a control system of sorts. But Gemini can’t always do things in apps. It’s more of a launcher.

There aren’t a ton of unique immersive Android XR experiences, unfortunately, even a year after the Samsung Galaxy XR debuted. The Aura can technically run almost all of those same apps, including many 2D ones that show up on the Google Play store in-headset. On the plus side, VR apps working at all on glasses this small feels like magic, despite some limits.

Demeo, one of several VR games I found that run on these glasses, looks great and is surprisingly playable. I can cast up a virtual tabletop RPG game in front of me, and my hands bring up cards that I can pick and play on the field. An included Galapagos immersive 3D documentary app looks lovely.

YouTube and Google Maps are once again stars of Android XR, just like they were on Galaxy XR when I reviewed it last year. YouTube has plenty of 3D and 360-degree videos you can view, and Google Maps’ immersive 3D earth modes and, occasionally, 3D scanned interior locations are still great to browse on the Aura’s smaller screens.

I fell in love with a demo of Sock Puppet Superstar, too. It’s a hand-puppet-singing VR game that works well on the Aura.

Mixed reality VR experiences that try to project a few simple things into a room work best, effectively turning the glasses into augmented reality. Cubism, a hand-tracking enabled puzzle game I’ve played on other VR headsets, works well here too. The accuracy of the hand tracking isn’t always great for precision gripping the corners of the virtual floating blocks, though.

The refresh rate on these VR apps isn’t as ultrasmooth as on Quest 3 or Steam Frame, but they do look sharp. Except, as I said before, the viewing area ends up clipped more narrowly, so immersion feels blindered.

Some VR apps didn’t run at all, though. A VR air hockey game on Android XR wouldn’t let me use my hands to control the pucks, for some reason. I know this is a prelaunch review of the Aura, but expect some apps to act oddly. You can sideload APKs of other VR apps, which is great. Google’s AI Studio tools also work in spatial 3D in these glasses, which means you could vibecode experiences on them.

Think of the Aura as a pair of super-powered Xreal glasses with a better viewing area and an included processor puck. Xreal’s existing line of other display glasses float microOLED displays via a USB-C tether in a similar way. The Aura glasses have similar Xreal controls on the arm, but they’re modified to Android XR interface controls that are a little different. There are volume buttons, a button that changes the dimming level of the electrochromic lenses from clear to nearly full black, and a top button that brings up the home app grid when clicked once, or launches live Gemini when held.

There’s also an array of three built-in cameras that handle room tracking, visual awareness for Gemini and hand tracking. Two are in the corners of the frame, one’s above the nose. Xreal’s other glasses, for the most part, are camera-free unless you buy a snap-in module.

The prism-like lenses that reflect the microOLED displays from the top of the frame are flatter like the Xreal One Pro line, and prescription lens inserts snap in the same way – I used the ones from the Pro and they work fine.

The display’s field of view, at 70 degrees, is bigger than Xreal’s largest size on the One Pro (57 degrees), and it feels like a larger projected display in front of me. The resolution is still just the same as Xreal’s other recent glasses, but things still look crisp, even for reading.

Sizewise, they’re like many other tethered glasses: bulkier and weirder than normal glasses, but a lot lighter than any VR headset. Three sets of nosepads are included for fit adjustment, and the arms bend at several angles, too.

I’m writing this review now in the Aura, at my dining room table, with a separately sold folding wireless keyboard made by Xreal. The keyboard performance in Chrome and Docs is fantastic. The trackpad, not quite as much. But I really feel like I can write on this.

Navigating Chrome and work apps also is possible: Logged into my office’s Google-based system, I’ve been handling emails and chats and little needs fine.

Getting files on and off the Aura is the trick. I’m Mac- and iPhone-based, so I’d need to put things in Drive and Google apps to triangulate more easily.

But what’s also impressive is that I can plug in other devices, including my MacBook, and use the Aura as a virtual screen. I can float my MacBook and the Aura apps side by side.

Here’s the catch: My MacBook keyboard only controls my Mac, and the Aura’s keyboard and hand tracking only work for the Aura apps. So I need two keyboards side by side to multitask.

To be clear, no one’s handled handing off of peripherals between connected devices well, not even Apple. But it points to the biggest thorn in Aura’s device-bridging dreams.

Connecting to lots of other devices via the Xreal Aura is a wild experience. You just need to cable in with a DisplayPort-ready USB-C cable to do it. The second cable included in the Aura box won’t do it; oddly, that’s just a charging cable.

Right now, I’m connecting the new iPad Mini and casting a second display up in the air. I’m typing on a Logitech keyboard and mouse paired to the iPad, because the Xreal inputs won’t control it. But the point, mainly, is that it connects. And Gemini can still give me feedback on what it sees on my iPad’s virtual screen.

Whatever you plug in can cast a virtual monitor in-glasses: MacBook, iPhone, Steam Deck. Shockingly, even a Nintendo Switch 2 works, something Xreal’s team has been excited about. There are caveats: The Switch 2 goes into docked mode and needs the Joy-Cons detached, and only certain higher-fidelity DisplayPort USB-C cables work. I played Ocarina of Time on the Aura’s screen and it looked great, but the framerate was a bit lower than what I get on the Switch 2 normally. But again, I can ask Gemini questions about the game as I’m playing, and it sees and gives me answers, provided I’ve clicked a little on-screen toggle to share my screen with Gemini’s visual mode.

Bridging between devices is exciting to me, but it’s really just limited to treating the input like a video-in that pops on a second screen in-glasses. Meta’s VR Glasses will do this too. It’s a great bonus addition, but having to cable both my glasses and my other device to the Aura puck means too many cables for my comfort.

The glasses also work on their own without the puck, defaulting to standard Xreal glasses firmware and controls. That’s great if I want to use them with my laptop/phone/etc on the fly without needing the Aura puck, at least.

Turning on Gemini Live with a press of the top button on Aura’s glasses means you can have Gemini in your life constantly, if you wish. Toggle a little upward-arrow icon to share your camera feed and on-screen apps, and suddenly Gemini can also describe YouTube videos for you, or read what you’re writing, or tell you what’s in your hand.

It’s an all-seeing assistant that can even work with Google’s circle-to-search, although that feature’s hard to trigger (press and hold my fingers and click to bring it up, it seems). But I can then circle something in front of me, capture it, and Google AI search brings up results instantly (a book I’m holding, a freezeframe on TV or something on one of my virtual screens).

This is a step beyond the type of live, camera-enabled AI modes in smart glasses. It can see the world via its cameras and all the virtual apps that get conjured.

That being said, it’s hit or miss. The video feed quality isn’t great, so the AI can’t always read things at a distance. But I wore the Xreal Aura across my kitchen, making coffee while floating a YouTube window in front of me and talking to Gemini, and it felt like some sort of cyberpunk future I’d only experienced in bits and pieces before. It’s something you could walk around with, technically, but not a device I’d wear all day (nor is it designed to be).

Xreal promises four hours of battery life on the Aura, which is more than most VR headset claims of 2 to 3 hours. In practice, it feels good. I can use it for several hours and still have a fair amount of battery left, which seems promising. I’ve only been testing for a week, though.

But the processor puck can overheat. The puck has venting fans that can pump very warm air, and it’s not meant to be put in a pocket, even though that’s exactly what I want to do with it when I’m wearing Aura on my face. Instead, there’s an included belt clip. I tried putting it in my pocket, and pretty soon I got an overheating warning pop-up message. Don’t put it in your pocket.

I don’t think I’ve ever been as fascinated and borderline overwhelmed as I have with the Xreal Aura. It points in all sorts of directions for where phones, AI assistants and glasses can be heading. Could this little tweener device be my portable workstation eventually?

Right now it’s more of an experiment with fascinating side benefits. It can’t replace a standard VR headset, though parts come close.

The Xreal Aura tested even my new-device tolerance, although I see amazing glimmers. It’s coming with me on my next trips for sure, and I’ll let you know what happens when I do. But it’s not yet the true fusion solution I’m waiting for. And yet, I’m still convinced that the concept, remixed and refined, will be.

#3028. Apple could build its AI health chatbot from this study – how to enroll

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Apple is leaning into AI-powered health tools with the launch of its Apple Health AI Usage Study.

Apple is exploring how people use AI for their health, presumably to build its own AI health coach. On Sunday, it launched the Apple Health AI Usage Study, which could contribute to the next AI health experience Apple builds by measuring the quality of AI health responses, comprehension, and everyday health behaviors, according to a press release.

Apple is conducting the study in collaboration with OpenEvidence, a clinical AI platform widely used by healthcare professionals. The study examines the relationship between conversational AI tools, like chatbots, and the people who use them.

“Insights from this study will help advance the broader scientific conversation and ensure that as technology evolves, we continue building trusted tools that genuinely support people wherever they are on their health journey,” Sumbul Desai, M.D., Apple’s vice president of Health and Fitness, said in the press release.

Also: Apple Watch Series 12 review: Finally, the health tracker I’ve been waiting for

Participants are encouraged to share their HealthKit data and query the health app with questions. The study will also explore how AI tools can best prepare patients ahead of clinical visits. Apple will monitor the AI’s clarity and approachability when providing medical information, and each response or recommendation will be linked to peer-reviewed clinical citations. Responses could be unclear or incomplete, which is why Apple is rolling this out as a study to explore a responsibly designed AI health assistant.

Apple often launches studies for features it would like to develop in the future. For example, many of the hearing health features launched on the AirPods were a direct result of the findings from Apple’s Hearing Study.

Also: Athenahealth patients can ask Claude about their medical records now

The AI usage study comes on the heels of the revamped Health app’s debut, which launches officially next month. It also arrives amid a bevy of AI health coaches, popping up alongside companion health devices. Google launched its AI Health Coach in Google Health Premium last year, and Oura launched a proprietary AI model for women trained on medical standards and research from Oura’s in-house team of board-certified clinicians.

A growing number of Americans are relying on AI for medical advice. A recent survey from Pew Research Center found that 34% of US adults have talked with a chatbot for medical advice. As AI proliferates, that percentage will only increase.

“Patients and clinicians are both turning to AI, but the tools they use are being built and tested in separate worlds,” said Robert M. Wachter, M.D., UCSF’s professor and chair of the Department of Medicine, in the press release.

Apple and other tech companies are building for this new health normal, and the AI usage study indicates that Apple isn’t taking the responsibility lightly.

If you’re interested in participating in Apple’s study, it’s open to 200,000 eligible participants age 21 and older in the US. You’ll need a phone with Apple Intelligence enabled (the iPhone 15 Pro or later), running iOS 26 or later. You can download the study app to learn more and enroll.

#3026. Nike Is Down 78% From Its High. Here's What That Does to the Yield.

Investors continue to feel dismayed by the lack of a revenue turnaround.

The overall market has done well over the last few years. Using the popular S&P 500 index as a proxy, large-cap stocks gained 61.5% over the last five years through Nov. 13.

That's been positive for many, but certainly not all, stocks. Naturally, there have been laggards.

Nike (NKE -6.30%) has been one. The shares are about 78% off the high price during this period. Here's a look at the sell-off and the dividend yield to see whether or not you should buy the stock.

This long-heralded company had big marketing budgets, famous commercials, multiple sports stars' endorsements, and growing sales. Investors did well by owning Nike's stock. However, over the last few years, a lack of product innovation, competition, and management missteps have led to sagging sales.

They don't look set to improve anytime soon, either. Nike's fiscal first-quarter revenue, adjusted to remove foreign-currency translations, dropped 5% year over year. The period ended on Aug. 31. Management forecasts revenue will fall by a high-single-digit percentage for the year.

With revenue persistently declining, it's no wonder the share price has dropped precipitously. Given the company's outlook, that doesn't look like it's going to reverse, at least not anytime soon.

Despite the company's struggles, Nike's board of directors has consistently raised dividends. In fact, the company has increased dividends annually for about a quarter of a century.

The lower stock price translates into a higher dividend yield. That's because you calculate a stock's yield by dividing the annual dividend by the share price. Hence, if a dividend stays constant or increases, the stock's yield rises.

Presently, Nike's shares yield 4.3%. That seems attractive, given that the S&P 500 yields 1.1%.

However, with weaker results, the company's operating cash flow has dropped over the past several years. Nike's fiscal 2026 operating cash flow fell from $3.7 billion to $2.9 billion. After subtracting $686 million for capital expenditures, it produced free cash flow (FCF) of $2.2 billion. This didn't cover the $2.4 billion of common and preferred stock dividends.

You can also look at dividends compared to earnings, called the payout ratio. Presently, Nike has a payout ratio of 79%.

However, earnings might not cover dividends for long. Management expects adjusted diluted earnings per share to come in at $1.15 to $1.35. Annualizing the $0.41 quarterly dividend results in $1.64.

With Nike's revenue slumping and dividend coverage shaky, I'd pass on the shares despite the higher-than-average dividend yield.

#3025. Oura’s new feature could help you kick jet lag – how to enable it

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Oura just launched a Jet Lag Plan to help you stay alert when you switch time zones, whether you're traveling for business or pleasure.

Oura developed a tool for its frequent-flying members that could help them stave off the worst of jet lag.

Ahead of the busy holiday travel season, on Tuesday, Oura announced Jet Lag Plan, a new feature designed to help travelers feel alert and energized after crossing several time zones.

Also: Oura Ring users may get in-app access to real doctors soon – what we know

Jet Lag Plan takes into account your travel itinerary, sleep patterns, and body responses to provide guidance for traveling members entering new time zones.

Jet lag happens when circadian rhythms are at odds with local time zones, but there are a few things people can do to adjust.

Oura factors in the direction of travel, how many time zones are crossed, individual light windows, and sleep timing.

Ring users will enter their flight details, including information like multi-stop trips, and also include the reason for the trip. Oura adjusts the Jet Lag Plan accordingly, and a business trip’s plan may differ in intensity from that of a vacation.

“Two people on the same flight can get different plans, because guidance reflects your itinerary, your typical sleep schedule, and your chronotype,” Oura writes in a blog post. The chronotype refers to Oura’s sleep chronotype, which categorizes users into six types (early morning, morning, early evening, and so on) based on their historical sleep activity.

After adding these details, Oura provides each user with timely guidance throughout their trip. This guidance could include recommendations on when to begin or end caffeine consumption or light exposure, and when to start preparing for sleep. The plan is designed for those crossing three or more time zones. Members can follow along with these recommendations by checking them off as they complete each one. Users can also talk to Oura’s Advisor in the event of flight or timing changes.

Jet Lag Plan is now available for Oura Members with Oura Ring Gen 3 or later.

Go to your home screen, tap the + and select Jet Lag Plan to get started. You can also tell Oura Advisor about a trip to initiate Jet Lag Plan. If the Oura app detects a time zone shift of 3 or more hours, Jet Lag Plan may appear as a push notification.

#3024. I Didn’t Expect to Like Xiaomi’s Bizarre Dual-Screen Phone So Much

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Review: Xiaomi's 18 Pro Max is a quirky Android phone that stands out from the crowd with its extra screen on the back. Shame Americans can't have it.

Editor at Large; Lead Photographer, Europe

Editor at Large; Lead Photographer, Europe

Xiaomi teased me with the 17 Pro, its bizarre dual-screen Android phone, last year. But it was sold only in China. Being from the UK, I went back to my regular boring phone with its boring single screen. Big sigh. So imagine my excitement when Xiaomi announced that its new flagship 18 Pro and Pro Max — complete with a second rear screen — would launch internationally, with a rollout including the UK and wider Europe. As with the rest of Xiaomi’s handsets, people in the US are flat out of luck.

That sucks for Americans because this phone is actually damn good. I worried that the rear screen would just be a dumb gimmick — something that tries to separate the phone from competitors but doesn’t actually add anything useful. But I actually like it. Need it? No. But it’s fun and has some genuine uses.

Beyond the screen, though, the 18 Pro Max packs the latest Qualcomm Elite Extreme Gen 6 processor, a fast-charging silicon-carbon battery and a potent camera setup that utilizes the same LOFIC sensor technology that impressed me so much in Xiaomi and Leica’s Leitzphone earlier this year.

The 18 Pro isn’t just smaller (6.4 inches vs. the Pro Max’s 6.9 inches) it misses some of the Max’s top tech as well. The processor is a lesser model, the main camera doesn’t use LOFIC tech and the smaller battery isn’t as capable. Shame.

But the 18 Pro Max is an all-round Android powerhouse, and I’ve really enjoyed getting to grips with it over the past couple of weeks. Here’s what I’ve found and what you need to know about this phone.

The extra display on the back is certainly this phone’s standout feature. It’s basically in the same place as the iPhone 18 Pro’s camera island, but instead of just being a piece of metal, it’s an actual functioning screen. If you’ve ever seen the cover display on a clamshell flip phone like Samsung’s Galaxy Z Flip 8, then it’ll seem quite familiar.

Like the Flip 8, the second display shows incoming notifications, acting as a camera viewfinder and offering a variety of basic built-in functions like calendar reminders. What really hooked me, though, was the ability to create Gen AI apps just by typing in a prompt.

For example, I asked for “a game where you just pop bubbles,” which the “Polish” tool elaborated on with deeper functions and visual styles before generating a finished game that was fully playable on the back screen, complete with a scoring system and, for some reason, a jellyfish mascot. It takes about 5 minutes for the app to be created each time, and its functions are limited. It’s not able to access any app data, so don’t expect to create a new email reader, and anything too technical will result in failure.

I asked it to create a camera overlay that showed exposure settings (shutter speed, ISO and so on) to serve as a light meter for an analog camera. I’m not sure whether the issue was my explanation or a technical limitation, but it took the phone two tries to get something close. It created an interface with dials and exposure information, but it didn’t open the camera to calculate exposure as I’d hoped. As a result, it looked nice but it was functionally redundant.

Another time, I asked it to create an app that showed real-time charging speeds. The resulting app showed current battery level but not charging speed. It did have a baffling “charging milestones completed” button that simply increased by one each time I tapped it. I also had no luck with my “rude word generator,” which just repeatedly came back with “Couldn’t generate.” Frustratingly, each time it fails to create an app, it doesn’t tell you why — like if you’re asking for information it’s unable to access — but just says to try again “in a minute or two,” which rarely resulted in success in my testing time. If I’m asking for something it can’t achieve, it’d be helpful to know that.

Even so, I’m impressed with this app creation tool and, like many of the AI tools that only mildly excite me right now, I can only assume it will improve over time.

One of my favorite uses of the rear screen, though, is for vlogging. Firstly, seeing yourself from the back of the phone means you’re able to accurately film yourself using the best quality camera, rather than limiting yourself to the front-facing camera, which won’t look as good. But there’s also an autocue function where you can input a script and have it overlaid as text, allowing you to read out your words as you present to camera.

It’s a powerful tool for vloggers and other video creators who rely on longer prewritten scripts for their videos. But it’s quite basic: the text simply auto-scrolls at a speed you set in advance. I’d love to see Xiaomi use voice recognition here to automatically progress the text as you read out the words, slowing down or speeding up as you naturally read aloud. This tech already exists, so I don’t think I’m asking for literal magic here.

Tucked into that second display is a 200-megapixel main camera and a 200-megapixel telephoto camera offering 3.2x optical zoom or 6.4x hybrid zoom. There’s also a really tiny 50-megapixel ultrawide camera by itself below the camera island, which makes it feel like an afterthought — something that I’ll come back to later.

The main sensor is physically slightly smaller than the one in Xiaomi’s Leitzphone, but it uses the same LOFIC sensor tech for better dynamic range in a single image. I’ve taken a lot of photos with it so far and I’m really impressed with what I’ve seen. The smaller 18 Pro has an almost identical camera setup but its main sensor doesn’t use LOFIC, which is a shame as it forces you to go for the larger phone if you want the best possible image quality.

Shots are well-exposed, with accurate colors and fine details that manage to look sharp but without the harsh over-sharpened look that’s all too often seen from phone cameras. Images look more natural as a result.

There are a lot of ways to tune your images in-camera — almost too many, in fact. There’s a whole host of built-in color presets, including a Leica-branded high-contrast black-and-white mode that I like, all of which you can customize further by adjusting the tones, colors, grain and white balance. Then there’s the option to shoot using the phone’s default color processing, going with “Leica Vibrant” for more popping colors or “Leica Authentic” for more natural tones. Each of these applies no matter what filter you then apply over the top.

Confused? Yeah, I’m not entirely surprised, there are a lot of variables at play when taking an image with this thing but it didn’t take me long to figure out how to get the look that I wanted. And let’s be honest, there aren’t many photographers who want fewer options in how to take a photo.

Then there’s Essential Moment, which is its own standalone mode where you can select from three distinct styles: a black and white mode, “modern vintage,” or “Iconic CCD.” Each of these is designed to replicate specific looks from cameras of the past, and Xiaomi says it uses AI to analyze the scene to authentically reproduce color tones, vintage lens effects and film grain (though crucially not generative AI to actually alter anything in the scene).

I actually love this, especially the black and white option, which produces monochrome images with beautiful contrast and genuinely authentic-looking film grain. It’s the mode I’d end up using most often, I’m sure, and I’ve taken a bunch of photos with it that I really like.

Oh, and that tiny ultrawide camera, weirdly separated from its friends? It’s not great, with nighttime shots being particularly disappointing here. On the upside, the main camera’s standard focal length is 23mm, which is already pretty wide, so you probably won’t miss the ultrawide much.

While the base 18 Pro uses Qualcomm’s latest Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6, the Pro Max ups the ante with the Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6. It’s no surprise that the Pro Max is a seriously powerful bit of kit, returning benchmark scores up there with the powerhouse Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra. Everything ran exceptionally smoothly, from playing demanding 3D games like Genshin Impact to editing photos or navigating the Android 17 interface. I found much the same with the 18 Pro, too — I didn’t see a noticeable difference in performance.

I don’t mind Xiaomi’s software skin, as it’s easy enough for anyone familiar with Android to get to grips with. What I don’t like, though, is the company’s insistence on preloading it with an armada of apps including AliExpress, Netflix, WPS Office, TikTok and others. Together with the variety of Xiaomi apps also on board, the phone feels somewhat cluttered before you’ve even had a chance to add anything of your own. I’ve seen worse examples (Oppo has been bad with this), but it still irks me that the phone ends up feeling almost like it’s ad-supported. And if it is, surely it should be cheaper?

It helps a bit, sure, but it won’t block those creeps entirely. My advice is: if you’ve got information so sensitive that even a glimpse would be career-ending, maybe wait until you’re alone before you put it on screen.

The 7,050-mAh silicon-carbon battery in the larger Pro Max packs a punch, putting in some solid scores on our demanding battery rundown tests. After one hour of YouTube streaming, it dropped to 97%, then to 89% after the third hour. That puts it above the Galaxy S26 Ultra and Google Pixel 11 Pro XL, although still below the current champion, the iPhone 18 Pro Max.

In everyday use, you won’t struggle to get through a full day of mixed use and you can likely be quite demanding with it and still not worry about it conking out mid-afternoon. Take photos, watch videos, listen to music – don’t stress over it; this thing should hold out fine.

The phone supports up to 100-watt wired fast charging, though you’ll need a Xiaomi fast charger to achieve the fastest speeds. I don’t have a Xiaomi charger (and the fastest it sells in the UK is 90W for £25), but I tried it with multiple third-party 100-watt chargers and the maximum I could get was around 65 watts. Even so, it went from 1% to 65% in 30 minutes of charging, which is still pretty quick — on par with the iPhone 18 Pro Max, in fact. Still, it should be able to go faster; you’ll just need to source a charger that will allow it.

With its smaller 6,000-mAh battery the Xiaomi 18 Pro didn’t fare as well on our battery drain tests (it dropped to 93% after an hour of YouTube streaming) but in general use you’ll still comfortably get through most of a day on a single charge.

If you’re in the US, it’s something of a moot point. You can’t buy it. Sorry. Sure, you can probably import it from some third-party resellers, but it’s not officially on sale.

If you’re somewhere where you can buy it, then lucky you — this phone is a blast. It ticks many of the boxes I’d expect from a flagship phone right now (camera quality in particular), and that second rear screen is the cherry on top. I expected it to feel like a pointless gimmick, and maybe it is a bit of a novelty, but it’s fun and I’ve already found it genuinely useful.

I don’t like that there are so many hardware differences between the two phone sizes, as it forces you to have a much bigger model if you want the best performance. I prefer Apple’s approach: With the iPhone 18 Pro, I can have the same exact potent camera setup and processor performance, no matter which size I choose. With Xiaomi’s phones I’m forced to compromise between performance and pocketability. If you want the best camera, then go for the bigger model. Battery life is better, too.

#3023. Why Evolution Metals & Technologies Stock Bumped Higher Today

A decent third quarter was almost overshadowed by a highly critical short seller report.

An estimates-topping quarterly earnings report from Evolution Metals & Technologies (EMAT +2.60%) published after market close on Monday was tempered by a scathing critique of the company. All in all, though, investors chose to focus on the positive, and collectively they sent Evolution's stock up by nearly 3% on the day.

Evolution, a relatively early-stage company that concentrates on the production of rare-earth magnets, earned revenue of $2.2 million in its third quarter. This was 36% higher than its take in the previous quarter; it earned no revenue in the third quarter of 2025. Its non-GAAP (adjusted) net loss deepened to $13.4 million, or $0.02 per share, from the year-ago quarter's $4 million shortfall.

Both headline figures were high enough to exceed the consensus analyst estimates. On average, prognosticators following Evolution stock were estimating revenue of $1.95 million and an adjusted net loss per share of $0.03.

Evolution also had encouraging news to report, but this concerned its current (fourth) quarter. In October, it received the entire order of 13 sintered rare-earth magnet production machines from a Korean unit of the vacuum equipment manufacturer Ulvac. Once installed at the company's expansion facility in that country, it will be able to significantly scale up its magnet production capacity.

One entity that surely wasn't as impressed with Evolution's third quarter is short-seller Capybara Research. On Monday, Capybara published a blisteringly critical report on the company. The headline of the document reflected Capybara's key criticisms, as it read "Evolution Metals: A cesspool of fraud. A $2 million payoff, convicted felons, insider trading, market manipulation and no material operations."

On Tuesday, Evolution fired off a detailed response to the report, categorically refuting all the allegations. It added that it is considering engaging legal counsel to pursue claims against Capybara.

While short-sellers have a material interest in publishing negative material on a stock, allegations as serious as this should be examined. Any investor should be very careful with Evolution and dig deeply into the report and the company's response before considering whether to buy the stock.

Tech > Services & Software > Operating Systems > Mobile OS > Android

If Android Fast Switch works like iPhone Handoff, one eSIM can be quickly switched between two phones.

In iOS 27, Apple announced iPhone Handoff, a networking feature that allows users to switch cell service between two eSIM-enabled iPhones. Text strings in Google’s SIM Manager app suggest the company is preparing a similar feature for compatible Android phones, according to Android Authority.

Code strings include “Use a SIM on two phones,” and note that the feature will be called Fast Switch. Little information is currently available about the feature’s limitations, including which phones or mobile carriers may not be compatible.

Also: Why your USB-C cables look alike, but work differently – and how to tell them apart

On Apple’s side, any iPhone in the US running iOS 27 with a T-Mobile or Verizon-provided eSIM can use iPhone Handoff. AT&T does not currently support iPhone Handoff.

However, the code strings uncovered by Android Authority show that Android’s Fast Switch will work similarly to iPhone Handoff, in that users must be signed in to both devices under the same Google account for the feature to work.

Strings in Google’s SIM Manager app also point to no sharing between two users, so this feature isn’t a way to circumvent carrier fees by adding service to someone else’s phone for the price of one.

If Fast Switch works anything like iPhone Handoff, which it appears it will, one eSIM can be switched between two phones. So, calls, messages, location services, and other information synced to your Apple ID can remain consistent between two devices.

Also: 5 hidden iOS 27 features that make older iPhones better

Some third-party apps, like banking, communications, or social media, may also remain consistent across the two phones, depending on the app’s syncing behavior.

Features like Apple’s iPhone Handoff and Google’s Fast Switch are ideal for people who regularly use two phones. Business owners and digital creators may want one phone strictly for business purposes and the other for personal use.

Also: Google Wallet turns your Android phone into a digital house key

In that case, one person can keep up with two phones without paying for two phone service lines through their carrier. Still, users will incur a fee, as T-Mobile charges $5/month for iPhone Handoff, while Verizon charges $10/month.

#3021. Ray Dalio says Bessent move is sign that a debt crisis is getting closer; recommends gold and bitcoin

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent's debt buyback announcement this week fits into a broader pattern that can signal a forthcoming crisis, according to billionaire investor Ray Dalio.

The Bridgewater Associates founder said Bessent's plan to increase government debt purchases may portend trouble for the U.S. economy. Coupled with the Japanese government reducing its U.S. bond market exposure and surging long-dated American bond yields, Dalio said investors may want to prepare their portfolios for increased risk by owning cryptocurrencies and gold.

"I am confident that the government's financial condition is at an inflection point," Dalio wrote in a LinkedIn post published Friday. "If this is not dealt with now, the debts will build up to levels where they can't be managed without great trauma."

Dalio noted that the Treasury Department has "only limited capacity" to buy back bonds. Bessent told CNBC on Thursday that his team was going to "make a market" and that the purchases would likely top $4 billion.

The U.S. is spending about 40% more than it's bringing in, resulting in the burgeoning budget deficit, Dalio said. The U.S. budget deficit topped $432 billion in July, but Bessent told CNBC that it's likely peaked under President Donald Trump's administration.

Bessent said in the interview that a team was looking at ways to shrink spending by hundreds of billions of dollars. But Dalio said there is "very little ability" to do so given that it is either committed or considered essential.

After years of overspending, Dalio said total debt now dwarfs what the U.S. brings in each year. If the U.S. government was a business, Dalio said debt service payments would come in at roughly $11 trillion — about 200% of annual revenue.

Dalio, 77, warned the cost of repaying principal and servicing the debt will only grow over time.

To solve this, Dalio said the U.S. needs to carefully employ a three-part strategy to get the budget deficit down to 3% of gross domestic product.

First, Dalio said the U.S. government needs to reduce its spending. Second, he said tax revenue needs to be raised. Finally, the New York native and Harvard Business School alumni said lower interest rates were needed.

"All three need to happen concurrently so as to prevent any one from being too large," Dalio said. "If any one is too large, the adjustment will be traumatic."

Dalio cautioned against ramming through these adjustments by "force." For instance, "it would be very bad if the Federal Reserve unnaturally forced interest rates down," he said.

Dalio said it's important to to take steps now, while the economy is healthy. An economy in recession requires increased government spending, he said.

Dalio said the exact timing of a debt crisis can be swayed by variables ranging from military conflict to political change. On its current trajectory, the U.S. could enter such a crisis in as early as one year or as late as five. "My guess, which I suppose will be a bad one, is that it will come in three years, give or take two, if the course we're on is not changed."

To prepare, Dalio recommended investors are underweight debt assets, such as bonds.

As much as 10% to 15% of a portfolio could land in gold, as well as "a bit" of bitcoin, the hedge fund founder said.

Dalio's post came at the tail end of a volatile week for U.S. financial markets. Rising long-term Treasury yields have pressured stocks, leading the S&P 500 to snap a a three-week-long advance.

#3019. Apple reveals daily limits on your Siri AI use – here’s how much you’ll have to pay

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

The more you pay for an iCloud+ plan, the more you’ll be able to use Siri AI and Apple Intelligence for advanced server-side tasks.

Have you been using the new Siri AI? If so, how much? I’ve been turning to it a lot since the release of iOS 27. Well, how we use it — and how often — will soon depend on how much we pay for an iCloud+ plan.

Also: 5 apps I need Siri AI to work with now that it’s open to third-party developers

Apple hasn’t been shy about stating that the use of Siri AI and Apple Intelligence for specific tasks would face daily access limits. Increased limits would be granted based on your iCloud+ subscription. Now the company has revealed how much it will cost you and when the limits will begin.

“Starting with the 2027 software releases, Siri AI and Apple Intelligence features are available for free for users with a supported device set to a supported language,” Apple said on a support page updated November 16. “Some features rely on powerful server models and have limits where increased access is available with eligible iCloud+ plans, starting with the 27.3 release.”

iOS 27.3 is expected to launch in early December, so that’s when the daily usage limits will kick in.

At that point, people with no paid iCloud+ plan and even those with the $0.99-per-month 50 GB plan will be the most limited, with Apple saying only that they’ll face a “Standard Device Limit.”

What is a standard limit? That depends not just on how many times you tap into Siri per day but on what tasks you assign it. Basic Siri commands, such as setting timers and alarms or sending standard text messages, will remain free and unlimited.

Also: Ready for a Siri AI agent? Apple under pressure to upgrade its assistant faster

Advanced Siri and Apple Intelligence tasks will bump into the usage limits. These include the following, according to Apple:

One positive here is that the limits are per device not per account. That means you can use Siri AI and Apple Intelligence with the same account across your iPhone, iPad, Mac, Apple Watch, Apple TV, and Vision Pro without fear of chewing up too much of your quota.

This all sounds like a way for Apple to steer people to more expensive iCloud+ accounts. But the limits are in place for a key reason. Basic commands are processed on your device, so they don’t require the use of Apple servers. More advanced tasks are processed using server-side AI models, which can feel the strain if too many people access them all at once.

Also: What you’ll pay for AI agents will be wildly variable and unpredictable

How will you know if you use up your daily allotment and what happens then? You’ll receive a notification if you hit your limit for a particular feature category. At that point, you can still give Siri basic tasks to perform. But advanced ones will be paused until your limit resets the next day. Otherwise, Apple is undoubtedly hoping that people who continually run into limits will upgrade to a pricier iCloud+ plan.

#3018. Try These Ways to Use Less Stuff (and Save More Money)

We believe everyone should be able to make financial decisions with confidence. While we don't cover every company or financial product on the market, we work hard to share a wide range of offers and objective editorial perspectives.

So how do we make money? Our partners compensate us for advertisements that appear on our site. This compensation helps us provide tools and services - like free credit score access and monitoring. With the exception of mortgage, home equity and other home-lending products or services, partner compensation is one of several factors that may affect which products we highlight and where they appear on our site. Other factors include your credit profile, product availability and proprietary website methodologies.

However, these factors do not influence our editors' opinions or ratings, which are based on independent research and analysis. Our partners cannot pay us to guarantee favorable reviews. Here is a list of our partners.

Personal finance writers and editors share their favorite ways to be resourceful.

Have you ever thrown away groceries that spoiled before you got around to using them? Or bought a new jacket despite already having half a dozen in your closet?

It’s easy to let things go to waste and accumulate more than we need.

Use Less Stuff Day, which lands on Nov. 19 this year, encourages us to rethink our consumption habits and make more mindful, environmentally friendly choices.

That might mean squeezing every last drop out of what you’ve got, finding creative ways to reuse things or simply buying less.

I keep a couple of simple tricks up my sleeve to extend the life of my family’s clothing: OxiClean soaks and basic sewing skills. You’d be surprised by how many things you can salvage with a little cleaning and mending.

I asked my fellow Nerds to share some of the ways they reduce waste and unnecessary spending. Maybe you’ll pick up an idea or two.

Pamela de la Fuente, managing editor: My husband grew up with a “make what’s in the house” kinda family. I didn’t. But this weekend while looking for spaghetti I found some crispy rice cereal, and I knew we had marshmallows from a bonfire a few weeks ago so I said, “I’m going to make crispy rice treats with this for the kids and get rid of this cereal.” (Surprisingly, it was not stale.) I still had cereal left, so I added it to some chocolate protein bars I love to make and my son said, “These are 9 out of 10. Usually they are 7 out of 10!”

Karen Gaudette Brewer, head of content: I’m a big “make big batches of food and freeze it” person, so I can drive everyone nuts reminding them that we really do have food at home. That freezer also holds grated lemon zest and cubes of those last little bits of chicken broth and wine so that I can easily make pan sauces and not waste that last half cup of goodness.

Jessica Cano, content coordinator: I save the tops from strawberries after cutting them for my kids. We use some to make strawberry balsamic vinegar, some to make strawberry syrup and the rest go in the freezer to be used for smoothies. Keeps me from having to buy frozen fruit and multiple vinegars.

Pantry shopping can result in less food in the trash and fewer trips to the grocery store. It can also make experimenting with new recipes a little more exciting. Take a page from Managing Editor Athena Cocoves, who says, “Sometimes we pretend we're on ‘Chopped.’”

Ryan Brady, lead writer: Rotating toys with our kids has helped them get more enjoyment out of the same toys versus constantly buying new toys. We put a bunch of toys they're bored with in a bin, and months later, take one out and bam — it's like a new toy all over again!

Kim Lowe, head of content: I invested a whole $12 in a lint remover last winter that transformed all my old sweaters into almost new!

Laura McMullen, editor: Almost all of my kids’ clothes are thrifted or hand-me-downs. My friend group of parents has kids from age 2 to 7, all of whom are about six months apart. We’ve developed a hearty clothing exchange. It’s fun to see my friends' kids wear hand-me-downs that we got from my brother’s family almost 10 years ago.

Look for other ways to salvage your belongings or get them secondhand. That might include watching a vacuum repair tutorial on YouTube, borrowing books from the library or purchasing used tools from Facebook Marketplace. The goal: Keep more stuff in circulation and out of landfills.

Abby Doyle, lead writer: Composting isn’t as fussy as it seems. Once you get into it, you start seeing would-be waste as stuff to feed your new backyard buddy. Junk mail, paper bags, slimy spring mix … it’s all food for my “pet dirt.” And my garden has legit never looked better.

Yuliya Goldshteyn, editor: Instead of throwing away kid art, I reuse it as wrapping paper throughout the year. Bespoke gift wrapping for everyone! I haven’t bought gift wrap for five years now.

Caitlin Constantine, editor: I repurpose glass jars and plastic containers. It always seemed like such a pity to throw perfectly good containers into the recycling after one use, so now I reuse them before I recycle them.

Before you toss something, ask yourself, “Is there another way I can use this?” An old T-shirt makes a good cleaning rag, for example.

Being resourceful often means getting as much mileage as possible out of what you have.

#3017. $1,000 Would Buy About 12 Anthropic Shares at the Top of the Expected IPO Range. Would That Be a Smart Bet?

History says the first few days of trading can be the most expensive time to buy.

Anthropic's initial public offering is finally almost here -- the AI start-up behind Claude plans to go public on the Nasdaq exchange on Nov. 19 under the ticker ANT, and plans to sell shares for between $70 and $78 apiece.

At the top of that range, $1,000 would get you 12 shares of Anthropic stock. But I wouldn't be in a hurry to buy right away.

Don't get me wrong -- I think Anthropic is going to be a good company to hold, and I plan to invest at some point. But I also think it's a mistake to rush in during the first few days of trading. And it could be a very expensive mistake.

Big IPOs attract a lot of attention. Retail investors tend to run up the stock price because they want in on the action, but often, those gains are short-lived.

Meta Platforms (META -1.20%) is a perfect example. Then known as Facebook, Mark Zuckerberg's company went public in May 2012 at $38 per share. By September that year, the stock had fallen to $17.55, a decline of nearly 54%. Of course, Meta has been a fantastic company in the last few years and currently is one of the biggest in the world, with a market cap of about $1.6 trillion. But I'm sure investors who bought at $38 wish they had waited and gotten their initial investment at less than $20.

More recently, Space Exploration Technologies (SPCX +3.16%) went public on June 12. It priced its IPO at $135, and shares began trading at $150. The stock surged above $225 in just a couple of days before falling apart. And today, you can get the stock for about $137.

Anyone who bought SpaceX at more than $200 is still licking their wounds.

Neither example means Anthropic will follow the same path. But they demonstrate why buying immediately after an IPO can be unnecessarily expensive.

Anthropic shows many signs of being a winning investment. It reported $17 billion in revenue for the third quarter, up more than 12-fold from a year ago. More than 11,900 of its customers generate at least $100,000 in annual revenue for Anthropic.

Then there's the other side of the coin -- Anthropic's latest S-1 discloses approximately $900.9 billion in infrastructure and other purchase and lease commitments extending over nearly two decades. That's a tremendous financial obligation, even for a company growing as quickly as Anthropic.

I like the company's business prospects, and its revenue growth gives investors plenty to be excited about. But buying a promising company and paying a sensible price for its shares are two different things.

I'd rather let Anthropic establish a trading history, allow the initial excitement to settle, and see where its valuation lands. There's no reason anyone’s $1,000 has to be invested on the first day.

#3016. I’ve Used VSCO’s Lightroom Rival Desktop Editor and It’s Great for Creatives

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

VSCO might be popular for iPhone photography, but its Studio Pro has rival Adobe firmly in its sights.

Editor at Large; Lead Photographer, Europe

Editor at Large; Lead Photographer, Europe

VSCO is best known these days for its iPhone and Android editing app that makes pics look all cool and analog. But the company is launching its first stand-alone desktop photo editor for Mac, called VSCO Studio Pro, bringing its famous filmic presets—and a wealth of editing tools. I’ve used it, and while it’s not yet my sole image-editing solution, it’s great for getting those dreamy vintage vibes out of your photos.

The desktop app will be immediately familiar to any photographer who’s spent any time in Lightroom or Capture One. There are exposure, contrast, highlight, and shadow sliders along with color sliders for white balance or individual color adjustments. It’s par for the course for any raw image editor.

VSCO’s wide range of color presets has always been where it shines the brightest. Numbering just north of 200, Studio Pro packs in all the presets, from color classics like the company’s A1-10 range to a wealth of black-and-white options and a host of presets designed to emulate real film stocks like Kodak Gold or Fuji Velvia. VSCO says these are modeled on real scans of these film stocks to make them as authentic as possible.

It’s the presets that I love the most in VSCO’s app. Years ago, the company sold its presets as a downloadable Lightroom preset pack, which I have used in my photography workflow almost daily for the past 13 years, and their look is identical here. While it hasn’t sold the Lightroom preset pack in about a decade, VSCO’s Studio Pro app finally lets photographers achieve those same looks in desktop editing.

With Studio Pro, VSCO clearly has its sights on Lightroom. While Adobe is increasingly filling its services with various generative AI tools that radically alter your image’s content, VSCO is taking a more stripped-back approach that focuses on the creative side of color and exposure adjustments.

It’s still quite bare-bones at launch, with several features I need for my own photography missing, like masking. I can’t make selective edits to my images—like using a gradient to tone down the highlights only in the sky. Apparently this is coming soon, as are bloom and halation tools, which are already in the app, but grayed out with a “soon” marker next to them. Ditto the spot removal tool for cleaning up dust or sensor spots.

The big thing for me, though, comes down to cataloging and archiving of my images. I have several terabytes of images cataloged in my Lightroom library, available to edit on any device I sign in on — including phone, tablet or desktop. While VSCO will have some basic organization options within the Studio Pro app (grouping images into “Projects”—again, coming soon), it’s not as full-featured as Lightroom’s archiving system. I worry that once I’m working with thousands of images across multiple photoshoots, things will quickly become cluttered and difficult to navigate. Time will tell.

I don’t imagine VSCO’s app will necessarily be the first choice for working pros who need strict cataloging, backups and remote access. I count myself in that category, and for me Lightroom’s cloud storage remains the biggest reason to stay with Adobe, while others swear by Capture One for its Sessions-based filing system and its tethered shooting workflow.

By contrast, I see VSCO Studio Pro appealing more to enthusiast photographers who want to efficiently add real creative flair to their images and don’t necessarily want to spend on the commercial tools, cloud storage, or AI options offered by Adobe.

#3015. I asked Gemini Notebook to ‘make me a site’ from my notes – it was satisfying

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

A new Gemini Notebook feature lets you create interactive sites from intricate data.

Google’s Gemini can now turn your notes and other sources in your Gemini Notebook (previously called NotebookLM) into interactive pages or sites to help you better process complicated information.

Complete with flashcards, dashboards, and colorful panels, the sites make it easier to study and understand intricate concepts. I tested the feature, announced Tuesday, to see how efficient it is at creating a navigable site that is actually helpful and stays loyal to sources.

Also: 4 ways Anthropic’s new Claude Sheets beat using a Google Sheets connector in my tests

Because Notebooks are built with the sources you provide, like textbooks, files, or notes, the sites are created with the data that is in your Gemini Notebook. Notebook has three tabs: Sources, Chat, and Studio. The site option is in the Studio tab, listed under what you can create.

If you’re taking a college class, you could put all the information you need to prepare for a test and use the interactive site as a study guide that you can share with others.

To test this, I gave Notebook the following prompt:

“Make me a site that visually explains how cellular respiration works, breaking down each stage with interactive diagrams and self-check flashcards.”

Since I’m not in a class that would give me those study materials, I gave Gemini online sources to use for this. Gemini cited the sources in my notebook, then spent a few minutes creating the interactive site. Gemini will give you a quick update when it’s done, including a summary of the source information as it pertains to your request and instructions on where to find the site.

Also: I checked Gemini’s new Memory summary to see what it knew about me – how to see and edit yours

As promised, my cellular respiration notes were complete and organized on an interactive, visually appealing site that was easy to navigate. The coolest feature on the site was the flashcards, which you can hover over to see which ones you’ve studied.

The interactive site feature is now available to Gemini Notebook users and will soon come to the mobile app. As someone who knows very little about coding, I was pretty satisfied to see the information Gemini put together presented in explorable, easy-to-understand tabs on a site.

So I wouldn't commit to it, but I think there's a good probability we'll close something. When you say end of the year, I assume you're talking fiscal year, not calendar.

Unknown Analyst: Yes, of course. And then how -- can you talk a little bit about how this product -- does it help your customers save money on token spend or just cut out steps in the process?

Roy Olivier: Yes, Josh, you can touch the token spend, but the steps in the process is big there because if you got 3,000 to 4,000 researchers, all of whom are high-income people, reducing steps is a big financial impact on your cost structure or your efficiency of the researchers. But Josh, do you want to touch on the token part of it?

Josh Nicholson: Yes. It's not really touching on kind of the token spend. If anything, in many of these kind of instances, they're using their tokens and not our tokens to do this. I think it's really the fact that they have a handful of different tools, their researchers, again, which can be in the hundreds or thousands, have to jump between these different tools and then they have to do this process, often medical writing, thousands of times a year. And so those steps that Roy mentioned as 11, like if you really break it down to all the steps, it's probably way more than that.

And so it's very clunky that they have, but they have to do certain things in certain ways. And so really, if you use Article Galaxy and Scite together, it's kind of a great one-two punch with AI to do things that still follow the regulatory steps that are necessary, but can help those humans cut down time and in some cases, cut down even the human work. And so I think it's really more about accelerating the time that the humans have to do and streamlining those workflows in, again, a copyright-compliant way.

If you need to check the reuse rights for hundreds of different articles and you have to do those one at a time, that's a huge pain, a lot of time. And if you can do that all automatically or even just at a glance, that alone is a big step in efficiency. And so we see that across a variety of different steps. And again, these calls are pretty fun to be in because you're untangling these big complex webs and providing a really nice solution to these groups.

Unknown Analyst: Yes, and meeting the customer where they are. I guess given your ability to grow organically and then to innovate organically and to generate cash flow organically, how come you're not aggressively buying back shares?

Roy Olivier: Well, we've talked about that before. I think everybody in the Board is in violent agreement that certainly where the share price is now, that's arguably the best use of cash. And as soon as we can announce something on that, that's more definitive, you'll see it. So it's not something we're doing today, but we agree that's a very, very good use of cash.

Operator: We will take our next question from George Melas with MKH Management.

George Melas: Can you guys talk a little bit about publisher participation? And I think, Josh, you talked -- in your prepared remarks, you talked about how your relationship with publishers is getting sort of deeper as you can show them more clearly which paper is read, which paper maybe people want to have access to but can't because of paywall. And how is that changing the conversation with some of your publishers?

Josh Nicholson: Yes. So across both products, we really want to be more strategic with publishers. And so we sit on a lot of very valuable data. What is being bought, what is being rented, what is being denied in AI, what is being used in AI. There is a new standard called COUNTER that is used to determine kind of the ROI or the value of subscriptions. And historically, that has been how do humans read content, right? How is it downloaded, how is it viewed, et cetera. COUNTER, as of the middle of October, put out new reports looking at Agentic usage. And so we are pretty uniquely able to, kind of, show that demand.

We have a public page that shows this broken down by publisher, broken down by journals, allows journals or publishers or societies to get these metrics and then to talk to us. And so that's a very active area of focus for us, where we are talking to publishers regularly, going to more events, and then I would say, evolving our current agreements that we have with them. These agreements with publishers can help publishers basically defend their subscription value in an AI world because we're giving them the metrics.

They can grow their subscription value again because we're giving them the metrics or -- and I think this is kind of the interesting area for some growth for both us and them, they can sell metered reads to their content into AI. And so there's a host of a few different start-ups also working in this area. There are some hosting agencies like Silverchair and Atypon also working in this area. But I think our big differentiators are our corporate customer base, which is by far the largest across anyone providing any sort of similar functionality and the fact that we already have these established relationships of sending royalties to publishers.

And so it's really nice narrative and data that we can show to publishers and say, "Hey, we want to work with you strategically to help bring your content into AI." And I really do think how content is consumed is transformationally, kind of, changing. If you look at print to web to AI, I think on average, people are reading maybe 20 articles a month. And now if you look at it an AI, the AI is consuming 300 to 600 articles per month. And so it's just a dramatic increase in kind of the consumption because AI can read an article instantly versus a human spending hours.

And so that is a big part of our strategy, is getting these publishers on board, exposing more of their content with them and then providing them strategic value through data and revenue so that they deeply engage with us. And so yes, a lot more kind of on the pipeline. We put out one press release on MDPI, and hopefully, there'll be some more coming soon, highlighting the traction we have there.

George Melas: Great. Okay. Lot to think about there. And maybe on the large transaction that you guys closed just a few weeks ago, how much is your content and access to publishers really important in that transaction? And how much is it really providing sort of the infrastructure to streamline their processes?

Josh Nicholson: Yes. So on that one, I think it's more kind of the latter. I think it's really the infrastructure there. Obviously, having good full text search across all these publisher relationships matter a ton. But if we had lost 1 or 2 publishers there, I don't think it would have changed the deal at all. And so I think we talk a lot about strategy, and we're giving you these kind of complex metered reads and all these different things. In this case, I think it's pretty simple, right? There are large customers out there that have simple challenges or maybe not simple challenges, large challenges.

And if we go in and leverage our long-standing relationship with them, we can show them, "Hey, here's how you can solve that." And that is a mixture of AI. It's a mixture of our content relationships on both products. And then I think also a testament to the sales team, right? We have some people that can really go and across and do these enterprise deals versus kind of tracking down at a smaller 6-figure deals, right? It takes some patience. It's a multi-stakeholder on both sides, their product and ours and a lot of listening and again, kind of, going to where the user is.

And so that, to me, is exciting because, again, we have a lot of very large customers. And in some cases, they're not paying the largest amount, right? And so that is an opportunity that I think we see.

Operator: At this time, there are no further questions in the queue. I would now like to turn our meeting back to Mr. Roy Olivier.

Roy Olivier: Thanks, everyone, for joining us on our call today. We look forward to speaking to you in February to discuss our second quarter FY '27 results. Have a great day.

Operator: Thank you. This brings us to the end of today's meeting. We appreciate your time and participation. You may now disconnect.

One of your Amazon Prime perks made a switch. GrubHub’s out and Uber Eats is in.

Amazon’s new meal delivery partner will offer free delivery, plus $20 off the first two Uber Eats eligible orders of $25 or more for the first 14 days. You can expect some Amazon-exclusive offers, and if you have a Prime Visa credit card, you’ll earn 5% back on all Uber Eats orders until Dec. 5 with a Prime membership. The Amazon and Uber Eats partnership is just in time for the holidays if you want convenient dinner option while you shop Black Friday deals and sales. But heads up, you won’t get the limited-time deal and free delivery if you order through the Uber Eats app. In order to get free delivery and $20 off your order, go to the Uber Eats tab at the top of your Amazon app or Uber Eats on Amazon’s website. Place your order as usual with a participating restaurant but make sure the $20 discount applies at checkout.

I tried the new perk and promo out for dinner. Aside from the meal, the tip, a nearly $10 service fee, tax and the delivery fee all added up to the cost of another meal — which is worth paying attention to when you order.

#3012. Google is making it easier to opt out of Gemini AI model training – here’s how

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

You’ll soon be able to turn off Gemini model training but still retain access to your previous chats with Google’s AI.

Also: I checked Gemini’s new Memory summary to see what it knew about me

In a change set to roll out in the coming weeks, you’ll be able to put the brakes on Gemini model training without losing access to your previous conversations with the AI. Here’s how this works now — and how it will work down the road.

Currently, Gemini offers a setting called Keep Activity that controls not only whether and for how long your chats are saved but also whether they’re used to train the AI. You can’t separate the two.

To correct this problem, Google will replace Keep Activity with two new settings. With the first setting, you’ll be able to keep or delete your past chats and choose how long your history will be saved. With the second setting, you’ll be able to decide whether your chats, including all text and attachments, will be used for model training.

Also: I asked Gemini Notebook to ‘make me a site’ from my notes

“With this change, you will be able to keep your history while independently controlling generative AI model training,” Google said in an announcement shared to Gemini users via email.

Here’s how this will play out. If your Keep Activity setting is off when this change is made, both new settings will be off. If your Keep Activity setting is on, both new settings will be on. That means you’ll need to head to Gemini’s Settings if you wish to opt out of model training but still be able to view and access your previous chats.

ChatGPT offers a setting called “Improve the model for everyone,” which is double-speak for model training. But this is easy enough to turn off. Microsoft Copilot provides settings for “Training on conversation activity” and “Training on voice conversations,” both of which you can disable to opt out of model training. Claude’s AI training option is turned off by default. But you can always control this by checking the setting for “Help improve our AI models.”
