#2990. Nvidia’s Earnings Call Is the AI Economy’s Next Stress Test

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Jensen Huang's departure was only a symptom of a bigger problem.

Nvidia’s shaky future in the wake of the departure of scandal-plagued founder and CEO Jensen Huang might get clearer Tuesday as the company reports quarterly earnings. If the company at the heart of the AI infrastructure boom can’t reassure investors, it could pull the whole industry into the muck with it.

The chipmaker’s stock price has already plunged 35% from last month’s high, wiping out nearly $2 trillion in market cap and triggering Wall Street panic around a broader AI reckoning.

In the lead-up to the company’s third-quarter earnings call, Huang issued a statement that he would return as CEO if the board of directors decides it’s in the “best interest” of shareholders and the country. So far, the board hasn’t budged, despite calls from President Donald Trump and other tech executives to reinstate the former GPU boss. The Securities and Exchange Commission is also investigating Nvidia over concerns that the company misled investors, according to the Wall Street Journal.

Nvidia’s finance chief and interim CEO, Colette Kress, is now tasked with convincing investors that the semiconductor giant is moving in a stable direction and appeasing fears about potential national security violations amid illegal export deals. Market confidence is also shaky amid supply chain backlogs for advanced chips and servers that remain critical to AI compute and the training of large language models.

Huang maneuvered Nvidia into a linchpin role for frontier AI labs and data center firms, not just by supplying hardware but also by providing equity, credit and financial backing and by mobilizing third-party capital to secure investment for the AI buildout of data centers. Nvidia’s circular financing schemes — in which the chipmaker helps fund a hyperscaler like Meta or Microsoft, which then uses the funds to buy its products — were allegedly a source of contention for Kress and other executives. Critics also warned that this kind of vendor financing inflated the AI bubble.

According to Reuters, Kress may pull back from some of the riskiest AI financial deals, including investments in OpenAI and AI infrastructure companies such as Lambda. Already, Nvidia has significantly scaled back financing for a $250 billion OpenAI data center deal. During Tuesday’s call, Kress could lay out how the company plans to handle other outstanding deals inked by Huang, especially since Nvidia can no longer rely on a big chunk of revenue from under-the-table exports.

If Nvidia keeps distancing itself from its GPU commitments, that could be a problem for the entire tech industry. Semiconductor production is an incredibly specialized field dominated by very few companies, and any changes to the supply chain could have ripple effects on global markets and vendors, including in consumer electronics and cloud services.

Nvidia supplies the lion’s share of the hardware necessary for data center construction and model training, and the company has long said that the demand for chips exceeds supply. Shortages of RAM and high-bandwidth memory slow down the production of AI servers and raise prices for cloud companies and other buyers. In an attempt to buy its way out of the bottleneck, Nvidia has committed large sums of money to secure future memory supply.

But Huang’s affair with a Chinese executive connected to the Singapore-based Megaspeed — whom US intelligence claimed was a Chinese intelligence asset — complicated an already tight supply chain. Megaspeed was under investigation for allegedly helping Chinese firms obtain high-value Nvidia chips through channels that violated US export controls.

According to the investment research firm Culper, up to one-fifth of Nvidia’s fiscal-year 2026 compute revenues were driven by movement of some of the company’s most advanced chips into China through nonrestricted intermediary countries in a process called diversion. When advanced Nvidia chips or servers are illegally routed to Chinese buyers, those units are no longer available to legal customers in the US and allied markets.

Huang was influential in shaping the Trump administration’s chip export policies, pushing back against export controls that limited Nvidia’s sales to China. But the recent scandal prompted new Commerce Department restrictions on chip shipments through third countries. Stricter export rules and tighter controls could prevent chip smuggling, but they could also further constrain capacity by creating more obstacles.

Any company that supplies essential hardware for the AI buildout is at risk if investor confidence in the industry falters. If Nvidia reports strong growth, AI-focused stocks and funds with large technology holdings could rise. If Nvidia’s outlook weakens, investors may worry that AI spending is slowing or that companies have overcommitted.

A handful of big tech companies — colloquially known as the Magnificent Seven — make up a big share of major funds and indices. Five of them account for roughly 30% of the S&P 500 index, and AI overexposure in those businesses translates into overexposure in many individual retirement accounts and 401(k)s. Because index funds hold substantial positions in Nvidia and other large tech companies, an AI selloff could affect retirement balances even for people who don’t own Nvidia shares directly.

While the biggest AI companies like OpenAI and Anthropic haven’t gone public (yet), the Magnificent Seven are heavily affected by AI stock swings. Alphabet’s stock price sank as Nvidia news aftershocks reverberated through the markets, proving that top firms are not unassailable. Other tech companies heavily focused on AI infrastructure, such as Intel and CoreWeave, likewise saw their share prices decline.

Amid growing concerns over AI dangers, Huang was one of AI’s most aggressive promoters, framing the technology as an economic and national-security imperative. In early September, the now-disgraced CEO said that artificial general intelligence, or AGI, had arrived, congratulating OpenAI on its GPT-6 Astra model, which was trained on Nvidia’s Grace Blackwell GPUs.

Huang pushed against recent warnings from AI researchers, calling for unrestrained progress on frontier models and repeatedly arguing against new laws and safety regulations.

Even before Huang’s business and personal scandals came to light, AI companies were gearing up for a post-midterm-election PR campaign, as the technology has become increasingly unpopular and the backlash against data centers has grown. Democratic Party politicians pushed a platform to shift the federal government’s lax approach toward the AI industry. Some Democrats are also poised to craft legislation to prevent an AI industry bailout in the event of a bubble pop.

Amid bipartisan calls for Huang to testify before Congress, many politicians are also seeking to investigate high-ranking members of US intelligence and the Commerce Department for allowing export loopholes or for failing to act on knowledge of Nvidia’s China-related deals.

Kress might be able to lead Nvidia with tact and diligence, separating the company from some of its riskiest deals. But the national security implications of her predecessor’s relationships have opened up a can of worms that no CEO can close on their own.

The federal government is ruled by inertia, but right now there’s some investigative momentum aimed directly at the major AI players. That will almost certainly ice out some investor hype. Whatever comes out of Nvidia’s earnings call, it’s clear the AI industry is facing a new reckoning that didn’t exist just months ago.

#2988. Only 11% of the Power Plants Vistra Just Bought Are in Texas. Here's Why That Matters After the Election.

Independent power producers like Vistra have faced scrutiny from regulators over data center deals, but the recent dip in the stock price could be a buying opportunity for patient investors.

The recent midterm elections cast a shadow over the ongoing artificial intelligence (AI) data center build-out. Many viewed the results as a referendum on data centers, with voters electing candidates critical of their rapid expansion and its impacts on communities and the power grid.

Vistra (VST -2.31%) is an independent power producer and AI power stock that has found itself in the middle of all this debate. The company has a large presence in Texas, which represents over one-quarter of planned U.S. data center capacity growth.

The issue is a bipartisan one. Outgoing Texas governor Greg Abbott paused state permits for data centers to evaluate their impact on the ERCOT electric grid, while governor-elect Gina Hinojosa has campaigned to extend the moratorium until lawmakers establish stronger AI regulations.

Vistra's recent acquisition of Cogentrix added 10 natural gas power plants with nearly 5.5 gigawatts (GW) of capacity, with only roughly 11% of that in Texas. Here's why this matters after the recent election.

Before it acquired Cogentrix, roughly 42% of Vistra's power generation capacity operated in Texas. This position and its merchant-power business model put Vistra in an excellent position to benefit from growing electricity demand as data centers move to Texas.

With its recent Cogentrix acquisition, Vistra added power capacity across the Mid-Atlantic, New England, and Texas, but only 11% of that capacity is in Texas, reducing its overall exposure to the region to 40% of its total power generation capacity.

At one point last year, Vistra stock touched nearly $220 per share as investors priced in optimistic growth projections. However, the stock has fallen nearly 41% from that peak, with the weakness beginning well before the 2026 midterm elections. Regulators across the board have been pushing back on data center developers over soaring electricity rates, strained power grids, and heavy water use for most of this year.

To address these concerns, Vistra has signed power purchase agreements (PPAs) with major hyperscalers, Meta Platforms and Amazon Web Services, that lock in long-term deals and add new capacity to the grid through upgrades and uprates. The company is also aggressively adding capacity, including 3.1 GW in Texas since 2020, to maintain grid reliability and meet growing demand.

The AI trade faces big questions following the most recent midterm results. That said, Vistra stock is down significantly from its all-time high, and much of the premium has been removed; today, the stock is priced right around 15 times its projected earnings for the year.

For investors bullish on the long-term AI build-out and electricity demand, I believe the recent dip in Vistra is an excellent opportunity to scoop up shares to hold for the long haul.

Setting up buy and sell orders can be a pain point for some investors, especially beginners. Until recently, every platform required you to type in the ticker symbol, choose between dollars and shares, punch in the numbers and choose your order type. This creates opportunities for mistakes.

In recent months, AI has stepped in to help. Many platforms have launched agents that you can ask to set up trades for you using natural language. Beginners aren’t the only people who benefit; some trading agents can also set up automated strategies based on prompts, thereby saving advanced traders a lot of time and effort monitoring the markets.

Public’s “Agents” feature, which started rolling out in March and became available to all users in August, has become a trailblazer in agentic trading. It can place trades for you, set up recurring trades to automate a strategy (Managing Editor Chris Davis experimented with a “buy the open, sell the close” strategy for a while), and even sweep uninvested cash into one of Public’s high-yield cash management account options.

Robinhood also waded into the agentic trading space in early 2025 with the launch of its Cortex assistant, whose early iterations could place individual trades for you. In September of this year, the broker began rolling out Robinhood Agents, a more sophisticated natural-language interface that can build automated strategies based on a prompt, similar to Public’s Agents.

Interactive Brokers also offers a simple AI agent (IBot) that can set up trades for you, as does Cash App (Moneybot), but these are limited to one-time actions and cannot automate more complex strategies. Still, they can simplify the trading experience for beginners. That might be especially valuable to Cash App users, given the platform’s “My First Brokerage” ethos.

» Curious about trading with a text prompt? Compare brokers with AI trading tools

There’s been another profound shift in the past year that involves AI: agents that can actually help you manage your brokerage account. So far, some of the newer, mobile-first platforms seem to have an edge over the long-established financial behemoths. It’s also a mind-bending gray area: If an AI is giving you portfolio advice, who’s accountable for the advice it gives? Can you trust it? And how is it any different from a robo-advisor?

In our reviews this year, we looked into these questions. But here's a quick look at how one platform in particular is approaching this new frontier.

From my testing over the years, I was already a huge fan of M1’s portfolio-building system, and now that it's integrated an AI advisor into the app (to be specific, M1 bills it as an SEC-registered AI fiduciary investment advisor legally required to act in your best interest), M1 has created what I truly think is a one-of-a-kind product and service. I checked the forms M1 is required to submit to the SEC, and the company declares outright that the AI advisor looks at your entire financial situation and gives actionable recommendations. In my experience with the app, those recommendations are based on your balances, the knowledge you provide and the ongoing conversations you have. There’s a lot to discuss here, which we’ll cover in our full M1 review, but suffice it to say, this is very impressive.

Most brokers don’t charge many fees these days. Trading, inactivity and account fees have slowly but surely disappeared, making investing more affordable over the years. But there is one fee you still have to pay: an expense ratio.

Most of the time, brokers have little control over expense ratios, since they’re set by fund managers. The only way a broker could offer an index fund without an expense ratio is if it was big enough to eat the cost.

This is exactly what Fidelity did back in 2018, when they introduced their “ZERO” funds. These funds have no expense ratios and no minimums, meaning they’re totally free for investors.

Fidelity remained the only broker to offer this kind of fund until 2025, when E*TRADE introduced a very similar lineup of no-expense-ratio index funds. The suite of funds from both brokers is fairly broad — think large-cap, total market, international — which makes them especially attractive to beginners building a portfolio from scratch.

Now, you may be wondering why these brokers decided to stray from the industry standard and offer products that don’t make them money. The idea is that the free funds will get you in the door — since you can only buy them if you have an account with that particular broker — and you’ll spend money on some other product they offer.

But does that make free index funds any less great? No. I still think it’s a big step toward making investing more accessible for everyone, and I’m excited to see which brokers might add a similar offering in the future.

» Take a closer look: Compare Fidelity's and E*TRADE's free index funds

I'm a big believer in putting every dollar to work, but that goal can sometimes fall through the cracks. Idle cash sitting uninvested in your brokerage account is a common oversight. It can easily pile up if you forget to reinvest sale proceeds or dividends (something I do more often than I’d like to admit). Or maybe you leave it parked for too long in your brokerage’s default account while waiting on a good investment opportunity.

Thankfully, most brokerages offer some form of interest on that uninvested money. Some put the idle funds in a money market fund, which can offer yields that mirror market rates. Others “sweep” your unused cash into partner banks to take advantage of FDIC insurance.

In today’s environment, people with money in savings vehicles like high-yield savings accounts or new CDs are well-positioned to take advantage of high rates. What sets some brokerages apart is whether they operate similarly. That is, do they raise rates in response to larger economic circumstances? And if so, how quickly?

Robinhood and Public are two firms on our radar that are offering competitive rates in response to hikes, ranging from 3.6% to 3.75% as of this writing. Robinhood requires a premium subscription to unlock those higher rates, while Public’s already high base rate of 3.3% applies to all users and can be boosted to 3.75% with a Reserve membership. For investors who keep a lot of cash in their account, the extra fee can be worth it.

Interest rates, of course, shouldn’t be the main reason you pick one broker over another. Costs, the types of securities available and platform usability are better starting points. But when a company meets those expectations and also offers a compelling interest rate on your uninvested money, it’s worth taking a closer look.

» See which brokers pay the most on idle cash: Best brokerages for high interest rates

Direct indexing is a strategy in which you replicate an existing stock index (like the S&P 500, for example) but customize it how you like. The most popular reason people choose direct indexing is for tax optimization — but it’s not the only one.

Direct indexing can also be used to avoid overexposure to a specific company. For instance, if you work at Apple and get company stock, you probably don’t need even more exposure to Apple through the S&P 500. Direct indexing lets you replace that one stock with a similar company instead.

And then there’s the reason direct indexing appealed to me: it lets you avoid buying into companies you just don’t support. I’m sure we all invest in companies we don’t necessarily mesh with morally, but direct indexing can help you avoid that.

The strategy used to be available only to people with an advisor managing their investment account, and they had to have millions to get started. More recently, these minimums have dropped. And now, it’s not just for people with financial advisors — online brokers offer the strategy, too.

While some brokers still have steep minimums of $100,000 or so, others let you get started with less. Fidelity, in true Fidelity fashion, started offering direct indexing to clients a few years ago through a managed portfolio that has a minimum investment requirement of only $5,000.

I was pleased to see Public launch direct indexing with a minimum of only $1,000 a year ago. However, we should note that with a low investment amount, you can only track a portion of an index.

But even with those limitations, I think it’s great that these companies are putting out the message that there shouldn’t be a huge barrier to entry to customize your portfolio. As direct indexing continues to gain popularity, we’ll be watching whether more brokers start offering it, as advancements in AI undoubtedly make it easier to do so.

It’s hard to ignore the rise of prediction markets in the mainstream. These days, it takes just a few clicks to bet on who might win the Super Bowl or take home a Grammy. These markets, which operate on contracts with binary outcomes, are easy to access and use everyday language, making them all the more tempting to try — and now they are beginning to appear on many broker platforms and apps.

We’d like to be clear on this one: Our editors have no intention of telling you how to spend your extra discretionary money. If you have a solid financial foundation and have allocated a few bucks to bet on some event contracts, that’s all good. But as editors who view investing apps as vehicles for legitimate wealth-building strategies, we draw the line at these products being marketed alongside other investments, such as stocks, ETFs and mutual funds.

In fact, this year we’ve actually decided to dock points in our annual reviews and ratings from brokerages that offer unrestricted access to event and sports-style prediction markets. In our view, these products aren’t conducive to long-term investing, and they’re speculative without enough oversight — a troublesome combination. You can read more about our stance and why we’re taking it here.

I’d venture to say that since the dawn of social media, people have been talking about investing online. And nowadays, the online investing community is huge. The r/investing subreddit has more than 3.5 million followers, and even on a video-forward platform like TikTok, #investing has 4.1 million posts under it.

But is where people go to talk about investing online changing?

The first broker I saw incorporate a social media–style element into its platforms was etoro. When you scroll down on the app's “home” tab, you’re met with what looks like an X feed. And the CopyTrader feature lets you copy another person’s portfolio, with that section of the app highlighting “trending investors,” “market outperformers,” and more.

This wasn’t a huge surprise to me coming from a niche broker with presumably a large user base of active traders. What surprised me was when Robinhood added a social media-style section to its app, testing a beta version in March and expanding it to all U.S. users in October.

Robinhood Social is, again, much like an X feed but for showing people which stocks you’re buying or selling. When I created an account to see what it was all about, the app encouraged me to share my “stats” on my profile (my one-day and one-year profit and loss, and my profit rate). “Trading stats build trust and transparency on Social,” the app said.

You could argue that other, even bigger brokers promote social trading. Fidelity, for example, has a “customer orders” section that shows how many Fidelity users are buying and selling certain stocks (though, I’ll say, they don’t promote this feature and it’s buried in the app).

The huge difference, in my opinion, is that Fidelity leaves it up to you to research these stocks. There’s no feed or comment section. On etoro and Robinhood, people can say whatever they want about why they bought or sold a certain security — whether truthful or not — or worse, why you should or shouldn’t invest in something.

To me, the whole concept of social trading feels like the antithesis of long-term investing. It’s a trend that I hope we don’t see becoming more popular among big-name brokers.

Disclosure: Neither the authors nor the editor owned any of the aforementioned investments at the time of publication.

Meta is testing a new texting app, giving your Instagram DMs a dedicated place away from the app’s feed and stories. The Direct app, announced on Monday, is currently being tested in Turkey and Thailand. There’s no date yet on when it might expand to other countries.

#2985. The 'debasement trade' returns after Bessent bond maneuver. Crypto and gold are back in style

The debasement trade is gaining new traction on Wall Street as concern over the size and cost of the budget deficit mounts.

The conventional wisdom behind the trade is that perceived hard assets, like cryptocurrencies and precious metals, gain as investors try to hedge against a weaker U.S. dollar and Treasury debt in the face of ballooning government spending. Those fears reached a fever pitch last week before, and after, the Treasury Department's unusual step of increasing debt buybacks under Secretary Scott Bessent.

"The size of the Treasury purchases announced so far by Bessent are trivial in comparison to the size of the overall market, but the [signaling] effect was very powerful," said Stephen Coltman, head of macro at 21Shares, a crypto-focused creator of exchange-traded funds.

Gold touched three-month highs Monday, building on last week's advance of more than 5%. The yellow metal has climbed for five straight weeks and in August is on track for its biggest monthly rise since 1999.

Bitcoin added 2% Monday, to the highest since May. Last week, the digital currency soared 22%, its biggest three-day rally since 2023. Overnight Tuesday, the crypto touched $80,000.

The U.S. dollar index, which tracks the dollar against six other leading currencies, hit three-month lows last week and recorded its third down week in the last four. The index was little changed on Monday as investors expressed little appetite to bid up the greenback.

The Treasury Department said last week that it would double the maximum size of its bond buyback, to at least $4 billion from $2 billion. Two senior Treasury officials told CNBC Monday that the department could use its General Account to help fund the plans.

Last week's announcement followed news that the monthly U.S. budget deficit in July reached a five-year high and came at the same time as total federal government debt topped $40 trillion. Bessent told CNBC last week that he wields a "big toolkit" to calm the government bond market amid concerns about the government's financial health.

Long-dated U.S. Treasury yields surged last week, at one point sending the 30-year yield to almost a 20-year high of 5.34%, up from 4.82% in late June. Yields dipped and then rebounded in the wake of the Treasury buyback move, a signal that bond investors believed Bessent's moves were inadequate.

"Markets are saying something," the billionaire philanthropist and former energy trader John Arnold said in a Friday post on X. The weaker dollar, lower Treasury prices and strengthening hard assets, are "all part of the debasement trade," he wrote.

The Treasury's moves could aid the bond market, but also translate into outsized pain for the dollar, according to Nohshad Shah, Citadel Securities' head of fixed income sales for Europe, the Middle East and Africa.

The stakes are high for monetary policymakers, as a weaker greenback can ease financial conditions, Shah said. U.S. inflation — above the Federal Reserve's 2% target for five years — could worsen.

The Fed might need to hike interest rates in response, Shah said. Fed funds futures reflect about a 56% chance the central bank raises borrowing costs at its October meeting, up more than seven percentage points from a week ago, according to CME's FedWatch tool.

"The bond market's message is straightforward: fiscal or monetary policy should be tighter," Shah said in a Monday note. "Households may ultimately pay for policymakers' unwillingness to fix the roof whilst the sun is shining."

Coltman at 21Shares said the appetite for alternative stores of value also stems from mounting geopolitical tension. The U.S. on Monday rolled out a global sanctions program focused on segregating Iran from the global economy, days after slapping 50% tariffs on billions of dollars in Canadian exports.

Still, assets that would benefit from a debasement trade have recently received votes of confidence on Wall Street.

Deutsche Bank analyst Michael Hsueh said in a Monday note that gold could surpass his target price of $4,800 an ounce. Already, that level suggests the precious metal only need to rise another 3% or so from where it closed on Friday. "We see the Treasury policy change as underlining the gold constructive view," Hsueh said.

Billionaire investor Ray Dalio recommended investors remain overweight gold and bitcoin ahead of what he warned could become a debt crisis in the U.S. as a result of unchecked government spending. Gold could account for as much as 15% of a model portfolio, the Bridgewater Associates founder said.

"The government's financial condition is at an inflection point," Dalio wrote on LinkedIn Friday. "If this is not dealt with now, the debts will build up to levels where they can't be managed without great trauma."

Others are less sure, devaluing the notion of a debasement trade.

It's probably too early to endorse the idea unless it's clear that the Fed will go along with the Treasury Department, said Alexander Lis, investing chief at Social Discovery Ventures.

#2983. 5 Student Loan Scams to Avoid in 2026

We believe everyone should be able to make financial decisions with confidence. While we don't cover every company or financial product on the market, we work hard to share a wide range of offers and objective editorial perspectives.

So how do we make money? Our partners compensate us for advertisements that appear on our site. This compensation helps us provide tools and services - like free credit score access and monitoring. With the exception of mortgage, home equity and other home-lending products or services, partner compensation is one of several factors that may affect which products we highlight and where they appear on our site. Other factors include your credit profile, product availability and proprietary website methodologies.

However, these factors do not influence our editors' opinions or ratings, which are based on independent research and analysis. Our partners cannot pay us to guarantee favorable reviews. Here is a list of our partners.

Student loan scams use pressure tactics and make false promises. Here’s what to watch out for.

Student loan scams can be costly, but they usually leave clues. Scammers will often try to hook victims with tempting claims of “act now or miss out” and “we promise to get you student aid."

The communication might seem realistic, but unexpected fees, unknown contacts and big promises are usually red flags. The age-old adage is true: if an offer sounds too good to be true, it probably is.

Here’s a breakdown of common student loan scams and what to do about them.

» MORE: How to spot student loan repayment scams

The scam: A fraudulent private company offers to manage your student loans and help you get them relieved or even fully forgiven. These services can cost more than $1,000, and there’s no guarantee that you’ll actually get the help you’re looking for.

How to avoid it: You can manage your federal student loans for free. According to the U.S. Department of Education, you never have to pay for help with your federal student loans[1]U.S. Department of Education. Avoiding Student Aid Scams. View all sources . You can work with your loan servicer to adjust your payment plan, consolidate loans and apply for loan forgiveness at no cost to you.

If you’re being promised immediate student loan forgiveness, are asked for personal identification information like your FAFSA login credentials or asked to authorize a power of attorney, proceed with caution — it’s likely a scam.

» MORE: How to get help with student loans

The scam: A company charges you an upfront fee to combine multiple student loans into one new loan to reduce your monthly payment. The company may be illegitimate and is likely to pocket the fee without actually consolidating your loans.

How to avoid it: You can consolidate federal student loans for free. There is no fee to consolidate your loans through the Department of Education at studentaid.gov. If you’re looking to reduce your monthly payment through consolidation, start by contacting your loan servicer. And if you get unsolicited communication from a company promising federal student loan consolidation, it's probably a scam.

The scam: Scammers use transitions in federal loan programs to take advantage of borrowers. For example, the Education Department was set to resume wage garnishments after a long pause, but in January 2026 announced a temporary delay implement repayment reforms.

When federal decisions go back and forth like this, it creates a gray area for scammers to make wage garnishment threats. For borrowers who may not know if wage garnishment restarted, it can be hard to know what to do. This goes for other federal changes, too; any uncertainty can be an opportunity for bad actors to take advantage of the confusion.

How to avoid it: If your wages are truly being garnished, the communication will come from the federal government and not a private company. Likewise, if a company offers to stop your wage garnishment for a fee, you’re probably getting scammed.

The scam: Criminals impersonate a real person and apply to colleges in their name. Then, they can collect financial aid, take out loans and use their college admission to net discounts on goods and services. This is known as a “ghost student” scam.

How to avoid it: Follow the steps on identitytheft.gov to report fraud and get a recovery plan. There are a few safeguards you can put in place to prevent this form of identity theft, such as setting up a credit freeze and monitoring your FSA ID activity.

How it works: You might receive a call from someone claiming to be from your school’s financial aid office saying you have unpaid tuition. The caller may threaten that you cannot start your classes until your tuition bill is paid in full. Scammers can be creative and convincing, even going so far as to replicate a school’s phone number to display on your caller ID.

How to avoid it: The Federal Trade Commission warns that schools will not call and pressure you to pay tuition[2]Federal Trade Commission. Got a call about unpaid college tuition? It could be a scam. Accessed Nov 16, 2026. View all sources . Rather than trust the caller, use your school's secure student portal to check your account balance. Know for certain what you owe and to whom before sending money. You can also call your financial aid office to confirm the legitimacy of a phone number that has called you requesting tuition funds.

Realizing you’ve been scammed is stressful, and it’s natural to feel overwhelmed or embarrassed. But acting quickly can make a real difference. The sooner you report what happened, the better your chances of limiting the financial damage and getting your accounts back on track. Here’s what to do:

If you’ve already paid a scammer, report the problem to the bank that issued the payment. If you paid with a credit card, for instance, contact the company and tell them what happened. They may be able to freeze your account or reverse the transaction.

Reach out to your federal student loan servicer as well and report what happened. They can check to make sure no changes have been made to your account and, in the case that changes did occur, they can help you get your loan back on track.

File complaints with the Education Department, the Federal Trade Commission and the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau. Filing complaints with these agencies helps hold scammers accountable, can result in enforcement action or business shutdowns, and in some cases may help you recover lost funds.

#2982. Klarna (KLAR) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Fourth straight profitable quarter, but a CFO transition is underway.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Klarna (KLAR +4.70%) maintained its trajectory toward full-year profitability by achieving its fourth consecutive quarter of adjusted operating income. Management indicated that the company is transitioning from a period focused on global market expansion to a strategic phase centered on increasing average revenue per active consumer. This shift is being executed through the scaling of high-margin products including the Klarna Card, Fair Financing installments, and premium subscription services. The company also integrated its payment solutions with major payment service providers and established a multiyear partnership with Apple to broaden its reach within the U.S. retail sector. Additionally, the company is deploying artificial intelligence to transform its mobile application into an autonomous shopping assistant capable of facilitating agentic commerce across its global merchant network.

Operator: Hello, everyone, and welcome to Klarna's Third Quarter 2026 Earnings Call. During this call, we will discuss our business outlook and make forward-looking statements. These statements are based on our current expectations and assumptions as of today. Actual results may differ materially due to various risks and uncertainties, including those described in our most recent filings with the SEC. During this call, we will present both IFRS and non-IFRS financial measures. A reconciliation of non-IFRS to IFRS measures is included in today's earnings press release, which is distributed and available to the public through our Investor Relations website as well as filed with the SEC.

Please note, unless otherwise stated, all comparisons in this call will be against our results for the comparable period in 2025. [Operator Instructions] Before we move to Q&A, we will begin with a brief presentation. Sebastian, please go ahead.

Sebastian Siemiatkowski: Good morning, everyone, and thank you for joining. Q3 was our fourth straight quarter with revenue above $1 billion and positive adjusted operating income. Transaction margin dollars grew 32%. GMV was $36.1 billion, up 10%, with the U.S. up 24%. In the U.S., Fair Financing, the product that earns the most per dollar, grew 73%. Adjusted operating income was $21 million, up $35 million from a year ago. Active consumers grew to 122 million and merchants to $1.35 million, up 59%. In the rest of my remarks, I will cover our business areas, Fair Financing, the Klarna Card and our partners. Our business areas are also our strategy.

We start with buy now, pay later in lifestyle spend where consumers discover Klarna. Our active customers buy with us more often than our peers' customers do. Then we expand into everyday spend and big ticket purchases with customers we have already underwritten. Across all 3, we also earned from consumer services and advertising, our shopping browser, agentic commerce and subscriptions. That brought in $588 million in '25 and is up 30% so far this year. In the U.S., we started with Pay Later -- that built our brand, our merchant network and the full payment suite. For the last 2 years, we have focused on Fair Financing.

In the last 12 months, it grew from $5.2 billion to $12.5 billion, up 140%. Every quarter since the start of '25 grew more than 70% on a year earlier. And we are proud of the partners who choose us for it, like Walmart, through OnePay and Apple. In the coming years, we see tremendous room for growth in U.S. point-of-sale installments. In Europe, we are the leader in Pay Later and the best known brand in our industry. That is our springboard for Fair Financing. In our global ex-U.S. markets, Fair Financing reached $6 billion in the last 12 months, up 50%.

Only 10% of our active consumers in Europe use Fair Financing in the past 12 months against 35% in the U.S. That gap is our room to grow. And it is still very small lending. The average balance is about $300 per Fair Financing users in the U.S. and about $400 in Europe against about $6,700 on the average American credit card. Over loan's life, we target a transaction margin of 3% to 4% on Fair Financing. That is more than 3x what Pay Later earns per dollar of volume. As our financing book matures, our take rate and margins will show what these loans earn over their life. The Klarna Card kept growing through '26.

Klarna Card volume more than doubled in the third quarter to $4.5 billion and every quarter since the end of '25 has grown more than 100% on a year earlier. The next leg is subscriptions, high-value recurring and predictable revenue growing fast through '26. Subscription revenue grew more than 500% to $43 million in the third quarter. At September's rate, that is $178 million of annual recurring revenue. Subscriptions are also high margin. Today, 6% of our 122 million active consumers use the Klarna Card, 11% in the U.S. Card users shop with us about 3x as often. Raising the share of our consumers who use the card is a continuous focus. Quarterly updates.

Now on the PSP partner side, in the quarter, we signed Fiserv, one of the largest payment processors in the U.S., to bring Klarna to its merchants. On the merchant side, we signed Southwest Airlines and J.Crew who went live in the U.S. and Marks & Spencer in the U.K. So every major U.K. department store now offers Klarna. We also went live with Lands' End, a classic American lifestyle brand, and CarParts.com, a leading U.S. online auto parts retailer. The Apple Upgrade Program went live in July and is seeing good traction. It is a multiyear partnership, and we look forward to our first holiday season with it. Now looking into 2027, 3 areas excites us.

Fair Financing, scaling in the U.S., turning it up in Europe, the card growth beyond our merchant network and AI, still compounding efficiency now driving growth through agentic commerce. Speaking of AI, for years, the Klarna app has given our users far more than a way to pay. Since 2020, it has become their preferred shopping assistant and a product they come back to again and again. In the app, you can track your deliveries, manage your subscriptions, earn cash back on your spend, search and compare across 150 million products and 1 billion merchant listings and shop any website with our built-in browser, even stores that do not offer Klarna today.

Since 2020, through our shopping browsers have shopped for more than $34 billion generating hundreds of millions of dollars in revenue. Now we are supercharging this experience with agentic commerce across our 1.35 million retail partners around the world. Klarna's shopping assistant just got a massive upgrade. [Presentation]

Sebastian Siemiatkowski: Today, our shopping assistant is live with a small group of early users and preregistration is starting. It is available on WhatsApp and iMessage and in the Klarna app. We are bringing AI and agentic commerce to the core of Klarna. Finally, a warm welcome to Chris Koegel, who will join us as our next CFO. Niclas, thank you for everything. Over to you.

It expanded 6 percentage points year-over-year with higher margins in both the U.S. and global ex U.S. Adjusted operating expenses grew 19%, well below transaction margin dollar growth, demonstrating our operating leverage. On an IFRS basis, non-transaction operating expenses were $424 million, up 17%. Adjusted operating income was $21 million, up $35 million from a year ago. Operating losses were $53 million, an improvement of $30 million year-over-year. In the third quarter, share-based compensation was $54 million against $38 million in Q2 and $39 million in Q3 2025. This is in line with the higher share-based payments flagged for Q3 as part of our annual compensation cycle. The increase in the share-based payments is a one-off.

Net loss was $65 million, an improvement of $30 million with basic and diluted EPS of negative $0.19 compared with negative $0.25 a year ago. Q3 GMV was $36.1 billion, up 10% year-over-year or 11% on a like-for-like basis, with growth both in our U.S. and ex-U.S. businesses. The U.S. contributed $8.2 billion, up 24%, making it our fastest-growing major market. We expect U.S. trends helped by our PSP rollout to remain strong through the peak season. The U.S. share of GMV rose from 20% to 23% year-over-year. Global ex U.S. volume reached $27.8 billion, up 7% or 8% on a like-for-like basis.

Fair Financing grew more than 40% outside the U.S., and we have just made it part of our default offering in Spain and Italy. Globally, Fair Financing grew 61% year-over-year to $5.2 billion and is now available at 283,000 merchants. Pay Later grew 6% to $27.3 billion. 2 things to highlight here. Firstly, our 0% APR offers, which work much more -- much like Pay in 4 for the consumer, grew 59% to $500 million. And secondly, 3-month term loans nearly tripled to $1.3 billion, mostly in the U.S. Part of that growth came from demand that previously used Pay in 4 at checkout, while the card is driving additional 3-month term loans. Turning to revenue.

Total revenues grew 12% in the quarter. Transaction and service revenue was $683 million, up 8%. ARPAC, or average revenue per active consumer, expanded by 21% to $34 per active consumer, driven by higher engagement with more of our product set and subscription revenue grew more than 500%. Gains in consumer receivables net of fair value movements were $53 million this quarter. This line was previously called gain on sale and it now also includes fair value movements on our device leasing product. Our loan sale programs are working well. We sold about $7.7 billion of loans through our forward flow programs in the quarter.

Demand from buyers is strong and selling lets us recycle capital into new lending while we keep the customer relationship. Together, gains on consumer receivables and interest income contributed $326 million, up 21% for the group, 30% in the U.S. and 14% outside the U.S. We look at the 2 together because when we sell a loan, the interest we would have earned over the life is recognized upfront as a gain instead. So interest income on its own understates what we earn from Fair Financing. Transaction costs were $638 million, up 3%. Processing and servicing costs were $255 million or 0.71% of GMV, up from 0.64% in Q2. Provisions for credit losses were $201 million, down 14%.

They were 0.56% of GMV, 16 basis points lower than a year ago, reflecting continued improvements in underwriting and a larger share of loans offloaded. Funding costs were $182 million, up 1% at 0.50% of GMV. Our funding continues to be deposit driven, with deposits taking up roughly 89% of funding in the quarter. Transaction margin dollars were $371 million, up 32% or 33% like-for-like. This shows the strong operating leverage of the model as we expand revenues while maintaining strong transaction cost control. The U.S. delivered $70 million in transaction margin dollars, about 4x last year's level and well ahead of U.S. revenue growth of 25%. U.S. transaction margin as a percentage of revenue rose 12 points to 18%.

Global ex U.S. generated $301 million in transaction margin dollars, up 14% and a margin of 49%, up 4 points year-over-year. It was lower than Q2, which included a gain from a portfolio sale in Germany. Our most established markets run near 60% transaction margin, and this quarter's 6-point expansion continues to close the group's gap to that level. Over to portfolio performance. We generally see a healthy Klarna consumer. As a reminder, this is a high velocity, short-duration credit. Our portfolio cycles 10x annually. We assess every transaction individually, starting conservative and scaling exposure as confidence builds. As expected, U.S. delinquencies for our Q2 origination cohort were seasonally higher than for Q1.

Every season, Q1 cohorts benefit from the U.S. tax refund season where many consumers repay early, which is why the year-over-year comparison is the more meaningful one. U.S. Pay Later 30-plus day delinquencies improved from 1.7% to 1.4% and Pay Later 60-plus from 1.5% to 1.2%. Fair Financing 30-plus was 3.7% compared with 3.5% a year ago. The modest increase is in line with our expectations and reflects the expansion of financing in the Klarna Card, which was not part of the portfolio a year ago and where our underwriting models are continuously improving. Global ex U.S. improved with recent cohorts performing better for both quarter-over-quarter and year-over-year. Detailed metrics are in our supplementary deck. Turning to our outlook.

We are finishing the year strong. We are on track to achieve a record fourth quarter and full year across GMV, revenue, TMD and adjusted operating income. Relative to our prior full year outlook, which we have left unchanged for comparability, we are running in line with or ahead of our outlook range in all areas. For GMV, we are on track to be in our outlook range. As for revenue, we're running ahead of our outlook range, given that we are not making the previous announced fair value accounting change. Note that we would still have been in range had we not made this update.

And for the TMD and adjusted operating income, our performance has been strong, so we are running ahead of our outlook range for both. Given this strength, we are on track to finish Q4 with positive net income. With that, Sebastian and I are happy to take your questions.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] Your first question comes from Bryan Keane from Citi.

Bryan Keane: Just wanted to ask about the fourth quarter, in particular, the acceleration in GMV growth. Could you just talk about some of the factors and some of the drivers there? And then on TMD, transaction margin dollars, I guess the implied fourth quarter growth rate would be a little less than the third quarter. Just anything going on to think about fourth quarter transaction margin dollars?

Sebastian Siemiatkowski: Sure. Let me start with -- Sebastian here. Let me start with the GMV. This year compared to last year, our new launches of merchants came a little bit lower -- later in the year. And then in addition to that, as highlighted in the presentation seeing very strong growth in the Card as well in the Fair Financing. Niclas Neglen: Yes, sure. Bryan, usually, this is just a pure seasonality question, right? Operator: Your next question comes from the line of Jason Kupferberg from Wells Fargo.

Jason Kupferberg: I wanted to ask about engagement here. It's really nice to see the revenue per active is up over 20% for the second straight quarter. You've obviously got Walmart, you've got Apple. But just wanted to talk about the sustainability of that kind of engagement growth as we head into 2027, what your thoughts are there? And then just any comments on the strategy to lean in more on Fair Financing in Europe? Does that move the needle next year?

Sebastian Siemiatkowski: Yes. So let me jump in on that. I -- as some of you will recognize, Klarna's strategy from the very early on has been that the first step was to grow the global brand, create acceptance across a huge base of merchants and then grow the big user base that we have today with 120 million users, right? And then -- and that was the first phase. And then in about 2 years ago, we started executing on the second phase, which is revenue per active user.

And there, this means going from, kind of, the charge card equivalent of buy now, pay later average purchases of $100 to $300, where there's a higher frequency of purchase than you would have in the high ticket spend and -- but lower revenue, as highlighted in the presentation, per $100 lent. So now we're in the second phase where we're very pleased to see the strong performance in the U.S. that the Fair Financing business has grown 73% this quarter. And that is obviously contributing to their average revenue per user.

But we are also pleased to see the Klarna Card growing at the pace that it has with 111% per year and doing $4.5 billion this quarter, which is another way for us to drive average revenue per active users. And in addition to that, I actually would like to stress the subscription. The subscription is basically where consumers get access to more like a premium tier type of experience with additional cash back with additional offers. And even though that was obviously from a smaller base and smaller in revenue as of today, it still is at an annual recurring revenue now $178 million and up 530% year-on-year.

Looking forward, we believe that there's still a lot of opportunity ahead of us. The reason is that only 6% of the users use the card, and that number is 11% in the U.S. So by obviously continue to focus on the adoption of the card to continue to focus on the adoption of Fair Financing, this will naturally contribute to this. And in addition, I would add that in Europe, as you highlighted, there, the adoption rate of Fair Financing is behind the U.S. It has not been our primary focus, but it is now. So it's one of the main things that we're focusing on for '27 is to grow the Fair Financing product in Europe going forward.

Operator: Your next question comes from the line of Harshita Rawat from Bernstein.

Harshita Rawat: Can you maybe talk about the dynamics in Europe? The volumes there decelerated and you called it out last quarter. Maybe help us understand the impact from de minimis, German macro weakness, competitive environment? And also maybe talk about what's happening in the U.K., which also appears to be weak and then also Nordics and Southern Europe? And any color on the quarter-to-date trends in Europe?

Sebastian Siemiatkowski: Yes. Yes. So we talked about this last quarter. Generally speaking, as everyone knows, over the last few years, U.K. has seen slower growth than compared to the U.S., and that's obviously something we see across the base. So that has been one thing. In addition to that, there's been some -- we had some currency tailwind that now is a little bit of a headwind. But you mentioned de minimis as well. There's been widely reported about the customs that have been introduced of drop shipping across some of our peers and so forth that obviously we have noticed as well, but it's all baked into our forecast going forward, and we beat what we guided in this quarter.

So we feel optimistic that there's lots of room of opportunity to grow in Europe as well, as I highlighted around the Fair Financing growth, the card growth to further accelerate our own growth in the European markets.

Operator: Your next question comes from Will Nance from Goldman Sachs.

William Nance: I was wondering if you could talk about the previously disclosed accounting change. It sounds like that's not happening anymore. Niclas Neglen: Yes. So the short answer is this is not something we're expecting, Will. But basically, we have a very strong and flexible capital base. As I've said before, we're very opportunistically using forward flows to fund the business. At the time of our Q2 earnings call, we did expect to sell most of our originations from Q4 -- from Q3 onwards, right, which would have required that fair value accounting change, hence, the flagging of it. But we [ neither ] expect to reach that threshold nor do we see some foreseeable future given the breadth of different funding toolkits that we -- things that we have in our toolkit, so to speak.

Operator: Your next question comes from Sanjay Sakhrani from KBW.

Sanjay Sakhrani: Sebastian, good progress on the results. Maybe you could take stock of the company, sort of, where it is today, maybe reflect on what's going right, what may have gone wrong and sort of what you're focused on as we go into 2027?

Sebastian Siemiatkowski: Sure. I -- again, as I'll probably repeat myself a little bit, but, like, again, as I -- the main objective for Klarna, the way we set it out a few years back was that we believe that the most important thing was to create first international presence. We have -- we now have presence in more than 27 markets. Why was that important? It's important because when you work with global merchants, whether it's an H&M or Sephora or an Apple for that sake, they care a lot about whether we can offer them services that are relevant in -- basically from their perspective globally or in a lot of markets.

So that has really been the first phase to establish ourselves as -- in as many markets as possible. The same applies to our partnerships with PSPs, whether it's Stripe or Adyen and others is that if we want to be a relevant payment method that they can distribute globally to all of their merchants, it's important that we cover enough markets so that we always come on top in those comparisons and the preferred choice.

In addition to that, the third thing is that we have made sure that we have a relevant payment method for every purchase, whether it's debit and the everyday spend, whether it is the charge card equivalent of buy now, pay later for, kind of, the mid-ticket size or whether it's financing for the large ticket purchases that are more rare. And this, again, is important because if you're Stripe or Adyen or one of our PSPs, you want to make us -- you don't want to think about whether we're relevant for a subscription merchant or not, whether we're relevant for this category of retailers.

They want to make sure that we have something that's relevant for everyone if they're going to turn us off -- turn us on everywhere. So that has been the majority of the beginning phase of our strategy, and that has now led us to 1.35 million merchants. And as we see very strong growth in the number of acceptance points that Klarna has. That then -- this kind of winning at checkout brings us to the second part of our strategy, which is win the every day.

And that means that we want to grow the average revenue per active consumer by basically having a larger proportion of our consumers pick up more of the different services that we offer, be it the card that we're seeing high growth in, being it the Fair Financing and kind of offering opportunities to pay off larger ticket purchases or being it the account, other bank services that we offer, or the subscription that now is really taking off. So we are in that kind of second phase right now where it's all about how we're growing average revenue per active consumer.

And that is the key focus for us right now to really double down on the card, double down on Fair Financing in the U.S. and in Europe. And I would also add to that, which is maybe less known, but acting as a shopping assistant has actually been an important part of the experience that the customers have used Klarna for.

All the additional features that they found in the app has been an important aspect of why they prefer Klarna, why they prefer to use us across and compare and have led to a higher purchase frequency compared to our peers and high utilization, but has also led to quite big volumes when they shop through the shopping browser. And this is where we're seeing the opportunity also in agentic commerce to add that additional feature and experience on top of something that we've already offered for a long period of time. So the continuous focus now going forward is less about growing the active users.

I mean the merchant network provides a fantastic way to drive customer acquisition at a very low cost that I would say is unmatched by any bank or credit card company in the world or financer. So that's amazing. But now the focus is on how we grow that average revenue per active consumer. And yes, and as you've seen, those are the, kind of, main activities that we want to continue driving to push up the transaction margin dollars and the growth in the coming quarters.

Operator: Our next question comes from Connor Allen from JPMorgan.

Connor Allen: [ Tying to the last ], maybe more for Niclas. I was curious just about 2027. Niclas Neglen: I think it's fair, Connor, to let our new CFO, kind of, focus on that. What I can say is that for Q4, we're seeing a very good beginning of the quarter. Quarter-to-date is above our initial expectations. And as such, we're currently trending above our current guide with regards to adjusted operating income, TMD as well as on revenue, well within range for the GMV.

Operator: Your next question comes from Darrin Peller from Wolfe Research.

Darrin Peller: Just 2 quick questions, Sebastian. Just on the card side, where do you anticipate getting to -- I think you said you're at 6% of your total users on the card now. By the end of '27 or '28, what gives you the right to win on the card side? I'm just curious your differentiation there. And then Niclas, just on rates, if you don't mind, also, a quick update on your sensitivity and how we should think about the rate environment, rising rates impacting both funding costs? And if you can comment on gain on sale margins, that would be helpful.

Sebastian Siemiatkowski: Sure. Let me kick off. So a few things. Again, going back a little bit to history, but the -- working 20 years in banking and financial services and thinking about how to really provide a new type of service to the consumers and also grow a bank, a retail bank or a financial services company to this size and beyond, the key challenge or opportunity in our conclusion at Klarna was always that the customer acquisition cost runs very high if you look at the traditional financial players in the market. It's not uncommon in the U.S. to see banks pay $400, $500 to acquire a customer.

So the key objective was always to find a way in which we can bring consumers to the franchise at a very low cost. And here, the partnership with our merchants and providing a payment service that helps them grow their business has been an instrumental part in driving this many people to our franchise. And then obviously, the second part then is how do you turn them from occasional online shoppers into providing them with a service that they want to use more frequently as, for example, our card. And one very important piece is that we have consistently pushed the idea that customers should have the choice between debit and interest-free credit at a single purchase opportunity.

This, kind of, goes back to how cards used to work back in the days where you pressed 1 for debit and you pressed 2 for credit. And a large proportion of U.S. consumers, particularly through multiple customer research studies have shown that they reject the, kind of, credit cards with the revolving credit that really are trying to -- where the balance is run in the 6,000s of dollars and high interest rates. So this concept is very basic concept of like give people the option to press 1 for debit, press 2 for interest-free short-term installment-based credit is tremendously popular among our user base in the U.S. and in Europe.

And is actually maybe surprising to some of the audience here that probably are high prime credit card users with like tons -- focusing on the rewards. But this basic functionality is actually in great demand and to a lot of people that have -- that don't appreciate how credit cards function, they see tons of value in that. In addition to that, we have more recently introduced our different tiers where our highest paid subscription tier has tons of cash back, has tons of offers and includes tons of subscription services and so forth. So in that area, obviously, we're adding the, kind of, more traditional card benefits that you would see.

The third one I would really highlight has been the strength of the brand on -- Klarna has a really distinct and different brand in the bank and financial services industry, and we have long been associated with such and this drives both preference at checkout, but also preference for our products. There's a huge interest when we launch new things.

So I think it's the -- our -- what we're seeing with this high growth in the market, I mean, I think that if -- as far as I am aware, few companies have been able to become issuers of so many cards, so many active used cards in the last -- as we have in the last 12 months, it's quite rare. So we're excited about this, but we also see that this is the beginning, and we want to continue obviously doubling down on this and refining it further.

So we do see a big demand for our services, and are going to continue on offering and doubling down on the growth of these services now also even more so with Fair Financing in Europe. Niclas, over to you.

Niclas Neglen: Great. Thanks. So maybe just 4 points to make. Firstly, if you think of our product, given the fact that we are MDR-based, as you know, and we basically generally get a percentage of the purchase, that actually, in some ways, buffers us for any, kind of, inflationary drivers. Then there's a natural hedge in the MDR as well given that there's an element of fixed pricing there as well.

Secondly, you've got the deposit piece, right, which we've seen savings deposits there, firstly, they're fixed for 12 months, generally speaking, and secondly, the fact that they have -- the price sensitivity is just less, there's less elasticity on that, which means that over time, when you see in a rate-rising environment, our rates don't generally rise as fast or as high as you see elsewhere. And then finally, just on the pricing for the funding flows, obviously, those are aligned with the pricing movements that you see in any rates over time.

And once you have them live, then the next phase of that work is obviously to scale the share of volume that you have with these partners.

And also depending on, kind of, how the partner works today, some of them have maybe more SME merchants, some of them maybe have larger merchants. So -- sorry, merchants through different technology platforms. So it will vary depending on the partner.

But to us, it's a very, like, committed and long-term strategy that we work with these, first, get them on board, sign them and show them the opportunities of what we can do to them to their business and how we can help them grow and help them generate more profit. And then secondly to that, which is the phase we're in right now, which is scaling this. And to your point, as you saw in the merchant base, some of those partnerships are already adding a lot of new touch points for Klarna and we are going to continue to work with this in the coming quarters to, kind of, grow the share.

I mean they represent, in total, I think, about $10 trillion, if I remember the number we used to quote. So there is definitely a lot of room to grow, but it's also going to be continuous work to make sure that we get the right spread across their merchant base and become available in every touch point. So this is continuous work but one that excites us. There are obviously a few new verticals as well in the U.S. that we're looking into where there's more opportunity. And I would argue again that, like, on the point-of-sale installments opportunity in the U.S.

This is still early days for buy now, pay later and Fair Financing, even including some of our peers that compete in that space because there is a legacy incumbent business that is still not offering the same quality of digital experience, the same brand experience, the same conversion rates and so forth in that. So I still see a lot of room for growth in U.S. and in Europe in growing these products and services through partnerships like the one you described. I think there was a second part to you, Niclas, or did I -- no, okay, sorry.

Operator: And your final question comes from Nate Svensson from Deutsche Bank.

Christopher Svensson: Going through the materials, I was just going to ask about the relationship between merchant growth and active consumer growth. But, Sebastian, in one of your prior answers, you talked about the focus shifting away from growing active users and more on ARPAC. So maybe taking both of those each in turn, just how should we think about the pace of adding new consumers on the platform specifically as you go live with a lot of these PSP relationships?

And then I guess, more color on your answer earlier about the shift in focus more on ARPAC, less on growing active users and kind of, confidence in that shift being able to sustain growth rates going forward?

Sebastian Siemiatkowski: Yes. Maybe I should adjust my answer slightly in the sense that, like, the growth in number of active payment -- paying customers and also active users are, kind of, coming a little bit for free so to say, because as you grow the merchant network, as you grow more touch points, there are more places where Klarna is visible to the consumer where it's available to the consumer. And then that actually in itself then creates new places for consumers to sign up and start using the service. I maybe more meant to say that, like, I think, kind of, that thing works really well and has delivered fantastically.

And I think if you look at our user base at Klarna, we're quite proud of the size and number of users and the brand recognition. I think as a company now, our main focus, though, is to think more about, like, how do we grow the average revenue per active consumer so that, that comes up and reaches the levels that we aspire for in that sense. So it's more a question of that focus. Now merchant base, the fact that the number of acceptance points grows actually has double impact what we've seen in a lot of markets.

We have some European markets where our merchant penetration is extremely high, and you're basically available in every checkout and we know by experience that as the merchant network grows, the more consumer get used to seeing you in the checkout, the more likely a new customer is willing to try you, and obviously, the existing user base will increase their purchase frequency even further because they now find it available. In addition to that, I think it's worth highlighting also that we are now live with Google Pay, Apple Pay and the card itself creates additional ways for our consumers to get the Klarna experience across merchants that are not integrated today.

So all of this, kind of, works in tandem to accelerate. So the focus for us right now is more on the on the average revenue per active consumer, while the growth in number of users is coming to some degree by itself and is, hence, less of a focus for us.

Operator: Thank you. And that was our final question for today. Thank you all for joining Klarna's Third Quarter 2026 Earnings Call. This concludes today's presentation. You may now log off, and we hope you have a wonderful rest of your day.

Inflation data, earnings reports and tensions in the Middle East have been influencing the market. In this volatile backdrop, investors seeking income can bolster their portfolios by adding dividend-paying stocks.

The recommendations of top Wall Street analysts can help inform investors in their search for attractive stocks from the vast universe of dividend-paying companies. These experts assign ratings after analyzing a company's financials and ability to consistently pay dividends while also seeking capital appreciation.

Here are three dividend-paying stocks that are highlighted by Wall Street's top pros, as tracked by TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance.

Integrated oil and gas giant Exxon Mobil has increased its dividends for 43 consecutive years. At a quarterly dividend of $1.03 per share (annualized dividend of $4.12), XOM stock offers a yield of 2.6%.

In his latest research report on energy players, Morgan Stanley analyst Devin McDermott reiterated a buy rating on Exxon Mobil stock and increased his price target to $177 from $168.

The analyst raised his free cash flow estimates to reflect Q2 guidance and the oil price strip, with the largest increase noted for integrated players due to higher refining margins. Notably, the five-star analyst raised his cash flow estimates by an average of 20% for the second half of 2026 and 7% for 2027.

McDermott highlighted that while pure-play refiners have rallied on stronger margins, integrated energy stocks have lagged, creating relative-value opportunities in major North American integrated producers, including Exxon Mobil, Suncor and Cenovus Energy.

Overall, McDermott is bullish on Exxon Mobil, as he expects the company to deliver strong earnings and cash flow growth, driven by robust upstream volumes, high-value projects in Product Solutions, and more than $5 billion of additional structural cost savings.

"XOM's large global integrated operations and strong balance sheet (0.0x 2027 net leverage) make it a clear defensive play in an uncertain macro backdrop," said McDermott.

McDermott ranks No. 726 among more than 12,490 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 59% of the time, delivering an average return of 9.80%. See Exxon Mobil Stock Buybacks on TipRanks.

Moving on to natural gas producer Expand Energy. The company announced a quarterly base dividend of $0.575 per share to be paid on Sept. 3. At an annualized dividend of $2.30 per share, EXE offers a yield of about 2.3%.

Recently, Goldman Sachs analyst Neil Mehta reaffirmed a buy rating on Expand Energy stock and increased his price target to $113 from $99. Mehta attributed his higher price target to cash flow improvement and a strong outlook for shareholder returns. He also cited the stock's attractive valuation, with an 11% free cash flow, or FCF, yield based on his 2027/2028 estimates compared with the peer average of 9%.

The five-star analyst expects Expand Energy to generate FCF per share of about $10 in FY28, up from the prior estimate of about $8 at his mid-cycle price forecast of $3.50/MMBtu Henry Hub. Mehta raised his FCF estimate to reflect an improved outlook for share repurchases, operational efficiencies, and gas pricing realizations.

Furthermore, the analyst expects the recently announced $1.25 billion Twin Eagle acquisition to enhance the competitive positioning of the combined business to expand to premium markets and capture incremental deals in the power and LNG end markets.

Mehta ranks No. 449 among more than 12,490 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been successful 64% of the time, delivering an average return of 12.1%. See Expand Energy Insider Trading on TipRanks.

Mehta is also bullish on Diamondback Energy, an independent oil and natural gas company focused on energy reserves that are primarily in the Permian Basin in West Texas. The company recently paid a base cash dividend of $1.10 per share for the second quarter of 2026. FANG stock offers a dividend yield of 2.2%.

Mehta increased his price target on FANG stock to $220 from $212 and reiterated a buy rating, citing the company's capital-efficient volume growth as oil prices remain high amid persistent supply disruption in the Middle East.

"We remain constructive on FANG, a high-quality, pure-play Permian Basin operator that continues to drive incremental capital efficiencies and strong well productivity relative to peers," said Mehta.

Also, the analyst said that the removal of a minimum return of capital commitment gives Diamondback more flexibility in taking capital allocation decisions amid high oil price volatility and macro uncertainty.

Mehta added that Diamondback sees a favorable environment for production growth, driven by the potential need for global inventory restocking. He highlighted that during Q2 2026, FANG's production volumes of 1,018 Mboe/d exceeded the high end of the company's guidance, driven by a stronger-than-expected natural gas output from Barnett development and improved downstream gas marketing.

Overall, Mehta is optimistic about Diamondback's growth and sees more upside in the stock, given higher production estimates, solid productivity and a deepening position in the Barnett shale formation. See Diamondback Energy Financials on TipRanks.

#2980. Survey: Gen Z Loves a Winter Challenge, but Money Goals Often Fizzle
