Gen Zers are apt to try cold-weather challenges like “winter arc.” But they’re also the generation most likely to say they generally quit challenges before finishing and set the same money goal more than once due to not sticking with it.

It’s not technically winter yet, but depending on where you live, it may feel like it. For many of us, this is a time of hibernation, but for others, it’s prime time for a glow-up.

“Winter arc” is a popular social media challenge through which people aim to improve themselves before the new year. It typically runs from October through December, but can be started any time during the cold months. The aim is to jump-start the “new year, new me” season before the ball even drops.

Whether they call it a winter arc or not, plenty of Americans are working on self-improvement as the chill sets in. According to a new NerdWallet survey, conducted online by The Harris Poll, 75% of Americans say they’re working on their physical health, and 69% say the same about their finances.

Popular as it is, winter arc isn’t the only cold-weather challenge out there. The survey found that half of Americans (50%) say they’ve tried some sort of winter improvement challenge. And no one likes a challenge like Gen Z: Nearly three-quarters of Gen Zers (74%) have tried a winter challenge, compared with 64% of millennials, 42% of Gen Xers and 29% of baby boomers.

Note: The survey defines Gen Zers as those 18-29; millennials, ages 30-45; Gen Xers, ages 46-61 and baby boomers, ages 62-80.

But there’s a difference between starting a challenge and successfully completing one. Gen Zers reign supreme as those most likely to hop on a winter challenge. But they’re also the most likely to say they generally quit challenges before finishing, buy products they saw on social media in an effort to stick with the challenges and set the same financial goal more than once.

Gen Zers are more likely than any other generation to say they:

Have tried a winter financial challenge other than no-spend January (21%, vs. 11% of millennials, 5% of Gen Xers and 2% of baby boomers).

Generally quit challenges before they finish them (59%, vs. 42% of millennials, 36% of Gen Xers and 22% of baby boomers).

Expect to spend more on at least one discretionary expense this winter than they would during another season (90%, vs. 83% of millennials, 61% of Gen Xers and 48% of baby boomers).

Put off dealing with money until after the holidays (60%, vs. 47% of millennials, 35% of Gen Xers and 15% of baby boomers).

Aren’t currently working on improving their finances, but want to make it a priority (15%, vs. 8% of millennials and 6% each of Gen Xers and baby boomers).

“Embracing the winter arc trend can be a great way to find motivation to make progress on a goal over the slower winter months,” says Kimberly Palmer, personal finance expert at NerdWallet. “Pick a winter challenge that aligns with a longer-term goal for the coming year.”

Winter challenges popular with Gen Z include diet- or fitness-related challenges (29%) and self-improvement challenges, like winter arc or 75 Hard, a mental toughness challenge that runs for 75 days and includes two workouts every day, a strict diet and daily nonfiction reading (25%).

While winter arcs typically focus on physical, mental and intellectual self-improvement, Gen Z is game to try a financial challenge as well: One long-standing financial challenge — no-spend January — is more popular among younger Americans (22% of Gen Zers and 20% of millennials) than their older counterparts (12% of Gen Xers and 6% of baby boomers). As for other types of financial challenges, Gen Z is more likely than any other generation to have tried at least one: 21% compared with 11% of millennials, 5% of Gen X and 2% of baby boomers.

Of course, it’s one thing to try a challenge, during wintertime or otherwise. It’s another thing entirely to follow through and complete it. That’s the hard part for many Gen Zers.

When taking on a self-improvement challenge, the beginning tends to be easiest. You’re motivated and excited to reach goals and better yourself. But as time goes on, it’s easy to slip back into old habits or for the shine of a brand-new challenge to dim. And Gen Zers report that they are most likely to quit early.

According to the survey, nearly 3 in 5 Gen Zers (59%) say they generally quit challenges before they finish them. That compares with 42% of millennials, 36% of Gen Xers and 22% of baby boomers.

Along with challenges in general, money goals can be difficult to follow through with, especially for younger Americans. Around two-thirds of Gen Zers (64%) say it’s been hard to stick to financial goals they’ve set in the past, compared with 52% of Gen Xers and 34% of baby boomers. Gen Zers are more likely than any other generation to say they’ve set the same financial goal more than once because they didn’t stick with it — 33%, compared with 20% of millennials, 15% of Gen Xers and 7% of baby boomers.

This isn’t for lack of desire, though. Seven in 10 Gen Zers (70%) say they’re working on improving their finances. All generations show high levels of effort here: 76% each of millennials and Gen Xers say the same, along with 59% of baby boomers.

So why is it so hard to stick with money goals? One possibility is that it’s difficult to see meaningful progress on finances, particularly when you’re young. According to the survey, 65% of Gen Zers say it’s harder to see progress on financial goals than on physical goals.

This makes perfect sense for this age group — for those light on money but rich in youthfulness, desired physical changes may show up faster than financial progress. On top of that, the current job market is tough for younger Americans. Recent college grads now have a higher unemployment rate than workers in general. Even if you’re still on the job hunt, your 20s are a great time to start taking steps, however small, toward building future wealth.» MORE: I’m 25. Here’s How I Got Started Investing

“To increase your chances of success, try coordinating winter arc plans with a friend or giving yourself smaller goals along the way,” Palmer says. “Leaning on the support or coaching from a loved one can make it easier to keep going, as can celebrating incremental progress.”

Self-improvement is a noble pursuit. But as with most things in life, it’s easy to lose sight of the ultimate goal in favor of buying things to help you reach it.

“It’s easy to feel like a quick purchase can help us meet our goals, and sometimes a product can be a useful tool, but the reality is that true winter arc progress comes from putting in the hard work. There’s no option for ‘purchasing’ it instead,” Palmer says.

According to the survey, more than a quarter of Gen Zers (26%) say they’ve bought a product they saw on social media to help with a personal goal or challenge. This is more than any other generation: 17% of millennials, 11% of Gen Xers and 7% of baby boomers say they’ve made social media buys for self-betterment.

Some self-improvement purchases may be billed on a monthly basis. More than 1 in 5 Gen Zers (23%) say they're still paying for a subscription or membership they signed up for during a past goal or challenge. This is also true for 17% of millennials, 9% of Gen Xers and 2% of baby boomers.

These challenge purchases may pile onto already higher winter expenses. A majority of Gen Zers (90%) say they expect to spend more on at least one discretionary expense this winter than they would during another season, more than any other generation. Top expenses include food delivery (38%), entertainment at home (35%) and indoor family entertainment (30%). A quarter of Gen Zers (25%) expect to spend more on fitness or wellness apps this winter compared to other seasons.

Some may be spending more to make themselves feel better during the cold, gray months. Nearly 1 in 5 Gen Zers (18%) say they tend to combat winter blues by spending money, compared with 10% of Gen Xers and 3% of baby boomers.

The holiday season is an expensive time of year for many of us, and it’s easy to sweep finances under the rug until the new year. According to the survey, 3 in 5 Gen Zers (60%) say they generally put off dealing with money until after the holidays. This is more than any other generation: 47% of millennials, 35% of Gen Xers and 15% of baby boomers say the same.

Even for those taking on financial challenges before the new year hits, it’s easy for the resulting “savings” to disappear. Nearly three-quarters of Gen Zers (74%) say money they save by cutting back in one area usually just gets spent somewhere else instead of staying “saved.” This is also true for 68% of millennials, 63% of Gen Xers and 45% of baby boomers.

For some, the holidays are just one thing competing for their money. Over half of Gen Zers (52%) say they’d rather spend money on how they look now than save it for their future financial security. This compares with 26% of Gen Xers and 13% of baby boomers.

We don’t begrudge anyone for their desire to look and feel their best this upcoming season. But that doesn’t have to mean you can’t level up your money at the same time.

More than 2 in 5 Gen Zers (43%) say they’re putting consistent work into improving their finances, and 27% are putting some work into this, but not consistently. Moreover, 15% of Gen Zers aren’t working on improving their finances but want to make them a priority. No matter your age, here are some ideas for a financial glow-up before the spring thaw.

Start small if you tend to quit. Nearly 2 in 5 Americans (38%) say they generally quit challenges before finishing them. Early-challenge motivation can make it easy to overcommit. If you often take on challenges impulsively then peter out a few weeks later, try starting small. For example, maybe no-spend January is a stretch, but you can still save by intentionally creating two no-spend days a week.

Move money the day you save it. Over 3 in 5 Americans (61%) say money they save by cutting back in one area usually gets spent somewhere else. If you’re cutting back, transfer the difference to savings that same day, so it can’t leak out elsewhere.

Make money progress measurable. Half of Americans (50%) say it’s harder to see progress on financial goals than physical goals. There’s a saying that what gets measured, gets managed. Choose one number to track. This might be down payment savings, debt payoff progress or an investment milestone. It may not move much month to month, but you’d be surprised at the difference a year can make, even without a ton of money each month to dedicate toward your goal.

Begin before January. More than a third of Americans (37%) say they put off dealing with money until after the holidays. Facing your finances during the often busy and expensive final months of the year can be daunting, but don’t put your head in the sand until after the holiday credit card balances come due. Put a cap on your winter spending before the new year to avoid going overboard during the tempting sales this time of year.

“If you’re trying to choose a winter arc, pick one that’s realistic but also a stretch goal, so it’s satisfying to accomplish while not being completely out of reach,” Palmer suggests. “Chances are you’ll be glad with what you got done over the colder months when springtime hits.”

#2979. AI Agents vs. Banks: Who Will Win? I'm Betting on Banks.

Doom-and-gloom predictions about AI agents destroying banks’ business model seem premature at best.

With the September launch of the Muse personal artificial intelligence (AI) agent from Meta Platforms (META -1.20%), and other recent advances in agentic AI, some AI industry observers believe AI agents could disrupt the banking industry.

Agentic AI assistants like Meta's Muse could help automate people's personal finances. With user permission to access personal banking accounts and credit card data, Muse can manage advanced personal financial tasks such as canceling subscriptions or negotiating bills.

If AI agents' capabilities improve to the point that people can easily move money between bank accounts, this could hurt banks' business models. What if an autonomous agent could quickly find better deals to move your extra cash from a zero-interest checking account to another bank's high-yield savings account? What if AI agents get into an online arms race to game the system for credit card rewards?

If AI agents become more active managers of people's money, it could drive up banks' costs of doing business, cut their profit margins, and deprive them of checking account funds, which are a key source of cheap deposits. Could banks lose market share or even lose market cap because of AI agents?I'm skeptical. I think there are a few reasons banks won't let their business get hijacked by AI agents.

Just because AI agents have the potential to get into bank accounts and upend the world of banking doesn't mean banks have to let them. Banks are not rolling out the red carpet for AI agents. Many major U.S. banks, including Citigroup (C -1.14%), Bank of America (BAC -1.28%), and JPMorgan Chase (JPM -2.44%), have already announced that they will not allow third-party AI agents or assistants to access customer accounts. JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon recently said he doesn't want "rogue agents" in customer accounts.

Rick Wurster, CEO of Charles Schwab (SCHW -1.18%), recently struck a similar chord, telling Bloomberg in an interview last month:

"We don't want someone just giving their password to Muse, and letting Muse come in and take action on that client's behalf. We can't control it, the client can't control it, something could go wrong and who's liable?"

Banks are required by law to know their customers. Banks must be able to verify that any requests to transfer funds or execute transactions are valid and authorized by a real person who controls the account. Unless regulations change to clarify new rules, limits, and liabilities for agentic AI banking, banks are likely to keep restricting third-party agents.

For example, on Sept. 30, Charles Schwab announced the launch of Charley, the company's new AI-powered assistant. Charley doesn't offer the same capabilities as a full-service automated AI agent, but it can help Schwab clients find answers, access account information, and enhance the customer service experience.

According to CNBC, JPMorgan Chase recently started a pilot for a new AI tool called "Smart Cash." This tool would analyze a customer's cash flow and help move money to maximize the customer's yield.

Banks aren't going to sit around and wait for AI companies to disrupt their business and take their deposits. It seems more likely that banks will use the competitive threat posed by AI agents as inspiration to develop their own "killer banking apps" powered by AI technology.

Do people really want to hand over their financial lives to AI? There's been a lot of hype in recent years about open banking, fintech apps, neobanks, and challenger banks. But despite all the digital banking hype, traditional brick-and-mortar banks seem to have a strong foothold with customers. Reporting from The Financial Brand in July found that major banks have opened more than 1,000 new bank branches in each of the past three years.

TL;DR: Mortgage rates continue to climb under pressure from inflation.

Mortgage rates keep rising as markets anticipate a near-certain Fed rate hike next month.

The average interest rate on a 30-year, fixed-rate mortgage rose to 7.34% APR, according to rates provided to NerdWallet by Zillow. This is seven basis points higher than yesterday and 34 basis points higher than a week ago. (A basis point is one one-hundredth of a percentage point.)

Here are the average APRs we're seeing today, as well as movement over the past month for context:

» Take the next step: Compare mortgage rates from NerdWallet’s top lenders

Mortgage rates are constantly changing, since a major part of how rates are set depends on reactions to new inflation reports, job numbers, Fed meetings, global news ... you name it. For example, even tiny changes in the bond market can shift mortgage pricing.

On Friday, the Bureau of Labor Statistics released the Producer Price Index for October, which tracks the change in prices that U.S. producers are able to get for their products. This is one way to measure inflation on the market end, rather than the consumer end.

The results were mixed. While prices didn’t rise quite as high as economists anticipated month-over-month (0.3% vs. 0.4%), year-over-year price growth did reach 6.5% — the largest increase in four years. This points to even higher costs for consumers coming in the near future.

Investors are convinced that the Federal Reserve will raise overnight borrowing rates again in December to pull inflation down. And higher overnight borrowing rates — called the federal funds rate, which is what banks pay to fund products like mortgages — usually lead to higher mortgage rates.

» MORE: How the Federal Reserve affects mortgage rates

Refinancing might make sense if today’s rates are at least 0.5 to 0.75 of a percentage point lower than your current rate (and if you plan to stay in your home long enough to break even on closing costs).

With rates where they are right now, you may want to start considering a refi if your current rate is around 7.84% or higher.

Also consider your goals: Are you trying to lower your monthly payment, shorten your loan term or turn home equity into cash? For example, you might be more comfortable with paying a higher rate for a cash-out refinance than you would for a rate-and-term refinance, so long as the overall costs are lower than if you kept your original mortgage and added a HELOC or home equity loan.

If you're looking for a lower rate, use NerdWallet's refinance calculator to estimate savings and understand how long it would take to break even on the costs of refinancing.

» Time to refi? Compare refinance rates from NerdWallet’s top lenders

There is no universal “right” time to start shopping — what matters is whether you can comfortably afford a mortgage now at today’s rates.

If the answer is yes, don’t get too hung up on whether you could be missing out on lower rates later; you can refinance down the road. Focus on getting preapproved, comparing lender offers, and understanding what monthly payment works for your budget.

NerdWallet’s affordability calculator can help you estimate your potential monthly payment. If a new home isn’t in the cards right now, there are still things you can do to strengthen your buyer profile. Take this time to pay down existing debts and build your down payment savings. Not only will this free up more cash flow for a future mortgage payment, it can also get you a better interest rate when you’re ready to buy.

» Is now a good time to buy? See NerdWallet’s analysis

If you already have a quote you’re happy with, you should consider locking your mortgage rate, especially if your lender offers a float-down option. A float-down lets you take advantage of a better rate if the market drops during your lock period.

Rate locks protect you from increases while your loan is processed, and with the market forever bouncing around, that peace of mind can be worth it.

🤓 Nerdy Reminder: Rates can change daily, and even hourly. If you’re happy with the deal you have, it’s okay to commit.

» Stay informed: Check out NerdWallet's mortgage news hub for all our latest coverage.

Even two people with similar credit scores might get different rates, depending on their overall financial profiles.

#2976. Billionaire Stanley Druckenmiller Says He's 'Staying Away' From Stocks. Here's What He Bought and Sold Last Quarter

The billionaire investor says he's focused on not losing money right now. His newest SEC filing shows how much he had already reshaped his portfolio by the end of September.

Stanley Druckenmiller, the billionaire founder of Duquesne Family Office, says he's sitting out the stock market for now.

"We are basically staying away," he said Tuesday at the TomorrowX Summit in Austin. "We are trying to not lose money as opposed to make money."

It's not clear exactly when he made that call. But a filing his firm sent to the SEC on Monday provides a detailed look at what he owned as of Sept. 30, showing a portfolio that was already shrinking.

Duquesne's latest 13F filing lists about $4.47 billion tied to U.S.-listed stocks and options as of Sept. 30, down from about $5.21 billion at the end of June, according to its previous filing. The number of positions fell to 65 from 95.

The firm sold out of dozens of companies and funds during the quarter, including Alphabet, AMD, Lam Research, Sandisk, Reddit, Delta Air Lines and United Airlines.

Perhaps most telling, it no longer listed call options on the S&P 500, the Russell 2000 and an equal-weight S&P 500 fund. Call options are bets that prices will rise. In June, those three positions covered about $341 million worth of the underlying funds.

The biggest holding by far is Natera (NTRA -0.35%), a genetic-testing company. It makes up about 29% of the disclosed portfolio, worth about $1.3 billion.

Druckenmiller didn't buy more to get there. Duquesne held about 3.16 million shares, slightly fewer than in June. The position grew because the stock did: Natera's shares gained about 50% during the quarter, and he let the winner run.

Among big shifts was one in semiconductors. Duquesne sold about 94% of its Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing (TSM -3.69%) shares, a stake worth about $282 million in June, and cut its STMicroelectronics shares nearly in half.

At the same time, it nearly tripled its Seagate Technology (STX +1.08%) shares and added call options on the stock, making Seagate its second-largest holding. It also opened a new position in Western Digital. Both companies make hard drives, which store much of the data that AI runs on.

Other notable moves include purchases of Unity Software (U -2.93%) (Duquesne's stake grew more than fivefold to about 4 million shares) and gold miners (with new stakes in Newmont, Barrick and Agnico Eagle, worth over $100 million combined). He also made new, smaller bets on Palantir, AppLovin and SpaceX, and bought more shares of Amazon, Sea Ltd and Fox.

A 13F has limits. It lists only the U.S.-listed stocks, funds and options a firm owns. It doesn't include short bets, currencies, bonds, or commodities, which are a big part of how Druckenmiller trades. And it's a snapshot from Sept. 30, seven weeks before Tuesday's comments.

That's how the filing and his "staying away" comment can both be true. His positions may have changed a lot since then.

By the time a 13F is public, the trades may already be undone. But the filing shows three habits worth borrowing.

First, conviction matters. Druckenmiller let Natera grow to nearly a third of his disclosed portfolio instead of trimming it.

Second, he seems to cut quickly when he loses confidence. In one quarter, his position count fell by 30, and his bullish bets on the overall market disappeared.

Third, cash can be a position. When one of the most successful investors of his generation says the outlook is unclear, it's fine to hold more cash and wait for a better opportunity.

For investors loaded up on semiconductor stocks, his quarter is worth a closer look. He didn't abandon tech, but he moved away from the chipmakers and toward the companies that store the data AI needs.

#2973. Nvidia’s 103% Revenue Growth Took a Backseat to Its Internal Drama

The AI chipmaker is growing like wildfire, but its future is still in flux.

Join Motley Fool analysts LIVE starting at 4 p.m. ET as they break down Nvidia's results and what they mean for your money. [Watch live →]

There's no denying that Nvidia (NVDA -0.44%) is the bellwether for the state of artificial intelligence (AI). That said, the drama surrounding its former CEO Jensen Huang continues to consume all the oxygen in the room. Reports alleging that a Chinese spy targeted Huang, that Nvidia's AI-centric chips were smuggled through other countries into China to circumvent export restrictions, and the resulting crackdown by the U.S. government are all front of mind for investors, who rightly wonder what the future holds.

As such, Wall Street and Main Street alike were sitting on the edge of their seats ahead of the company's quarterly financial report after the market close on Tuesday. Given the nature of recent events, the numbers took a back seat to the internal drama and to what the future holds for the chipmaker.

The fact that Nvidia's growth continued to accelerate may have served to remind shareholders why they invested in the company in the first place. For its fiscal 2027 third quarter (ended Oct. 25), the company generated record revenue of $115.8 billion, up 103% year over year and 20% quarter over quarter. This drove adjusted earnings per share (EPS) up 111% to $2.68. The highlight was Nvidia's sustained gross margin, which clocked in at 74.9%.

For context, analysts' consensus estimates were calling for revenue of $108.7 billion and adjusted EPS of $2.47, so Nvidia sailed past expectations with room to spare.

The data center segment, which includes processors used for AI, cloud computing and high-performance computing -- and, of course, data centers -- continued to accelerate, delivering another record-setting performance. Segment revenue of $107.6 billion soared 110% year over year and 21% sequentially.

The edge computing segment (previously the "gaming" segment) -- which includes PCs, workstations, game consoles, robotics, and automotive -- reported respectable growth, up 42% year over year and 14% quarter over quarter.

In a move designed to restore investor confidence, the board of directors increased Nvidia's buyback authorization by an additional $150 billion (with no expiration).

Management's forecast suggests the company's impressive growth will continue in Q4. Nvidia's outlook calls for revenue of $130 billion, representing year-over-year growth of 90%. The company also reminded investors that its gross margin is poised to moderate, falling to 72% at the midpoint of its guidance -- in keeping with the company’s previous forecast.

Nvidia also increased its fiscal 2028 guidance, forecasting 75% growth for the year, up from its previous outlook of 70% -- on top of its beat-and-raise quarter.

Board chair Harvey Jones sought to reassure investors, saying of interim CEO and CFO Colette Kress, "We have an incredibly talented leadership team, and we have every confidence in Colette's leadership, integrity, and ability to deliver as interim CEO." He went on to say that the board "has no intention" of taking Huang back.

In her own opening remarks, Kress chimed in, saying, "Our ambition will not change. Our passion to innovate will not change. And our commitment to customers, partners, and shareholders will not change." Of the company's results and future potential, Kress had this to say: "Our momentum is real. Nvidia is an exceptional technology leader, powered by the relentless innovation of our people." She closed the earnings call by saying, "We've got this."

These comments, the robust guidance, and the increased buyback authorization were all a coordinated effort to ease investor concerns about Nvidia's future in a post-Jensen Huang world. The efforts seemed well received, with Nvidia stock up more than 5% in after-hours trading (as of this writing).

There are still many unknowns, with the biggest being who will ultimately fill Nvidia's CEO position. There are also recent reports that the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) has launched an investigation into Nvidia, though the exact nature of that probe is unclear, according to a report that first appeared in The Wall Street Journal.

Nvidia stock is selling for less than 20 times earnings, so the valuation may seem intriguing. At this juncture, however, remember the old adage: "Caveat emptor" -- Let the buyer beware.

#2963. Viking: 3 Key Takeaways for Long-Term Investors

Goodwill vouchers and a 60% rebooking rate suggest river guests stayed loyal through a costly disruption, a test many cruise operators have yet to face.

On its third-quarter 2026 earnings conference call, held on Nov. 17, 2026, Viking (VIK +4.43%) reported total revenue of $2.2 billion, an increase of 9.2% year-over-year. The company's fleet diversification into ocean cruising and its guest retention efforts help cushion earnings against seasonal disruptions in river cruising. Three key takeaways from management explain where the business is headed next.

Unprecedented low water levels across European rivers reduced third-quarter revenue and adjusted gross margin, defined as total revenue minus direct variable costs, by $100 million each. Management issued goodwill vouchers to preserve guest trust, and 60% of rebooked guests selected 2027 river itineraries.

Viking is expanding its presence in ocean cruises, where it holds a 27% market share in the luxury category. Revenue per passenger cruise day, which measures daily guest ticket revenue, increased in the ocean segment as advance bookings for 2026 rose 17% year over year.

The company ended the quarter with $4.1 billion in cash and cash equivalents while maintaining net leverage, calculated as net debt divided by adjusted earnings, at 1.2 times. Management deployed $350 million to repurchase shares under its $1.0 billion authorization while securing options for 10 additional river vessels.

Advance bookings across core products reached 68% of 2027 capacity by early November, proving that consumer demand isn't waning despite temporary weather impacts. Fleet expansion options, strong brand equity, and high repeat customer rates provide structural protection while management maintains pricing discipline.

Viking continues to balance fleet expansion across river and ocean segments with a conservative balance sheet.

#2959. The Biggest Problem In Accounting Firms Isn’t Strategy; It’s Alignment

David Marquis is the Chief Executive Officer of Caseware.

Few professions are as steeped in tradition as accounting, and few are changing as fast. Technology, business models and client expectations are all shifting at once.

That can create tension, particularly for auditors. Their business is to manage risk, yet they are being asked to change at a pace that can feel at odds with that.

Across the industry, I see firms embracing change with vigor, firms that are more measured in their approach and everything in between. The good news is that nobody is alone in this. These pressures are happening across the profession and beyond it.

One pattern stands out, however: The firms that seem most confident and adaptable are rarely the ones that simply have the better strategy. More often, they are the ones that are aligned enough to act on it.

Accounting firms are often partnerships, and that structure creates its own challenges. The ownership model tends to make firms more consensus-driven by default. That is not necessarily a problem when the big decisions are clear. The difficulty appears in the day-to-day decisions. Smaller issues accumulate until a firm becomes divided across details. Partners may agree that standardization is necessary while reluctant to cede control over how their own teams function. Or, a firm may make a deliberate technology investment, but teams don’t use it consistently. In these scenarios, execution will start to slow.

I see a version of this in my own role as a CEO. Organizations may be aligned on the big things, but once you break those decisions down by functional silo, complexity or detail, alignment becomes harder. The more alignment you can create, the less you slow yourself down in terms of organizational execution.

For accounting firms, that challenge can be even more pronounced because it is not always clear who makes the judgment call on what. The gap is often less about the strategy and more about having the confidence to move with pace across the firm.

The fastest-moving firms don’t pretend the tension between individual partner autonomy and firm-wide consistency does not exist. They acknowledge it. That’s the first step.

From there, the question becomes one of clarity: determining what the firm’s call is and what the partners are individually responsible for. That might include client relationships, judgment calls on specific work items or how they manage their book of business.

Then there are the things, such as common processes, common technology decisions, common workflows and quality standards the firm needs to handle consistently. Knowing who is responsible for what, and what becomes a firm-level decision versus an individual partner decision, is incredibly important.

Judgment alone is valuable, but it doesn’t scale reliably. At some point, you need process. You need workflow. You need a system approach that holds the structure together as the organization grows. That is why I increasingly think about successful firms as systems rather than simply collections of individual partners.

This need for alignment is increasingly important because several forces are converging simultaneously.

AI is one. Some firms are experiencing and adopting it at speed. Some are just beginning to experiment. Accounting firms have good reasons to approach AI carefully and judiciously because the risk of being wrong can carry high stakes.

Talent is another pressure. Firms are dealing with fewer people entering the profession, higher expectations from those who do and less patience for antiquated ways of working.

Then there is private equity (PE), which is raising the bar on operational discipline across the profession. PE-backed firms are being pushed to improve how they serve clients, run internal operations and use technology. That creates a new reference point for what best practice can look like, even for firms that have no intention of pursuing private equity themselves. Not every firm will take the PE route, and none needs to. The operational discipline that makes PE-backed businesses attractive is available to anyone willing to build it.

The cumulative impact is more critical than any one of these trends. Firms increasingly have to be deliberate about how they operate and how systematically they can execute.

I sometimes hear firms say, “We’ll just wait this whole thing out.” I understand the impulse, but I think it can be the wrong one. That doesn’t mean chasing every trend. It means asking the harder questions earlier, even when the answers aren’t entirely clear.

Which aspects of the organization currently function effectively? Where do things work solely due to the presence of “human glue,” where one person holds it all together? In what areas does alignment fall apart among the partners? What has the organization been avoiding addressing due to too much friction in doing so?

Technology investment is one example. In a partnership, capital that might otherwise go toward technology may instead go toward profit sharing. That can limit the firm’s ability to invest in what will make it better over time.

Some of the strongest firms are intentional about setting that capital aside. They have a system for it. Everybody contributes, but it pays back over time.

Readiness isn’t always size-dependent. Ownership structure and leadership matter, but culture matters, too. I see firms where partners have agreed to invest in technology and systems not only for themselves but for the partners coming up behind them. They want to hand the next generation an effective legacy. They care about the brand and what the partnership means while other firms remain focused primarily on maximizing current profit.

The firms that ask the hard questions, invest for the future and build alignment now are the ones keeping their options open. Nobody knows exactly what the profession will look like several years from now, but the goal is to build a firm that can move with confidence and certainty when the answer becomes clear.​

On the operational side, Motor Vessel Evridiki G incurred 69 days of planned off-hire due to its scheduled drydocking between July 1 and September 7, 2026. Otherwise, we recorded no commercial off-hire during the quarter. Please turn to Slide 5. Our operating fleet currently consists of 20 vessels with a combined carrying capacity of about 59,000 TEU and a TEU-weighted average age of 12.5 years. The fleet comprises 6 intermediate containerships with a combined carrying capacity of approximately 25,000 TEU and an average age of around 18 years, alongside 14 feeder containerships with a [Technical Difficulty] capacity of approximately 33,000 TEU and an average age of around 8 years.

We have 12 newbuilding vessels on order, comprising 8 feeder and 4 intermediate containerships, with deliveries scheduled from the third quarter of 2027 through the first quarter of 2029. Upon completion of our newbuilding program, our fleet will expand to 32 vessels and a total carrying capacity of approximately 95,000 TEU. Please turn to Slide 6 for a further update on our fleet employment and forward coverage. Our chartering coverage stands at 100% for 2026, 90% for 2027 and almost 50% for 2028 at attractive average daily rates of approximately $30,000, $32,500 and $31,000 respectively. Even if all our open days in 2028 earned zero charter, the year would still be profitable as well.

Moving on to Slide 8, let's walk through the key market developments that shaped the containership sector during the third quarter. The containership market firmed further through the third quarter, helped by resilient demand after the peak season and logistical bottlenecks down the whole supply chain. Charter rates have climbed again in recent weeks, with current rates for feeder to post-Panamax tonnage well above third quarter averages as liners continue to compete for scarce ships. Freight rates have also held firm, rising further in October.

On the asset side, secondhand prices rose about 2.5% over the quarter and remain near the highest levels since mid-2022, while newbuilding prices held steady at elevated levels, reflecting strong yard demand and high construction costs. Idle capacity, excluding vessels under repair, was just 250,000 TEU, or 0.7% of the global fleet, as of early November. This is a historic low and confirms the structural tightness in the cycle. Recycling has also remained totally subdued, with only 11 vessels totaling 27,000 TEU sent to scrap year-to-date, reflecting again how valuable tonnage remains. Scrap prices have recently increased to about $530 per lightweight ton. Meanwhile, the global fleet has already grown by 4.2% year-to-date.

Please turn to Slide 9, which illustrates the development of 6- to 12-month time charter rates over the past decade. Across the board, from the smaller feeders through to the larger intermediate container segments, current charter rates remain well above both their 10-year median and average levels. Across the 4 size segments shown, today's rates are roughly 65% to 80% higher than the 10-year averages. These vessel classes remain essential to maintaining network flexibility and supporting regional and intra-regional trade flows, a role that has only grown in importance amid the ongoing geopolitical uncertainty and supply chain realignment. Please turn to Slide 10, where we review the global macroeconomic backdrop and its implications for container shipping demand.

According to the IMF's October 2026 World Economic Outlook, global economic activity has remained resilient despite ongoing geopolitical disruptions and elevated energy prices and trade uncertainty. Global GDP growth is projected at 3.1% in 2026, but recovering to 3.4% in 2027. The resilience has been supported by continued investment in artificial intelligence, technology-related demand and the ability of economies to adapt to geopolitical and trade disruptions. However, performance remains uneven. Technology-linked economies and energy exporters are holding up better, while energy importers outside the technology supply chain face a tougher outlook.

Meanwhile, inflationary pressures remain elevated, with global headline inflation projected to rise to 4.7% by the end of 2026, largely on higher energy prices, before easing to 4.1% in 2027. Risks remain tilted to the downside, particularly from further geopolitical escalation, renewed trade tensions, fiscal vulnerabilities and the potential reassessment of AI-related investment expectations. Turning to the major economies, U.S. growth is projected to remain steady at 2.3% in both 2026 and 2027. The IMF has revised China's growth forecast slightly lower, down by 0.1 percentage points to 4.5%, noting that resilient exports are no longer sufficient to fully offset persistent weakness in domestic demand. Growth is expected by the IMF to moderate further to 4% in 2027.

In the ASEAN-5 economies, growth is projected at 4.4% in 2026 and 4.3% in 2027, putting the region ahead of China in 2027 for the first time. Looking at global trade, world trade volume growth is slightly moderating in 2026 compared to 2025 whilst remaining quite strong at 4.2%, and it will stabilize there in 2027. Importantly, however, for our sector, Clarksons expects TEU-miles to turn slightly negative in 2027 and grow by just 1% in 2028 due to the normalization of the trade routes they expect to see within the next 24 months. Turning on to Slide 11, you can see the total fleet age profile and containership outlook.

The overall containership fleet remains relatively young, with a majority of vessels under 15 years of age and only about 15% of the fleet over 20 years old. However, this aggregate view is totally different when examining the feeder and intermediate segments in isolation. Turning to vessel deliveries, the top right chart illustrates scheduled new deliveries as a percentage of the existing fleet. Deliveries are projected at approximately 5.5% for 2026, 9.9% for 2027 and just under 30% for 2028 onwards, although actual fleet growth is expected to be somewhat lower due to slippage and future demolition activity. The bottom chart places the current order book in historical context.

At approximately 44.4% of the existing fleet as of November 2026, the order book stands at its highest level in more than 15 years, which warrants close attention as we assess the medium-term supply outlook for the sector. The overall containership order book is now up about 26% since the start of 2026. Turning to Slide 12, we highlight the age profile and order book for the 1,000 to 3,000 TEU feeder segment. The supply picture here is very different from the broader market, starting with a striking age profile difference.

Approximately 23% of the fleet is between 15 and 19 years old, and 31% is over 20 years old, meaning more than half of the feeder fleet is approaching scrapping age. As environmental regulations tighten and compliance costs rise, a meaningful portion of these older vessels will likely exit the market over the coming years, depending on how challenging market conditions become. Against this aging backdrop, newbuilding activity in the sub-3,000 TEU segment remains very limited at below 20% of the existing fleet, well below the 44.4% for the global containership fleet, pointing to a more favorable supply outlook for smaller vessels.

Scheduled deliveries represent just 3.2% of the existing fleet in 2026, 8.5% in 2027 and 9.4% in 2028 and beyond. Let's move to Slide 13 to focus on the intermediate segment, the other core segment of our fleet. As of November 2026, the order book in this segment stands at approximately 31% of the existing fleet. Whilst that is higher than in the feeder segment, it remains modest relative to the larger mainline vessel classes, where newbuilding activity has been considerably more pronounced. What makes this segment particularly compelling from a supply perspective is the age profile.

Approximately 32% of the vessels in this size range are over 20 years old, with a further 34% between 15 and 19 years old. This means roughly 2/3 of the fleet is approaching the age where retirement becomes likely, especially as environmental compliance requirements grow more stringent and costly, as we have noted before. Scheduled deliveries are predicted at 4% of the fleet in 2026, rising to 8.3% in 2027 and around 20% in 2028 and beyond. When weighed against the potential for accelerated scrapping among the older segments, net fleet growth in the segment is expected to remain contained over the coming years.

The interplay between a maturing fleet and a measured newbuilding pipeline continues to underpin a structurally supportive environment for intermediate containership operators. Moving on to Slide 14, which sets what we have just discussed against the containership sector as a whole. The most striking feature is how heavily newbuilding activity is concentrated in the larger sectors. Order books in the neo-Panamax and post-Panamax segments range from approximately 36% to 112% of their existing fleet, as capacity is added for the main lane routes between major hubs. These are the vessel classes where oversupply concerns are most acute. At the same time, though, regional distribution relies on feeders, so more main lane volume increases the need for them as well.

With a significant portion of the fleet approaching replacement age, net fleet growth in these segments is likely to remain constrained and capacity could even shrink, while the larger classes and the overall fleet continue to expand. This underpins our conviction that Euroseas' fleet is positioned in segments with a supportive supply outlook and limited risk of oversupply. Please turn to Slide 15, where we summarize our outlook on the container sector. As we already discussed, the container market stayed strong through the third quarter of 2026 and continues to improve due to resilient trade growth, market disruptions and the lack of available tonnage.

Looking ahead to 2027, however, the outlook becomes more challenging, as a record wave of newbuilding deliveries and a possible return to normal Red Sea routing could weaken the supply-demand balance. Importantly, regardless of when traffic returns to Suez, our modeling indicates that fundamentals could deteriorate significantly from the second half of 2027 onwards, as the delivery schedule accelerates and fleet growth outpaces trade growth. Geopolitical uncertainty, however, could still alter this picture. Our modeling suggests the imbalance could widen further in 2028, adding to the pressure on freight and charter rates. But again, geopolitics, inefficiencies and logistical supply constraints may keep the market higher than fundamentals alone would suggest. Please turn now to Slide 16.

The left chart traces the 1-year time charter rate for 2,500 TEU containerships over the past decade. As of November 13, the 1-year rate for a 2,500 TEU vessel stands at $42,000 per day, well above the 10-year average of $25,000 per day and the median of $17,500. This strength, of course, is also reflected in asset values. The right chart shows newbuilding prices of $46 million, compared with a 10-year median of $40 million and an average of $37 million, while a 10-year-old vessel is valued at $44 million, more than double its 10-year median of $20 million and well above its average of $23.5 million.

These elevated secondhand valuations, particularly without attached employment, offer a less attractive risk-reward profile at this stage of the cycle. Newbuildings, by contrast, offer greater pricing flexibility and cost predictability. This conviction has driven our decision to expand our order book to the 12 vessels, building on the 9 vessels we completed in early 2025. This strategy, combined with our strong balance sheet and substantial liquidity, leaves us well-capitalized to pursue accretive opportunities as they arise, while our fleet's lower operating costs and environmental advantages set us apart competitively. On its third-quarter 2026 earnings call, held on Nov. 17, 2026, Klarna (KLAR +4.70%) reported that total revenue rose 12% year over year to $1.09 billion. The payment provider is shifting its long-term focus from acquiring new users to increasing average revenue per active consumer. Three key takeaways from management highlight how this strategic pivot is shaping up.

Fair Financing offers longer installment loans that generate higher profit margins per dollar spent than short-term payment options. Scaling these loan products in the U.S. and introducing them into European markets helps boost average customer revenue over time.

The company's payment card lets consumers choose between debit and interest-free installments at checkout. Card users make purchases roughly three times as frequently as non-card users, making card adoption a key driver of engagement.

The company offloads consumer loans through forward-flow programs, in which outside buyers commit to purchasing loans upfront. This setup allows the business to recycle capital into new lending while maintaining direct customer relationships.

Fourth-quarter transaction volume is accelerating toward 30% year-over-year growth in the U.S., supported by expanding payment card adoption and point-of-sale financing. Deep integrations with payment service providers (third-party distribution partners that connect payment software to online merchants) provide a steady source of low-cost merchant expansion.

Management is prioritizing deeper monetization over pure user acquisition, using high-margin subscription plans and flexible lending products to increase revenue per customer in established markets.
